title: Fasteners and keys
cards: Fasteners clamp parts together. A key locks a hub to a shaft so torque can pass between them.
A hex bolt has a hex head and a straight threaded shank. Carriage bolts have domed heads and lag screws taper to a point.

Screw heads: a socket head cap screw takes an Allen key and sits in a counterbore; a button head is low and rounded; a flat head is countersunk to sit flush. Nuts: a nyloc nut has a nylon ring that grips the thread so it resists loosening, a jam nut is a thin second nut tightened against the first, and a flange nut has a built-in washer that spreads the load.

qs.q: Which fastener is this?
qs.ans: Hex bolt
wrong: Carriage bolt
Lag screw
Hex nut
qs.why: Hex head, straight threaded shank. Carriage bolts have domed heads and lag screws taper to a point.

qs.q: A shaft key is there mainly to…
qs.ans: Transmit torque between shaft and hub
wrong: Carry axial thrust between the two
Center the hub on the shaft bore
Seal the keyway against oil leaks
qs.why: The key sits in a keyway in both parts so the hub can’t spin on the shaft. Fits and shoulders handle centering and thrust.

qs.q: A screw head has to sit flush with the surface. Which head do you pick?
qs.ans: Flat (countersunk) head
wrong: Button head
Socket head cap screw
Hex head
qs.why: A flat head is cone-shaped and sits in a countersink, flush with the surface. A button head is low but still stands proud; a socket head cap screw sits flush only in a counterbore; a hex head always sticks out.

qs.q: A nut must not shake loose on a vibrating machine, and you only have room for one nut. Which one?
qs.ans: Nyloc nut
wrong: Jam nut
Flange nut
Wing nut
qs.why: The nyloc’s nylon ring grips the thread and resists loosening. A jam nut needs a second nut locked against it; a flange nut spreads load but doesn’t lock; a wing nut is made to be loosened by hand.

qs.q: Match each fastener to what sets it apart.
pairs: Allen key, sits in a counterbore
qs.why: Head shape decides the tool and how far it stands proud; a flange nut’s washer is part of the nut.

p.x: A **fastener** such as a bolt squeezes parts together. A **hub** is the center of a part, such as a gear, that fits around a shaft.
A **shaft key** sits in matching slots in the shaft and hub. It makes them turn together so the shaft can transmit torque, a turning effect, to the hub.
A key stops relative rotation. A fitted bore centers the hub, and a shoulder or retainer locates it along the shaft.

g.q: What motion does the key in matching slots mainly stop?
o: Turning relative to the shaft
The slot sides press on the key when the hub tries to turn relative to the shaft.
Sliding along the shaft
The key bears against the slot sides to stop turning. A shoulder or retainer handles sliding.

p.x: A **hex bolt** has a six-sided head and a straight threaded shank, the part below the head.
A **carriage bolt** has a [[domed]] head. The round top has no wrench flats.
A **lag screw** tapers to a point so it can thread into wood. A **hex nut** has internal threads that fit over a bolt.
A **socket head cap screw** takes an Allen key and can sit in a counterbore, a flat-bottomed recess.
A **button head** is low and rounded. A **flat head** sits flush in a countersink, a cone-shaped recess.
A **nyloc nut** has a nylon ring that grips the threads to resist loosening.
A **jam nut** is a thin second nut tightened against the first. A **flange nut** has a built-in washer to spread the clamp load.

title: Fits and gears
cards: A fit says how tightly a shaft sits in a hole. Interference: shaft bigger than hole. Clearance: always smaller.
Gear ratio = teeth out ÷ teeth in. Speed falls by that ratio and torque rises by the same ratio, ignoring losses.

qs.q: A shaft is slightly larger than its hole and is pressed in. This is a…
qs.ans: Interference fit
wrong: Transition fit
Clearance fit
Sliding fit
qs.why: Interference means the shaft is bigger than the hole at every tolerance extreme. Transition fits can go either way.

qs.q: Gear 1 has 20 teeth and turns at 1200 rpm. It drives gear 2, which has 60 teeth. Ideally, what are gear 2’s speed and torque?
qs.ans: 400 rpm, 3× the torque
wrong: 400 rpm, 1/3 the torque
3600 rpm, 3× the torque
3600 rpm, 1/3 the torque
qs.why: Speed falls by the tooth ratio, so torque rises by the same ratio (power is conserved, minus losses).

qs.q: A 15-tooth pinion at 1800 rpm drives a 45-tooth gear. Output speed in rpm?
qs.why: Speed falls by the tooth ratio: 1800 × 15/45 = 600.

p.x: A **fit** describes how tightly a shaft sits in a hole. A tolerance is the range of sizes a part is allowed to have.
With a **clearance fit**, the shaft is always [[smaller]] than the hole.
Even the largest allowed shaft leaves a gap in the smallest allowed hole.
With an **interference fit** the shaft is larger at every allowed size. A **transition fit** can give either a gap or interference.

p.cap: One meshing gear pair. In drives out.
Meshing teeth pass at the same rate.
At steady speed with negligible losses.

p.x: A larger driven gear turns more slowly and delivers more torque.

g.q: The driven gear has three times the teeth. How do its speed and torque compare?
o: ⅓ the speed, 3× the torque
Three times the teeth means one turn for three input turns. With no losses, torque triples.
⅓ the speed, ⅓ the torque
The speed falls, but reducing torque too would lose power in an ideal pair.
3× the speed, ⅓ the torque
That reverses the driver and driven gears. The larger gear takes longer to make a turn.

title: Joints and fatigue
cards: A preloaded bolt clamps the joint. Outside loads mostly reduce the clamp force instead of stretching the bolt.
Fatigue cracks start where stress concentrates: sharp corners, notches, holes. A bigger radius helps.

qs.q: A well-preloaded bolted joint gets an external tensile load. The bolt sees…
qs.ans: Only a small fraction of it
wrong: All of it, since it is in tension
About half, shared with the plates
None, the plates take it all
qs.why: The clamped plates are much stiffer than the bolt, so most of the extra load just reduces clamp force. That’s why preload helps fatigue.

qs.q: Which change most improves the fatigue life of a stepped shaft?
qs.ans: A larger fillet radius at the shoulder
wrong: A switch to higher-strength alloy steel
A keyway next to the shoulder
A finer finish on the middle only
qs.why: Fatigue starts at stress concentrations. Higher-strength steels are often more notch-sensitive, so they don’t fix a sharp shoulder.

p.x: **Preload** is the bolt tension from tightening. It squeezes the plates together.
While stiffer plates stay clamped, a pull mainly reduces their squeeze and adds little bolt tension.
**Fatigue** cracks start at a **stress concentration**, where local stress rises at a sharp corner. A **fillet** rounds the step where the shaft diameter changes.
A larger fillet radius lowers the local stress rise under the same load.

title: Symbols and diodes
cards: Resistors limit current. A diode lets current flow one way: from anode (triangle side) to cathode (bar).
Learn the symbols first, and schematics read like sentences.

qs.q: Which symbol is this?
qs.ans: Resistor
wrong: Thermistor
Varistor
Inductor
qs.why: A zigzag is a resistor in US-style schematics. Thermistors and varistors add a slash or angled line.

qs.q: Conventional current flows easily through this symbol…
qs.ans: Left to right
wrong: Right to left
Both ways
Neither way
qs.why: Current flows from anode to cathode, the direction the triangle points. The bar is the cathode.

p.x: A **resistor** limits current: for a given voltage, more resistance means less current.
A **diode** lets current flow [[one way]] only, from anode (the triangle side) to cathode (the bar).
A conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 V.
A schematic shows how parts connect, not where they sit on the board. Learn the symbols first, and it reads like a sentence.
Read it as: current leaves the supply, passes through the resistor, then the LED, and returns to ground.

title: Series, parallel, floating pins
cards: Series resistors add. Parallel resistors: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
A digital input with nothing driving it floats and reads noise. A pull-up or pull-down resistor sets its default.

qs.q: Two 100 Ω resistors in parallel, in series with 50 Ω. Total?
qs.why: The parallel pair is 50 Ω, plus 50 Ω in series is 100 Ω.

qs.q: A microcontroller input reads random values when a switch is open. Best fix?
qs.ans: A 10 kΩ pull-up or pull-down resistor
wrong: A 100 nF capacitor across the switch only
A diode in series with the switch
A 10 Ω resistor in series
qs.why: The input is floating. A pull-up or pull-down gives it a defined level. A capacitor only helps with bounce.

p.cap: same current through both
same voltage across both

p.x: In parallel, the total comes out below the smaller resistor.

g.q: Put 1 kΩ in parallel with 4 kΩ. The total is…
o: 5 kΩ
That's the series total. In parallel the reciprocals add, not the resistances.
2.5 kΩ
That's the average. A second path lets more current through, so the total falls below 1 kΩ.

p.x: A digital input with nothing driving it **floats**: it picks up stray charge and reads random 1s and 0s.
A pull-up or pull-down resistor gives it a [[default]] state.
A button or another chip can still drive the pin the other way when it needs to.

title: LEDs and filters
cards: LED resistor: R = (Vsupply − Vf) / I. Round up to a standard value so current stays under the limit.

An RC low-pass has cutoff f = 1/(2πRC). Well below f the input changes slowly, so the capacitor has time to charge and follow it: the signal passes. Well above f the input flips faster than the capacitor can charge through R, so the output barely moves: each 10× rise in frequency cuts it about 10×. At f itself the output is about 0.71 of the input.

qs.q: 5 V supply, LED drops 2 V. Which standard E12 resistor gives the most current without going over 10 mA?
qs.why: R = (5 − 2)/0.010 = 300 Ω, which isn’t an E12 value, so round up. 330 Ω gives 9.1 mA. 270 Ω (11.1 mA) and 220 Ω (13.6 mA) go over the limit; 390 Ω (7.7 mA) is safe but dimmer than it needs to be.

qs.q: A 10 kΩ and 100 nF RC low-pass has a cutoff near…
qs.ans: 160 Hz
wrong: 1.6 kHz
16 Hz
1 kHz

qs.q: Order the steps to size an LED resistor.
items: Round up to a standard value
qs.why: R = (Vs − Vf) / I, then pick the next standard value so current stays at or below the target.

p.cap: resistor in series with the LED

p.x: Red LED, $V_f$ = 1.8 V, on 5 V, at most 20 mA:
Standard values near 160 Ω are 150 and 180 Ω. Round up:

g.q: 160 Ω isn't a standard value. Pick…
o: Rounding down raises the current: 3.2 / 150 = 21.3 mA, over the 20 mA limit.
Rounding up keeps the current under the limit: 3.2 / 180 = 17.8 mA.

p.cap: first-order RC, nothing loading the output

p.c: C has time to charge and follow
input flips faster than C charges through R

p.x: Above $f_c$, each 10× rise in frequency cuts the output about 10×.

g.q: Well above the cutoff, raise the frequency 10×. The output…
o: drops about 10×
Above f_c a single RC's output falls as 1/f: 10× the frequency, a tenth the output.
drops about 100×
That's a second-order filter (two RC stages). One RC falls as 1/f.
halves
Well above f_c, halving takes only a 2× frequency step. A 10× step cuts a single RC's output about 10×.

title: Op-amps and MOSFETs
cards: Inverting op-amp gain is −Rf/Rin. Non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf/Rin.

A MOSFET used as a switch should be fully on, so it acts like a tiny resistor, RDS(on). Only partly on, its resistance is much higher and it heats up, because power lost = I² × R. Check RDS(on) at the gate voltage you actually drive, not just Vgs(th), the voltage where it barely starts to conduct.

qs.q: Inverting op-amp amplifier: Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 100 kΩ. Gain?
qs.why: Gain = −Rf/Rin = −10. +11 would be the non-inverting gain, 1 + Rf/Rin.

qs.q: A MOSFET switching a motor runs hot from a 3.3 V gate drive (datasheet Vgs(th) = 2.5 V). Best fix?
qs.ans: Use one rated for low RDS(on) at 3.3 V
wrong: Add a flyback diode across the motor
Use a larger gate resistor for slower edges
Raise the motor supply voltage
qs.why: Vgs(th) is where it starts to turn on, not where it’s fully on. A flyback diode handles spikes, not heating.

p.cap: ideal op-amp with negative feedback, output inside the supply rails

p.x: Same resistors, gain 11 instead of 10, and the sign doesn't flip.

g.q: $R_f$ = 10 kΩ, $R_{in}$ = 1 kΩ. The non-inverting gain is…
o: That's the size of the inverting gain. Non-inverting adds 1: G = 1 + 10.
That's the inverting gain. A non-inverting stage keeps the sign.

p.x: Used as a switch, a MOSFET should be **fully on**, so it acts like a tiny resistor, $R_{DS(on)}$.
Only partly on, its resistance is [[much higher]], and it heats up: power lost $P = I^2 R$.
Check $R_{DS(on)}$ at the gate voltage you actually drive, not $V_{GS(th)}$, where it only barely starts to conduct.

title: Four forces
cards: Steady level flight balances four forces: lift up, weight down, thrust forward, drag back.
Lift = ½ρv²·S·CL. Double the speed and lift becomes four times larger, all else equal.
ρ is air density, S is wing area and CL is the lift coefficient, set by wing shape and angle of attack. Hold S and CL fixed and lift follows ρv².

qs.q: A plane flies level at constant speed. Which statement is true?
qs.ans: Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
wrong: Lift exceeds weight, which keeps it level
Thrust exceeds drag, which holds speed constant
Weight equals thrust
qs.why: Constant velocity means zero net force: lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

qs.q: One wing at a fixed angle of attack. Rank these by lift, highest first.
qs.why: Lift ∝ ρv². With ρ ≈ 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level and 0.909 kg/m³ at 3,000 m, ρv² is 4410, 3272, 1960 and 1454 kg/(m·s²).

qs.q: Same wing and air, but you double airspeed. Lift becomes how many times larger?
qs.why: Lift ∝ v², so doubling speed gives 2² = 4.

p.x: Four forces act on an airplane: lift up, weight down, thrust forward, drag back.
In **steady level flight**, speed and height don't change, so nothing accelerates.
So the forces cancel in pairs: lift equals weight, thrust equals drag (thrust along the flight path).

p.eq: L = ½ ρ V^2 S C_L

p.x: Hold $ρ$, $S$ and $C_L$ fixed and change only the speed.
Lift grows with the square of speed: $L ∝ V^2$.

g.q: Double the airspeed, everything else fixed. Lift…
o: doubles
That treats lift as proportional to V. Speed enters squared, through ½ρV².
becomes 4×
Lift goes as V², and 2² = 4.
becomes 8×
That's a cube. Lift goes as V², so 2² = 4.

p.x: $C_L$ is set by the wing's shape and its angle of attack. It has no units.
Same weight, same $C_L$: in thinner air the wing has to fly [[faster]] to make the same lift.

p.cap: level flight, lift = weight W, true airspeed

title: Orbits and rockets
cards: Orbiting means falling around Earth fast enough to keep missing it. Low Earth orbit is about 7.8 km/s.

Rocket equation: Δv = ve·ln(m0/mf), with ve the exhaust speed, m0 the mass at ignition and mf the mass at burnout. Flip it and m0/mf = e^(Δv/ve): the mass ratio you need grows exponentially with Δv. Staging drops empty tanks so the next burn starts lighter; dropping hardware adds no Δv by itself.

qs.q: Why do rockets drop stages?
qs.ans: Dropping dead mass raises the mass ratio m0/mf
wrong: Each stage is tuned to a different gravity
Engines can only burn for a few minutes
Smaller tanks are cheaper to build and fly
qs.why: Δv = ve·ln(m0/mf). Dropping dead mass raises m0/mf for the remaining burn.

qs.q: ve = 3000 m/s, m0 = 10 t, mf = 2 t. Find Δv in m/s.

p.x: An orbiting spacecraft is falling the whole time. It moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away as fast as it falls.

p.cap: circular orbit, Earth's gravity only

p.x: Farther out, slower orbit: $v ∝ 1/√{r}$

g.q: A satellite much farther out, in geostationary orbit, moves…
o: slower
Gravity is weaker out there, so less speed keeps it in a circle: v = √(GM/r) ≈ 3.07 km/s.
faster
A bigger circle doesn't need more speed. Gravity weakens with distance, so v = √(GM/r) falls.

p.cap: constant v_e, no gravity or drag losses

p.x: Flip it, and the mass ratio you need grows [[exponentially]] with Δv:
Staging drops empty tanks so the next burn starts lighter. Dropping hardware adds no Δv by itself.

title: Growth rates
cards: Big-O describes how run time grows with input size n, ignoring constants.

Binary search on sorted data is O(log n): each step halves what’s left. A scan, checking every item once from start to end, is O(n). A loop inside a loop is O(n²): for each of the n items, the inner loop goes through all n again, like comparing every item with every other.

qs.q: Binary search on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items needs about…
qs.ans: 20 comparisons
wrong: 1,000 comparisons
500,000 comparisons
1,000,000 comparisons
qs.why: Each step halves the range: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20.

qs.q: Order by growth rate, fastest-growing first.
qs.why: Quadratic, then linear, then logarithmic, then constant.

qs.q: How many times can you halve 1,024 before reaching 1?
qs.why: 1,024 = 2¹⁰, so ten halvings.

title: Bits and overflow
cards: A byte is 8 bits. An 8-bit unsigned integer holds 0 to 255.

Signed integers use two’s complement: the top bit counts as −128 instead of +128. So 8 bits hold −128 to 127: still 256 values, and zero takes one of the non-negative ones, leaving one more negative value than positive.
Overflow wraps around. 255 + 1 becomes 0 in 8 bits.

qs.q: In two’s complement, what range of values can a signed 8-bit integer hold?
qs.why: 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 values. Zero uses one of the non-negative slots, so there is one more negative value: −128 to 127. −127 to 128 puts the extra value on the wrong side; 0 to 255 is the unsigned range; −255 to 255 would need 511 values (9 bits).

qs.q: In an 8-bit unsigned register, what is 255 + 1?
qs.why: The value wraps around: 256 mod 256 = 0.

title: Parts and forces
cards: A bushing is a sleeve that wears so the housing doesn’t.
Torque is a twisting moment: force × perpendicular distance from the axis.

qs.q: A bushing is…
qs.ans: A sleeve that takes the wear in a hole
wrong: A threaded insert for soft materials
A flexible coupling between two shafts
A collar that locates a shaft axially
qs.why: It’s a simple plain bearing, cheap to replace so the housing isn’t worn.

qs.q: Torque is…
qs.ans: Force × perpendicular distance from the axis
wrong: Force × distance moved along its path
Energy transferred per unit of time
Force per unit area of the contact
qs.why: Torque is a twisting moment in N·m. Force × distance moved is work, and energy per time is power.

title: Edges and fits
cards: A chamfer is an angled cut on an edge. A fillet is a rounded blend at a corner.
Fit codes like H7/g6 name tolerance classes: capital letter for holes, lowercase for shafts.

qs.q: A chamfer differs from a fillet because it is…
qs.ans: A flat angled cut on an edge
wrong: A rounded inside corner
A groove at the end of a thread
A conical hole entrance only
qs.why: Chamfers are angled cuts on edges. Fillets are rounded blends at corners.

qs.q: A hole is 10 H7 and the shaft is 10 g6. This is a…
qs.ans: Clearance fit
wrong: Press fit
Transition fit
Locational interference fit
qs.why: H7/g6 is a close sliding fit: the shaft is always slightly smaller than the hole.

title: Gears and drawings
cards: Backlash is the gap between mating gear teeth.
A datum is the reference feature every other measurement starts from.

qs.q: Backlash in a gear train is…
qs.ans: Clearance between mating tooth flanks
wrong: Axial play of the gear shaft
Whine from the teeth at speed
Tooth bending under load
qs.why: It prevents binding but creates lost motion when direction reverses.

qs.q: A datum on a drawing is…
qs.ans: A reference that measurements are taken from
wrong: The shape of a feature’s tolerance zone
A modifier for the material condition
A symbol that specifies surface finish
qs.why: Datums anchor GD&T so every inspector measures the part from the same place.

title: Manufacturing talk
cards: Poka-yoke means mistake-proofing: the part only fits one way.
MMC, maximum material condition, is the size with the most metal: smallest hole, largest shaft.

qs.q: Poka-yoke in design means…
qs.ans: Making wrong assembly physically impossible
wrong: Holding a very tight tolerance everywhere
Adding a redundant load path for safety
A heat treatment applied after welding
qs.why: Think keyed connectors or asymmetric holes: the part only fits one way.

qs.q: The maximum material condition (MMC) of a hole is when it is…
qs.ans: At its smallest allowed size
wrong: At its largest allowed size
Perfectly round
At the nominal size
qs.why: MMC is the size with the most material: smallest hole, largest shaft.

title: Corners and edges
cards: Parts fail at sharp inside corners and at holes near edges.
Add fillets, and keep a hole about two hole-diameters from an edge.

qs.q: This bracket cracked at the circled corner. What should change?
qs.ans: Add a fillet at the inside corner
wrong: Thicken only the horizontal leg
Move the holes closer to the corner
Switch to a harder material
qs.why: A sharp inside corner concentrates stress. Harder materials are often more crack-sensitive.

qs.q: A bolt hole sits 0.5 mm from a part’s edge. Best fix?
qs.ans: Move it about 2× its diameter from the edge
wrong: Enlarge the hole to spread out the stress
Add a hardened washer under the bolt head
Chamfer the hole to remove the burr
qs.why: Too little material tears out. 1.5 to 2× the hole diameter is a common rule of thumb.

title: Make it buildable
cards: Cutters are round, so inside corners in pockets get a radius. Specify one a little bigger than the cutter.
Traces carry current like pipes carry water: thin ones heat up.

qs.q: Why avoid sharp inside corners in a machined pocket?
qs.ans: Round cutters can’t make them without extra steps
wrong: Sharp corners make the pocket much less stiff
They trap coolant and chips while cutting
They remove too much material from the pocket
qs.why: Specify a radius a bit larger than the cutter’s. It’s cheaper, and sharp corners also concentrate stress.

qs.q: A high-current PCB trace runs hot and is very thin. Fix?
qs.ans: Widen it or add a copper pour
wrong: Lengthen it so heat spreads out
Add a series resistor to it
Move it to a thinner copper layer
qs.why: A wider or thicker trace has less resistance, so it heats less.

title: Process limits
cards: 3D prints are weakest between layers, so load along layers.
Sheet-metal holes need space from bend lines.

qs.q: A 3D-printed bracket splits between layers under load. Best fix?
qs.ans: Reorient so load runs along the layers
wrong: Raise infill from 20% to 40%
Add chamfers to every outside edge
Print it with a larger nozzle
qs.why: Layer bonds are the weak direction. Infill helps little when the failure is at the layer line.

qs.q: A sheet-metal hole sits right on a bend line. Risk?
qs.ans: It distorts or tears when bent
wrong: Springback doubles
The bend radius doubles
Nothing, holes relieve stress
qs.why: Keep holes a few material thicknesses from bends so they stay round.

title: Casting and cycles
cards: Thick sections cool last and shrink. Even out wall thickness.
A part can pass a short test and still fail from fatigue at a stress raiser.

qs.q: A cast part has a thick boss joined to a thin wall. Likely defect and fix?
qs.ans: Shrinkage voids; blend thickness gradually
wrong: Warping; thicken the whole thin wall
Flash; reduce the mold clamp force
Cold shuts; remove the boss entirely
qs.why: Thick sections freeze last and shrink. Even out wall thickness or use coring and generous blends.

qs.q: A snap-fit passes a 100-cycle test but breaks near 10,000 cycles at a sharp notch. Best change?
qs.ans: Radius the notch to cut peak strain
wrong: Switch to a stiffer material
Add more latches around the part
Increase the load in the test
qs.why: Fatigue cracks start at stress raisers. A stiffer material can raise peak stress for the same deflection.

cards: In plain English: A beam’s material and cross-section determine how far it bends; neither alone tells you whether it will fail.
Our model is a straight, uniform, slender cantilever: fixed at one end, free at the other, with a transverse tip force. It assumes small deflection and linear-elastic material behavior.
For this elastic, small-deflection cantilever, δ = PL³/(3EI). P is tip force, L length, E Young’s modulus and I the section’s second moment. At fixed P and L, larger EI reduces deflection.
For rectangular elastic bending, I = bh³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to width b. Height h lies in the bending direction. At fixed b, doubling h multiplies I by eight.
For the same cantilever, hold P, L and E fixed: doubling width halves deflection; doubling height divides it by eight; doubling both section dimensions divides it by sixteen.
For elastic bending, a 20 mm-wide, 40 mm-tall rectangle has I = 106,667 mm⁴. Rotating it gives I = 26,667 mm⁴. At fixed load, length and modulus, the upright orientation bends one-quarter as far.
Small-deflection elastic example: P = 100 N, L = 500 mm, E = 200,000 N/mm², b = 20 mm, h = 40 mm. Thus δ = 100(500³)/(3×200,000×106,667) = 0.1953 mm.
At fixed load and geometry, increasing E reduces elastic deflection without reducing this cantilever’s bending stress. Strength needs separate material data, which the next lesson uses.
title: Cantilevers, stiffness and section orientation
plain: A beam’s material and cross-section determine how far it bends; neither alone tells you whether it will fail.
demoNeeded: Reuse the cantilever demo. Add an orientation comparison for b=20 mm, h=40 mm versus b=40 mm, h=20 mm at P=100 N, L=0.500 m and E=200 GPa. Show I=106666.7 versus 26666.7 mm⁴ and δ=0.1953125 versus 0.78125 mm. Visually distinguish doubling width, doubling height and doubling both. Preserve the b25 assumptions and model-check display.
figNeeded: Show a fixed wall, free tip, downward tip force P, length L and tip deflection δ. Beside it, show both orientations of the same 20×40 mm rectangle. Label b, h and the centroidal bending axis; do not confuse section area with second moment I.

qs.q: Which situation matches δ = PL³/(3EI) without changing the load or support model?
qs.ans: A slender elastic beam fixed at one end, loaded by a force at its free tip, bending only slightly
wrong: The same beam supported by a pin and roller at its ends, with a force at midspan
The same cantilever carrying a uniformly distributed load whose total equals P
The same tip-loaded cantilever after its material has yielded substantially
qs.why: The stated formula applies to the fixed-free, tip-loaded, small-deflection elastic case. A pin-and-roller beam has different boundary conditions. A distributed load has a different moment distribution even when its total force equals P. Substantial yielding violates the linear-elastic assumption.

qs.q: “The beam calculator returned a number, but our bracket is short, thick and permanently bent.”
qs.ans: The slender-beam and linear-elastic assumptions need checking before trusting the deflection.
wrong: A numerical result proves that the beam assumptions are satisfied.
Permanent bending can be represented just by increasing the elastic modulus.
Matching the total force is sufficient even if the support and load distribution differ.
qs.why: A calculator evaluates an equation; it does not establish that the equation fits the physical case. Permanent deformation cannot be repaired within the model by arbitrarily increasing E. Equal total force does not make different support conditions or load distributions equivalent.

qs.q: A rectangular section is 20.0 mm wide and 40.0 mm tall in the bending direction. Using I = bh³/12 about its centroidal axis parallel to b, calculate I in mm⁴. Give 3 significant figures.
qs.why: I = 20.0×40.0³/12 = 106666.7 mm⁴, or 1.067×10⁵ mm⁴. The area bh=800 mm² is not I. Cubing the width instead of the height gives the other bending orientation. Using metres without converting the fourth-power result produces incompatible units.

qs.q: A cantilever bar is 40 mm wide and 20 mm tall, and its tip deflects 0.7813 mm. Turn the same bar on edge: 20 mm wide, 40 mm tall. That makes I four times bigger. Same load, length and material. What is the new tip deflection?
qs.ans: About 0.195 mm
wrong: 0.781 mm: same bar, same area, same deflection
About 0.098 mm: height is cubed, so 8× less
About 3.13 mm: bigger I, bigger deflection
qs.why: Deflection goes as 1/I, so 4× the I gives a quarter of the deflection: 0.7813 / 4 = 0.195 mm. Same area doesn’t mean same I. The height is cubed, but the width also halves, so I grows 8 × ½ = 4×, not 8×. Bigger I means a stiffer beam, so the deflection shrinks.
qs.hint: δ = PL³/(3EI): I is on the bottom.

qs.q: Four slender rectangular cantilevers have the same tip force, length and E, and remain in the small-deflection elastic regime. Rank their tip deflections, largest first. Here b and h describe the original section.
items: Original section: width b, height h
Width doubled only: width 2b, height h
Height doubled only: width b, height 2h
qs.why: Since I=bh³/12, the four I values are I₀, 2I₀, 8I₀ and 16I₀. At fixed P, L and E, the corresponding deflections are δ₀, δ₀/2, δ₀/8 and δ₀/16. Width enters linearly; height enters cubically; scaling the whole section changes both.

qs.q: A tip-loaded cantilever remains linear-elastic with small deflection. Its material is replaced by one with twice E, while load, supports and geometry remain unchanged. No strength data for the new material are supplied. What can you conclude?
qs.ans: Deflection halves; calculated bending stress is unchanged; strength adequacy remains undetermined.
wrong: Deflection and bending stress both halve, proving the replacement is safe.
Deflection is unchanged because only cross-section geometry controls stiffness.
Deflection doubles, while the higher E proves that yield strength doubles.
qs.why: Deflection varies inversely with E, but the bending stress from the imposed force and geometry does not contain E. Halving stress incorrectly applies the deflection relationship to stress. Ignoring E omits material stiffness. Doubling deflection reverses the dependence, and E does not determine yield strength.

p.x: **Deflection** is how far a beam moves under load. A **cross-section** is the shape you see when you cut across the beam.
Material stiffness and cross-section geometry work [[together]] to control how far it bends for a given support and load.
A beam can bend very little and still fail. Strength needs its own check.
A **cantilever** is fixed at one end and free at the other. This beam is straight, slender, and uniform along its length.
This model applies a **transverse tip force**, a force across the beam at its free end.
It assumes small deflection and a linear-elastic material, so stress is proportional to strain and the material recovers when unloaded.

g.q: What should happen after this model’s load is removed?
o: The beam returns to its original shape
Elastic deformation reverses when the load goes away.
The beam stays permanently bent
A permanent bend means the material has left the elastic range.

vars: second moment of area about the bending axis

p.cap: Slender, linear-elastic cantilever with a tip force and small deflection.

p.x: At the same load and length, a larger $EI$ means less deflection.

vars: second moment of area, weighted by distance squared from the axis

p.x: At fixed width, $I$ grows [[cubically]] with depth.

p.cap: Rectangular section. The axis passes through its center, parallel to b.

p.x: Double the depth at fixed width and $I$ grows eightfold.
Hold the tip force, beam length and material fixed. Change only the size of the rectangular section.
Width counts once, depth counts three times: $δ ∝ 1/(bh^3)$.

g.q: Double both width and depth. What happens to tip deflection?
o: Drops to one sixteenth
The width doubles I and the depth multiplies it by eight, so deflection falls by sixteen.
Drops to one eighth
That accounts for the depth change only. Doubling the width divides deflection by two again.
Drops to one quarter
That follows area. The second moment scales with width times depth cubed.

p.x: Turn a rectangular bar on its edge. Its area stays the same, but its depth in the bending direction doubles and its width halves.
Four times the second moment gives one quarter of the deflection at the same load, length and modulus.
Use the upright section for a slender elastic cantilever and assume the tip moves only a small distance.
In millimeter units, $E = 200,000$ N/mm². Use the unrounded second moment in the calculation.
With the same force, supports and geometry, a higher $E$ makes this elastic cantilever bend [[less]].
Nominal bending stress, the stress predicted by the beam model, depends on the imposed force and section geometry. It stays the same.
Young's modulus is a stiffness measure. A strength check needs separate data, such as the stress at which the material yields.

cards: In plain English: A beam bends less when its material sits far from the middle. Making it taller helps far more than making it wider.

Deflection of a cantilever with a tip load: δ = PL³/(3EI). More load or a longer beam bends it more, and length counts cubed. A stiffer material (bigger E) or a deeper section (bigger I) bends it less. Assumes a slender, linear-elastic beam and small deflection.
I says how far the material sits from the bending axis. For a rectangle I = bh³/12: width counts once, height counts cubed. A tube puts its material far out, so it gets a big I for little area.

Stress: the wall carries the biggest moment, M = PL, and the outer edge works hardest: σ = Mc/I, where c is the distance from the middle to that edge. E isn’t in it: a stiffer material bends less but carries the same stress at the same load.
Small-deflection elastic example: P=100 N, L=500 mm, b=20 mm, h=40 mm. Then I=106,667 mm⁴ and c=20 mm; σ=(100×500×20)/106,667=9.375 MPa. E does not enter this force-controlled stress calculation.
Same load, length and material: make the beam twice as tall and it bends 8× less, with 4× less stress. Make it twice as wide and both halve. That’s why floor joists stand on edge.
Same material, same amount of it: a tube 25 mm across with a 15 mm hole is about 2× stiffer than a 20 mm solid rod, because its material sits farther from the middle.

Compare deflection and nominal-stress targets separately. A target stress is not a verified material allowable. Yielding, fatigue, local buckling, connections and load uncertainty need separate checks; passing these calculations does not establish overall safety.
title: Beam calculations and design checks
plain: A beam bends less when its material sits far from the middle. Making it taller helps far more than making it wider.
demoNeeded: Extend the cantilever model with rectangle, solid circle and concentric circular tube choices. Display section area, centroidal I, outer-fiber distance c, wall moment PL, tip deflection and maximum nominal bending stress. Include a same-area comparison: solid d=20 mm versus tube OD=25 mm, ID=15 mm, both A=100π mm². At P=100 N, L=500 mm and E=200000 N/mm², solid I=7853.9816 mm⁴ and δ=2.6525824 mm; tube I=16689.7110 mm⁴, δ=1.2482741 mm and σ=37.4482219 MPa. Label model predictions and preserve assumption checks. Do not label material strength adequate from E.
figNeeded: Show a cantilever with a wall-section cut identifying M=PL and c. Show rectangle b/h, solid diameter d, and concentric tube OD D/ID dᵢ about centroidal bending axes. For the design question, compare the same 40×20 mm rectangle flat and upright, with no change in area.

qs.q: A slender steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa) is 0.500 m long and carries a 100 N tip load. Its section has I = 133,333 mm⁴. Using δ = PL³/(3EI), what is the tip deflection in mm?
qs.why: δ = 100 × 500³ / (3 × 200,000 × 133,333) = 0.156 mm. Using E = 200 mixes GPa with N/mm² and gives an answer 1000× too big. Leaving L in metres while I is in mm⁴ mixes units. Dropping the 3 gives 3× too much.
qs.hint: Work in N and mm: L = 500 mm and E = 200,000 N/mm².

qs.q: A cantilever 500 mm long carries a 100 N tip load. Its section is 40 mm tall with I = 106,667 mm⁴, so the outer edge is c = 20 mm from the middle. Using σ = Mc/I with M = PL, what is the bending stress at the wall, in MPa?
qs.why: M = 100 × 500 = 50,000 N·mm, so σ = 50,000 × 20 / 106,667 = 9.375 MPa. Using c = 40 mm (the full height) doubles it. P divided by the section area is a direct stress, not bending. E isn’t needed: the stress comes from the load and the shape.
qs.hint: M = 100 N × 500 mm = 50,000 N·mm. N/mm² is the same as MPa.

qs.q: A solid rod is 20 mm across. A tube is 25 mm outside with a 15 mm hole, so it has the same area. How many times bigger is the tube's I? (Round section: I = πd⁴/64. Tube: subtract the hole's I.)
qs.why: The π/64 cancels: (25⁴ − 15⁴) / 20⁴ = 340,000 / 160,000 = 2.125. Same area doesn't mean same I. Subtracting the diameters first (10⁴) or using d² (area) gives the wrong ratio.

qs.q: Steel tube cantilever: 25 mm outside, 15 mm inside, 500 mm long, 100 N at the tip. E = 200,000 N/mm² and I = 16,690 mm⁴. Using δ = PL³/(3EI) and σ = PLc/I, which pair is right?
qs.ans: δ ≈ 1.248 mm and σ ≈ 37.45 MPa
wrong: δ ≈ 2.653 mm and σ ≈ 63.66 MPa
δ ≈ 1.248 mm and σ ≈ 74.90 MPa
δ ≈ 0.6241 mm and σ ≈ 18.72 MPa
qs.why: δ = 100 × 500³ / (3 × 200,000 × 16,690) = 1.248 mm and σ = 100 × 500 × 12.5 / 16,690 = 37.45 MPa. 2.653 / 63.66 is the solid 20 mm rod with the same area. 74.90 MPa uses the full diameter instead of the radius. 0.6241 / 18.72 uses J = 2I, which is for twisting, not bending.
qs.hint: c is the outer radius: 25/2 = 12.5 mm.

qs.q: A steel cantilever (elastic, small deflection; 100 N at the tip, 500 mm long) has a flat section, 40 mm wide and 20 mm tall: δ = 0.781 mm and σ = 18.75 MPa. Targets: δ ≤ 0.25 mm and σ ≤ 10 MPa. Which single change meets both?
qs.ans: Turn it on edge, 20 wide × 40 tall: δ ≈ 0.195 mm, σ ≈ 9.38 MPa
wrong: A material with twice the E: δ ≈ 0.391 mm, σ = 18.75 MPa
Double the width to 80 mm: δ ≈ 0.391 mm, σ ≈ 9.38 MPa
A stronger steel, same E: δ = 0.781 mm, σ = 18.75 MPa
qs.why: On edge, I grows 4× and c doubles: δ drops 4×, σ halves, both targets met. Twice the E halves δ but leaves σ alone. Twice the width halves both, so δ still misses. A stronger steel with the same E changes neither number. Meeting these targets alone doesn't make it safe.

qs.q: “The cantilever model says the tip drops 20% of the length. We only entered E, but the spreadsheet says it's safe.”
qs.ans: Recheck the model, that's too much bending for it, and get real strength data.
wrong: A drop of 20% of the length proves the small-deflection model works.
E tells you the yield strength, so the material is approved.
Show fewer decimal places and both problems go away.
qs.why: The formula assumes small deflection; a 20% drop breaks that assumption rather than confirming it. E is stiffness, not strength. Rounding changes how the numbers look, not what's missing. Also check the supports, buckling and joints.

p.x: A beam resists bending better when more of its cross-section lies far from the bending axis through its middle.
That is why adding height in the bending direction reduces deflection more than adding the same proportion of width.

vars: length from fixed end to tip

p.cap: Straight, slender, linear-elastic cantilever. Small deflection under a tip force.

p.x: Length enters cubed. With everything else fixed, twice the length gives eight times the deflection. A larger $E$ or $I$ reduces it.

g.q: With the same tip force, section and material, doubling the beam length makes deflection…
o: Twice as large
That treats length as linear. Each factor of length gets doubled.
Four times as large
That treats length as squared. The tip displacement depends on length cubed.
Eight times as large
Deflection scales with length cubed when the load, section and material are fixed.

p.x: The second moment $I$ adds up the effect of area at different distances from the bending axis. Area farther out counts more.
A rectangular section has a [[cubic]] dependence on depth at fixed width.

p.cap: Rectangular section, about the axis through its center parallel to b.

p.x: A tube can put much of its area far from the axis without needing a solid center.

vars: distance from the centerline to the edge

p.cap: At the fixed end of a tip-loaded cantilever.
Nominal bending stress of a slender, linear-elastic beam.

p.x: Same force and shape: a higher modulus reduces deflection, and stress stays the same.
E doesn't appear. With the force given, stress depends only on the load and the section; E sets how far the beam bends.
Elastic cantilever. Keep P, L and E fixed and change only the cross-section.
Depth pays off most: $δ ∝ 1/(bh^3)$ and $σ ∝ 1/(bh^2)$.

g.q: Make the beam twice as deep. The tip deflection…
o: halves
That treats deflection as 1/h. δ = PL³/(3EI) and I = bh³/12, so δ goes as 1/h³.
drops to a quarter
That's the stress, which goes as 1/h². Deflection goes through I, which grows with h³.
drops to an eighth
I = bh³/12 grows 2³ = 8 times, and δ = PL³/(3EI) falls by the same factor.

p.x: A 25 mm outer-diameter tube with a 15 mm centered hole has the same area as a solid 20 mm rod.

vars: hole diameter, zero for a solid rod

p.cap: Circular section, bending about a diameter through the center.

p.x: The tube has 2.125 times the bending stiffness $EI$ at the same modulus. Its area lies farther from the bending axis.
Screen deflection and nominal stress [[separately]]. Each limit answers a different question.
A deflection target limits motion. A stress target limits the calculated value, and a verified material allowable needs strength data.
Check yielding, fatigue, local buckling, connections, and uncertain loads separately. Passing both screening targets cannot establish overall safety.

cards: A streamline is a line that follows the local flow direction everywhere. In steady flow, air particles travel along streamlines, and where streamlines squeeze together in a channel, the flow speeds up.
Static pressure p is the local fluid pressure. Dynamic pressure q = ρV²/2 measures a speed-related pressure scale, where ρ is air density and V is flow speed.

For steady, incompressible flow with negligible friction and elevation change, Bernoulli’s equation gives p + q = constant along a streamline. Slowing that flow to rest produces stagnation pressure p₀ = p + q.
title: Pressure and airflow

qs.q: Which quantity is represented by q = ρV²/2?
qs.ans: Dynamic pressure
wrong: Local static pressure
The pressure measured after bringing the flow to rest
Aerodynamic drag force
qs.why: The expression defines dynamic pressure. Stagnation pressure includes both static and dynamic pressure; drag additionally depends on area and a coefficient.

qs.q: Air has density ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ and speed V = 10 m/s. What is its dynamic pressure q in Pa?
Along one streamline, steady incompressible airflow accelerates with negligible friction and elevation change. What happens to static pressure p?
qs.ans: It decreases
wrong: It increases because faster air has greater pressure
It remains fixed at atmospheric pressure
It becomes equal to dynamic pressure q
qs.why: Bernoulli’s equation keeps p + q constant. Increasing speed raises q and lowers p; greater dynamic pressure does not mean greater static pressure.

qs.q: What is the name of the pressure obtained by bringing airflow to rest without losses?
qs.why: Stagnation pressure, also called total pressure, includes the static pressure and the recoverable contribution associated with flow speed.

figNeeded: Draw horizontal airflow along a streamline toward a stagnation point. Label upstream speed V, density ρ, static pressure p, and stagnation pressure p₀ where V = 0. State the incompressible, negligible-loss assumptions.

p.x: A **streamline** follows the local flow direction at every point. In steady flow, air particles travel along streamlines.
Where streamlines squeeze together in a channel, the same flow passes through less area, so it [[speeds up]].

p.cap: steady, incompressible flow along a channel

p.x: **Static pressure**: the local pressure of the air itself.
**Dynamic pressure**: a pressure scale set by the flow's speed.

p.cap: along a streamline: steady, incompressible, no friction, no height change

p.x: Where the flow slows, static pressure rises. Brought to rest, it reaches the highest pressure on the streamline:
Stagnation pressure $p_0 = p + q$.

g.q: Air slows to rest at the nose. Its pressure, compared with upstream, is…
o: higher
p + q stays constant, so when q drops to zero, p rises by q.
lower
Low pressure goes with fast flow. Slowing the flow trades q for static pressure, so p rises.

cards: Lift and drag coefficients describe aerodynamic forces relative to dynamic pressure and reference area. Lift L = qSCL and drag D = qSCD, where S is reference area and CL and CD are dimensionless.
Dynamic pressure is q = ρV²/2. For a wing, S usually means planform area viewed from above. Coefficients depend on operating conditions; changing speed does not guarantee unchanged coefficients.
In steady, level flight with negligible vertical thrust, L = W, where W is weight. Thus CL = W/(qS). Using the same reference area for both coefficients gives lift-to-drag ratio L/D = CL/CD.
title: Aerodynamic force coefficients

qs.q: A wing flies at V = 20 m/s in air of density ρ = 1.0 kg/m³. With area S = 2 m² and lift coefficient CL = 0.5, what is lift L in N?
An aircraft weighs W = 600 N and flies steadily and level at V = 20 m/s in air with ρ = 1.2 kg/m³. For S = 5 m², what CL is required?
qs.why: q = 1.2 × 20²/2 = 240 Pa. Level flight requires CL = W/(qS) = 600/(240 × 5) = 0.5.

qs.q: A wing has CL = 0.6 and CD = 0.03 using the same reference area. If its lift is L = 1000 N, what is drag D in N?
An aircraft maintains steady level flight at unchanged weight W, density ρ, and area S. If speed V doubles, what happens to required CL?
qs.ans: It falls to one quarter of its original value
wrong: It halves because speed doubled
It remains unchanged as a property of the wing
It becomes four times larger to match dynamic pressure
qs.why: Doubling V quadruples q. Since L = W remains fixed, CL = W/(qS) must fall by four; it is not a fixed geometric constant.

figNeeded: Draw a wing in plan view with reference area S shaded. Add a separate side view labeling relative airflow V, lift L perpendicular to airflow, and drag D parallel to airflow.

vars: lift and drag coefficients, no units

p.x: Dividing out $q$ and $S$ leaves a pure number. That lets a wind-tunnel model and the full-size wing be compared, if their Mach and Reynolds numbers match.
For a wing, the reference area $S$ is usually the planform: its outline seen from above.
The coefficients aren't fixed numbers. They change with angle of attack, and also with Mach and Reynolds number, so a new speed can mean new coefficients.
$L = W$ holds when thrust has no vertical part. $L/D = C_L/C_D$ only if both coefficients use the same $S$.

cards: Angle of attack α is the angle between the wing’s chord line and incoming airflow. Beyond a critical α, extensive flow separation causes stall. Pitch attitude alone does not determine α.
Maximum lift coefficient CL,max limits lift. At load factor n = L/W, stall speed is Vstall = √[2nW/(ρSCL,max)]. Here W is weight, ρ density, and S wing area.
In a coordinated level turn, n = 1/cos φ, where φ is bank angle. Stall speed scales with √n, so a 60° bank (n = 2) raises it by √2, about 41%.
title: Stall during maneuvers

qs.q: An aircraft stalls at Vstall = 20 m/s in straight, level flight. At unchanged density and configuration, what is its stall speed in a coordinated level turn with bank angle φ = 60°, in m/s?
qs.why: n = 1/cos 60° = 2. Stall speed becomes 20 × √2 ≈ 28.3 m/s.

qs.q: A pilot holds airspeed above the aircraft’s straight-and-level stall speed while tightening a coordinated level turn. Why can the wing still stall?
qs.ans: The required lift can exceed the available lift at CL,max
wrong: Bank angle itself becomes the wing’s angle of attack
Turning reduces dynamic pressure even at unchanged density and speed
Exceeding the straight-flight stall speed rules out a stall
qs.why: A level turn requires L = nW. At fixed speed, increasing n raises required CL until it reaches CL,max; bank angle and angle of attack are different quantities.

qs.q: An aircraft’s straight-and-level stall speed is 20 m/s. It flies at 30 m/s with unchanged density, weight, and configuration. What maximum aerodynamic load factor n is available before reaching CL,max? Ignore structural limits.
qs.why: At unchanged CL,max, available lift scales with V². Therefore nmax = (30/20)² = 2.25.

qs.q: For unchanged load factor n, area S, and CL,max, weight W increases by 44% while density ρ falls to 81% of its original value. By what factor does true stall speed increase?
qs.why: The factor is √(1.44/0.81) = 4/3. The value 16/9 omits the square root; 6/5 ignores density; 27/25 incorrectly multiplies by the density ratio.

figNeeded: Draw a wing section labeling chord line, incoming airflow, and angle of attack α. Separately draw a rear view of a level banked aircraft with bank angle φ, weight W, lift L, and vertical lift component L cos φ.

p.x: **Angle of attack**: the angle between the wing's chord line and the oncoming air.
Past a critical $α$, the flow separates from the upper surface and lift drops: a **stall**.
α is measured from the oncoming air, not the horizon. A wing stalls at its critical α in any attitude.

g.q: True or false: a nose-low airplane can't stall.
o: True
Attitude isn't α: a dive pull-out can stall nose-low.
False
Stall depends on α, measured from the oncoming air, not on attitude.

p.x: A wing can only reach a certain lift coefficient before it stalls: $C_{L,max}$.
Pull more g and the wing must make more lift at the same speed, so the stall speed [[rises]].

p.cap: steady flight at load factor n
vars: load factor L/W: 1 in level flight

p.x: In a coordinated level turn at bank angle $φ$, lift tilts with the wings, and its vertical part must still hold the weight.

p.cap: coordinated, level turn

p.x: Stall speed grows with $√{n}$: a 60° bank raises it about 41 %.

g.q: At 60° bank, n = 2. The stall speed…
o: doubles
That's n itself. Stall speed goes as √n, and √2 ≈ 1.41.
rises about 41 %
V_stall ∝ √n, and √2 ≈ 1.41.
stays the same
The stall angle stays the same, but the wing needs twice the lift, so it reaches that angle at a higher speed.

cards: A simple drag polar is CD = CD0 + kCL². Here CD0 is a constant baseline drag coefficient and k is the induced-drag factor. Induced drag is the drag associated with producing lift.
In steady level flight, D = qSCD0 + kW²/(qS), where D is drag, q dynamic pressure, S area, and W weight. At minimum drag, these two terms are equal and CL = √(CD0/k).
Power required is P = DV. In this model, minimum power occurs at a lower speed than minimum drag, where induced drag is three times baseline drag. Both points must stay above stall.
title: Minimum drag tradeoffs

qs.q: An aircraft has W = 4000 N, S = 10 m², ρ = 1.0 kg/m³, CD0 = 0.02, and k = 0.08. Assuming the optimum is unstalled, what true airspeed V minimizes drag in level flight, in m/s?
At speed V₀, an aircraft’s baseline and induced drag are each 100 N. In level flight at 2V₀, with unchanged density, weight, and polar, what is total drag D?
qs.why: Baseline drag becomes 400 N, while induced drag becomes 25 N. The total is 425 N. Scaling both terms with V² incorrectly gives 800 N.

qs.q: An aircraft is at its minimum-drag speed in level flight. The simple polar remains valid and stall margin is ample. Which speed change initially reduces aerodynamic power P = DV?
qs.ans: A small decrease in speed
wrong: A small increase to reduce the time spent airborne
No change, because minimum drag also minimizes power
An immediate reduction to the stall boundary
qs.why: At minimum drag, induced and baseline drag are equal. Minimum power occurs at a lower speed, where induced drag is three times baseline drag; it need not coincide with stall.

qs.q: A polar gives minimum-drag CL = 1.0, but the wing’s CL,max is 0.8. Assuming the model holds up to that boundary, what is the least-drag feasible point in steady level flight?
qs.ans: CL = 0.8, at the stall boundary
wrong: CL = 1.0, because the mathematical optimum governs
CL = 0.4, to halve the induced-drag coefficient
CL approaching zero, to remove lift-dependent drag
qs.why: With fixed weight, D/W = CD0/CL + kCL decreases up to CL = 1.0. The feasible boundary is therefore 0.8; practical operation requires additional stall margin.

figNeeded: Plot drag D against true airspeed V for fixed weight and density. Label baseline drag, induced drag, total drag, and minimum-drag speed V₀. Mark the minimum-power speed to the left of V₀ and indicate a separate stall-speed boundary.

p.x: Part of a wing's drag comes from making lift: **induced drag**. In a simple model it grows [[with the square of]] the lift coefficient.

p.cap: simple parabolic model

p.x: The first term doesn't change with lift. The second is the induced drag.

p.cap: steady level flight, lift = weight W

p.x: The first term grows with speed; the induced term shrinks. Drag is lowest where they're equal:
Power required is drag times speed: $P = D V$.
Both speeds must stay above the stall speed.

g.q: Compared with the minimum-drag speed V₀, the minimum-power speed is…
o: lower
P = DV: just below V₀ drag barely changes, but V falls, so power keeps dropping. It bottoms out near 0.76 V₀.
higher
Above V₀ both drag and speed rise, so P = DV only grows.

cards: A data structure organizes values and their relationships. An array stores elements in consecutive slots. With zero-based indexing, index 0 identifies the first element and index 3 identifies the fourth.
A singly linked list stores nodes containing a value and a link to the next node. Its head identifies the first node; the last node’s next link is null, meaning no next node.

An array locates a slot directly from its index. A singly linked list reaches a position by following links from its head. Inserting inside a packed array requires shifting later elements to preserve order.
title: Arrays and linked nodes

qs.q: A zero-indexed array contains [12, 7, 19, 4]. What value is stored at index 2?
qs.why: Index 0 contains 12, index 1 contains 7, and index 2 contains 19.

qs.q: What information does a singly linked list node’s next link represent?
qs.ans: A reference to the following node
wrong: The number of nodes remaining in the list
An array index that must increase by one
A second copy of the following node’s value
qs.why: The link identifies another node. It does not require consecutive storage or encode how many nodes remain.

qs.q: Starting with only a singly linked list’s head reference, how do you reach its fourth node?
qs.ans: Follow the next link three times
wrong: Read array slot 3 directly
Add three node sizes to the head’s memory address
Read the head’s previous link
qs.why: The head is already the first node. Three links reach the fourth; linked nodes need not occupy consecutive memory.

qs.q: A packed array has spare capacity and currently stores [A, B, C]. To insert X between A and B while preserving order, what happens to existing elements?
qs.ans: B and C move one slot to the right
wrong: B is overwritten by X
A new next link is attached to A
X is placed after C at the end of the array
qs.why: Shifting B and C opens the required slot. Appending preserves existing positions but places X in the wrong order.

figNeeded: Draw an array with slots indexed 0 through 3. Beside it, draw a singly linked list with head, four value-and-next nodes, and a final next link labeled null. Show nodes separated rather than adjacent.

cards: A stack removes the most recently added item first. Push puts a new item on top; pop takes the top item (the one added most recently) off and hands it back. Stacks suit nested operations that must finish in reverse order.

A queue removes the item that has waited longest. Enqueue adds at the back; dequeue removes and returns the front. Use a queue when work should be handled first come, first served, like print jobs or messages waiting to send.
A circular queue reuses an array of capacity C. With head at the front and count items stored, the next insertion goes at index (head + count) mod C, wrapping past the end.
title: Stacks and queues

qs.q: A stack holds 3, then 8 on top. You push 5, then pop twice. What does the second pop return?
qs.why: Push puts 5 on top: 3, 8, 5. The first pop takes 5, the second takes 8. Answering 5 stops after one pop; answering 3 takes from the bottom, like a queue.

qs.q: A queue holds 4 at the front, then 7. You enqueue 9, then dequeue twice. What does the second dequeue return?
qs.why: Enqueue adds 9 at the back: 4, 7, 9. Dequeue takes from the front: first 4, then 7. Answering 9 takes from the back, like a stack.

qs.q: A circular queue has 8 slots, numbered 0–7. The front item is in slot 7 (head = 7) and it holds 2 items. Which slot does the next item go in? next = (head + count) mod 8
qs.why: (7 + 2) mod 8 = 9 mod 8 = 1: the queue wraps past slot 7 back to the start. Answering 9 forgets the wrap; there is no slot 9.

qs.q: You check the brackets in “( [ ] )”. Each closing bracket must match the most recent opener that is still unmatched. Which structure hands you that opener?
qs.ans: A stack
wrong: A queue
A counter of how many openers you’ve seen
A list of which opener types appeared
qs.why: A stack returns the newest item first, which is exactly the most recent unmatched opener. A queue returns the oldest one; a counter or a list of types loses the order.

figNeeded: Draw a stack with a labeled top and a queue with labeled front and back. Add a circular array with indices 0 through 7, head = 6, and occupied indices 6, 7, and 0.

cards: A hash table maps keys to buckets with a hash function. Different keys can collide in one bucket. With separate chaining, each bucket holds a list that is searched for the exact key.
Load factor α = n/m, where n is entry count and m is bucket count. With well-distributed hashes, chained lookup takes expected O(1 + α) time. If every key collides, lookup can take O(n).

Growing a table means moving every entry, because its bucket index (h mod m) changes with m. One resize costs O(n). Doubling the capacity each time keeps resizes rare, so the cost is amortized O(1) per insertion. Amortized means averaged over a long run: most insertions are cheap, the occasional resize is expensive, and the average per insertion stays constant.
title: Hash collisions and growth

qs.q: A chained hash table holds n = 600 entries in m = 200 buckets. It grows to 800 buckets without changing its entries. What is its new load factor α?
qs.why: After growth, α = n/m = 600/800 = 0.75. The original load factor was 3.

qs.q: A table selects buckets using index = h mod m. A key has hash h = 29. When m grows from 8 to 16, what must happen to this key’s entry?
qs.ans: It must move from bucket 5 to bucket 13
wrong: It stays in bucket 5 because the key has not changed
Its key must be changed to avoid a collision
It belongs in bucket 29 once the table grows
qs.why: 29 mod 8 = 5, while 29 mod 16 = 13. A stable hash value does not imply a stable bucket index.

qs.q: A separately chained table has load factor α = 0.5, but all n keys hash to one bucket. What is the worst-case lookup time in terms of n?
qs.ans: O(n)
wrong: O(1), because the load factor is below one
O(log n), because each key check halves the candidates
O(n²), because every stored pair must be compared
qs.why: A lookup may scan all n entries in the single chain. A low average load factor cannot compensate for a badly concentrated hash distribution.

qs.q: A hash table doubles capacity when needed and has amortized O(1) insertion under well-distributed hashing. Which claim about one insertion is justified?
qs.ans: An insertion that triggers resizing can still take O(n)
wrong: Each insertion has a fixed constant-time upper bound
Doubling capacity makes the resize itself O(log n)
Amortized cost is the same as the most likely measured latency
qs.why: Amortized analysis spreads occasional expensive work across an operation sequence. It does not bound each operation’s latency or describe a probability distribution.

figNeeded: Draw a chained hash table with bucket indices and two distinct keys sharing one bucket. Add before-and-after tables with m = 8 and m = 16, showing hash h = 29 moving from index 5 to index 13.

cards: A binary min-heap keeps each parent key no larger than its children. It provides minimum access in O(1) and insertion or minimum removal in O(log n). Searching for an arbitrary key can require O(n).

A balanced binary search tree maintains key order and logarithmic height. Lookup, insertion, and deletion take O(log n). Reporting k keys in a specified range takes O(log n + k) with suitable ordered traversal.
Sorted arrays search in O(log n) but insert in O(n), since elements shift. To keep a stream’s k largest values, use a size-k min-heap and replace its root when a bigger value arrives.
title: Ordered structure tradeoffs

qs.q: A service stores n distinct numeric keys. Each cycle inserts one key, deletes a specified key, and reports k keys within a numeric interval. Which structure supports the complete cycle in O(log n + k) worst-case time?
qs.ans: A balanced binary search tree
wrong: A binary min-heap, because its root is the smallest key
A sorted array with binary search for the interval endpoints
A hash table with a low load factor
qs.why: The balanced tree supports logarithmic updates and ordered range reporting. Binary search finds array positions quickly, but maintaining sorted order can still require linear shifting.
qs.hint: List what each cycle needs: insert a key, delete one specific key, and report the keys between two values in order. Which structure keeps keys sorted and still updates in O(log n)?

qs.q: A size-3 min-heap retains the three largest values seen so far: {8, 12, 15}. New values arrive in order: 10, then 9. What is the heap’s minimum after both values are processed?
qs.why: 10 replaces the current minimum 8, leaving {10, 12, 15}. Then 9 is discarded because it is below 10. The final minimum is 10.

qs.q: A binary min-heap contains n distinct keys. You must locate a specified key but have no index mapping keys to heap positions. Why is an O(log n) lookup not guaranteed?
qs.ans: Parent-child order does not identify one search branch
wrong: The heap can have height n even when stored correctly
Only the root is ordered; every parent-child relation below it is unrestricted
Finding any key requires sorting the entire heap first
qs.why: Heap order allows the target in either child subtree, so many nodes may need inspection. A binary search tree provides the additional left-right ordering needed to choose one branch.

qs.q: You keep the k largest of n values in a min-heap of size k. Each new value costs at most O(log k). What is the total for all n values?
qs.ans: O(n log k)
wrong: O(n log n), because every arrival must remain stored
O(nk), because each update must scan all retained values
O(log k), because the heap never exceeds k entries
qs.why: n values × O(log k) each = O(n log k). O(n log n) assumes all n values are stored; O(nk) assumes each update scans the whole heap; O(log k) is the cost of one value, not all n.

figNeeded: Draw a valid binary min-heap and a balanced binary search tree using the same distinct keys. Label the heap’s parent-child inequality and the tree’s left-smaller/right-larger rule. Show a size-3 heap retaining {8, 12, 15} before processing 10.

cards: A closed system contains a fixed amount of matter. Energy can cross its boundary, but matter cannot. Internal energy U describes energy stored microscopically within the system.

Heat Q transfers energy because of a temperature difference. Work W transfers energy through mechanisms such as a moving piston or rotating shaft. Heat and work describe transfers, not stored contents.
Use Q > 0 for heat entering and W > 0 for work leaving. With negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, ΔU = Q − W. Adiabatic means no heat transfer, not constant temperature.
title: Heat, work, and energy

qs.q: Gas is sealed inside a cylinder with a movable, leak-free piston. Which system description applies to the gas?
qs.ans: A closed system
wrong: An isolated system because the cylinder is sealed
A control volume with mass flowing through its boundary
A constant-volume system
qs.why: No matter crosses the gas boundary, so it is closed. Sealing does not prevent energy transfer, and piston motion changes the volume.

qs.q: A motor turns a paddle inside a thermally insulated tank, increasing the liquid’s internal energy. How does energy cross the liquid’s boundary?
qs.ans: As shaft work
wrong: As heat because the liquid becomes warmer
As internal energy carried by incoming matter
As heat stored in the rotating paddle
qs.why: The shaft transfers energy mechanically. A temperature increase does not mean heat crossed the boundary.

qs.q: A closed system receives heat Q = 90 J and does work W = 30 J. Neglecting kinetic and potential energy changes, what is ΔU in J?
qs.why: With heat entering and work leaving positive, ΔU = Q − W = 90 − 30 = 60 J.

qs.q: What does an adiabatic boundary require?
qs.ans: Zero heat transfer across the boundary
wrong: Equal initial and final temperatures
No work performed by a moving boundary
Constant internal energy throughout the process
qs.why: Adiabatic means Q = 0. Work can still change internal energy and temperature.

figNeeded: Draw sealed gas beneath a movable piston. Label the gas boundary, heat Q entering, work W leaving through piston motion, and stored internal energy U.

p.x: A **closed system** contains a fixed amount of matter. Its boundary marks what is inside.
Energy [[can]] cross that boundary.
For example, a sealed piston can move and transfer energy without letting gas escape. An **isolated system** exchanges neither matter nor energy.
**Internal energy** is energy stored in the system at the microscopic level, such as in molecular motion.
**Heat** transfers energy because of a temperature difference.
**Work** transfers energy through a mechanism, such as a moving piston or a rotating shaft.
Heat and work describe transfers, not stored contents. A hot coffee holds internal energy U, not heat.

g.q: True or false: a hot cup of coffee contains heat.
o: True
That's the everyday meaning. The coffee holds internal energy; heat only names energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference.
False
Heat only exists while energy crosses a boundary. What sits in the coffee is internal energy.

p.x: Heat input $Q$ is positive, and work output $W$ is positive. With negligible changes in motion and elevation, the difference is the change in internal energy $ΔU$.
**Adiabatic** means no heat crosses the boundary. Work can still change internal energy and temperature.

cards: For a closed system, changes in stored energy come from heat and work crossing its boundary. Neglect bulk motion and elevation changes so ΔU = Q − W, with work leaving positive.
For an ideal gas with constant specific heat cv, ΔU = mcvΔT. Here m is mass and ΔT is temperature change. Boundary work at constant pressure p is W = pΔV.
Keep pressure-volume units consistent: 1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ. Compression gives ΔV < 0 and therefore negative boundary work. Include other work transfers, such as shaft work, when present.
title: Closed-system energy balances

qs.q: An ideal gas expands at p = 100 kPa from 0.02 to 0.05 m³ while receiving Q = 8 kJ. Boundary work is the only work transfer. What is ΔU in kJ?
A rigid tank contains m = 2 kg of ideal gas with cv = 0.75 kJ/(kg·K). It receives Q = 30 kJ, with no work transfers. What is the temperature increase ΔT in K?
qs.why: No work crosses the boundary, so ΔU = 30 kJ. Then ΔT = ΔU/(mcv) = 30/(2 × 0.75) = 20 K.

qs.q: An adiabatic closed system receives 12 kJ of shaft work. It contains m = 2 kg of ideal gas with cv = 1 kJ/(kg·K). What is ΔT in K?
qs.why: Work entering means W = −12 kJ. Thus ΔU = 0 − (−12) = 12 kJ and ΔT = 12/(2 × 1) = 6 K.

qs.q: A gas expands at constant p = 200 kPa by ΔV = 0.01 m³ while losing 1 kJ of heat. With boundary work as the only work transfer, what is ΔU?
qs.ans: −3 kJ
wrong: 1 kJ
−1 kJ
−2 kJ
qs.why: Q = −1 kJ and W = 200 × 0.01 = 2 kJ, so ΔU = −1 − 2 = −3 kJ. 1 kJ reverses the work sign; −2 kJ ignores the heat loss.

figNeeded: Draw initial and final piston positions with gas volumes V1 and V2. Label constant pressure p, heat Q, and displacement corresponding to ΔV = V2 − V1.

p.x: A **closed system** keeps the same matter inside its boundary. Heat and work can cross it.

vars: net work out of the system

p.x: To find the change in internal energy, [[subtract]] work out from heat in.

p.cap: Neglect changes in bulk speed and elevation.

p.x: For an ideal gas, $m$ is mass and $ΔT$ is final minus initial temperature.
If the specific heat at constant volume $c_v$ stays fixed, $ΔU = mc_v ΔT$.
In compression, volume decreases, so $ΔV$ is negative. The pressure is positive.
At constant pressure, compression makes $pΔV$ negative. That is work entering the gas.
Use $1$ kPa·m³ = $1$ kJ. Include any other work, such as energy delivered by a turning shaft.
An **adiabatic** boundary passes no heat. A rigid tank cannot do moving-boundary work.

g.q: Which way does the piston transfer work during compression?
o: Into the gas
The volume falls, so pΔV is negative. The sign convention counts work into the gas as negative.
Out of the gas
That is the sign for expansion. A contracting volume makes pΔV negative.

cards: A control volume is a region through which matter may flow. Specific enthalpy h combines specific internal energy u with flow work: h = u + p/ρ, where p is pressure and ρ density.
For steady, adiabatic flow with one inlet, one outlet, and negligible elevation change: ws = h1 − h2 + (V1² − V2²)/2. Here ws is shaft work output per mass; V is speed.
Use h and ws in J/kg when V is in m/s. Shaft power is Ps = ṁws, where ṁ is mass flow rate. A nozzle with no shaft can convert enthalpy into kinetic energy.
title: Flowing energy and enthalpy

qs.q: An adiabatic nozzle has no shaft work. Enthalpy falls by 20 kJ/kg, inlet speed V1 is negligible, and elevation is unchanged. What is outlet speed V2 in m/s?
qs.why: With ws = 0, V2²/2 = h1 − h2 = 20,000 J/kg. Therefore V2 = √40,000 = 200 m/s.

qs.q: An adiabatic turbine has h1 − h2 = 100 kJ/kg, V1 = 200 m/s, V2 = 100 m/s, and ṁ = 2 kg/s. Neglect elevation change. What is shaft power output Ps in kW?
qs.why: Kinetic energy decreases by (200² − 100²)/2 = 15,000 J/kg. Thus ws = 115 kJ/kg and Ps = 2 × 115 = 230 kW.

qs.q: A steady adiabatic nozzle has no shaft and negligible elevation change. Its outlet speed exceeds its inlet speed. What follows from the energy balance?
qs.ans: Outlet enthalpy is lower
wrong: Enthalpy stays constant because no heat enters
The fluid gains total energy from the narrowing passage
Shaft work input supplies the increase in speed
qs.why: The kinetic energy increase comes from an enthalpy decrease. Adiabatic flow conserves total energy here, not enthalpy alone.

qs.q: An adiabatic compressor raises enthalpy by 40 kJ/kg. Its inlet and outlet speeds are equal, and ṁ = 0.5 kg/s. What shaft power input is required?
qs.ans: 20 kW
wrong: 80 kW
40 kW
qs.why: Input power is ṁ(h2 − h1) = 0.5 × 40 = 20 kW. 40 kW ignores mass flow; 80 kW divides by it instead of multiplying.

figNeeded: Draw a control volume with inlet 1 and outlet 2. Label ṁ, h1, V1, h2, V2, and shaft power Ps leaving. Add a nozzle variant with no shaft and a faster outlet stream.

p.x: A **control volume** is a region with a boundary that matter can cross. A **specific** quantity is measured per unit mass.
Enthalpy [[includes]] the work per mass needed to push fluid through the boundary.

p.cap: For fluid at pressure p and density ρ.

p.x: At each opening, $h$ is specific enthalpy and $K = V^2/2$ is kinetic energy per mass at speed $V$.

p.cap: Shaft work out per mass. Steady, adiabatic flow from inlet 1 to outlet 2 at equal elevation.

p.x: Compare kinetic energy and enthalpy in J/kg when speed is in m/s.
A steady adiabatic compressor raises the fluid’s enthalpy. Inlet and outlet speeds and elevations are equal.
In this compressor, work enters through the shaft. Its work output per mass $w_s$ is negative.

p.cap: Steady flow. ṁ is mass per second and P_s is shaft power out.

p.x: In a steady adiabatic nozzle with no shaft or elevation change, a fall in enthalpy supplies a rise in kinetic energy.

g.q: Which way does work cross the compressor boundary?
o: Into the fluid
The enthalpy rises and neither speed nor elevation changes. The shaft supplies the energy increase.
Out of the fluid
Work output would require a drop in the energy carried by the flow, as in a turbine.

cards: A cyclic heat engine receives heat Qh from a hot reservoir and rejects Qc to a cold reservoir. Taking both heat magnitudes positive, net work output W = Qh − Qc.
Thermal efficiency η = W/Qh cannot exceed 1 − Tc/Th for two reservoirs. Th and Tc are absolute temperatures in kelvin. Equality requires a reversible engine, with no entropy generation.
Entropy generation measures irreversibility. For this cycle, Sgen = Qc/Tc − Qh/Th ≥ 0. An energy-balanced proposal can still be impossible if it requires negative Sgen.
title: Heat-engine feasibility

qs.q: An engine operates only between reservoirs at Th = 600 K and Tc = 300 K. It receives Qh = 900 kJ per cycle. What is the maximum possible work output W in kJ per cycle?
qs.why: ηmax = 1 − 300/600 = 0.5. Thus Wmax = ηmaxQh = 0.5 × 900 = 450 kJ.

qs.q: An engine between Th = 600 K and Tc = 300 K claims Qh = 100 kJ, Qc = 40 kJ, and W = 60 kJ per cycle. What identifies the flaw?
qs.ans: It requires negative entropy generation
wrong: Its heat and work violate energy conservation
Its 60% efficiency is allowed because it is below 100%
Nothing, since 1 − 27/327 ≈ 92% allows 60%
qs.why: Energy balances, but ηmax = 1 − 300/600 = 50% < 60%, so Sgen = 40/300 − 100/600 ≈ −0.033 kJ/K. The 92% figure wrongly uses Celsius temperatures.

qs.q: A cyclic engine receives Qh = 120 kJ at Th = 600 K and rejects Qc = 80 kJ at Tc = 300 K. What is Sgen in kJ/K per cycle?
qs.why: Sgen = Qc/Tc − Qh/Th = 80/300 − 120/600 = 0.2667 − 0.2 ≈ 0.0667 kJ/K. It is positive, so the cycle is possible but irreversible.

qs.q: Rank these reversible engines from highest to lowest efficiency using their reservoir temperatures Th and Tc.
qs.why: Using η = 1 − Tc/Th gives 75%, 50%, 40%, and 25%. Hot-reservoir temperature alone does not determine efficiency.

figNeeded: Draw an engine between reservoirs Th and Tc, with Qh entering from Th, Qc leaving toward Tc, and net work W leaving sideways. Label Qh and Qc as positive heat magnitudes.

p.x: A **cyclic heat engine** returns to its initial state each cycle. Hot and cold **reservoirs** supply and absorb heat at fixed temperatures.
Net work is the [[difference]] between the incoming and outgoing heat magnitudes.

p.cap: Both heat magnitudes are positive; stored energy returns to its initial value.

p.x: Efficiency $η = W/Q_h$ compares work out with heat in. Use kelvin for $T_h$ and $T_c$ in the two-reservoir limit.
Only a **reversible** engine reaches this limit. Its ideal cycle generates no entropy.
**Entropy generation** $S_{gen}$ measures irreversibility, the effect of processes such as friction or heat flow across a finite temperature gap.

p.cap: Per complete cycle with only the two reservoirs. Use kelvin.

p.x: A cycle can balance energy and still be impossible. The second law requires $S_{gen} ≥ 0$.

g.q: A proposal balances heat and work but needs negative entropy generation. Is the proposal possible?
o: Possible
Energy conservation alone allows it, but the second law also has to hold.
Impossible
The second law requires entropy generation to be zero or positive.

cards: A sensor converts a physical quantity into a usable signal. Calibration compares its readings with reference values to establish the relationship between input and output.
Measurement error e = xmeas − xref, where xmeas is the measured value and xref the reference value. A consistent offset is bias; closely grouped repeated readings indicate good repeatability.
A thermometer repeatedly reads 22 °C in a stable 20 °C reference bath. Its observed error is +2 °C. Good repeatability does not establish agreement with the reference.
title: Measurement error and repeatability

qs.q: A pressure sensor repeatedly reports nearly the same reading in a stable reference pressure, but every reading is too high. Which property do the closely grouped readings demonstrate?
qs.ans: Good repeatability
wrong: Small bias
High sensitivity to pressure changes
Fine display resolution
qs.why: Repeatability concerns agreement among repeated readings. A consistent high reading can be repeatable while still having substantial bias.

qs.q: A temperature sensor reads xmeas = 24 °C when the reference is xref = 21 °C. What is measurement error e in °C?
qs.why: e = xmeas − xref = 24 − 21 = +3 °C.

qs.q: What is the purpose of calibration?
qs.ans: Relate sensor readings to reference values
wrong: Increase the number of digits on the display
Remove random variation by repeating measurements
Make the sensor’s output voltage as large as possible
qs.why: Calibration establishes a measurement relationship. Repetition can characterize variation, but it cannot establish accuracy without a reference.

qs.q: What term describes a consistent offset in repeated sensor readings relative to a reference?
qs.why: Bias is the systematic component of measurement error, unlike the variation seen between repeated readings.

figNeeded: Draw repeated temperature readings clustered around 22 °C with a reference line at 20 °C. Label xmeas, xref, and the observed offset e.

p.x: A **sensor** converts a physical quantity into a usable signal.
**Calibration** compares its readings with reference values to find the relationship between input and output.
Measurement error is measured minus reference: $e = x_{meas} − x_{ref}$.
**Bias**: a consistent offset, the same size and sign every time.
**Repeatability**: how closely repeated readings group together.
Good repeatability doesn't show agreement with the reference. Calibration finds the +2 °C bias so it can be corrected.

g.q: Its readings repeat within 0.1 °C. So it's accurate…
o: true
Tight grouping is repeatability. Every reading can still sit 2 °C off the reference.
false
Repeatable readings can share the same bias: these all read about 2 °C high.

cards: A linear sensor model separates sensitivity from offset: V = sx + b. Here V is output voltage, x the measured physical quantity, s sensitivity, and b the voltage at x = 0.
Two reference points determine s = (V2 − V1)/(x2 − x1), then b = V1 − sx1. Recover an unknown input using x = (V − b)/s.
A pressure sensor produces 1 V at 0 kPa and 5 V at 200 kPa. Its sensitivity is 0.02 V/kPa, so a 3 V reading corresponds to 100 kPa.
title: Linear sensor calibration

qs.q: A linear pressure sensor produces 0.5 V at 0 kPa and 4.5 V at 200 kPa. What pressure x in kPa corresponds to V = 2.5 V?
A linear temperature sensor produces 1 V at 10 °C and 3 V at 50 °C. What output V in volts should it produce at 30 °C?
