qs.why: s = (3 − 1)/(50 − 10) = 0.05 V/°C. From the first reference point, V = 1 + 0.05(30 − 10) = 2 V.

qs.q: A pressure sensor has sensitivity s = 0.02 V/kPa. A zero-pressure check now reads 0.7 V. Assuming only offset changed, what pressure corresponds to V = 2.7 V?
qs.why: The zero-pressure check sets the new offset b = 0.7 V. Thus x = (2.7 − 0.7)/0.02 = 100 kPa.

qs.q: A sensor follows V = 0.02x + 0.5, with x in kPa and V in volts. Software instead calculates x = V/0.02. What error does this introduce?
qs.ans: A constant +25 kPa error
wrong: A 2% error that grows with pressure
An offset of +0.5 kPa
No error after averaging enough readings
qs.why: Ignoring b adds b/s = 0.5/0.02 = 25 kPa to every result. This is a systematic offset, so averaging does not remove it.

qs.q: Order the dependent steps for converting an unknown voltage using a new two-point linear calibration.
items: Record the two reference input-output pairs
Calculate sensitivity s from their differences
Calculate offset b using s and one pair
Convert the unknown voltage using s and b
qs.why: The reference pairs determine sensitivity. Sensitivity then determines offset, and both are needed to invert V = sx + b.

figNeeded: Plot output voltage V vertically against pressure x horizontally. Label calibration points (0 kPa, 0.5 V) and (200 kPa, 4.5 V), offset b, slope s, and the point for V = 2.5 V.

vars: sensitivity, volts per unit of x

p.cap: inside the sensor's rated range

p.x: The model keeps sensitivity (the slope) apart from offset (where the line starts), so each can be calibrated.

g.q: The sensor reads 3 V. The pressure is…
o: 100 kPa
Take off the 1 V offset first: (3 − 1) / 0.02 = 100 kPa.
150 kPa
3 / 0.02 forgets the offset: 1 V of the reading is there even at 0 kPa.
120 kPa
3/5 of 200 kPa assumes the line starts at 0 V. It starts at 1 V.

cards: Standard uncertainty is the typical size of a measurement’s error (one standard deviation). Independent errors combine by root-sum-square: square each, add them, take the square root. They partly cancel because two independent errors are rarely both at their worst, so 0.3 K and 0.4 K combine to 0.5 K, not 0.7 K. Errors that move together (correlated) don’t follow this rule.
For independent measurements a and b, difference d = a − b has uncertainty ud = √(ua² + ub²). Averaging N independent readings reduces random uncertainty from u to u/√N.

A shared additive offset cancels when subtracting two readings, but remains in their average. Repeating measurements cannot average away a fixed calibration bias. Distinguish repeatability uncertainty from uncertainty in the calibration.
title: Uncertainty and shared errors

qs.q: Two independent temperature measurements have standard uncertainties ua = 0.3 K and ub = 0.4 K. What is the standard uncertainty ud of their difference in K?
qs.why: ud = √(ua² + ub²) = √(0.3² + 0.4²) = 0.5 K. Independence allows root-sum-square combination even though the readings are subtracted.

qs.q: The mean of 16 readings has a random uncertainty of 0.5 K (2 K/√16) and a separate, independent calibration uncertainty of 1.2 K. What is their combined standard uncertainty, in K?
qs.why: Root-sum-square: √(0.5² + 1.2²) = √1.69 = 1.3 K. Adding them directly (1.7 K) treats independent errors as if they always line up.

qs.q: One thermometer reads every temperature 0.5 K too high, the same offset b in both readings. You measure Ta and Tb and subtract. What happens to b in Ta − Tb?
qs.ans: It cancels out
wrong: It adds √2 × its uncertainty
It doubles, because there are two readings
It only goes away after averaging many readings
qs.why: (Ta + b) − (Tb + b) = Ta − Tb, so b drops out. √2 treats the two offsets as independent errors, but they are the same error. Doubling would need them to add. Averaging never removes a fixed offset; subtracting does.

qs.q: Random uncertainty in a mean is 0.1 K, while an independent calibration uncertainty is 1 K. What best explains why collecting four times as many independent readings gives little improvement?
qs.ans: The calibration contribution dominates
wrong: Random uncertainty falls as 1/N, so it is already zero
Independent errors must be added with their signs
The calibration uncertainty shrinks by the same factor as random uncertainty
qs.why: Random uncertainty falls to 0.05 K, but calibration remains 1 K. Combined uncertainty changes only from about 1.005 K to 1.001 K.

figNeeded: Draw an uncertainty budget for a mean with separate random and calibration contributions. Label the random term u/√N and the unchanged calibration term. Also show the same additive offset b applied to Ta and Tb before subtraction.

p.x: **Standard uncertainty** $u$ is the typical size of a measurement's error: one standard deviation.
Independent errors [[partly cancel]]: two are rarely both at their worst at once.

p.cap: independent (uncorrelated) errors

p.x: Not 0.7 K. Errors that move together (correlated) don't follow this rule.
For independent $a$ and $b$, the difference $d = a − b$ still adds uncertainty: $u_d = √{u_a^2 + u_b^2}$.

p.cap: independent random errors

p.x: 4 readings halve it; 100 cut it 10×.
A **shared additive offset** shifts every reading by the same amount, for example one calibration error in both.
Repeating can't average away a fixed calibration bias. Keep repeatability uncertainty apart from calibration uncertainty.

g.q: Two readings share a +0.5 K calibration offset. In their difference, it…
o: cancels
(a + 0.5) − (b + 0.5) = a − b: the shared part drops out.
doubles
Subtracting removes the shared offset; it would only add up in a sum.
adds as root-sum-square
RSS is for independent errors. A shared offset is fully correlated.

cards: Sampling records a continuous signal at discrete times. Aliasing makes different input frequencies produce indistinguishable samples. Once those signals overlap in sampled data, digital filtering cannot uniquely separate their original contributions.

For a signal limited to bandwidth B, sample at fs > 2B. A sine at f shows up at fa = |f − k·fs|, where k·fs is the multiple of fs nearest to f. Example: fs = 1000 Hz and f = 900 Hz: the nearest multiple is 1000 (k = 1), so it appears at 100 Hz.

An analog anti-alias filter attenuates unwanted frequencies before the analog-to-digital converter. Its transition band requires margin above twice the wanted bandwidth. The path is sensor, analog filter, converter, then digital processing.
title: Sampling and aliasing

qs.q: A sensor samples at fs = 1000 Hz. Interference at f = 900 Hz is not filtered out. Using fa = |f − k·fs| with k = 1 (1000 Hz is the multiple of fs nearest 900 Hz), at what frequency fa does it show up, in Hz?
qs.why: fa = |900 − 1 × 1000| = 100 Hz. Using k = 0 gives back 900 Hz, which is above fs/2 = 500 Hz and so cannot appear in the sampled data.

qs.q: You want real 100 Hz vibration. Interference at 900 Hz, sampled at 1000 Hz, also shows up at 100 Hz. Why can’t a digital filter at 100 Hz fix it?
qs.ans: It would remove the wanted 100 Hz vibration too
wrong: A digital filter moves the interference back to 900 Hz
900 Hz cannot alias because it is below fs
Recording more samples separates the two
qs.why: After sampling, the alias and the real signal are both at 100 Hz, so any filter that removes one removes the other. Digital filters can’t move a signal back to 900 Hz; anything above fs/2 (500 Hz) aliases, not only signals above fs; and more samples of the same mix are still mixed.

qs.q: You need signals up to 200 Hz. The analog filter only blocks noise well from 350 Hz up, so half the sample rate must be above 350 Hz. Which sample rate works?
qs.ans: 800 Hz
wrong: 400 Hz
500 Hz
700 Hz
qs.why: fs/2 must exceed 350 Hz, so fs > 700 Hz: 800 Hz works. 400 Hz is just 2 × 200 Hz and ignores the filter; 500 Hz gives fs/2 = 250 Hz; 700 Hz puts fs/2 exactly at 350 Hz, not above it.

qs.q: Order the signal path so unwanted analog frequencies are attenuated before they can alias.
items: Convert the physical input into a sensor signal
Attenuate unwanted frequencies with an analog filter
Sample and digitize the filtered signal
qs.why: Anti-alias attenuation must occur before sampling. Digital processing acts on data that may already contain irreversible frequency overlap.

figNeeded: Draw the sensor-to-filter-to-converter-to-processing path. Add a frequency plot labeling B = 200 Hz, attenuation boundary 350 Hz, and fs/2 = 400 Hz for fs = 800 Hz. Separately show 900 Hz aliasing to 100 Hz at fs = 1000 Hz.

p.x: **Sampling** records a continuous signal at discrete times.
**Aliasing**: different input frequencies can give exactly [[the same]] samples.
At $f_s$ = 1 kHz, a 900 Hz cosine gives the same samples as a 100 Hz cosine.
Once signals overlap in the samples, no digital filter can tell them apart. Filter before sampling.
To sample a signal limited to bandwidth B, the sampling rate must be [[more than twice]] B.
A tone above f_s/2 still shows up in the samples, at a false frequency:

vars: the whole number that puts f_a between 0 and f_s/2

p.x: An analog anti-alias filter cuts unwanted frequencies before the signal is sampled.
A real filter can't cut off instantly, so sample with margin above 2B to leave room for its roll-off.

cards: Heat moves through three mechanisms. Conduction transfers energy through matter; convection transfers heat between a surface and moving fluid; radiation transfers energy through electromagnetic waves.
For one-dimensional steady conduction through a uniform slab, Qdot = kAΔT/L. Qdot is heat-transfer rate, k thermal conductivity, A area, ΔT temperature difference, and L thickness.

Doubling slab thickness halves conduction for unchanged k, A, and ΔT. Radiation can cross a vacuum; conduction and convection require matter. A hot object can lose heat through several mechanisms simultaneously.
title: Heat transfer mechanisms

qs.q: Heat travels along a stationary metal bar from its hot end toward its cold end. Which mechanism describes this transfer within the bar?
qs.ans: Conduction
wrong: Natural convection
Thermal radiation
Bulk fluid transport
qs.why: Conduction transfers energy within the stationary metal. Natural convection requires fluid motion rather than energy transfer through a solid.

qs.q: A slab has k = 2 W/(m·K), area A = 1 m², thickness L = 0.1 m, and temperature difference ΔT = 10 K. What is steady heat-transfer rate Qdot in W?
Which heat-transfer mechanism can carry energy between two surfaces separated by a vacuum?
qs.ans: Thermal radiation
wrong: Conduction through the gap
Forced convection
Natural convection
qs.why: Electromagnetic radiation does not require matter. Conduction through the gap and both forms of convection require a material medium.

qs.q: Four slabs have identical thermal conductivity k, area A, and temperature difference ΔT. Rank them by steady conduction rate Qdot, largest first.
qs.why: Qdot is inversely proportional to L. The rates therefore have the ratio 8:4:2:1 in the listed order.

figNeeded: Draw a slab with hot and cold faces, thickness L, face area A, conductivity k, and heat-transfer arrow Qdot. Label face temperatures Th and Tc and define ΔT = Th − Tc.

p.x: **Conduction** transfers heat through matter without bulk motion, as in a stationary metal bar.
**Convection** transfers heat between a surface and moving fluid. A fan can force motion; buoyancy can drive natural convection.
**Radiation** transfers heat by electromagnetic waves.
Radiation can carry heat across empty space.

g.q: Which mechanism can carry heat between two surfaces with a vacuum between them?
o: Conduction
Conduction across the gap needs material between the surfaces.
Convection
Convection needs a fluid in contact with a surface.
Radiation
Electromagnetic waves can carry energy across a vacuum.

p.x: $Q̇$ is heat rate, $k$ is conductivity, $A$ is face area and $L$ is thickness.
$ΔT$ is the temperature drop straight through the slab. Assume steady flow, uniform material and insulated edges.
For steady conduction, fix conductivity, face area and the temperature difference. Double the slab thickness.
The conductive heat rate [[halves]].
At fixed $k$, $A$ and $ΔT$, $Q̇ ∝ 1/L$.
A hot object can lose heat by several mechanisms at once. Across a vacuum gap, radiation can still carry heat.

cards: Thermal resistance measures temperature difference per heat-transfer rate. For steady heat flow, Qdot = ΔT/R, where ΔT is temperature difference and R is thermal resistance in K/W.
A slab has Rcond = L/(kA); convection has Rconv = 1/(hA). Here L is thickness, k conductivity, A transfer area, and h the convection coefficient relating surface heat flux to temperature difference.
Resistances in series add because the same heat rate passes through each. If Rtotal = 3 K/W and ΔT = 60 K, Qdot = 20 W. Each resistance’s temperature drop is QdotR.
title: Thermal resistance networks

qs.q: Two layers in series have thermal resistances R1 = 0.2 K/W and R2 = 0.3 K/W. Their outer faces differ by ΔT = 50 K. What is steady heat-transfer rate Qdot in W?
qs.why: Rtotal = R1 + R2 = 0.5 K/W. Then Qdot = ΔT/Rtotal = 50/0.5 = 100 W.

qs.q: A surface rejects Qdot = 60 W to air at Tair = 25 °C. Its area is A = 0.2 m² and convection coefficient h = 10 W/(m²·K). What is surface temperature Ts in °C?
qs.why: Rconv = 1/(hA) = 0.5 K/W. The rise is QdotRconv = 30 K, so Ts = 25 + 30 = 55 °C.

qs.q: A wall has layers R1 = 0.1 K/W and R2 = 0.4 K/W between faces at 100 °C and 20 °C. R1 touches the hot face. What is the interface temperature in °C?
qs.why: Qdot = (100 − 20)/(0.1 + 0.4) = 160 W. The drop across R1 is 160 × 0.1 = 16 K, giving 84 °C.

qs.q: A slab and its external convection resistance are in series, each initially 1 K/W. Doubling slab conductivity k leaves everything else unchanged. By what factor does heat-transfer rate increase at fixed ΔT?
qs.why: Slab resistance halves, so total resistance falls from 2 to 1.5 K/W. Heat rate increases by 2/1.5 = 4/3; doubling it would ignore convection resistance.

figNeeded: Draw thermal nodes Th, Ti, and Tc connected by series resistances R1 and R2. Label heat-transfer rate Qdot through both. Add a surface-to-air resistance Rconv with surface Ts and air Tair.

p.x: **Thermal resistance** $R$ measures how much temperature difference a path needs per watt of heat flow. Its unit is K/W.
At a fixed temperature difference $ΔT$, larger resistance passes [[less]] heat per second.

p.cap: Steady heat flow, from the hot side to the cold side.

vars: convection coefficient: heat rate per area per kelvin

p.cap: Steady, straight-through conduction in a uniform slab.
Uniform h and surface temperature over area A.

g.q: Double only the slab conductivity k. What happens to the slab's thermal resistance?
o: It halves
Conductivity is in the denominator. Doubling k cuts the slab's resistance in half.
It doubles
Better conductivity makes heat easier to transfer, so resistance falls.
It stays the same
The size is unchanged, but the material property k matters too.

p.x: Resistances in **series** lie one after another on the same steady heat path. Use their sum as the total resistance.
Multiply the heat rate by a layer's resistance to find that layer's temperature drop.

cards: The lumped thermal model treats an object as one uniform temperature. Check Bi = hLc/k, where Lc = V/A uses object volume V and exposed area A. Bi < 0.1 is a common guideline.
With constant properties and convection to fixed ambient temperature Tair, θ/θ0 = exp(−t/τ). Here θ = T − Tair, θ0 is its initial value, t is time, and τ = mc/(hA).
Here m is mass and c specific heat. After one time constant τ, 36.8% of the initial temperature difference remains. Scaling an object up increases both τ and Bi at unchanged material and h.
title: Transient temperature response

qs.q: A lumped object has m = 0.2 kg, c = 500 J/(kg·K), h = 20 W/(m²·K), and exposed area A = 0.1 m². How long in seconds does its initial temperature difference take to fall to 10%?
qs.why: τ = mc/(hA) = 100/2 = 50 s. Solving 0.1 = exp(−t/50) gives t = 50 ln(10) = 115.1 s.

qs.q: An object has h = 100 W/(m²·K), Lc = 0.01 m, and k = 2 W/(m·K). What should you conclude before using a uniform-temperature cooling model?
qs.ans: Internal temperature gradients need evaluation
wrong: The model is justified because Lc is only 10 mm
Use the model once enough cooling time has elapsed
A larger external h makes uniform temperature more reliable
qs.why: Bi = hLc/k = 0.5, exceeding the 0.1 guideline. Small size alone is insufficient; external cooling can outpace internal conduction.

qs.q: A lumped object starts at 100 °C in air at 20 °C. What is its temperature after one time constant τ?
qs.why: T = 20 + (100 − 20)e⁻¹ = 49.4 °C. Applying e⁻¹ to absolute Celsius temperature instead of the ambient-relative difference gives 36.8 °C.

qs.q: Geometrically similar solid objects share material, convection coefficient h, and exposed-surface proportions. All satisfy the lumped criterion. Rank their cooling time constants τ, largest first, using linear scale factor s.
qs.why: Mass scales as s³ and exposed area as s². Thus τ = mc/(hA) scales as s, rather than s² or s³.

figNeeded: Draw an object with volume V, exposed area A, uniform modeled temperature T, and surrounding air Tair. Plot (T − Tair)/(Tinitial − Tair) against t/τ, marking 0.368 at t/τ = 1.

p.x: A **lumped model** uses one temperature for the entire object.
This works when resistance to heat flow inside is [[small]] compared with resistance to convection at the surface.

vars: object volume divided by exposed area

p.cap: Convection at the exposed surface, conduction inside.

p.x: $Bi < 0.1$ is a common guideline for treating internal temperature differences as small.
The gap $θ = T − T_{air}$ compares the object with the air. Its initial value is $θ_0$, and $t$ is elapsed time.

p.cap: Fixed air temperature, constant h and properties. m is mass and c is specific heat.

p.x: After one time constant $τ$, 36.8% of the initial gap from air temperature remains.
Scale up the same solid shape. Keep material, convection coefficient and exposed-surface proportions fixed.
Both $τ$ and $Bi$ rise. The volume grows faster than the exposed area, so both mass per area and $L_c$ increase.

g.q: As the object gets larger, what happens to its time constant and Biot number?
o: Both rise
Both depend on volume per exposed area, which grows with linear size.
Both fall
Area grows, but volume grows faster. Both ratios increase.
Both stay fixed
Keeping material fixed keeps its properties fixed, not the ratio of volume to area.

cards: Parallel thermal paths split heat between the same two temperature nodes. For path resistances R1 and R2, Req = R1R2/(R1 + R2). A shared upstream resistance Rc still carries the total heat.
For heat generation P and ambient temperature Ta, source temperature Ts = Ta + P[Rc + Req]. Each branch carries Qi = ΔTb/Ri, where ΔTb is the temperature difference across the parallel branches.
Adding cooling paths cannot eliminate a shared contact bottleneck. With Rc = 2 K/W, even zero downstream resistance leaves a 20 K source rise at P = 10 W.
title: Cooling bottleneck decisions

qs.q: A source generates P = 20 W through shared contact resistance Rc = 0.5 K/W. Downstream paths R1 = 2 K/W and R2 = 2 K/W both end at Ta = 25 °C. What is Ts in °C?
A 10 W source uses Rc = 2 K/W in series with one downstream resistance Rd = 2 K/W. Which change gives the greatest source-temperature reduction at fixed ambient temperature?
qs.ans: Reduce Rc to 0.5 K/W
wrong: Add a second 2 K/W path parallel to Rd
Reduce Rd to 1 K/W
Reduce Rc to 1.5 K/W and Rd to 1.5 K/W
qs.why: Reducing Rc to 0.5 gives total resistance 2.5 K/W. Each alternative gives 3 K/W; the extra parallel path does not bypass the shared contact.

qs.q: A source must stay at or below Ts = 65 °C in Ta = 25 °C air while generating P = 20 W. Shared resistance Rc = 1 K/W precedes parallel paths R1 = 3 K/W and R2. What is the largest allowable R2 in K/W?
qs.why: Total resistance must be at most 40/20 = 2 K/W, leaving Req ≤ 1 K/W. Solving 3R2/(3 + R2) = 1 gives R2 = 1.5 K/W.

qs.q: A source sends P = 30 W through shared Rc = 1 K/W, then splits between R1 = 2 K/W and R2 = 4 K/W to the same ambient. What heat rate Q1 passes through R1?
qs.why: Req = 4/3 K/W, so the branch temperature difference is 30 × 4/3 = 40 K and Q1 = 40/2 = 20 W. 15 W assumes an equal split; 30 W sends all heat down the easier path.

figNeeded: Draw a source node Ts receiving heat P, shared series resistance Rc, then a junction splitting through R1 and R2 to the same ambient node Ta. Label branch rates Q1 and Q2 and branch temperature difference ΔTb.

p.x: **Parallel** heat paths connect the same two temperature points. Each has the same temperature drop, and their heat rates add.

p.cap: Two steady parallel paths with resistances R_1 and R_2.

p.x: The shared contact carries the full heat rate. Its resistance [[adds to]] the equivalent parallel resistance.

p.cap: Steady state, all generated heat leaves through the network.
Branch i carries heat rate Q̇_i through R_i; ΔT_b is the drop across the branches.

p.x: Imagine the downstream paths reach zero equivalent resistance. The shared contact still carries all the heat.
To get below this temperature rise at the same power, reduce the shared contact resistance.

g.q: What is the source temperature rise over ambient in this limit?
o: Zero
Zero downstream resistance removes only the downstream drop. The contact still carries 10 W.
The contact alone takes a 10 W × 2 K/W temperature drop.
That would require another 2 K/W downstream, but the example sets it to zero.

cards: Networks move data in structured units. An IP packet carries network-layer addressing information. A router forwards packets between networks; a link-layer frame carries a packet across a particular local link.
In a simplified sender stack, application data enters a transport protocol, then IP, then the link layer. Encapsulation means adding the information each layer needs around the data it receives.
An IP address identifies a network-layer destination; a transport port identifies a service endpoint. A router forwards using network information rather than the application’s document name.
title: Packets and network layers

qs.q: Which device primarily forwards IP packets between different networks?
qs.ans: A router
wrong: An Ethernet repeater
A link-layer switch
A domain-name resolver
qs.why: A router uses network-layer information to forward packets between networks. A link-layer switch ordinarily forwards local frames using link-layer addresses.

qs.q: What term describes adding a layer’s control information around data received from a higher layer?
qs.why: Encapsulation packages higher-layer data with the control information needed by the next layer.

qs.q: What does a transport port number help identify?
qs.ans: A service endpoint on a host
wrong: The next physical router on the path
A network cable’s hardware connector
The destination’s link-layer address
qs.why: Ports distinguish transport endpoints such as application services. They are logical identifiers, not physical connector numbers.

qs.q: Order these layers as outgoing application data moves downward through the simplified sender stack.
qs.why: Application data receives transport information, then IP information, then link-layer framing before transmission.

figNeeded: Draw nested application data, transport segment, IP packet, and link frame. Label destination IP address in the IP header and destination port in the transport header.

cards: Transmission delay is the time needed to place a packet’s bits onto a link. Propagation delay is the time a signal takes to travel that link. Faster transmission does not shorten the physical path.
Transmission time tx = L/R; propagation time tp = d/v. L is packet length in bits, R link rate, d distance, and v signal speed. Use 8 bits per byte.
With no other delays, a packet’s last bit arrives after tx + tp. A store-and-forward router receives the complete packet before transmitting it onward. Here Mb/s means 10⁶ bits per second.
title: Transmission and propagation

qs.q: A 1500-byte packet crosses a 12 Mb/s link with propagation delay tp = 2 ms. Ignore other delays. How long after transmission begins does its last bit arrive, in ms?
A 1000-byte packet crosses two 8 Mb/s links through a store-and-forward router. Each link has propagation delay 0.5 ms. Ignore processing and queueing. What is total last-bit delivery time in ms?
qs.why: Each link needs 8000/8,000,000 = 1 ms to transmit. Total time is 2 × 1 + 2 × 0.5 = 3 ms.

qs.q: A 2000-byte packet uses a 16 Mb/s link over d = 200 km. Signal speed is v = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Ignoring other delays, what is last-bit arrival time in ms?
A packet’s transmission delay is 4 ms and propagation delay is 6 ms. The link rate doubles while packet size and path stay unchanged. What is its new last-bit arrival time?
qs.ans: 8 ms
wrong: 5 ms
7 ms
6 ms
qs.why: Only transmission delay halves: 4/2 + 6 = 8 ms. Halving the whole original delay incorrectly treats propagation as rate-dependent.

figNeeded: Draw a packet crossing a link of distance d at signal speed v. Label packet length L and link rate R. Add a two-link path with a store-and-forward router and separate transmission and propagation intervals.

cards: A sliding window limits how much sent data may remain unacknowledged. Even a fast link can sit idle if its sender must wait for acknowledgments before sending more.
Ideal steady throughput is bounded by min(R, 8W/RTT). R is bottleneck rate in bits/s, W usable window in bytes, and RTT round-trip time. Ignore losses, overhead, and startup.
At R = 8 Mb/s and RTT = 0.1 s, full utilization needs W ≥ R·RTT/8 = 100,000 bytes. Faster links require larger windows when RTT stays fixed.
title: Windows and throughput limits

qs.q: A connection has bottleneck rate R = 20 Mb/s, usable window W = 50,000 bytes, and RTT = 0.1 s. Under the ideal model, what throughput bound applies in Mb/s?
qs.why: The window bound is 8W/RTT = 8 × 50,000/0.1 = 4 Mb/s. The smaller of 20 and 4 Mb/s is 4 Mb/s.

qs.q: A connection must fully utilize R = 40 Mb/s with RTT = 0.05 s. Ignoring losses and overhead, what minimum usable window W is required in bytes?
A connection has R = 10 Mb/s, W = 25,000 bytes, and RTT = 0.1 s. Only the bottleneck rate is upgraded to 100 Mb/s. What is the new ideal throughput bound?
qs.ans: 2 Mb/s
wrong: 20 Mb/s
100 Mb/s
10 Mb/s
qs.why: The unchanged window still limits throughput to 8 × 25,000/0.1 = 2 Mb/s. Scaling throughput with the link upgrade ignores acknowledgment waiting.

qs.q: All connections have R = 100 Mb/s. Rank their ideal throughput bounds from largest to smallest using their usable window W and RTT.
qs.why: The window bounds are 16, 8, 4, and 1 Mb/s. Each is below R, so the window determines the ranking.

figNeeded: Draw a sender-receiver timeline with data traveling forward and acknowledgments returning. Label RTT, usable window W, and an idle interval after the sender exhausts its window.

cards: A lost response leaves a client uncertain whether a request completed. Retrying a non-idempotent operation, whose repetition changes the result, can duplicate its effect even when each network connection reliably delivers bytes.

An idempotency key identifies one logical operation across retries. The server can return a stored result for that key. Durable storage survives restart; atomic storage commits the operation and its completion record together.

A transport acknowledgment confirms receipt at the transport layer, not durable application completion. If an effect is committed before its duplicate-prevention record, a crash between them can allow the effect to happen again.
title: Retries and duplicate operations

qs.q: A server creates a job and durably records its result under key K, but its response is lost. Which retry best preserves one logical job creation?
qs.ans: Resend the same operation with key K
wrong: Generate a new key so the retry is distinguishable
Open a new connection and omit the key
Rely on the transport acknowledgment as the job result
qs.why: Reusing K lets the server recognize the completed operation and return its result. A new key identifies a different operation and can create another job.

qs.q: Requests A, B, and C each create one job. The server creates A and records A’s key, then creates B but crashes before recording B’s key. After restart, all three are retried. Recorded keys are skipped; other requests execute. How many jobs exist afterward?
qs.why: Two jobs exist before the crash. The retry skips A, creates B again, and creates C. Total jobs = 2 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4.

qs.q: A server atomically commits an operation and its idempotency record, but deletes records after one hour. A client may retry after two hours. What gap remains?
qs.ans: An old retry can execute after its record expires
wrong: Atomic storage prevents retries from receiving the saved result
A reliable transport retains expired application records
Using a longer random key extends record retention
qs.why: Duplicate prevention lasts only while the relevant record remains available. Key uniqueness and transport reliability do not restore expired application history.

qs.q: For a new key K, order this successful request lifecycle. The effect and completion record share one atomic transaction.
items: Send the operation with key K
Confirm K has no completed operation
Atomically commit the effect and result for K
Return the committed result to the client
qs.why: The request identifies K before checking it. The effect and record commit together before success is reported, preventing a crash gap between them.

figNeeded: Draw client and server timelines with request key K, an atomic commit containing both job creation and the saved result, a lost response, and a retry using K. Contrast a separate effect-then-record sequence with a crash between those steps.

cards: Injection molding melts plastic pellets, forces the melt into a closed steel mold, cools it solid, then ejects the part. The mold is expensive; each part then takes seconds.
One cycle: the clamp closes the mold, the screw injects melt, packing pressure adds material as it shrinks, the part cools, and ejector pins push it out.
Why cooling usually dominates: plastic conducts heat poorly, so the part must sit in the mold until its core is solid enough to eject without distorting.
Example: a 30 s cycle in a 4-cavity mold makes 4 parts every 30 s, which is 3600 / 30 × 4 = 480 parts per hour.
title: The molding cycle

qs.q: In the molding cycle, what happens right after the melt fills the cavity?
qs.ans: Packing pressure pushes in more melt as it shrinks
wrong: Ejector pins push the finished part out of the cavity
The mold cracks open a little to vent trapped air
The screw pulls back so the fresh melt can cool
qs.why: After filling, the machine holds pressure to pack in extra melt and offset shrinkage. Ejection only happens after cooling.

qs.q: Order the stages of one injection molding cycle.
items: Cool the part in the mold
qs.why: The mold must be clamped before injection, packed while the gate is open, cooled until rigid, then opened.

qs.q: A mold has 8 cavities and a 24 s cycle. How many parts does it make per hour?
qs.why: 3600 / 24 = 150 shots per hour, and 150 × 8 cavities = 1200 parts.

qs.q: Which stage usually takes the largest share of the cycle time?
qs.ans: Cooling
wrong: Injection
Mold opening
Ejection
qs.why: Filling takes about a second or two; cooling often takes more than half the cycle because plastic conducts heat slowly.

qs.q: What are the small plastic beads fed into the machine’s hopper usually called?
qs.why: Resin is supplied as pellets, which the heated screw melts and meters.

demo.title: Cycle time and output
demo.hint: Output is shots per hour times cavities. Shaving a few seconds off a short cycle adds far more parts than the same cut on a long one.

p.x: **Injection molding** melts plastic pellets, forces the melt into a closed steel mold, cools it solid, then ejects the part.
The mold is the big cost. Once it's made, each part takes seconds.
So molding pays off at [[high volume]]: the mold's cost is spread over many parts.
Every shot runs the same cycle:
**Packing** pressure keeps adding melt as the part shrinks, so it doesn't come out undersized or sunk.
Ejector pins push the solid part out, and the clamp closes for the next shot.
Clamp, inject, pack, cool, eject: one of these steps usually sets the cycle time.
**Cooling** usually dominates. Plastic conducts heat poorly, so the core stays soft long after the surface has set.
The part waits in the mold until its core is solid enough to eject without distorting.

g.q: Which step usually takes longest?
o: injecting the melt
Filling is fast: high pressure pushes the melt in within a second or two.
cooling
Plastic conducts heat poorly, so the core takes the longest to go solid.
ejecting
Ejection is one quick mechanical stroke of the pins.

p.x: Output is shots per hour times cavities. Cut the cycle to 25 s and it's 144 shots, 576 parts an hour.

cards: Molded parts should have uniform walls, about 1 to 4 mm for many plastics. Thick zones cool last and shrink after the surface has set.
Cooling time grows with wall thickness squared: t ≈ C·s², where s is wall thickness and C depends on the plastic and mold temperatures.
Why squared: heat must travel from the middle to the mold surface, and a thicker wall both stores more heat and puts it farther away.
Ribs add stiffness without thick walls. Keep a rib about half the wall thickness, or the thick junction it makes will show a sink mark.
Example: if a 2 mm wall cools in 10 s, a 3 mm wall needs about 10 × (3/2)² = 22.5 s.
title: Walls, ribs and cooling

qs.q: A 2 mm wall cools in 8 s. About how long does a 4 mm wall need in the same plastic and mold, in seconds?
qs.why: Cooling time scales with s²: 8 × (4/2)² = 8 × 4 = 32 s, not 16 s.

qs.q: A part has 2 mm walls. A stiffening rib on the back is 3 mm thick. What is most likely to show on the front face, right opposite the rib?
qs.ans: A sink mark along the rib line
wrong: A weld line running along the rib
A short shot at the tip of the rib
The whole panel warping into a bow
qs.why: Where the 3 mm rib meets the 2 mm wall the plastic is thickest, so it stays molten after the front skin has frozen. As that core shrinks it pulls the surface in: a sink mark. Rule of thumb: ribs about 50–60% of the wall.

qs.q: A stiffening rib causes a sink mark on the show face. Which design change fixes it best?
qs.ans: Thin the rib to about half the wall
wrong: Thicken the rib so it stays stiffer
Raise the melt temperature by 50 °C
Remove all draft from the rib faces
qs.why: A thick rib makes a thick junction that shrinks late. A thinner rib, with more ribs if needed, keeps the junction close to wall thickness.

qs.q: Rank these walls by cooling time in the same plastic, longest first.
qs.why: Cooling time goes with s², so the times are in the ratio 16 : 9 : 4 : 1.

qs.q: Cooling time grows with wall thickness raised to what power?
qs.why: t ∝ s². Doubling the wall roughly quadruples the cooling time.

demo.title: Wall thickness and cooling time
demo.hint: Cooling time grows with the square of thickness, so one thick boss can set the cycle for the whole part. C here is an illustrative 2.5 s/mm².

verify: Wall range 1–4 mm and rib at about half the wall are common guidelines; exact values vary by resin.

p.x: Molded parts should have **uniform walls**, about 1 to 4 mm for many plastics.
A thick zone cools **last**. It keeps shrinking after the surface around it has set, and pulls that surface in.
Keep the walls even, and core out thick spots.

g.q: A part has thin walls and one thick boss. The boss cools…
o: first
More plastic holds more heat, and its middle is farther from the cold mold, so it takes longer.
last
It holds more heat and its core is farther from the mold surface, so it's the last to go solid.

p.x: Cooling time grows with the [[square]] of the wall thickness.

p.cap: same plastic, melt and mold temperatures
vars: constant set by the plastic and the mold temperatures

p.x: Heat has to travel from the middle of the wall out to the mold surface.
Both grow with thickness, so the time goes as $s^2$.
**Ribs** add stiffness without making the wall thick.
Keep a rib about half the wall thickness. A thicker rib makes a fat junction that shrinks late and shows a **sink mark**.
A wall 50% thicker needs 2.25 times the cooling time, and the cycle grows with it.

cards: Melt pressure in the cavity pushes the mold halves apart. The clamp must resist that pressure acting on the part’s projected area, the shadow it casts along the opening direction.
Clamp force F = p × A, where p is the average cavity pressure and A is the projected area of all cavities plus runners.
Why projected area, not surface area: pressure on side walls pushes sideways and balances out. Only area facing the opening direction pushes the halves apart.
Example: 100 cm² at 40 MPa needs 0.01 m² × 40 × 10⁶ Pa = 400 kN, about 41 tonnes-force.
Too little clamp force lets melt escape between the halves as flash; far too much wastes press capacity and wears the mold.
title: Clamp force

qs.q: A part has 150 cm² projected area, runners included, and 30 MPa average cavity pressure. What clamp force is needed, in kN?
An open box 10 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm deep is molded opening-down toward the parting line. Which area sets the clamp force?
qs.ans: The 10 × 10 cm footprint seen from above
wrong: The total surface area of all its walls
The four 10 × 5 cm side walls added up
The box volume divided by wall thickness
qs.why: Only the projected area along the opening direction separates the halves. Side-wall pressures act sideways and cancel.

qs.q: A press clamps about 2940 kN. At 35 MPa average cavity pressure, what is the largest projected area it can hold, in cm²?
Which defect points to clamp force that is too low?
qs.ans: Flash at the parting line
wrong: Sink marks over thick ribs
Short shots at the far end
Splay streaks near the gate
qs.why: If the halves separate under pressure, melt squeezes into the gap as flash. Sink and short shots come from packing and filling problems.

qs.q: Rank these parts by the clamp force they need, largest first.
qs.why: F = p × A, and cm² × MPa ÷ 10 = kN: 200 × 40 ÷ 10 = 800 kN, 100 × 60 ÷ 10 = 600 kN, 300 × 10 ÷ 10 = 300 kN. The biggest part needs the least.

demo.title: Clamp force against press capacity
demo.hint: Force grows in proportion to projected area and cavity pressure. Cross the press line and the mold will flash. 1 tonne-force is about 9.81 kN.

verify: Average cavity pressures of roughly 20–70 MPa are typical; check for the specific resin and flow length.

p.x: Melt pressure in the cavity pushes the two mold halves apart.
The clamp holds against that pressure acting on the part's **projected area**: the shadow it casts along the opening direction.

vars: projected area of all cavities plus runners

p.cap: average cavity pressure over the projected area

p.x: Handy units: cm² × MPa ÷ 10 gives kN.
Melt pressure pushes on every surface it touches, side walls too.
Pressure on opposite side walls pushes sideways and cancels out.
Only area facing the opening direction pushes the halves apart: projected area, not surface area.
That's about 41 tonnes-force (1 tf = 9.81 kN), the unit press ratings often use.
Pick a press whose rated force covers $F = pA$, with some margin.
Too little clamp force: melt escapes between the halves as **flash**, a thin fin along the parting line.
Far too much wastes press capacity and wears the mold.

g.q: The press can't quite hold the mold shut. The parts come out with…
o: flash
The halves crack open a little and melt squeezes into the gap along the parting line.
a short shot
A short shot is melt freezing before the cavity fills, from low injection pressure or cold melt. A weak clamp lets melt out, not in short.
sink marks
Sink comes from thick sections shrinking after the skin sets, not from the halves opening.

cards: Most molding defects trace to one of four causes: not enough material, too much pressure, trapped gas, or uneven cooling and shrinkage.
Short shot: melt freezes before the cavity fills, from low pressure, cold melt or a long thin flow path. Flash: melt escapes past the parting line.
Sink and voids: thick sections keep shrinking after the skin freezes. Warp: regions shrink by different amounts, from uneven walls, cooling or fiber orientation.
Weld lines form where flow fronts meet, around holes or between two gates. They are weaker; moving the gate moves where they land.
title: Diagnosing defects

qs.q: Parts fill fully near the gate, but a thin far corner is incomplete. What is the most likely cause?
qs.ans: Melt freezes before reaching the thin far corner
wrong: Clamp force is too high for the projected area
Packing pressure is held on for far too long
The mold coolant runs too warm in that corner
qs.why: A thin, distant section loses heat fastest and freezes off before the melt arrives. Too little injection pressure or speed is one reason it gets there too late, so raising pressure or speed is a fix, along with warmer melt or mold or a thicker flow path. The cause the part shows is the freeze-off.

qs.q: A flat glass-filled nylon panel with uniform walls warps after ejection. What is the best first suspect?
qs.ans: Fibers aligned with flow shrinking unevenly
wrong: Too little clamp force letting the mold open
A short shot leaving the panel hollow
Weld lines weakening the panel middle
qs.why: Glass fibers shrink less along their length than across it, so flow-aligned fibers create different shrinkage in different directions, even with uniform walls.

qs.q: A snap-fit keeps cracking at a weld line behind a hole. Which change most directly helps?
qs.ans: Move the gate so the weld line lands elsewhere
wrong: Increase the cooling time by 20 percent or more
Add more draft to the snap-fit hook faces
Raise the clamp force to the press limit
qs.why: Weld lines are weaker because the flow fronts meet partly cooled. Relocating the gate puts the weld line in a low-stress area.

qs.q: Sink marks appear over thick bosses, and the design can’t change yet. Which process change helps most?
qs.ans: Increase packing pressure and hold time
wrong: Lower the clamp force to relieve stress
Shorten the hold time to cut the cycle
Raise the injection speed only
qs.why: Longer, higher packing feeds more melt into the shrinking core before the gate freezes. Injection speed mostly affects filling, not shrinkage.

qs.q: What is the name for thin excess plastic squeezed out at the parting line?
qs.why: Flash forms when melt escapes between mold halves, usually from excess pressure, low clamp force or a worn parting line.

demo.title: Will it fill?
demo.hint: Each plastic can only flow so far relative to wall thickness before it freezes. A thinner wall or a longer flow path pushes you toward a short shot. Flow ratios are illustrative.

verify: Flow-length-to-thickness ratios vary widely by grade and conditions; the demo values are for illustration.

p.x: Most molding defects trace to one of four causes.
**Not enough material**: short shots.
**Too much pressure**: flash.
**Trapped gas**: burn marks and bubbles.
**Uneven cooling and shrinkage**: sink, voids and warp.
Name the cause before changing settings: each one needs a different fix.
**Short shot**: the melt freezes before the cavity fills, from low pressure, cold melt or a long thin flow path.
**Flash**: melt escapes past the parting line, leaving a thin fin where the mold halves meet.
**Sink and voids**: a thick section keeps shrinking after its skin freezes. The skin dents in (sink) or the core pulls apart inside (void).
**Warp**: regions shrink by different amounts, from uneven walls, uneven cooling or fiber orientation.
Even walls help, but uneven cooling or fiber orientation can still warp a part.

g.q: True or false: a part with perfectly uniform walls can't warp.
o: True
Uniform walls remove one cause. A hot side of the mold or fibers lined up with the flow still make regions shrink differently.
False
Uneven cooling or fiber orientation can still make regions shrink by different amounts.

p.x: **Weld lines** form where two flow fronts meet: around a hole, or between two gates.
The fronts have started to cool when they meet, so the line is [[weaker]] than the plastic around it.
Moving the gate moves where weld lines land. Keep them away from highly loaded spots.

cards: A datum is a theoretically exact plane, axis or point that measurements start from. A real surface or hole, the datum feature, establishes it.
A feature control frame reads left to right: the geometric symbol, the tolerance zone size, then datum letters in order: primary, secondary, tertiary.
Why datums matter: without a shared origin, two inspectors can measure the same part differently and both be right. Datums make measurement repeatable.
The 3-2-1 idea: the primary datum plane touches at 3 points, the secondary at 2, the tertiary at 1, removing all 6 degrees of freedom.
title: What a datum is

qs.q: In a feature control frame, the first datum letter listed is the…
qs.ans: Primary datum, contacted first
wrong: Least important datum, checked last
Datum with the tightest tolerance
Feature that the tolerance applies to
qs.why: Datum references are listed in order of precedence. The part is located on the primary datum first, then secondary, then tertiary.

qs.q: What is the real, physical surface that establishes a datum called?
qs.ans: The datum feature
wrong: The tolerance zone
The basic dimension
The feature control frame
qs.why: The datum is the ideal plane or axis; the datum feature is the actual surface or hole on the part that sets it up.

qs.q: In the 3-2-1 principle, how many points of contact does the primary datum plane need?
qs.why: Three points define a plane and remove three degrees of freedom: one translation and two rotations.

qs.q: How many degrees of freedom does an unconstrained rigid part have?
qs.why: Three translations and three rotations. The primary, secondary and tertiary datums remove 3, 2 and 1 of them.

qs.q: Why does a drawing reference datums in a feature control frame?
qs.ans: So everyone measures from the same origin
wrong: To tell the machinist which face to cut first
To mark the surfaces that need a finer finish
To show which features are only cosmetic
qs.why: Datums define the reference frame for inspection and assembly, so a tolerance means the same thing to the designer, machinist and inspector.

demo.title: Locking down a part, 3-2-1
demo.hint: Each datum removes degrees of freedom: the primary plane takes 3, the secondary 2, the tertiary the last 1. Slide to engage them in order.

p.x: Two words that sound alike but aren't the same thing:
**Datum**: a theoretically exact plane, axis or point that measurements start from. Drawings name it with a letter.
**Datum feature**: the real surface or hole on the part that establishes it.
The machined face is the datum feature. Datum A is the perfect plane; in inspection, the surface plate it rests on simulates it.

g.q: The machined face labelled A on the part is datum A itself. True or false?
o: true
The face is real, so it has bumps and tilt. It's the datum feature; the datum is the exact plane that face establishes.
false
A real face is never perfectly flat. It establishes the datum, an exact plane, usually simulated by the surface the part rests on.

p.x: A **feature control frame** is a row of boxes, read left to right.
Example: position, Ø0.2, A, B, C. The axis must lie in a Ø0.2 mm zone, located from datum A first, then B, then C.
The letter order matters: it says which face the part is set on first.
One inspector rests a part on its bottom face; another rests it on its side. Both measure the same hole.
Without a shared origin, they can get different results and [[both be right]].
Datums give everyone the same starting point, so the measurement repeats.
A loose rigid part has 6 degrees of freedom: 3 slides and 3 rotations. The 3-2-1 idea removes them all.
3 + 2 + 1 = 6: three datum planes at right angles hold the part completely when it's pressed against them.

cards: Position controls where a hole’s axis may lie. True position is set by basic dimensions: boxed, exact values with no tolerance of their own.
A position tolerance of Ø0.2 means the axis must lie inside a cylinder 0.2 mm in diameter, centered on true position.
Check it from measured offsets: actual position = 2√(Δx² + Δy²). The factor 2 turns the radial offset into a diameter.
Why round: a ±0.1 mm square zone fits inside a Ø0.283 circle. That circle treats every direction equally and gives 57% more area than the square.
title: Position tolerance

qs.q: A hole’s axis measures Δx = 0.03 mm and Δy = 0.04 mm from true position. What is its actual position, as a diameter in mm?
qs.why: Radial offset = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = 0.05 mm. Actual position = 2 × 0.05 = Ø0.10.

qs.q: That same hole has a position tolerance of Ø0.08. Does it pass?
qs.ans: No: it needs Ø0.10
wrong: Yes: its radial offset is only 0.05
Yes: each offset is under 0.08
No: Δy alone exceeds the tolerance
qs.why: Compare diameters, not radii. The axis sits on a Ø0.10 circle, which is outside the Ø0.08 zone.

qs.q: What do boxed dimensions on a drawing mean?
qs.ans: Exact values that locate true position
wrong: Reference values given for information only
Dimensions to check on every single part
Critical values with a tighter ± tolerance
qs.why: Basic dimensions are exact; the tolerance lives in the feature control frame. Reference dimensions are shown in parentheses.

qs.q: A ±0.05 mm square coordinate zone fits inside a round position zone of what diameter, in mm?
qs.why: The square’s corner is √(0.05² + 0.05²) = 0.0707 mm from center, so the circle is Ø0.141.

qs.q: Rank these measured holes by actual position, largest first.
qs.why: 2√(Δx² + Δy²) gives Ø0.20, Ø0.18, Ø0.141 and Ø0.08.

demo.title: Accept or reject a hole
demo.hint: Position combines both offsets into one diameter. A hole can be inside ± limits on each axis and still fail the round zone, or the reverse near the corners.

p.x: **Position** controls where a feature's axis may lie, such as a hole's.
**Basic dimension**: a boxed, exact value with [[no tolerance]] of its own.
**True position**: the exact location the basic dimensions set.
The allowed error comes only from the position callout, not from the title block's ± tolerances.
A position tolerance of Ø0.2 means the hole's axis must lie inside a cylinder 0.2 mm in diameter, centered on true position.
So the axis may stray up to [[half]] the tolerance from true position, in any direction.

p.cap: Δx, Δy: measured axis offsets from true position

p.x: The factor 2 turns the radial offset into a diameter. 0.10 > 0.08, so this hole is rejected.
Separate ±0.1 mm limits on x and y allow 0.141 mm of offset at the square's corners, but only 0.1 mm straight along x.
A mating pin doesn't care which direction the hole is off. Only the distance matters.
So position uses a round zone: the same limit in every direction.

cards: With position at MMC (a circled M), the stated tolerance applies when the hole is at its smallest. As the hole grows, the extra clearance becomes bonus tolerance.
Hole: allowed position = stated tolerance + (actual size − MMC size). Shaft: stated tolerance + (MMC size − actual size).
Why it’s fair: a bigger hole still clears the mating pin even if it sits farther off position, so the assembly still works and more good parts pass.
Virtual condition of a hole = MMC size − position tolerance. It is the worst-case boundary the mating pin must always fit through.
Example: hole Ø10.0–10.2 with Ø0.1 position at MMC. At Ø10.15, the allowed position is 0.1 + 0.15 = Ø0.25.
title: Bonus tolerance at MMC

qs.q: A hole’s size limits are Ø8.0–8.3, with Ø0.2 position at MMC. It measures Ø8.25. What position tolerance is allowed, in mm?
A hole has MMC Ø12.0 and Ø0.3 position at MMC. What is its virtual condition, in mm?
qs.why: For a hole, VC = MMC − position tolerance = 12.0 − 0.3 = Ø11.7, the largest pin guaranteed to fit.

qs.q: A shaft is Ø19.8–20.0 with Ø0.1 position at MMC. It measures Ø19.85. What position is allowed?
qs.why: A shaft’s MMC is its largest size, 20.0. Bonus = 20.0 − 19.85 = 0.15, so Ø0.25. Ø0.15 measures the bonus from the wrong limit.

qs.q: Why doesn’t MMC bonus tolerance hurt a clearance fit?
qs.ans: A larger hole leaves room for more offset
wrong: Inspectors skip position once size passes
Bonus applies only to perfectly round holes
The mating pin is made at its smallest size
qs.why: The pin needs a clear path. When the hole is bigger, the axis can wander farther and the pin still fits, so the extra tolerance is functional.

qs.q: All these holes have MMC Ø10.0 and Ø0.1 position at MMC. Rank them by allowed position, largest first.
qs.why: Allowed position is 0.1 plus the departure from MMC: Ø0.28, Ø0.22, Ø0.15 and Ø0.10.

p.x: **MMC**, maximum material condition: the size at which a feature holds the most material. For a hole, that's its [[smallest]] size.
With position at MMC, the stated tolerance applies when the hole is at that smallest size.
As the hole is made bigger, the extra clearance is added to the position tolerance as **bonus tolerance**.

p.cap: position at MMC; d_{M} is the smallest hole
position at MMC; d_{M} is the largest pin

p.x: Either way, the bonus is how far the size has moved away from MMC.

g.q: For a pin, the bonus tolerance grows as the pin gets…
o: bigger
That's the hole rule. A pin at MMC is at its largest, so it moves away from MMC by getting smaller.
smaller
A pin holds the most material when largest. A smaller pin leaves more clearance, and that clearance is the bonus.

p.x: Why it's fair: the mating pin has a fixed size.
A bigger hole leaves more room around that pin, so the hole can sit farther off position and the pin still clears.
The assembly still works, and more good parts pass inspection.

p.cap: position at MMC; d_{M} smallest hole, t_{M} stated tolerance

p.x: Hole Ø10.0–10.2 with Ø0.1 position at MMC.
Every good hole leaves a perfect Ø9.9 opening clear: the worst-case boundary a pin must fit through.

g.q: The largest perfect pin that fits every good hole is…
o: Ø10.0 is the smallest hole, but that hole may also sit 0.05 mm off position, which closes the clear opening.
The smallest hole, shifted by its full Ø0.1 position zone, still leaves Ø10.0 − 0.1 = Ø9.9 clear.
That's the middle of the size range. Holes can be as small as Ø10.0, so a Ø10.1 pin won't fit them all.

p.x: At the largest hole, Ø10.2, the allowed position reaches Ø0.3.

cards: A stack-up adds tolerances along a chain of dimensions to find the worst possible gap. Choosing datums at functional features keeps that chain short.
Worst case: gap tolerance = sum of all the tolerances. Statistical (RSS): √(sum of squares), assuming independent, centered variation.
Why RSS is smaller: it is unlikely every part sits at its limit at once. Four parts at ±0.1 give ±0.4 worst case but ±0.2 by RSS.
Dimension each feature from one datum instead of chaining feature to feature, and tolerances stop accumulating between features.
title: Datum choice and stack-ups

qs.q: Five dimensions in a chain each carry ±0.05 mm. What is the worst-case tolerance on the resulting gap, in ±mm?
qs.why: Worst case adds them: 5 × 0.05 = ±0.25 mm.

qs.q: For the same chain, what is the RSS tolerance on the gap, in ±mm?
qs.why: √(5 × 0.05²) = 0.05 × √5 ≈ ±0.112 mm, under half the worst case.

qs.q: Holes are dimensioned in a chain, A to B then B to C, each ±0.1. What is the worst-case tolerance from A to C?
qs.why: Two chained dimensions add: ±0.1 + ±0.1. ±0.14 is the RSS value, which is not guaranteed.

qs.q: The designer re-dimensions both holes directly from datum A, each ±0.1. What can A to C now hold?
qs.ans: ±0.1, one dimension from the datum
wrong: ±0.2, two holes are still involved
±0.14, root-sum-square of two
±0.05, the datum removes error
qs.why: A to C is now a single dimension, so it carries only its own tolerance. B to C, however, now stacks to ±0.2.

qs.q: When is an RSS stack-up risky to rely on?
qs.ans: Few parts, or processes not centered
wrong: Many parts with independent variation
Dimensions measured on a CMM
Tolerances given in millimeters
qs.why: RSS assumes many independent, centered, roughly normal contributors. With few parts or biased processes, the worst case is much more likely.

qs.q: Rank these gap predictions for four parts at ±0.1 mm, largest first.
qs.why: Worst case adds all four, RSS is √4 × 0.1 = 0.2, and a 1.5 factor on RSS gives 0.3.

demo.title: Worst case against RSS
demo.hint: Worst case grows in proportion to the number of parts; RSS grows only with its square root. The gap between them widens with every part in the chain.

p.x: A **stack-up** adds tolerances along a chain of dimensions to find the worst possible gap.
Pick datums at the functional features, the ones that touch mating parts, and the chain stays [[short]].
Fewer links in the chain, fewer tolerances adding up.

vars: ± tolerance of dimension i in the chain

p.cap: every part at its limit at once
independent variations, each centered in its range

p.x: Four parts in a chain, each ±0.1 mm.
RSS is smaller because every part at its limit at once is unlikely. It grows with √n, worst case with n.

g.q: By RSS, the gap tolerance is about…
o: That's the worst case, 4 × 0.1. RSS adds squares: √(4 × 0.1²).
That's one part alone. Adding parts always widens the gap's spread, just more slowly by RSS.

p.x: Four holes in a row, every dimension ±0.1 mm. Dimension each hole from one datum, not from the hole before it.

p.c: hole 4 to the datum, through 4 dimensions
hole 4 to the datum, one dimension

p.x: From one datum, the spacing between any two holes stays within ±0.2, however many holes there are.

cards: A Python variable is a name bound to a value: `F = 250.0`. Python infers the type from the value: `int`, `float`, `str` or `bool`.
Arithmetic uses `+ - * /`, with `**` for powers, `//` for floor division and `%` for remainder. `/` always returns a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`.
Why `//` matters: `7 // 2` is `3`, dropping the fraction. Mixing up `/` and `//` is a classic bug when computing counts or indices.
`print(f"σ = {sigma:.1f} MPa")` puts numbers inside text. The `:.1f` means one digit after the decimal point.
title: Values, types and arithmetic

qs.q: What does `7 / 2` evaluate to in Python 3?
qs.why: `/` is true division and always gives a float. `7 // 2` would give `3`.

qs.q: What does `2 ** 10` evaluate to?
qs.why: `**` is exponentiation: 2 to the 10th power is 1024. `^` in Python is bitwise XOR, not a power.

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
n = 17
print(n // 5, n % 5)
```
qs.why: 17 // 5 is 3 (whole times 5 fits), and 17 % 5 is the remainder, 2.

qs.q: What does `print(f"{3.14159:.2f}")` print?
qs.why: `.2f` formats the float with two digits after the decimal point, rounding as needed.

qs.q: What is `type(True)`?
qs.ans: `bool`
wrong: `str`
`float`
`NoneType`
qs.why: `True` and `False` are the two values of type `bool`.

demo.title: Division, floor division, remainder
demo.hint: `/` keeps the fraction, `//` drops it, and `%` is what’s left over. For positive numbers, `(a // b) * b + a % b` always gives back `a`.

cards: A list holds items in order: `loads = [120, 340, 95]`. Indexing starts at 0, so `loads[0]` is 120, and `loads[-1]` is the last item.
`for x in loads:` visits each item in turn. `range(n)` gives 0 up to n − 1, so `range(3)` is 0, 1, 2.
Why off-by-one bugs happen: ranges and slices stop before the end value. `range(1, 5)` is 1 to 4, and `loads[0:2]` is items 0 and 1.
Example: `total = 0`, then `for x in loads: total += x` sums the list. The built-in `sum(loads)` does the same in one call.
title: Lists and loops

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
for i in range(3):
    print(i * 2)
```
qs.ans: 0, 2 and 4 on separate lines
wrong: 2, 4 and 6 on separate lines
0, 2, 4 and 6 on separate lines
0, 1 and 2 on separate lines
qs.why: `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2, and each is doubled. It stops before 3, so there is no 6.
Indexing starts at 0: v[0] is 4, v[1] is 8, v[2] is 15.

qs.q: With the same `v`, what is `len(v[1:4])`?
qs.why: The slice takes indices 1, 2 and 3 and stops before 4: three items, [8, 15, 16].
Negative indices count from the end: v[-1] is 42, v[-2] is 23.

qs.q: Order these lines to print the sum of the squares of a list `xs`.
qs.why: Initialize before the loop, accumulate inside it (indented), and print once after the loop ends.

demo.title: What range(a, b, s) produces
demo.hint: range stops before b, so the last value is always less than b. Count = ceil((b − a) / s), and an empty range happens whenever a ≥ b.

cards: `def stress(F, A): return F / A` defines a reusable function. Names created inside a function are local and disappear when it returns.
Arguments are passed as references. Changing a list in place (`xs.append(1)`) changes the caller’s list; rebinding the name (`xs = []`) does not.
Why default lists bite: `def add(x, xs=[])` creates one list when the function is defined, so it keeps growing across calls. Default to `None` instead.
`b = a` copies the reference, not the list. `b = a.copy()` or `list(a)` makes an independent copy of a flat list.
title: Functions, references and copies

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
```
qs.why: `b = a` makes both names refer to the same list, so appending through `b` changes what `a` shows.

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
def f(xs):
    xs = [0]
a = [1, 2]
f(a)
print(a)
```
wrong: `None`
qs.why: Inside f, `xs = [0]` rebinds the local name to a new list. The caller’s list is untouched.

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
def add(x, xs=[]):
    xs.append(x)
    return len(xs)
add(1)
add(2)
print(add(3))
```
qs.why: The default list is created once and shared by every call, so after three calls it holds three items.

qs.q: Which change fixes that growing-default bug?
qs.ans: Default to `None` and build the list inside
wrong: Rename the parameter so it becomes private
Move the function inside a class body
Call `del xs` at the end of the function
qs.why: With `xs=None`, write `if xs is None: xs = []` so each call gets a fresh list.

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
def area(d):
    r = d / 2
    return 3.14 * r ** 2
print(area(2))
```
qs.why: r = 1.0, and `**` binds tighter than `*`, so 3.14 × 1² = 3.14.

demo.title: The shared default list
demo.hint: With `xs=[]` the same list is reused, so its length grows with every call. With `xs=None` and a fresh list inside, each call starts empty.

bars.label: len(xs) after the last call, xs=[] default
len(xs) after the last call, xs=None default

cards: Floats are binary approximations, so `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False`. Compare computed floats with a tolerance, such as `math.isclose(a, b)`.
NumPy arrays apply an operation to every element at once: `sigma = F / A` works on whole arrays and runs in compiled code instead of a Python loop.
Why it’s faster: a Python loop pays interpreter overhead on every element, while a vectorized call pays it once. On large arrays that is often 10 to 100 times faster.
Watch shapes: adding a shape (3,) array to a (3, 1) array broadcasts to (3, 3). Check `.shape` when a result is unexpectedly large.
title: Floats, NumPy and speed

qs.q: What does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluate to?
qs.ans: `False`
wrong: `True`
`None`
qs.why: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their sum is 0.30000000000000004.

qs.q: What is the most reliable way to test two computed floats for equality?
qs.ans: `math.isclose(a, b)` with a tolerance
wrong: `a is b`, comparing object identity
`str(a) == str(b)`, comparing text
`int(a) == int(b)`, dropping decimals
qs.why: `isclose` compares within a relative or absolute tolerance. Identity, text and truncation all give misleading answers.

qs.q:
What does this print?
```
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print((a * 2).sum())
```
qs.why: a * 2 is [2, 4, 6], applied element-wise, and its sum is 12.

qs.q: An array of shape (4,) is added to one of shape (4, 1). How many elements does the result have?
qs.why: Broadcasting stretches both to (4, 4), so the result has 16 elements, not 4.

qs.q: A Python loop over 1,000,000 floats takes 0.5 s. Roughly how long would the equivalent NumPy vectorized operation take?
qs.ans: About 5 to 50 ms
wrong: About 0.5 s, it’s the same work
About 5 s, NumPy adds overhead
Under 1 µs, it’s instant
qs.why: Vectorized code removes per-element interpreter overhead, typically giving 10 to 100 times speedups on large arrays, not infinite ones.

demo.title: Loop against vectorized
demo.hint: For tiny arrays the fixed call overhead dominates and the loop can win. Past a few hundred elements the per-element cost takes over. Per-element costs are illustrative.

cards: Each tool and material pair has a recommended cutting speed Vc: how fast the cutting edge moves through the material, in m/min.
Spindle speed n = 1000·Vc / (π·D), with n in rpm, Vc in m/min and tool diameter D in mm.
Why diameter matters: a bigger tool’s edge travels farther each turn, so it needs fewer rpm for the same edge speed. Small tools need very high rpm.
Example: Vc = 100 m/min with a 10 mm end mill gives 1000 × 100 / (π × 10) ≈ 3183 rpm.
Material sets the speed. With carbide, aluminum runs fastest because it is soft and carries heat away. Mild steel is slower; stainless and titanium trap heat at the edge and run slowest.
title: Spindle speed

qs.q: Vc = 150 m/min and D = 12 mm. What spindle speed is needed, in rpm?
Switching from a 6 mm to a 12 mm end mill at the same cutting speed, the rpm should…
qs.ans: Halve
wrong: Double
Stay the same
Drop to a quarter
qs.why: n is inversely proportional to D, so doubling the diameter halves the rpm for the same edge speed.

qs.q: With carbide tools, which material usually allows the highest cutting speed?
qs.ans: Aluminum alloy
wrong: Titanium alloy
Stainless steel
Hardened tool steel
qs.why: Aluminum is soft and conducts heat away, so it tolerates very high edge speeds. Titanium holds heat at the edge and needs low speeds.

qs.q: A 20 mm cutter runs at 800 rpm. What cutting speed is that, in m/min?
Rank these materials by typical carbide cutting speed, highest first.
qs.why: Speed falls as materials get tougher and hold heat at the cutting edge: aluminum, then mild steel, stainless and titanium.

demo.title: Spindle speed and tool size
demo.hint: rpm rises steeply as the tool shrinks. Small cutters in aluminum can ask for more rpm than the spindle can give, so you run slower and accept a lower cutting speed.

cards: Chip load fz is the chip thickness each tooth takes, in mm per tooth. Too thin and the edge rubs and heats; too thick and it chips or breaks.
Feed rate vf = n × z × fz: spindle rpm times number of teeth times chip load, in mm/min.
Why chip load comes first: tool makers rate an edge for a chip thickness. Cutting speed sets the heat at the edge; chip load sets the force on it.
Example: 3000 rpm, 3 flutes and 0.05 mm per tooth give 3000 × 3 × 0.05 = 450 mm/min.
title: Feed rate and chip load

qs.q: 4000 rpm, 4 flutes, 0.04 mm per tooth. What is the feed rate, in mm/min?
A 2-flute cutter at 6000 rpm feeds at 600 mm/min. What chip load is that, in mm per tooth?
qs.why: fz = vf / (n × z) = 600 / (6000 × 2) = 0.05 mm per tooth.

qs.q: You double the rpm but leave the feed rate unchanged. What happens to the chip load?
qs.ans: It halves, and the tool may rub
wrong: It doubles, and the tool may chip
It stays the same, since feed is fixed
It quarters, with speed squared
qs.why: fz = vf / (n × z). Doubling n at fixed vf halves each chip, which can drop below the edge’s cutting threshold.

qs.q: A tool squeals and its chips look like fine dust. What is the most likely fix?
qs.ans: Raise the feed to thicken the chip
wrong: Lower the feed to reduce the load
Raise the rpm to clear chips faster
Switch to a tool with more flutes
qs.why: Dust-like chips and squeal mean the chip is too thin and the edge is rubbing. More rpm or more flutes at the same feed thin the chip further.

qs.q: All four cutters have 4 teeth. Rank these setups by feed rate, highest first.
qs.why: With z the same, compare n × fz: 180, 150, 120 and 80. Times 4 teeth gives vf = 720, 600, 480 and 320 mm/min.

demo.title: Feed rate from chip load
demo.hint: Feed rate is just rpm × teeth × chip load. Change rpm without changing the feed and you’ve silently changed the chip load.

cards: Material removal rate Q is the volume cut per minute: Q = ap × ae × vf, with axial depth ap and radial width ae in mm and feed vf in mm/min.
Cutting power P = Q × u, where u is specific cutting energy: roughly 0.7 W·s/mm³ for aluminum and about 3 for low-carbon steel. Use Q in mm³/s.
Why it matters: if P exceeds what the spindle delivers at that speed, the cut stalls or chatters. Doubling the depth doubles both Q and power.
Example: ap 5 mm, ae 10 mm, vf 600 mm/min gives Q = 30,000 mm³/min = 500 mm³/s. In aluminum, P ≈ 500 × 0.7 = 350 W.
title: Removal rate and power

qs.q: ap = 2 mm, ae = 8 mm, vf = 900 mm/min. What is Q, in mm³/min?
A cut with ap = 2 mm, ae = 8 mm and vf = 900 mm/min is in steel with u = 3 W·s/mm³. What cutting power does it need, in W?
Which change doubles the removal rate without changing chip load?
qs.ans: Double the axial depth of cut
wrong: Double the spindle speed alone
Make two passes instead of one
Use a tool with half the flutes
qs.why: Q = ap × ae × vf. Doubling rpm alone leaves vf, and so Q, unchanged while halving chip load. Two passes double the time, not the rate.

qs.q: A spindle delivers 2 kW, but a planned steel cut needs 2.6 kW. Which fix keeps the tool and chip load the same?
qs.ans: Reduce the radial width of cut
wrong: Raise rpm and feed together
Switch to a 4-flute tool at the same feed
Add flood coolant to cut power use
qs.why: Power follows Q, so less width means proportionally less power. Raising rpm and feed together increases Q; coolant barely changes cutting energy.

qs.q: Rank these cuts by material removal rate, largest first.
qs.why: Q = ap × ae × vf gives 20,000, 16,800, 14,400 and 12,000 mm³/min.

demo.title: Removal rate against spindle power
demo.hint: Power grows in proportion to depth, width and feed. Cross the spindle line and the cut stalls. Specific energies are typical values; check your material’s data.

verify: Specific cutting energy values (about 0.7 W·s/mm³ aluminum, about 3 for low-carbon steel, 4–5 for stainless) are typical textbook ranges.

cards: Two terms first. Radial engagement ae is how far the cutter steps sideways into the material; D is the cutter diameter. ae/D = 0.5 means half the cutter is in the cut; ae/D = 0.1 means a tenth.
Chip load fz is how far the cutter moves forward per tooth (mm per tooth). When ae/D is 0.5 or more, each tooth’s chip reaches that full thickness at its thickest point.
In a light side cut, each tooth only skims its arc: it leaves the material before it reaches the thick part of the chip. So its thickest chip, hex, is smaller than fz. That is radial chip thinning.

For r = ae/D at or below 0.5: hex = fz × 2√(r(1 − r)). At r = 0.5 the factor is 1, so hex = fz. At r = 0.1 the factor is 2√(0.1 × 0.9) = 0.6, so hex = 0.6 fz. (Model: a round cutter, feed per tooth small compared with D.)

Why it matters: cutting edges are slightly rounded. A chip thinner than that rounding is smeared instead of cut, which makes heat, rubbing, flank wear and a poor finish. The fix is to raise the programmed feed: fz = target hex ÷ 2√(r(1 − r)).

Stickout L is how far the tool hangs out of the holder. Treated as a cantilever with the same tip force, deflection ∝ L³/d⁴ for tool diameter d. So 50% more stickout gives 1.5³ ≈ 3.4 times the deflection, and a 10 mm tool is (10/6)⁴ ≈ 7.7 times stiffer than a 6 mm one at the same stickout.
title: Chip thinning and stickout

qs.q: fz = 0.06 mm per tooth at ae/D = 0.1. What is the actual maximum chip thickness, in mm?
To get a real 0.06 mm chip at ae/D = 0.1, what chip load should be programmed, in mm per tooth?
qs.why: Divide by the thinning factor: 0.06 / 0.6 = 0.10 mm per tooth.

qs.q: Stickout grows from 30 mm to 45 mm, all else equal. How does tool deflection change?
qs.ans: About 3.4 times larger
wrong: About 1.5 times larger
About 2.25 times larger
About 5 times larger
qs.why: Deflection ∝ L³: (45/30)³ = 1.5³ ≈ 3.4. 2.25 squares the ratio instead of cubing it.

qs.q: A finishing pass at ae/D = 0.05 gives poor finish and fast flank wear at the catalog chip load. Best first change?
qs.ans: Raise feed to offset chip thinning
wrong: Lower the feed to reduce the load
Raise rpm while keeping feed fixed
Cut the depth of cut in half
qs.why: At r = 0.05 the real chip is only about 0.44 fz, so the edge rubs. Raising feed restores the chip; lower feed or higher rpm thin it more.

qs.q: A 6 mm end mill chatters at 40 mm stickout. Which change raises stiffness the most?
qs.ans: A 10 mm tool at shorter stickout
wrong: A 6 mm tool with one more flute
Slowing the spindle by 10 percent
A longer holder for more reach
qs.why: Tool stiffness ∝ d⁴ / L³, so a larger diameter and less stickout multiply. An extra flute barely changes the core size.

demo.title: Radial chip thinning
demo.hint: Below half-diameter engagement the real chip gets thinner than the programmed chip load. Raise the feed by the factor shown to keep the edge cutting.

cards: Supervised learning fits a model to examples with known answers. A linear model predicts ŷ = w·x + b, with weight w and bias b learned from the data.
The loss measures how wrong predictions are. Each error is e = ŷ − y. Mean squared error is the average of e². Training means finding the w and b that minimize it.
Why squared: it makes every error positive and punishes big misses far more than small ones, so a single wild outlier can drag the whole fit.
Example: w = 2 and b = 1 predict ŷ = 7 at x = 3. If the true y is 8, the squared error is (7 − 8)² = 1.
title: Fitting a line

qs.q: A linear model has w = 0.5 and b = 4. What does it predict at x = 10?
Predictions ŷ = [3, 5, 7] against targets y = [2, 5, 10]. What are the errors e = ŷ − y?
qs.why: e₁ = 3 − 2 = 1, e₂ = 5 − 5 = 0, e₃ = 7 − 10 = −3. Dropping the sign of −3 gives 1, 0, 3. Subtracting the other way (y − ŷ) gives −1, 0, 3. Adding instead of subtracting gives 5, 10, 17.

qs.q: In ŷ = w·x + b, what are w and b called during training?
qs.ans: Learned parameters
wrong: Hand-set hyperparameters
Input features
Target labels
qs.why: Training adjusts w and b to reduce the loss. Hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, are chosen outside training.

qs.q: One point has an error of 10 while the rest are near 1. Under mean squared error, that point…
qs.ans: Dominates the loss because its error is squared
wrong: Counts exactly as much as each other point does
Gets dropped automatically as an outlier
Lowers the loss since positive and negative errors cancel
qs.why: 10² = 100 against 1² = 1, so one point can outweigh dozens of others. That is why outliers pull least-squares fits.

qs.q: Rank these errors by their contribution to mean squared error, largest first.
qs.why: Squares are 16, 9, 4 and 1. The sign doesn’t matter once squared.

qs.q: Predictions [3, 5, 7] against targets [2, 5, 10] give errors e = ŷ − y of 1, 0 and −3. What is the mean squared error?
qs.why: Square each error: 1, 0, 9. Their mean is 10 / 3 ≈ 3.33. Averaging the errors first (−2/3) and then squaring loses the big miss: square first, then average.

demo.title: Fit a line by hand
demo.hint: Move w and b to bring your line onto the best fit. Watch how quickly the squared error grows as you tilt away. Data: x = 1 to 5, y = 3.1, 4.9, 7.2, 8.8, 11.0.

cards: Gradient descent lowers the loss by stepping downhill: w ← w − η·dL/dw, where η is the learning rate and dL/dw is the slope of the loss.
The gradient points uphill, so subtracting it moves toward lower loss. Near the minimum the slope shrinks, so the steps shrink on their own.
Why the learning rate matters: too small and training crawls; too large and each step overshoots the minimum, bouncing or blowing up.
Example: L = (w − 3)², so dL/dw = 2(w − 3). From w = 0 with η = 0.1: w ← 0 − 0.1 × (−6) = 0.6.
title: Gradient descent

qs.q: L = (w − 3)², starting at w = 0 with η = 0.1. What is w after two steps?
L = (w − 5)², w = 1, η = 0.25. What is w after one step?
On L = (w − 3)², which learning rate makes gradient descent diverge?
qs.why: Each step multiplies the distance to 3 by (1 − 2η). That factor is −1.4 at η = 1.2, so it grows. At 0.9 it is −0.8: it oscillates but converges.

qs.q: Loss falls fast at first, then barely moves for thousands of steps. What is a likely reason?
qs.ans: The gradient flattens near a minimum or plateau
wrong: The learning rate keeps growing on its own each epoch
Shuffling the data between epochs stalls progress
The loss function itself changed partway through
qs.why: Step size is η times the gradient. Where the loss surface flattens, the gradient and so the steps get tiny.

qs.q: On L = (w − 3)², rank these learning rates by how fast w approaches 3, fastest first.
qs.why: The remaining distance shrinks by |1 − 2η| each step: 0, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.9. At η = 0.5 it lands on the minimum in one step.

demo.title: Learning rate and convergence
demo.hint: Each step multiplies the distance to the minimum by (1 − 2η). Below η = 0.5 it creeps in, between 0.5 and 1 it zigzags in, and above 1 it blows up.

cards: A model that memorizes its training data can score perfectly there and still fail on new data. That gap is overfitting.
Hold out data the model never trains on. Training error shows fit; validation error estimates performance on new data. Choose models by validation error.
Why complexity cuts both ways: simple models miss real patterns (high bias), very flexible ones chase noise (high variance). Validation error is lowest in between.
Data leakage, such as scaling with statistics from the whole dataset or duplicates crossing the split, makes validation scores look better than reality.
title: Overfitting and validation

qs.q: Training error is 1% but validation error is 25%. What is most likely happening?
qs.ans: Overfitting: the model memorized noise
wrong: Underfitting: the model is far too simple
The validation labels are probably mislabeled
The learning rate is too small to fit anything
qs.why: A big gap between low training error and high validation error is the signature of overfitting.

qs.q: Training and validation error are both high and close together. What is the best next step?
qs.ans: Use a more flexible model or better features
wrong: Add much stronger regularization to the model
Stop training early to avoid overfitting
Copy a share of training rows into validation
qs.why: High, similar errors mean high bias. Regularization and early stopping fight variance, which isn’t the problem here.

qs.q: In 5-fold cross-validation on 1000 examples, how many examples train each model?
qs.why: Each fold holds out one fifth, 200 examples, and trains on the other 800.

qs.q: Which step leaks information into the validation score?
qs.ans: Scaling features with the mean of all the data
wrong: Shuffling all the rows before splitting them up
Fitting the scaler on the training rows only
Holding back a final test set until the very end
qs.why: Using the full dataset’s statistics lets validation data influence training. Fit preprocessing on training data only.

qs.q: Validation error by polynomial degree: 1 → 9.0, 3 → 2.1, 6 → 2.6, 12 → 7.8. Which degree should you choose?
