qs.why: Pick the lowest validation error. Training error would keep falling with degree, which is exactly the overfitting trap.

demo.title: Model complexity, training and validation
demo.hint: Training error keeps falling as the model gets more flexible. Validation error falls, bottoms out, then climbs as the model starts fitting noise. More noise moves the best point lower. Curves are illustrative.

cards: When one class is rare, accuracy misleads. If 1% of parts are defective, a model that always says “good” is 99% accurate and catches nothing.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the parts flagged, how many were truly bad. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the bad parts, how many were caught.
Why they trade off: lowering the alarm threshold catches more defects, raising recall, but also flags more good parts, lowering precision.
Rare events crush precision: with 1% defects, 90% recall and a 5% false-alarm rate, only about 15% of alarms are real defects.
title: Metrics for rare events

qs.q: 1000 parts, 10 of them defective. The model flags 20 parts, 8 of which are truly defective. What is its precision?
qs.why: Precision = TP / flagged = 8 / 20 = 0.40.

qs.q: Same case: what is its recall?
qs.why: Recall = TP / all defective = 8 / 10 = 0.80.

qs.q: Same case: what is its accuracy?
qs.why: False positives = 12, so true negatives = 990 − 12 = 978. Correct = 8 + 978 = 986 of 1000.

qs.q: A plant must miss almost no cracked turbine blades, even if that means extra inspections. Which metric should set the threshold?
qs.ans: Recall
wrong: Precision
Accuracy
Training loss
qs.why: Missing a crack (a false negative) is the costly error, so maximize recall and accept more false alarms.

qs.q: Lowering the alarm threshold usually…
qs.ans: Raises recall and lowers precision
wrong: Raises both recall and precision
Lowers recall and raises precision
Raises accuracy but leaves recall alone
qs.why: More parts get flagged: more true defects are caught, but more good parts are flagged too.

demo.title: Precision when defects are rare
demo.hint: Even an excellent detector produces mostly false alarms when defects are rare, because false alarms scale with the huge number of good parts.

cards: An open-loop system acts without checking the result, like a toaster on a timer. A closed-loop system measures the output and corrects, like cruise control.
The loop: setpoint r, measured output y, error e = r − y. The controller turns the error into a command u that drives the plant.
Why feedback helps: it corrects for disturbances and model errors that open loop can’t see, such as a hill under the car or a weaker motor.
The cost: feedback needs a sensor, passes sensor noise into the system, and badly tuned gains can make a stable plant oscillate.
title: Open and closed loop

qs.q: Which of these is a closed-loop system?
qs.ans: A thermostat switching heat from a room sensor
wrong: A microwave running for a set number of minutes
A sprinkler running on a fixed daily timer
A washing machine on a fixed cycle program
qs.why: Only the thermostat measures the result (room temperature) and adjusts based on it.

qs.q: Setpoint 80 °C, measured 74 °C. What is the error e = r − y, in °C?
qs.why: e = 80 − 74 = 6 °C. A positive error tells the controller to add heat.

qs.q: Order the signals around a feedback loop, starting from the setpoint.
qs.why: The error compares setpoint and measurement, the controller acts on it, the plant responds, and the sensor closes the loop.

qs.q: Cruise control holds speed up a hill where a fixed throttle would slow down. Why?
qs.ans: It measures speed and adds throttle as error grows
wrong: It reads the hill’s slope from a stored road map
It runs the engine at a higher fixed throttle setting
It lowers the setpoint until the measured speed matches
qs.why: The disturbance shows up as a speed error, and the controller responds to it without needing to know its cause.

qs.q: What is a real downside of feedback compared with open loop?
qs.ans: Bad tuning can make it oscillate
wrong: It can’t reject outside disturbances
It works without any sensor at all
It only suits electrical systems
qs.why: Feedback adds dynamics. Too much gain or delay can turn a well-behaved plant into an oscillating one.

demo.title: Disturbance rejection
demo.hint: Open loop passes every disturbance straight to the output. Feedback divides it by (1 + loop gain), so a loop gain of 9 cuts the error to a tenth.

p.x: An **open-loop** system acts without checking the result: a toaster runs its timer whether the bread is pale or burnt.
A **closed-loop** system measures the output and corrects: cruise control reads the speed and adjusts the throttle.
A thermostat is closed loop: it switches the heater by the room temperature it is controlling.

g.q: A thermostat switches a heater on and off by the room temperature. It is…
o: open loop
It does check the result: the room temperature it measures is the output it controls.
closed loop
It measures the output (room temperature) and corrects the heater from it.

vars: output, as the sensor measures it

p.x: The controller turns $e$ into a command $u$ that drives the **plant**: the thing being controlled.
Feedback corrects for what open loop can't see: **disturbances** and **model errors**.
On a hill, a fixed throttle lets the car [[slow down]]. Cruise control sees the speed drop and opens the throttle.
With a weaker motor than planned, the loop simply pushes harder until the measured speed matches.
Feedback works from the measurement, so it doesn't need a perfect model.
Feedback isn't free. It costs three things.
**A sensor**: extra parts, cost, and one more thing that can fail.
**Noise**: the loop acts on what the sensor reports, so sensor noise reaches the actuator.
**Instability**: badly tuned gains can make a plant that is stable on its own oscillate.

cards: Many systems answer a step like a first-order lag: a heater, an RC circuit, a motor’s speed. The output rises fast at first, then levels off.
Step response: y(t) = K·(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with steady-state gain K and time constant τ. At t = τ the output reaches 63% of its final change.
Why 63%: e^(−1) ≈ 0.37 of the gap remains after one time constant. After 4τ under 2% remains, a common definition of settling time.
Example: a heater with τ = 60 s and a 30 °C final rise is about 19 °C up after one minute and settled after about four.
title: First-order response

qs.q: τ = 5 s and the final change is 100 °C. How far has the output risen after 5 s, in °C?
Same system, τ = 5 s: what is the approximate 2% settling time, in s?
qs.why: Settling to within 2% takes about 4τ = 4 × 5 = 20 s, since e^(−4) ≈ 0.018.

qs.q: After 2τ, what percentage of the final change has been reached?
Doubling τ with the same K changes the step response how?
qs.ans: Same final value, reached twice as slowly
wrong: Twice the final value, reached at the same speed
Half the final value, reached twice as fast
The same speed, but now with some overshoot
qs.why: K sets the final value; τ sets the speed. A first-order system never overshoots.

qs.q: Rank these systems by the time to reach 95% of the final value, longest first.
qs.why: 95% takes about 3τ: 24 s, 15 s, 6 s and 1.5 s.

demo.title: First-order step response
demo.hint: Every first-order system has the same shape, just stretched by τ. Drag the time marker to τ and you’ll always read 63% of the final change.

p.x: A **step** input jumps to a new value and stays there, like switching a heater on.
Many systems answer a step as a **first-order lag**: a heater, an RC circuit, a motor's speed.
The output rises fastest at the start, then levels off at a new steady value.

vars: steady-state gain: final change per unit of input

p.cap: unit step at t = 0, starting at rest

p.x: At $t = τ$: $y = K(1 − e^{−1}) = 0.632 K$, so the output has made **63 %** of its final change.

g.q: At t = τ, how far has the output got toward its final value?
o: about half
Half is reached a bit earlier, at t ≈ 0.69 τ. At t = τ it is further along.
about two-thirds
1 − e^−1 = 0.632: about 63 % of the final change.
all the way
An exponential never quite arrives; after one τ about 37 % of the gap is still left.

p.x: In every time constant, the gap left to the final value shrinks by the [[same factor]].
Each row is $e^{−1}$ ≈ 0.37 times the one before.
Under 2 % is left after 4τ, a common definition of **settling time**: $t_s ≈ 4τ$.
About 19 °C up after one minute, and within 2 % of the final 30 °C after about four minutes.

cards: A proportional controller sets u = Kp·e: more error, more push. It is simple, but against a constant setpoint it leaves a steady-state error.
For a plant with steady-state gain K, the closed-loop error after a step is e_ss = r / (1 + Kp·K). The product Kp·K is the loop gain.
Why an offset remains: P control needs a nonzero error to produce any output, so holding the output above zero requires some error to persist.
Integral action adds Ki × (the error added up over time). That running total keeps growing while any error remains, so it drives the steady-state error to zero for a constant setpoint.
title: Proportional control and offset

qs.q: Kp·K = 9 and the setpoint steps by 1. What is the steady-state error, as a percent of the step?
What loop gain Kp·K gives a 2% steady-state error?
A P-controlled heater settles 3 °C short of setpoint. Which change removes the offset entirely?
qs.ans: Add integral action
wrong: Double the proportional gain
Add derivative action
Use a faster sensor
qs.why: Doubling Kp shrinks the offset but can’t eliminate it. Integral action accumulates error until it is gone.
qs.hint: Look back at the last card: the integral term adds up the error over time, so it keeps growing as long as any error is left.

qs.q: Raising Kp shrinks the offset, so what usually limits how high it can go?
qs.ans: Oscillation and actuator saturation
wrong: The error starts growing again as Kp rises
The plant’s own gain falls whenever Kp rises
Integral windup builds up inside the P loop
qs.why: High gain amplifies delays and noise into oscillation, and real actuators have limits. A pure P loop has no integrator to wind up.

qs.q: Rank these loop gains by steady-state error, largest first.

demo.title: Proportional gain and offset
demo.hint: Offset falls as 1 / (1 + loop gain): fast at first, then slowly. Getting from 10% to 1% needs the loop gain to go from 9 to 99, which is why integral action exists.

p.x: More error, more push. Zero error, zero push.
Simple, but against a constant setpoint it leaves a steady error, called the **offset**.

p.cap: plant steady-state gain K, step setpoint r, stable loop

p.x: Offset ∝ 1/(1 + loop gain): it shrinks, but reaches zero only at infinite gain.

g.q: Raise the loop gain from 9 to 99. The offset…
o: drops to about 1 %
1/(1 + 99) = 1 %: about ten times smaller, but not zero.
drops to zero
r/(1 + K_pK) is zero only for infinite gain; finite gain always leaves some offset.

p.x: P control pushes with $u = K_p e$: with zero error, it pushes with zero.
Holding a room above outdoor temperature takes steady heater power, so P control needs a [[nonzero]] error to supply it.
The loop settles where the error is just big enough to make the power needed.

vars: the error added up over time

p.x: That running total keeps growing while any error remains.
The integral can hold a steady output with zero error, so the offset goes to zero (constant setpoint, stable loop).

g.q: With integral action, the steady error to a constant setpoint ends up…
o: smaller, but not zero
That's P control with more gain. The integral keeps growing until the error is exactly zero.
zero
The total stops changing only when the error is zero, and it then holds the output needed.

cards: Many closed loops behave like a mass, spring and damper. Their step response depends on the damping ratio ζ and the natural frequency ωn.
Underdamped loops (ζ < 1) overshoot. Percent overshoot = 100·e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)): about 16% at ζ = 0.5 and 4.6% at ζ = 0.7.
Why ζ ≈ 0.7 is a common target: it rises quickly with little overshoot. The 2% settling time is about 4 / (ζ·ωn).
Derivative action adds damping by reacting to how fast the error changes. Too much proportional gain lowers damping and adds overshoot.
title: Damping and overshoot

qs.q: What is the percent overshoot for ζ = 0.5?
With ζ = 0.5 and ωn = 4 rad/s, what is the approximate 2% settling time, in s?
A positioning stage overshoots 30% on every move. Which change most directly reduces the overshoot?
qs.ans: Add derivative action for more damping
wrong: Raise the proportional gain for more speed
Add integral action to remove the offset
Lower the position sensor’s sample rate
qs.why: Overshoot comes from low damping. Derivative action damps; more P or I action typically adds overshoot.

qs.q: Which damping ratio gives the fastest response with no overshoot at all?
qs.ans: ζ = 1, critically damped
wrong: ζ = 0.2, lightly damped
ζ = 0.7, the usual target
ζ = 2, heavily overdamped
qs.why: Below 1 there is some overshoot (4.6% at 0.7). Above 1 the response is slower. ζ = 1 is the fastest without overshoot.

qs.q: Rank these damping ratios by percent overshoot, largest first.
qs.why: Overshoot is about 53%, 25%, 9.5% and 1.5%.

demo.title: Second-order step response
demo.hint: Low damping rings and overshoots; damping near 0.7 is quick with a small bump. ωn only stretches the time axis.

p.x: Many closed loops behave like a mass, spring and damper. Two numbers describe their step response.
**Damping ratio**: how fast oscillation dies out. At 1 and above, there's no overshoot.
**Natural frequency**: how fast it would oscillate with no damping, in rad/s.
Higher ζ, less overshoot. Higher ω_n, faster response.

p.cap: standard second-order loop, no zeros, step input, ζ < 1

p.x: A little more damping cuts overshoot sharply: it falls off steeply as ζ rises.

g.q: Raise ζ from 0.5 to 0.7. Overshoot falls to about…
o: That scales overshoot down in step with ζ. The formula is exponential, so it drops much faster.

p.x: Low ζ overshoots and rings. High ζ doesn't overshoot, but is [[slow]] to rise.
$ζ ≈ 0.7$ is a common compromise: a quick rise and about 5 % overshoot.

p.cap: underdamped second-order loop, ζ < 1

p.x: **Derivative** action reacts to how fast the error changes. It acts like the damper, so it adds damping.
**Proportional** gain acts like the spring. On a mass-like plant with PD, raising it alone makes the loop stiffer.

g.q: Raise K_p alone. Overshoot…
o: grows
A stiffer spring with the same damper means lower ζ, so more overshoot.
shrinks
That's what more D gain does. More P gain lowers the damping ratio.

cards: A sketch is a 2D profile that features turn into 3D geometry. Its shape comes from geometric constraints and dimensions, not from where you clicked.
Each entity has degrees of freedom: a point has 2, a line segment 4, a circle 3 (center x, center y, radius). Every constraint or dimension removes some.
Why fully define: an under-defined sketch can shift when you edit something else, silently moving features. Zero remaining DOF means every change is deliberate.
Example: four lines with joined corners and horizontal and vertical constraints still have 4 DOF: width, height, and the x and y position.
title: Sketches and constraints

qs.q: How many degrees of freedom does a free circle in a 2D sketch have?
qs.why: Center x, center y and radius.

qs.q: A rectangle has joined corners plus horizontal and vertical constraints. How many more dimensions or constraints fully define it?
qs.why: Width and height set its size, and two more fix its position. 16 line DOF − 8 for corners − 4 for horizontal and vertical leaves 4.

qs.q: What does a fully defined sketch guarantee?
qs.ans: Nothing moves unless you edit a value
wrong: Every feature will mesh cleanly for analysis
It can extrude without errors in any direction
It contains no construction geometry at all
qs.why: Fully defined means zero remaining DOF: the geometry is pinned by its constraints and dimensions, so edits only happen on purpose.

qs.q: Which of these is a geometric constraint rather than a dimension?
qs.ans: Tangent
wrong: Length 40 mm
Angle 30°
Radius 5 mm
qs.why: Constraints set relationships such as tangent, parallel or coincident. Dimensions set sizes and positions with numbers.

qs.q: Rank these sketch entities by degrees of freedom, most first.
qs.why: Ellipse 5 (center, two radii, rotation), line 4 (two endpoints), circle 3, point 2.

demo.title: Counting sketch degrees of freedom
demo.hint: Each line brings 4 DOF, each coincident corner removes 2, each horizontal or vertical constraint and each dimension removes 1. Aim for exactly zero; below zero is over-defined.

cards: Parts are built as an ordered list of features: extrude, revolve, cut, fillet, pattern. Each feature can reference geometry made by earlier ones.
Those references create parent-child links. Change or delete a parent and every child that depends on it can fail or move.
Why design intent matters: dimension from what matters functionally. If a hole must stay centered, constrain it to the midpoint, not 37.5 mm from an edge.
Fillets and chamfers usually go near the end of the tree, so edits to the base shape don’t break the edges they reference.
title: Features and design intent

qs.q: A bracket’s hole must stay centered whenever its width changes. What is the best way to locate the hole?
qs.ans: Constrain it to the edge’s midpoint
wrong: Dimension it 25 mm from the left edge
Place it by eye, then fix it in place
Dimension it 25 mm from the right edge
qs.why: A midpoint relation captures the intent, so the hole follows any width change. A fixed distance keeps it 25 mm from one edge instead.

qs.q: You delete an early sketch and several later features fail with errors. Why?
qs.ans: They referenced geometry from that sketch
wrong: The tree is recomputed in alphabetical order
Deleting a sketch resets the part material
Errors show until the file is saved again
qs.why: Later features were children of the sketch. Removing a parent breaks every reference to it.

qs.q: Which feature makes a shaft from a 2D profile and an axis?
qs.ans: Revolve
wrong: Extrude
Sweep
Loft
qs.why: A revolve spins a profile about an axis. A sweep needs a path, and a loft blends between profiles.

qs.q: A bolt circle has 6 equally spaced holes. What is the angle between neighboring holes, in degrees?
Order these features for a robust model of a mounting plate with a hole pattern and rounded outer edges.
qs.why: The base comes first, a hole must exist before it can be patterned, and fillets go last so base edits don’t break their edge references.

demo.title: Bolt circle pattern
demo.hint: More holes on the same circle means a smaller angle and a shorter gap between neighbors. The straight-line spacing is D·sin(π/n), not the arc length.

cards: In an assembly, each free part has 6 degrees of freedom. Mates remove them, just as constraints do in a sketch.
A face-to-face coincident mate removes 3 DOF; a concentric mate removes 4. A pin concentric in a hole and seated on a face keeps just 1: rotation.
Why not fix everything: leave the motion the real mechanism has, so you can drag it to check range, clearance and interference.
For planar linkages, Gruebler’s equation gives mobility: M = 3(n − 1) − 2j, with n links including ground and j pin or slider joints. A four-bar gives 1.
title: Assemblies and mates

qs.q: A part is mated concentric to a shaft, with no other mates. How many degrees of freedom remain?
qs.why: It can still rotate about the axis and slide along it: 6 − 4 = 2.

qs.q: A planar linkage has 5 links, including ground, and 5 pin joints. What is its mobility M?
qs.why: M = 3(5 − 1) − 2 × 5 = 12 − 10 = 2, so it needs two inputs to fully define its motion.

qs.q: A shaft sits in a bore (concentric mate), and its shoulder rests against the housing face (coincident mate). What can the shaft still do?
qs.ans: Spin about its own axis
wrong: Slide in and out along its axis
Nothing: it is fully fixed
Tip over the edge of the shoulder
qs.why: Concentric leaves only spin and slide along the axis. The shoulder against the face stops the slide, so only the spin is left. “Fully fixed” forgets that neither mate stops rotation; tipping was already removed by the concentric mate.

qs.q: Why leave a hinge’s rotation unconstrained in the assembly?
qs.ans: To drag it through its range and check clearance
wrong: Because CAD cannot constrain any rotation of a hinge pin
To keep the assembly file noticeably smaller
So the drawing can show a hidden-line view
qs.why: Keeping the real degree of freedom lets you test motion, interference and limits before parts are made.

qs.q: A free part has 6 DOF. Rank these single mates by the DOF the part has left, most first.
qs.why: They remove 1, 3, 4 and 6 DOF, leaving 5, 3, 2 and 0. A distance mate only sets one gap; fixed locks everything.

demo.title: Gruebler mobility
demo.hint: Each moving link adds 3 DOF and each pin or slider removes 2. A four-bar has exactly 1, so one motor drives it; at 0 or below it locks up as a structure.

cards: Robust models survive edits. Drive key sizes from a few named parameters or equations, such as hole spacing = width − 2 × edge distance.
Fragile references cause most rebuild failures: picking a face or edge that a later edit renames or deletes. Reference base sketches, planes and axes instead.
Why configurations help: one model can carry a family of sizes, such as lengths 50, 75 and 100 mm, without copied files that drift apart.
Model-based definition puts dimensions, tolerances and notes on the 3D model itself, so inspection and CAM read the same source as the designer.
title: Robust parametric models

qs.q: Plate width W = 120 mm and edge distance e = 15 mm, with holes placed by spacing = W − 2e. What is the spacing, in mm?
qs.why: 120 − 2 × 15 = 90 mm. Change W and the holes follow automatically.

qs.q: A fillet fails every time you change the base extrude depth. What is the most robust fix?
qs.ans: Move it later and pick edges from stable geometry
wrong: Suppress the fillet whenever you edit the depth
Convert the part into a non-parametric solid
Raise the fillet radius until the model rebuilds cleanly
qs.why: The fillet referenced edges that the edit renamed. Later placement and stable references fix the cause; the other options hide it.

qs.q: Why use configurations instead of copied files for a family of bracket lengths?
qs.ans: Edits to shared features update every size
wrong: Copied files can’t be referenced in drawings or assemblies
Configurations make each part lighter
Copies lose their material assignment
qs.why: One source means a fix or change happens once. Copies drift apart as people edit some and forget others.

qs.q: What does model-based definition mainly change?
qs.ans: Tolerances live on the 3D model, not a drawing
wrong: Parts are modeled without using sketches
Assemblies are built without using mates
Simulation results replace the dimensions entirely
qs.why: MBD makes the annotated 3D model the authority for manufacturing and inspection.

qs.q: A bracket comes in 8 lengths, and every length comes in 5 hole-pattern options. How many configurations does the table need?
qs.why: Every length pairs with every hole pattern: 8 × 5 = 40. Adding them (13) counts the options, not the combinations.

demo.title: Driving holes from parameters
demo.hint: Change the width and the hole pitch updates itself, because both come from one equation. Hard-coded positions would leave holes stranded near one edge.

cards: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model, so complex internal shapes cost little extra. It suits prototypes, low volumes and lattices.
Main families: material extrusion (FDM) melts filament; vat photopolymerization (SLA) cures resin with light; powder bed fusion (SLS, metal) fuses powder with a laser.
Why layer height matters: thinner layers smooth the stair steps on slopes, but more layers mean a longer build. Build time scales with height ÷ layer height.
Example: a 60 mm tall part at 0.2 mm layers needs 300 layers; at 0.1 mm it needs 600.
title: Printing processes

qs.q: A part is 45 mm tall. How many layers does it take at a 0.15 mm layer height?
Which process cures liquid resin with light, layer by layer?
qs.ans: Vat photopolymerization (SLA)
wrong: Material extrusion (FDM)
Selective laser sintering (SLS)
Binder jetting into powder
qs.why: SLA and related processes cure photopolymer resin with a laser or projector. SLS fuses powder; FDM extrudes melted filament.

qs.q: Which process usually needs no support structures for nylon parts, because loose powder holds them up?
qs.ans: Selective laser sintering
wrong: Fused deposition modeling
Stereolithography
Directed energy deposition
qs.why: In selective laser sintering (SLS) the unfused powder surrounds and supports the part, so overhangs print freely. HP Multi Jet Fusion works the same way. FDM and SLA both need supports for steep overhangs; directed energy deposition is mostly for metal.

qs.q: Rank these settings by build time for the same 50 mm tall part, longest first.
qs.why: Layer count is 1000, 500, 250 and about 167, and time scales roughly with layer count.

qs.q: What three-letter abbreviation names printing by melting and extruding a thermoplastic filament?
qs.why: Fused deposition modeling (FDM), also called fused filament fabrication (FFF).

demo.title: Layer height and build time
demo.hint: Halving the layer height doubles the layer count and roughly doubles the build. Use thin layers only where curved or sloped surfaces need them. Time per layer is illustrative.

p.x: **Additive manufacturing** builds a part layer by layer from a digital model.
Complex internal shapes cost little extra, unless they need supports or clean-out: the printer traces each layer's outline whatever its shape.
It suits prototypes, low volumes and lattices.

g.q: Add internal cooling channels to a printed part. The printing time and cost…
o: rises a lot
That's true for machining, where every internal feature needs its own tool path or a split part. A printer just traces different outlines in the same layers.
change little
The printer traces each layer's outline whatever its shape, so internal detail costs little extra, unless a channel needs supports or powder or resin cleaned out.

p.x: Three main process families:
**Material extrusion** (FDM) melts filament and lays it down through a nozzle.
**Vat photopolymerization** (SLA) cures liquid resin with light.
**Powder bed fusion** (SLS, metal) fuses powder with a laser.
Thinner layers smooth the stair steps on slopes, but take more layers to reach the same height.

p.cap: build time ∝ N for a fixed time per layer

p.x: Half the layer height, twice the layers: $N ∝ 1/h$

g.q: Switch to 0.1 mm layers. The layer count…
o: doubles
N = H/h, so halving h doubles N, and roughly doubles the build time.
halves
Thinner layers mean more of them to reach the same height. N = H/h goes up as h goes down.

cards: FDM can print overhangs up to about 45° from vertical without support on almost any printer, because each new layer still rests partly on the one below. A well-tuned printer with strong part cooling can often hold 60–75°.
Each layer steps out by about layer height × tan(θ) beyond the one below it, where θ is the wall’s angle from vertical.
Why 45°: there each layer steps out one layer height, about half a typical extrusion width, so it is still half supported. Steeper overhangs droop.
Short bridges between two supports print fine; long ones sag. Reorienting the part can often remove most supports entirely.
title: Overhangs and supports

qs.q: Layer height is 0.2 mm and a wall leans 60° from vertical. How far does each layer step out, in mm?
qs.why: 0.2 × tan 60° = 0.2 × 1.732 ≈ 0.346 mm, most of a 0.4 mm extrusion width, so it will droop.

qs.q: Which feature most likely needs support in FDM?
qs.ans: A flat shelf jutting straight out
wrong: A 30° chamfer along the part’s top edge
A tall, vertical cylinder wall
A wall sloping 40° from vertical
qs.why: A horizontal shelf is a 90° overhang with nothing below it. The others stay within about 45° of vertical.

qs.q: Why does reorienting a part often beat adding supports?
qs.ans: It removes overhangs and the marks supports leave
wrong: Supports weaken whatever surface they touch
Reorienting shortens every layer’s tool path length
Printers can’t make supports in some plastics
qs.why: Fewer overhangs means less support material, less cleanup and no rough scars where supports were broken off.

qs.q: Extrusion width 0.4 mm and layer height 0.2 mm. At what angle from vertical does each layer step out by half the extrusion width, in degrees?
qs.why: Half the width is 0.2 mm, so tan θ = 0.2 / 0.2 = 1 and θ = 45°.

qs.q: Rank these overhangs by risk of drooping, highest first.
qs.why: The step per layer is h·tan θ, which grows quickly toward 90°.

demo.title: Overhang angle
demo.hint: The step per layer grows with tan θ, slowly at first and then very fast. Past the point where it exceeds half the extrusion width, the new layer mostly hangs in air.

p.x: FDM can print overhangs up to about 45° from vertical without support on almost any printer.
Each new layer still rests partly on the one below it.
A well-tuned printer with strong part cooling can often hold 60–75°.

p.cap: each layer compared with the one below

p.x: Typical FDM settings: 0.2 mm layers and 0.4 mm wide beads.
One layer height: half of each bead still sits on the layer below.
Steeper wall, much bigger step: step ∝ $tan θ$
Past 45° most of each bead hangs in air and droops.

g.q: Tilt the overhang to 60°. The step per layer is about…
o: That scales the step with the angle, 0.2 × 60/45. It goes as tan θ, which grows faster: tan 60° = 1.73.
0.2 mm × tan 60° = 0.2 × 1.73 ≈ 0.35 mm, most of a 0.4 mm bead.

p.x: A **bridge** spans the gap between two supports.
Short bridges print fine; long ones sag.
Reorienting the part can often remove most supports entirely.

cards: Printed parts are weakest across their layers, along the build direction, because each layer bonds to the last only where they fuse.
For FDM, strength across layers is often around half to three quarters of the in-layer strength, and lower when layers cool before the next lands.
Why orientation is a design decision: the same part can be strong or weak depending on how it sits on the bed. Run the main tensile load along the layers.
Perimeter walls usually matter more than infill for strength, because bending and twisting stresses peak at the outer surface.
title: Orientation and strength

qs.q: A hook printed standing upright snaps between layers at the bend. What is the best fix?
qs.ans: Print it lying flat so layers follow the hook
wrong: Raise the infill from 20% to 60% or more
Increase layer height so it prints faster
Print it upright with a wide brim at the base
qs.why: Upright, the bend pulls layers apart. Lying flat, the load runs along the layers. Infill barely helps a layer-bond failure.

qs.q: In-layer strength is 50 MPa and across-layer strength is 60% of that. What is the across-layer strength, in MPa?
For a bracket loaded in bending, which change usually adds the most strength per gram?
qs.ans: More perimeter walls
wrong: A denser infill pattern
A wider brim at the base
A higher print speed
qs.why: Bending stress is highest at the outer surface, so solid perimeters there carry the load. Infill sits near the neutral axis where stress is low.

qs.q: Why can printing very fast with the cooling fan on full weaken the bond between layers?
qs.ans: Each layer cools before the next fuses to it
wrong: Fast prints lay down less plastic in walls
Cooling makes the plastic absorb moisture
The fan blows each new layer out of alignment
qs.why: Layers fuse by melting into the one below. If the lower layer is already cold, interdiffusion is weak and the bond is poor.

qs.q: Rank these orientations by strength for a tensile load along the part’s length, strongest first.
qs.why: Strength falls as the load turns from along the layers toward pulling them apart.

demo.title: Strength versus load angle
demo.hint: Turn the load from along the layers (0°) to straight across them (90°). Strength falls slowly at first, then quickly, toward the layer-bond strength. Model is illustrative.

verify: Across-layer strength as a fraction of in-layer strength varies widely with material and process settings.

p.x: A printed part is built up in layers, stacked along the build direction.
It's weakest **across** its layers, along the build direction: each layer bonds to the last only where they fuse.

g.q: Pull a printed bar along the build direction, straight across its layers. Compared with pulling along the layers, it's…
o: weaker
The load has to pass through every layer-to-layer bond, and those are the weakest part of the print.
stronger
Across the layers the load pulls on the bonds between them, which are weaker than the beads themselves.
about the same
Printed parts aren't the same in every direction: the bonds between layers are weaker than the beads.

p.x: For FDM, strength across the layers is often around half to three quarters of the strength along them.
It drops further when each layer cools before the next one lands on it.
The same part can be strong or weak depending on how it sits on the bed.
Run the main tensile load [[along]] the layers.
Then the load pulls on continuous beads, not on the bonds between layers. Orientation is a design decision.
A printed part has **perimeter walls** around the outside and **infill** inside.
Perimeters usually matter more: bending and twisting stresses peak at the outer surface and are small near the middle.

g.q: A printed bracket bends too much. Which change helps more?
o: more perimeter walls
Extra walls add material at the surface, where bending and twisting stresses are largest.
denser infill
Infill sits near the middle, where bending stress is small, so it adds weight and time for little stiffness.

cards: Metal powder bed fusion melts powder with a laser, layer by layer. Rapid heating and cooling lock in residual stress that can warp parts or crack supports.
Supports in metal also conduct heat away and anchor the part against distortion, so they are needed even where an overhang would otherwise hold.
Why build height drives cost: recoating every layer takes time regardless of part area, so a tall build costs more than a wide one. Nesting parts shares that time.
Typical post-processing: stress relief while still on the plate, support removal, then machining of critical surfaces and holes.
title: Metal printing tradeoffs

qs.q: A build takes 30 h on a machine billed at $100/h, with 10 parts on the plate. What is the machine cost per part, in dollars?
qs.why: 30 × 100 = $3,000 for the build, shared by 10 parts: $300 each.

qs.q: Why stress-relieve metal parts before cutting them off the build plate?
qs.ans: So locked-in stress doesn’t warp them on release
wrong: So the powder fuses into a denser structure
So the supports can be dissolved chemically
So surface roughness drops to its final finished values
qs.why: The plate restrains the part. Cut it free while stressed and it springs out of shape; heat treatment first relaxes that stress.

qs.q: The same part can be built tall and upright or laid flat. If supports allow, which usually costs less in powder bed fusion?
qs.ans: Laid flat, since it needs fewer layers
wrong: Upright, since each layer is smaller
Either, since the volume is the same
Upright, since recoating gets faster as layers shrink
qs.why: Every layer costs a recoat cycle, so fewer layers means a shorter build. Smaller layer area saves some laser time but rarely as much.

qs.q: A designer merges an 8-piece welded manifold into one printed part. What is the main benefit?
qs.ans: Fewer joints, leak paths and assembly steps
wrong: Lower material cost per kilogram
Higher strength than wrought metal in every direction
No need for any post-machining
qs.why: Part consolidation removes welds and fittings, which are leak and failure points, and cuts assembly labor. Printed metal costs more per kilogram, is usually weaker across its layers than wrought metal, and still needs machining on sealing faces and threads. Build time can go either way, so it isn’t the main benefit.

qs.q: For a 40 h build billed at $80/h, rank these plate loads by machine cost per part, highest first.
qs.why: $3,200 per build shared gives $1,600, $640, $320 and $80 per part.

demo.title: Cost per part and nesting
demo.hint: Machine time is shared by everything on the plate, so cost per part falls steeply as you nest more. Past a point, material dominates and nesting stops helping.

p.x: Metal **powder bed fusion** melts metal powder with a laser, layer by layer.
Rapid heating and cooling lock in **residual stress**.
That stress can warp the part or crack its supports.
In metal, supports also conduct heat away and anchor the part against distortion.
So they're needed even where an overhang would otherwise hold.
For every layer, the machine spreads a fresh coat of powder, then the laser melts that layer's outline.
A tall build costs more than a wide one: recoating takes the same time each layer, whatever the part area.
Nesting several parts on one plate shares that time between them.

g.q: Two builds hold the same volume of parts: one tall, one wide and flat. Which takes more machine time?
o: the tall one
It has more layers, and every layer costs a full recoat regardless of how much area gets melted.
the wide one
Melting area takes laser time in both, and the volumes match. The tall build adds many more recoats.
about the same
Equal volume means similar laser time, but the tall build has many more layers to recoat.

p.x: Typical post-processing for a metal print:
Stress relief comes while the part is still on the plate, so it doesn't warp when it's cut free.
Machining then brings critical surfaces and holes to size.

cards: Every physical quantity is a number times a unit. Treat units like algebra: they multiply, divide and cancel.
Convert by multiplying by a fraction equal to one, such as 1000 mm / 1 m. Pick the fraction so the unit you don’t want cancels.
Why squares and cubes trip people: 1 m = 1000 mm, so 1 m² = 10⁶ mm² and 1 m³ = 10⁹ mm³. Convert every power, not just once.
Prefixes: k = 10³, M = 10⁶, G = 10⁹, m = 10⁻³, µ = 10⁻⁶. 1 MPa = 1 N/mm², which is why drawings use MPa.
title: Units and conversions

qs.q: How many mm² are in 0.5 m²?
A 2,000 N force acts on a 40 mm² area. What is the stress, in MPa?
qs.why: 2000 N / 40 mm² = 50 N/mm², and 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.

qs.q: A car goes 90 km/h. What is that in m/s?
qs.ans: 25 m/s
wrong: 15 m/s
qs.why: 90 × 1000 m / 3600 s = 25 m/s. Dividing by 3.6 is the shortcut.

qs.q: Which quantity has the same units as a pascal?
qs.ans: Newtons per square meter
wrong: Newton-meters per second
Joules per kilogram
Kilograms per cubic meter
qs.why: Pressure is force over area: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

qs.q: Rank these lengths, largest first.

demo.title: Length scale and area scale
demo.hint: Scale a length by a factor and the area scales by the square, the volume by the cube. Halving a part’s size cuts its weight to an eighth.

p.x: Every physical quantity is a number times a unit: 250 N means 250 times one newton.
Treat units like algebra. They multiply and divide:
And they cancel, top against bottom:
To convert, multiply by a fraction equal to one:
Pick the fraction so the unit you don't want cancels.
1 m = 1000 mm, and an area is a length times a length.
Convert every power, not just once: $(1000 mm)^2 = 10^6 mm^2$.

g.q: So 1 m² is…
o: 1000 mm²
That converts the metre only once. A square metre is 1000 mm × 1000 mm.
10⁶ mm²
Both lengths convert: 1000 × 1000 = 10⁶.
10⁹ mm²
That's 1000³, the cube, for a volume. An area has two lengths.

p.x: Case matters: m is milli, M is mega.
Drawings give sizes in mm, so a stress in MPa is simply newtons per square millimetre.

cards: Every valid equation is dimensionally consistent: both sides reduce to the same base units of mass M, length L and time T.
Check a formula by substituting dimensions. Kinetic energy ½mv² gives M·(L/T)² = ML²/T², which matches a joule (N·m).
Why it is powerful: you can catch a wrong formula, or guess the form of one, before doing any detailed physics.
Functions like sin, exp and log need dimensionless arguments. exp(t) is meaningless unless t is divided by a time constant.
title: Dimensional analysis

qs.q: Which expression has the dimensions of power?
qs.ans: Force × velocity
wrong: Force × distance
Mass × acceleration
Pressure × area
qs.why: Power is energy per time: N·m/s = force × velocity. Force × distance is energy.

qs.q: A student writes v = √(2gh²). What does dimensional analysis say?
qs.ans: Wrong: the right side has units of L^1.5/T
wrong: Correct: both sides reduce to a length per unit time
Wrong: the right side is dimensionless
Can’t tell without plugging in numbers
qs.why: g·h² is (L/T²)·L² = L³/T², whose root is L^1.5/T, not L/T. The correct form is √(2gh).

qs.q: In e^(−t/τ), what must the units of τ be if t is in seconds?
qs.ans: Seconds
wrong: Per second
Dimensionless
Seconds squared
qs.why: The exponent must be dimensionless, so τ carries the same units as t.

qs.q: A pendulum’s period depends only on its length L and g. It goes as √(L/g). If L is made 4 times longer, by what factor does the period grow?
qs.why: √4 = 2. Dimensional analysis alone gives the √(L/g) form.

qs.q: Rank these by the power of length in their dimensions, highest first.
qs.why: L³, L², L¹ (L/T) and L⁻³ (M/L³).

demo.title: Scaling a pendulum
demo.hint: Dimensions force the period to go as √(L/g). Quadruple the length and the period only doubles; drop g to the Moon’s and it slows by about 2.5×.

p.x: A valid equation is dimensionally consistent: both sides reduce to [[the same]] combination of M, L and T.
Check a formula by substituting dimensions. Kinetic energy:
They match: KE comes out in joules (N·m). The ½ is a pure number, so dimensions can't check it.
Dimensions can catch a wrong formula, or suggest the form of one, before any detailed physics.
A pendulum's period can depend only on its length L and on g (L/T²). The one mix with units of time:

p.cap: C is a pure number dimensions can't find (2π for small swings)

p.x: 4× the length, 2× the period: $period ∝ √{L}$

g.q: Make the pendulum 4× longer. Its period…
o: doubles
Period goes as √L, and √4 = 2.
quadruples
That treats period as proportional to L. Only √(L/g) has units of time, so period goes as √L.
stays the same
Length sits inside √(L/g). It's mass that drops out, since nothing else carries M.

p.x: Functions like sin, exp and log need [[dimensionless]] arguments.

p.cap: t/τ has no units

p.x: exp(t) alone is meaningless: its value would change if you measured t in minutes instead of seconds.

cards: A vector has magnitude and direction. Split it into components: Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ, with θ measured from the x-axis.
Add vectors by adding components, then rebuild: magnitude = √(Fx² + Fy²), angle = atan2(Fy, Fx).
Why atan2: plain atan(Fy/Fx) can’t tell (1, 1) from (−1, −1). atan2 uses both signs to pick the right quadrant.
Sanity check: a 30° angle puts most of the force along x, since cos 30° ≈ 0.87 and sin 30° = 0.5.
title: Vector components

qs.q: A 200 N force acts at 30° above the x-axis. What is its x-component, in N?
Two forces add to Fx = 30 N and Fy = 40 N. What is the resultant magnitude, in N?
A vector has components (−3, −3). What is its direction?
qs.why: Both components are negative, so it points into the third quadrant. atan would wrongly give 45°.

qs.q: Which change to a 100 N force at 60° increases its x-component?
qs.ans: Lower the angle toward 0°
wrong: Raise the angle toward 90°
Flip the force to 240°
Keep the angle but halve it to 50 N
qs.why: Fx = F cos θ, and cos θ grows as θ falls toward 0°.

qs.q: For a 100 N force, rank these angles by y-component, largest first.
qs.why: 100 sin θ gives 100, 86.6, 50 and 0 N.

demo.title: Splitting a force
demo.hint: As the angle rises, the x-share falls along a cosine and the y-share rises along a sine. Their squares always add to F².

p.x: A vector has a magnitude and a direction.
Split it into components along x and y.
With θ measured from the x-axis, cos goes with x and sin with y.
Add vectors by adding their components, then rebuild the magnitude and angle.
Plain atan only sees the ratio F_y/F_x. For (1, 1) and (−1, −1) that ratio is 1 both times.

p.c: for (−1, −1): uses both signs (−135° is the same as 225°)

p.x: atan2 uses both signs to pick the right quadrant.
Sanity-check components against the angle. Take a force F at 30° from the x-axis.
Between 0° and 45°, mostly along x: $cos θ > sin θ$

g.q: Which way does most of the force point?
o: along x
cos 30° ≈ 0.87 is bigger than sin 30° = 0.5, so the x-component is larger.
along y
That swaps sin and cos. With θ from the x-axis, Fx = F cos θ, and cos 30° ≈ 0.87.
half and half
An even split happens at 45°, where cos and sin are both about 0.71. At 30° the force leans toward x.

cards: The dot product a·b = |a||b| cos θ gives a scalar. It measures how much one vector points along another: work is F·d.
The cross product a × b gives a vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude |a||b| sin θ. Moment is r × F.
Why both: dot picks out the parallel part, cross the perpendicular part. Pushing a door along its plane does no turning.
In 2D, the cross product’s z-value is rx·Fy − ry·Fx. A positive result means counterclockwise.
title: Dot and cross products

qs.q: a = (3, 4) and b = (2, −1). What is a·b?
A 50 N force pulls a cart 10 m, at 60° to the direction of motion. How much work is done, in J?
r = (0.3, 0) m and F = (0, 20) N. What is the moment about the origin, in N·m (counterclockwise positive)?
qs.why: rx·Fy − ry·Fx = 0.3 × 20 − 0 = 6 N·m, counterclockwise.

qs.q: Two nonzero vectors have a dot product of zero. What does that tell you?
qs.ans: They are perpendicular
wrong: They are parallel
One must be a unit vector
Their cross product is zero
qs.why: cos 90° = 0. Perpendicular vectors have the largest cross product, not zero.

qs.q: For a fixed wrench length and force, rank these force angles to the wrench by moment produced, largest first.
qs.why: Moment = rF sin θ: 1, 0.87, 0.5 and 0 times rF.

demo.title: Dot versus cross
demo.hint: At 0° the dot product is largest and the cross is zero; at 90° it flips. Work follows the dot, turning follows the cross.

p.cap: the result is a scalar

p.x: It measures how much one vector points along the other. Work is one: $W = F·d$. A constant 10 N force, 2 m of motion:
Only the part of F along d does work: $W = F d cos θ$

g.q: Now push at 90° to the motion. The work done is…
o: zero
cos 90° = 0: none of the force points along the motion.
still 20 J
Only the part of F along d counts, and at 90° that part is zero.
negative
Negative work needs θ above 90°, with the force partly against the motion. At exactly 90°, cos θ = 0.

p.x: The cross product $a × b$ is a vector [[perpendicular]] to both a and b.

p.cap: θ: angle between a and b; direction by the right-hand rule

p.x: Moment is one: $M = r × F$, with r from the pivot to where F acts.

p.l: 20 N at 90°, 0.8 m from a hinge

p.x: Dot uses the part of b along a; cross uses the part of b across a.
Push a door along its own plane, toward the hinge: F lines up with r, so sin θ = 0 and nothing turns.

p.cap: z-value of r × F, with x right and y up

p.lab: Bar from a pin at the origin to (1, 0)

p.x: Positive M_z: counterclockwise. Negative: clockwise.

g.q: The force pushes up on the bar's right end. It turns the bar…
o: counterclockwise
Pushing up on the right end swings it up and to the left. M_z = 1·10 − 0·0 = +10 N·m, and positive means counterclockwise.
clockwise
Clockwise needs the right end pushed down (F_y < 0), which makes M_z negative.

cards: In MATLAB everything is a matrix. A scalar is 1×1, a row vector 1×n. x = 0:0.5:2 makes [0 0.5 1 1.5 2].
Indexing starts at 1, not 0. x(1) is the first element, x(end) the last, and x(2:3) a slice.
Why semicolons matter: ending a line with ; hides its output. Leave it off and MATLAB prints the result, which floods the console in loops.
linspace(a, b, n) gives exactly n evenly spaced points, which is handy for plotting.
title: Arrays and indexing

qs.q: How many elements does 0:0.25:2 contain?
qs.why: (2 − 0)/0.25 + 1 = 9 elements, counting both ends.

wrong: An index error
qs.why: MATLAB indexing starts at 1, so x(2) is the second element.

qs.q: x = [5 6 7 8 9]. What does x(end-1) return?
qs.why: end is the last index (5), so end − 1 is index 4, which holds 8.

qs.q: What does size(zeros(3, 5)) return?
qs.why: zeros(3, 5) has 3 rows and 5 columns; size returns rows then columns.

qs.q: x = linspace(0, 10, 6). What is x(3)?
qs.why: Six points from 0 to 10 are spaced by 2: [0 2 4 6 8 10]. The third is 4.

demo.title: Colon ranges and linspace
demo.hint: start:step:stop counts how many steps fit, so the last value may stop short. linspace fixes the count instead and always lands on the end.

cards: * is matrix multiplication; .* is element by element. The same goes for / versus ./ and ^ versus .^.
For vectors x and y of the same size, x.*y multiplies matching entries. x*y fails unless the inner dimensions agree.
Why it bites: y = x^2 on a row vector errors, because it asks for x*x. Write x.^2 to square each element.
Transpose with '. A row times a column, x*x', gives a scalar: the sum of squares.
title: Element-wise operators

qs.q: x = [1 2 3]. Which line squares every element?
wrong: x*x
qs.why: .^ works element by element. x^2 and x*x try matrix multiplication of a 1×3 by a 1×3, which errors.

qs.q: x = [1 2 3]. What is x*x'?
qs.why: A 1×3 times a 3×1 gives a scalar: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.

qs.q: x = [1 2 3]. What is the size of x'*x?
qs.why: A 3×1 times a 1×3 is an outer product: a 3×3 matrix.

qs.q: a = [2 4 6] and b = [1 2 3]. What is a./b?
wrong: An error
qs.why: ./ divides matching entries: 2/1, 4/2, 6/3.

qs.q: For x = [1 2 3], rank these by the number of elements in the result, most first.

demo.title: Result sizes of vector products
demo.hint: For a 1×n row x: x*x' collapses to one number, x.*x stays n long, and x'*x blows up to n×n. Matrix rules depend on inner dimensions; dotted ones need equal sizes.

cards: Vectorized code acts on whole arrays at once: y = sin(x) instead of a loop. It is shorter and usually much faster.
A comparison like x > 5 returns a logical array of 1s and 0s. Use it as a mask: x(x > 5) keeps only the matching values.
Why preallocate: growing an array inside a loop, y(end+1) = …, copies it every time. y = zeros(1, n) first avoids that.
sum, mean, max and cumsum work along a dimension. sum(x > 5) counts how many values pass the test.
title: Vectorizing and logical masks

qs.q: x = [3 8 1 9 6]. What does sum(x > 5) return?
qs.why: x > 5 is [0 1 0 1 1], whose sum counts the 3 values above 5.

qs.q: x = [3 8 1 9 6]. What does x(x > 5) return?
qs.why: The logical mask selects the values themselves. find(x > 5) would return the indices [2 4 5].

qs.q: Why does preallocating with zeros(1, n) speed up a loop?
qs.ans: The array isn’t copied each time it grows
wrong: Zeros are faster to multiply than other values
It turns the loop into vectorized code
MATLAB skips type checks on zero arrays
qs.why: Without preallocation, every growth step may reallocate and copy the whole array.

qs.q: x = [3 8 1 9 6]. Which line sets every value below 5 to zero?
wrong: x = x < 5
qs.why: Masked assignment changes only the selected entries. x = x < 5 replaces x with logicals; == only compares.

qs.q: x = [1 2 3 4]. What is the last element of cumsum(x)?
qs.why: cumsum gives running totals [1 3 6 10]; the last is the total sum.

demo.title: Thresholding a signal
demo.hint: A mask like x > t is just a test applied to every sample. Raise the threshold and fewer samples pass; the count is what sum(x > t) returns.

cards: Solve A x = b with x = A \ b. Backslash picks a good method and is faster and more accurate than inv(A)*b.
If A is tall (more equations than unknowns), A \ b gives the least-squares solution: the best fit to all equations at once.
Why that fits lines: for y ≈ m t + c, stack [t, ones] as A, and A \ y returns [m; c]. polyfit(t, y, 1) does the same.
Check conditioning with cond(A). A huge value means tiny input changes cause big swings in x, so trust the result less.
title: Solving systems and fitting

qs.q: Which is the recommended way to solve A x = b in MATLAB?
qs.ans: x = A \ b
wrong: x = inv(A) * b
x = b / A
x = A .\ b
qs.why: Backslash solves the system directly. Forming inv(A) is slower and loses accuracy.

qs.q: A = [2 0; 0 4] and b = [6; 8]. What is the second element of A \ b?
qs.why: The system is diagonal: 2x₁ = 6 and 4x₂ = 8, so x = [3; 2].

qs.q: A has 50 rows and 2 columns. What does A \ y return?
qs.ans: The least-squares fit for 2 unknowns
wrong: An error, since A isn’t a square matrix
A 50-element vector of residuals
The exact solution of all 50 rows
qs.why: With more equations than unknowns, backslash minimizes the squared error.

qs.q: p = polyfit(t, y, 1). What is p(1)?
qs.ans: The slope
wrong: The intercept
The R² value
The first residual
qs.why: polyfit returns coefficients from the highest power down, so p(1) is the slope and p(2) the intercept.

qs.q: Rank these matrices from most to least trustworthy to solve, by condition number.
qs.why: Lower condition numbers amplify errors less. Near 10¹⁶ the matrix is effectively singular in double precision.

demo.title: Ill-conditioned systems
demo.hint: A = [1 1; 1 1+ε]. As ε shrinks the two rows become nearly the same equation, and cond(A) explodes: small errors in b swing x wildly.

cards: Stress σ = F/A is force per area, in MPa. Strain ε = ΔL/L is stretch per length, with no units.
In the elastic region they are proportional: σ = E ε. Young’s modulus E is a material property: about 200 GPa for steel, 70 for aluminum, 3 for nylon.
Why E is not strength: E sets how much a part deflects, not when it breaks. A hardened steel and a mild steel have nearly the same E.
Example: a 100 MPa stress in steel gives ε = 100/200,000 = 0.0005, so a 1 m bar stretches 0.5 mm.
title: Stress, strain and stiffness

qs.q: A 10 kN load acts on a rod with a 50 mm² cross-section. What is the stress, in MPa?
Aluminum (E = 70 GPa) carries 140 MPa. What is the strain?
A steel bracket deflects too much under load but never yields. Which change helps least?
qs.ans: Switch to a stronger alloy steel
wrong: Make the cross-section deeper
Switch to a material with a higher E
Shorten the unsupported span
qs.why: All steels have E near 200 GPa, so a stronger steel deflects the same. Depth, span and modulus set the deflection.

qs.q: A 2 m bar stretches 1 mm under load. What is the strain?
Rank these materials by Young’s modulus, highest first.
qs.why: About 200, 110, 70 and 3 GPa.

demo.title: Same load, different materials
demo.hint: Stretch is F·L/(A·E). Swap steel for aluminum and the rod stretches about three times as much, even if both stay well below yield.

p.x: **Stress**: force per unit area, in MPa.
**Strain**: stretch per unit length.
Strain is a length over a length, so it has no units. A stress in MPa is newtons per square millimetre.
In the elastic region, stress is [[proportional]] to strain.

p.cap: elastic region, load along one axis

p.x: Same stress, about 3× the strain in aluminum as in steel: $ε = σ/E$.
For a given shape and load, $E$ sets how much a part deflects. Strength sets the stress at which it yields or breaks.
Hardening raises strength, not stiffness. To deflect less, change the shape or the kind of material.

g.q: Harden a steel shaft so its yield strength rises 5×. Under the same load, it deflects…
o: about a fifth as much
That mixes up strength with stiffness. Deflection depends on E, and hardening barely changes E.
about the same
Deflection depends on E, which stays about 200 GPa. Only the stress it can take before yielding goes up.

p.x: 100 MPa is below the yield strength of common steels, so the bar springs back to 1,000 mm when unloaded.

cards: The stress-strain curve is straight up to the yield strength. Past it, the material deforms permanently.
Ultimate tensile strength is the peak stress. After it, a ductile bar necks down and breaks; elongation at break measures ductility.
Why design to yield: a part that has yielded no longer fits or works, even though it hasn’t broken. Safety factor = yield strength / working stress.
Brittle materials such as cast iron, glass and ceramics barely yield, so they break with little warning.
title: Yield, ultimate and ductility

qs.q: A shaft has a yield strength of 350 MPa and sees 140 MPa. What is the safety factor against yield?
A bolt is loaded past its yield strength but below its ultimate strength, then unloaded. What happens?
qs.ans: It stays permanently stretched
wrong: It returns to its original length
It snaps as soon as it is unloaded
It gets shorter than it started
qs.why: Past yield, part of the strain is plastic. Unloading recovers only the elastic part.

qs.q: Which property best measures how much warning a part gives before it fractures?
qs.ans: Elongation at break
wrong: Young’s modulus
Ultimate tensile strength
Density
qs.why: High elongation means the part bends and stretches visibly before breaking.

qs.q: Required safety factor is 2 and yield strength is 250 MPa. What is the maximum allowed working stress, in MPa?
Rank these by typical elongation at break, most ductile first.
qs.why: Roughly 45%, 25%, 12% and under 1%.

demo.title: Stress-strain curve
demo.hint: Linear up to yield, then the curve flattens and rises to the ultimate strength. Steeper start means stiffer; a longer tail means more ductile. Curve shape is idealized.

p.x: On a stress–strain curve, stress first rises in a straight line, with slope $E$: the elastic region.
The **yield strength** $σ_y$ ends that line. Unload below it and the bar returns to its original length.
Unloaded from past yield, it springs back along a line parallel to the elastic one and keeps a permanent stretch: plastic strain.

g.q: Stretch a steel bar past yield, then take the load off. Its length…
o: returns to the original
That's true only below yield. Past it, part of the stretch is plastic and stays.
stays a little longer
Only the elastic part springs back; the plastic stretch stays.

p.x: **Ultimate tensile strength** $σ_{uts}$ is the peak of the curve: the highest stress the bar carries.
After the peak, a ductile bar thins in one spot, called necking, and breaks there.
**Elongation at break** measures ductility.
A part that has yielded is bent for good: it may no longer fit or work, even though it hasn't broken. So design checks it against yield.

p.cap: steady load, ductile material

p.x: Bracket: $σ_y$ = 250 MPa, working stress 100 MPa.
Codes and companies set the $n$ a part must reach.
Brittle materials such as cast iron, glass and ceramics barely yield, so they break with [[little warning]].

p.c: gray cast iron, stretch at break

p.x: With no yield to design to, brittle parts are checked against ultimate strength, with larger safety factors.

cards: Material indices compare candidates for a job. For a light, stiff tie rod, rank by E/ρ; for a light, stiff beam, by √E/ρ.
Why the beam index differs: a beam can be made deeper to gain stiffness, so a low-density material can afford a thicker section.
E/ρ is nearly the same for steel, aluminum and titanium, about 25 MPa·m³/kg. In bending panels, aluminum and magnesium pull ahead.
Real choices add cost, corrosion, joining and manufacturability. Indices just shrink the list.
title: Picking materials by index

qs.q: Steel has E = 200 GPa and ρ = 7850 kg/m³. What is E/ρ, in MPa·m³/kg?
For a light, stiff tie rod in tension, which material ranks highest?
qs.ans: Carbon-fiber composite
wrong: Aluminum alloy 6061-T6
Structural steel
Titanium Ti-6Al-4V
qs.why: Composite E/ρ is several times higher, about 100 versus 25 for the three metals, which are nearly equal.

qs.q: Why does aluminum beat steel for a light, stiff panel in bending but not for a rod in tension?
qs.ans: Bending rewards low density more, via √E/ρ
wrong: Aluminum is stiffer than steel when it bends
Steel is weak in bending specifically
Panels see much lower loads than rods do
qs.why: Stiffness grows with thickness cubed, so a lighter material can be made thicker. The √E/ρ index captures that.

qs.q: Aluminum: E = 70 GPa, ρ = 2700 kg/m³. Steel: E = 200 GPa, ρ = 7850 kg/m³. What is aluminum’s √E/ρ divided by steel’s? Use E in GPa.
qs.why: √70/2700 = 0.00310 and √200/7850 = 0.00180, a ratio of about 1.72: aluminum gives about 70% more bending stiffness per kilogram.

qs.q: Rank these by density, highest first.

demo.title: Stiffness per kilogram
demo.hint: Switch between a tie rod (E/ρ) and a beam (√E/ρ). In tension the metals tie; in bending the light metals pull ahead.

p.x: A **material index** ranks candidate materials for one job. Higher is better.

p.cap: set length and stiffness, lowest mass
square section free to grow, set length and stiffness

p.x: Keep the length and the needed stiffness fixed, and switch to a material with a quarter of the $E$.
A square beam's $I$ grows as $A^2$, so its stiffness does too. A low-density material can afford the thicker section: beam mass ∝ $ρ/√{E}$.

g.q: With a quarter of the E, a square beam needs how much more area to stay as stiff?
o: That's the tie rod, where stiffness ∝ EA. A beam's stiffness goes as EI, and I grows with area squared.
Stiffness ∝ EA² for a square beam, so A² must rise 4× and A only 2×.

p.x: For tie rods, the common metals score almost the same on $E/ρ$:
Panel index $E^{1/3}/ρ$, length and width fixed, thickness free: stiffness grows with thickness cubed, so a low density buys a much thicker sheet for the same mass.

g.q: A light, stiff panel in bending. Against steel, aluminum scores…
o: about the same
That's the tie-rod index E/ρ. In bending, thickness counts cubed, so low density pays off.
about 2× better
The panel index is E^{1/3}/ρ: aluminum 1.53 against steel 0.75.

p.x: An index ranks one need, such as stiffness per kilogram.
Real choices add cost, corrosion, joining and how the part will be made.

Unidirectional carbon-fiber composite (CFRP), loaded along its fibers, beats aluminum on the beam index by more than 2×. But it costs far more, is weak across the fibers and is usually bonded or bolted, not welded.
Use indices to shrink the list, then judge the few that remain on everything else.

cards: Fatigue is failure under repeated loads well below yield. Cracks start at stress raisers such as holes, scratches and sharp corners, and grow each cycle.
An S-N curve plots stress amplitude against cycles to failure. Many steels have an endurance limit, around half the ultimate strength for polished samples.
Why aluminum needs care: it has no true endurance limit, so any cyclic stress eventually causes failure. Aircraft parts get finite design lives.
Real parts last less than test samples: surface finish, size and notches cut the endurance limit, often by half or more.
title: Fatigue and endurance

qs.q: A polished steel sample has an ultimate strength of 600 MPa. Using the half rule, what is its estimated endurance limit, in MPa?
qs.why: About 0.5 × 600 = 300 MPa for a polished test specimen.

qs.q: A shaft breaks after years of service at a stress well below yield, at a sharp shoulder. What is the most likely cause?
qs.ans: Fatigue starting at the stress raiser
wrong: Static overload of the shaft section
Creep from the shaft’s operating temperature
Low Young’s modulus of the steel
qs.why: Cyclic loading plus a sharp corner is the classic fatigue setup. Fatigue failures happen below yield after many cycles.

qs.q: Which change most improves fatigue life at a shaft shoulder?
qs.ans: A larger fillet radius at the shoulder
wrong: A stiffer material with the same strength
A rougher, machined surface finish
A sharper corner to save material
qs.why: A larger radius lowers the stress concentration, which slows crack initiation.

qs.q: Why are aluminum aircraft parts given finite fatigue lives?
qs.ans: Aluminum has no true endurance limit
wrong: Aluminum yields at very low stress
Aluminum corrodes in every environment
Aluminum’s modulus drops with each cycle
qs.why: Its S-N curve keeps falling, so cyclic stress eventually causes a crack. Parts are inspected and retired on schedule.

qs.q: Rank these by fatigue strength for the same steel part, highest first.
qs.why: Smoother surfaces have fewer crack starters; shot peening adds compressive stress that slows cracks.

demo.title: S-N curve
demo.hint: Lower the stress amplitude and the life grows by orders of magnitude. Steel flattens at its endurance limit; a surface factor below 1 drops the whole curve. Basquin-style model, illustrative.

p.x: **Fatigue**: failure under repeated loads, which can happen at stresses [[well below]] yield.
Cracks start at stress raisers such as holes, scratches and sharp corners.
An **S–N curve** plots stress amplitude $S$ against cycles to failure $N$, with $N$ on a log scale. Lower stress, longer life.
Many steels level off at an **endurance limit** $S_e$. Below it, a test sample survives 10^6–10^7 cycles, and design treats that as infinite life (steady amplitude, no corrosion).

p.cap: polished steel samples in rotating bending, σ_{uts} up to about 1,400 MPa

g.q: For polished steel samples, the endurance limit is about…
o: the yield strength
Fatigue cracks grow at stresses well below yield, so the endurance limit sits lower.
half the ultimate strength
For polished steel samples, S_e ≈ 0.5 σ_uts, up to about 1,400 MPa.
a tenth of ultimate
Too low for a polished sample. Notches, rough surfaces and corrosion can pull a real part down a long way, but the sample's limit is about half.

p.x: Aluminum's S–N curve never levels off: at every stress amplitude its life is [[finite]], though it can be very long.
So aluminum gets a fatigue strength at a stated life, often 5×10^8 cycles, and aircraft parts get finite design lives with inspections.
$S_e$ comes from small polished samples. A real part is rougher, bigger and notched, and each of these lowers its endurance limit.
Machined steel shaft in rotating bending, 25 mm diameter, $σ_{uts}$ = 600 MPa:
At a shoulder with fatigue notch factor $K_f$ = 2, the local stress doubles:
Estimated endurance limit at the shoulder: about 110 MPa of nominal stress amplitude, at 50 % reliability. Less than half the sample's 300.

cards: C has fixed-size types. On most microcontrollers and PCs, `uint8_t` holds 0–255, `int16_t` −32,768 to 32,767, `int32_t` about ±2.1 billion.
Integer division truncates toward zero: `7 / 2` is 3, and `-7 / 2` is −3. `7 % 2` gives the remainder, 1.
Why overflow matters: unsigned values wrap around, so `uint8_t x = 250; x += 10;` gives 4. Signed overflow is undefined behavior.
Mixed math promotes: `7 / 2.0` is 3.5 because one operand is a double.
title: Types and integer math

qs.q: In C, what is `17 / 5`?
qs.why: Integer division drops the fraction: 3.4 becomes 3.

qs.q: `uint8_t x = 200; x = x + 100;` What is x?
qs.why: 300 does not fit in 0–255, so it wraps: 300 − 256 = 44.

qs.q: What does `(float)7 / 2` evaluate to?
qs.why: The cast makes 7 a float before dividing, so the division is floating-point.

qs.q: How many distinct values can a 12-bit ADC reading take?
qs.why: 2¹² = 4096 values, from 0 to 4095.

qs.q: Rank these types by the largest value they can hold, largest first.
qs.why: About 4.29 billion, 2.15 billion, 65,535 and 127.

cards: A pointer holds a memory address. `int *p = &x;` stores x’s address; `*p` reads or writes x through it.
An array name acts like a pointer to its first element. `a[i]` means `*(a + i)`, and `a + i` moves i elements, not i bytes.
Why C crashes: nothing checks array bounds. Writing `a[10]` in a 10-element array silently overwrites whatever sits next in memory.
Pass a pointer to let a function change the caller’s variable: `void inc(int *n) { (*n)++; }`.
title: Pointers and arrays

qs.q: `int x = 5; int *p = &x; *p = 9;` What is x now?
wrong: The address of x
Undefined
qs.why: *p refers to x itself, so writing through p changes x.
a + 2 points to a[2], which holds 30.

qs.q: An `int32_t` array starts at address 1000. At what address is element 3?
qs.why: Each element is 4 bytes: 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012.

qs.q: Why doesn’t `void inc(int n) { n++; }` change the caller’s variable?
qs.ans: C passes a copy of the value
wrong: n++ only works on pointers
The function must return void*
Local variables can’t be changed
qs.why: Arguments are passed by value. To change the caller’s variable, pass its address.

Why not `reg = (1 << n)`: plain assignment wipes every other bit in the register, turning off things you didn’t mean to touch.

In parallel, every branch sees the same voltage and conductances add: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. For two resistors, R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Why parallel is always smaller: each branch is another path for current, so the total resistance falls below the smallest branch.
Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value: two 1 kΩ make 500 Ω.

cards: Kirchhoff’s current law: currents into a node sum to zero. Voltage law: voltages around any loop sum to zero.
A voltage divider gives Vout = Vin × R₂/(R₁ + R₂), with R₂ the bottom resistor. It is how sensors and level shifters often work.
Why loads break dividers: a load in parallel with R₂ lowers the bottom resistance, so Vout sags. Keep the load at least 10× R₂.

cards: Power is P = VI = I²R = V²/R. A resistor’s power rating, such as ¼ W, is how much heat it can shed without overheating.
Wires have resistance too. Loss in a wire is I²R, so doubling the current quadruples the heat.
Why high-voltage transmission: for the same power, raising V lowers I, and wire loss falls with I². Ten times the voltage cuts loss 100-fold.
Derate: run parts at about half their rating to keep them cool and long-lived.

wrong: It falls to 1/10
It stays the same
It rises 10 times
qs.why: Current falls 10×, and loss goes as I², so it falls 100×.

wrong: Add a second identical one in series with it

Leave it, since it is under its rating

o: yes
P = V²/R = 100/100 = 1 W, four times the rating.
no

cards: Any linear two-terminal circuit acts like one voltage source in series with one resistor: Vth and Rth.
Find Vth as the open-circuit voltage, and Rth by zeroing sources (shorting voltage sources) and looking back into the terminals.
Why it helps: a battery’s sag under load, a sensor’s output impedance and a divider’s loading are all Rth problems.
Load power peaks when RL = Rth, with efficiency then only 50%. Power systems avoid this; RF and audio sometimes match on purpose.
title: Thévenin and max power

qs.q: A 12 V source with R₁ = 4 kΩ on top and R₂ = 4 kΩ on the bottom. What is the Thévenin resistance at the output, in kΩ?
qs.why: Short the source: R₁ ∥ R₂ = 4 × 4 / 8 = 2 kΩ.

qs.q: A battery reads 9.0 V open-circuit and 8.4 V while supplying 0.3 A. What is its internal resistance, in Ω?
A source has Vth = 10 V and Rth = 5 Ω. Which load gets the most power?
qs.ans: 5 Ω
qs.why: Maximum power transfer happens when RL = Rth.

qs.q: Why don’t power grids match the load to the source resistance?
qs.ans: Matching wastes half the power in the source
wrong: Matched loads draw no current at all
Grids have no source resistance to match
Matching only works for AC signals at radio frequencies
qs.why: At RL = Rth, efficiency is 50%. Grids want high efficiency, so RL is much larger than Rth.

qs.q: Vth = 10 V and Rth = 5 Ω feed a 5 Ω load. How much power does the load get, in W?
qs.why: I = 10/10 = 1 A, and P = I²RL = 5 W.

demo.hint: Load power peaks where RL equals Rth, but efficiency there is only 50%. Make the load larger and efficiency climbs while power falls.

equal to $R_{th}$

cards: Pressure in a still fluid grows with depth: p = p₀ + ρgh. Only depth matters, not the container’s shape.
Water adds about 9.81 kPa per meter, so 10 m of water is roughly one atmosphere, 101 kPa.
Why gauge pressure: tire and tank gauges read pressure above atmospheric. Absolute = gauge + about 101 kPa.
Pressure pushes equally in all directions at a point, so dam walls and tank bottoms see the most load.

qs.q: What is the gauge pressure 5 m below the surface of fresh water, in kPa? Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
A tall thin tube and a wide tank are filled with water to the same height. Which has the higher pressure at the bottom?
qs.ans: Both are the same
wrong: The wide tank
The thin tube
It depends on the volume of each
qs.why: Hydrostatic pressure depends only on depth, density and g.

qs.q: A tire gauge reads 220 kPa. What is the absolute pressure, in kPa? Use 101 kPa for the atmosphere.

qs.q: At the same depth, which fluid gives the highest pressure?
qs.ans: Mercury
wrong: Seawater
Fresh water
Oil

qs.why: About 196, 133, 98 and 83 kPa.

cards: Volume flow rate Q = A × V, in m³/s. For an incompressible fluid in a pipe, Q is the same at every section.
So A₁V₁ = A₂V₂: where the pipe narrows, the fluid speeds up. Halve the diameter and the area drops 4×, so speed rises 4×.
Why nozzles work: a garden hose nozzle shrinks the exit area, so the same flow leaves much faster.
Mass flow ṁ = ρQ. For gases with changing density, it is mass flow that stays constant.

A pipe splits into two identical branches. How does the speed in each branch compare to the main pipe, if each branch has half the main pipe’s area?

wrong: Half the speed
Twice the speed
Four times the speed

wrong: Volume flow rate

cards: Along a streamline in steady, frictionless, incompressible flow: p + ½ρV² + ρgz is constant.

Why diameter matters so much: at fixed flow, V ∝ 1/D², so Δp ∝ 1/D⁵ in turbulent flow. A slightly larger pipe saves a lot of pump power.
Water at 1 m/s in a 25 mm pipe gives Re ≈ 25,000: turbulent, as most plumbing is.

o: Lowers it

Raises it

Leaves it unchanged

p.x: For developed laminar flow in a round pipe, the Darcy factor $f$ varies [[inversely]] with Reynolds number.

cards: Thrust comes from pushing mass backward: F = ṁ(Ve − V₀), plus a pressure term if the exhaust isn’t at ambient pressure.
ṁ is mass flow, Ve the exhaust speed, V₀ the flight speed. A rocket carries all its propellant, so V₀ drops out: F = ṁVe.
Why big fans: the same thrust comes from a lot of air pushed gently or a little air pushed hard. Gentle is far more efficient.
Example: 100 kg/s of air sped up from 200 to 500 m/s gives 30 kN.
title: Thrust from momentum

wrong: The engine burns less fuel per second
The intake air gets denser with speed
The nozzle area grows with speed

wrong: The one moving less air much faster
Both waste exactly the same energy
Whichever burns its fuel hotter

cards: Specific impulse Isp is thrust per unit weight flow of propellant, in seconds: Isp = F/(ṁg₀) = Ve/g₀, with g₀ = 9.81 m/s².
Higher Isp means more momentum per kilogram of propellant. Solid rockets reach about 250 s, kerosene-oxygen about 300–350 s, hydrogen-oxygen about 450 s.
Why ion engines are different: Isp of 1500–4000 s, but thrust of only millinewtons. Great for long missions, useless for launch.
Jets breathe air, so their Isp is several thousand seconds: only the fuel counts as propellant.

qs.q: An engine has Isp = 300 s. What is its effective exhaust speed, in m/s? Use g₀ = 9.81.

qs.ans: Their thrust is far below the rocket’s weight
wrong: They only work inside a perfect vacuum chamber
Their exhaust speed is too low for orbit
They need oxygen from the air to run
qs.why: Launch needs thrust greater than weight. Ion engines give millinewtons.

qs.q: Why does a turbofan have a much higher Isp than a rocket?
qs.ans: It carries only fuel; air is free mass
wrong: Its exhaust is much faster than a rocket’s
It burns its fuel at a higher temperature
It runs at a higher chamber pressure
qs.why: Isp counts only carried propellant. Most of a jet’s reaction mass is atmospheric air.

qs.why: Roughly 3000, 450, 330 and 250 s.

cards: The rocket equation Δv = Ve ln(m₀/mf) punishes dead weight: empty tanks keep being accelerated after their propellant is gone.
Staging drops empty structure partway up. Each stage’s Δv adds, and each uses a mass ratio for just its own part of the stack.
Why not one big stage: with 10% structure, a single stage tops out near Δv = Ve ln 10 ≈ 2.3 Ve, even with no payload.
Low orbit needs about 9.4 km/s including losses, more than a single kerosene stage can reasonably give.

wrong: Each stage gets a higher exhaust speed
Engines run more efficiently when lit late
Gravity losses vanish after staging

qs.ans: About 6.9 km/s
wrong: About 9.4 km/s
About 3.0 km/s
About 30 km/s

cards: A turbofan splits intake air: the core burns fuel, the bypass stream is pushed by the fan only. Bypass ratio = bypass flow / core flow.
Propulsive efficiency ≈ 2/(1 + Ve/V₀). It rises as the exhaust speed approaches the flight speed.
Why airliners use bypass ratios of 9–12: a big, slow jet stream makes thrust with less waste. Fighters use about 0.3–1 for compact size and high speed.
The limit is fan diameter: weight, drag, ground clearance and fan-tip speed cap how big it can get.
title: Bypass ratio and efficiency

qs.q: A jet flies at 250 m/s with an average exhaust speed of 350 m/s. What is its propulsive efficiency, in %?
A turbofan has a core flow of 50 kg/s and a bypass flow of 500 kg/s. What is its bypass ratio?
Why do fighters use low bypass ratios despite worse fuel economy?
qs.ans: A small, fast jet suits high speed and drag
wrong: Big fans can’t make useful thrust above Mach 0.5
Low-bypass engines weigh far less per newton
Afterburners only fit high-bypass engines
qs.why: At high flight speed a fast jet is needed, and a small frontal area keeps drag down.

qs.q: What happens to propulsive efficiency as exhaust speed falls toward flight speed?
qs.ans: It approaches 100%, but thrust approaches zero
wrong: It falls toward zero along with the thrust it makes
It stays constant while thrust drops
It rises past 100% at very low speeds
qs.why: η = 2/(1 + Ve/V₀) → 1 as Ve → V₀, but thrust ∝ (Ve − V₀) vanishes. Hence huge fans to move lots of air.

qs.q: Rank these engines by typical bypass ratio, highest first.

demo.title: Propulsive efficiency
demo.hint: Bring the exhaust speed down toward flight speed and efficiency rises toward 100%, while thrust per kilogram of air shrinks. Real engines balance the two.

flag.yes: No thrust: exhaust slower than flight

p.x: A turbofan splits the air it takes in. The **core** stream goes through the compressor, burners and turbine.
The **bypass** stream goes around the core, pushed by the fan alone.
Bypass ratio = bypass flow ÷ core flow. A ratio of 10 sends 10 kg around the core for each 1 kg through it.

A slower jet gives less thrust per kilogram, but it leaves less energy in the wake, so efficiency rises.

p.x: A high bypass ratio moves a lot of air in a big, slow jet, making thrust with less waste.
A low-bypass engine is slim, and its fast jet still makes thrust at high flight speed.
