To keep tip speed down, a bigger fan has to turn [[slower]]. Some engines put a gearbox between fan and turbine for that.

cards: Sheet metal parts are cut flat, then bent on a press brake. The inside of a bend compresses and the outside stretches.
Somewhere between them is the neutral axis, which keeps its length. It sits at a fraction K of the thickness from the inside, typically K ≈ 0.3–0.5.
Why the inside radius matters: too tight a radius cracks the outside of the bend. A common minimum is about one material thickness.
Bend lines across the rolling direction (the grain) crack less than bends along it.
title: Bending basics

qs.q: During a bend, which side of the sheet stretches?
qs.ans: The outside of the bend
wrong: The inside of the bend
Neither side changes length
Both sides stretch equally
qs.why: The outside goes the long way round and is in tension; the inside is compressed.

qs.q: Sheet thickness is 2 mm and K = 0.4. How far is the neutral axis from the inside surface, in mm?
A 3 mm aluminum bracket cracks along the outside of a bend. What is the best first fix?
qs.ans: Increase the inside bend radius
wrong: Decrease the inside bend radius
Bend it faster on the press brake
Use a thinner punch tip on the brake
qs.why: A larger radius lowers the strain on the outer fibers.

qs.q: Which bend orientation is least likely to crack?
qs.ans: Bend line across the grain
wrong: Bend line along the grain
Bend line at exactly 0° to the grain
Grain makes no difference to bending
qs.why: Bending across the rolling direction stretches fibers along their strong direction.

qs.q: For the same sheet, rank these inside radii by strain on the outer surface, highest first.
qs.why: Outer strain ≈ 1/(2R/t + 1): about 50%, 33%, 20% and 11%.

cards: After bending, the elastic part of the strain recovers, so the part springs open a little. Brakes overbend to compensate.
Springback grows with yield strength over modulus, and with R/t. High-strength steel and aluminum spring back more than mild steel.
Why flanges need a minimum length: the press brake die needs something to push against. A rule of thumb is at least about 4 × t plus R.
Holes too close to a bend distort into ovals. Keep them about 2.5 t plus R from the bend line.

For the same R/t, springback grows with yield strength over modulus, Sy/E. Typical values: 7075-T6 aluminum 500 MPa / 70 GPa ≈ 7.1. Spring steel about 1000 / 200 = 5.0 (harder grades go higher). Mild steel 250 / 200 = 1.25. Annealed copper: 70 / 117 ≈ 0.6. Strong but flexible metals spring back most.

qs.ans: High-strength aluminum
wrong: Annealed copper sheet

Soft, annealed aluminum

cards: A neuron computes a weighted sum plus a bias, z = w·x + b, then applies an activation: a = f(z).
Common activations: ReLU, max(0, z); sigmoid, 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ), between 0 and 1; tanh, between −1 and 1.
Why activations matter: without them, stacked layers collapse into one linear map. Nonlinearity lets a network bend its decision boundary.
A dense layer from n inputs to m outputs has n × m weights plus m biases.
title: Neurons and activations

wrong: Any smooth function, given enough units
Only functions with outputs between 0 and 1
The same functions as five ReLU layers

wrong: ReLU

cards: Training adjusts each weight against its gradient: w ← w − η ∂L/∂w. Backpropagation computes all these gradients with the chain rule, layer by layer.
The learning rate η sets the step size. Too small crawls; too large overshoots the minimum and the loss bounces or explodes.
Why gradients vanish: sigmoid’s slope is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can shrink a gradient by 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶. ReLU avoids this for positive inputs.
Mini-batches estimate the gradient from a sample of data: noisier steps, but far cheaper and often better at escaping bad spots.

wrong: The model has too few parameters
The validation set is too small
The learning rate is too low
qs.why: Steps that overshoot the minimum make the loss oscillate or diverge.

qs.why: 0.25⁶ ≈ 0.000244: vanishing gradients.

qs.ans: Each step is much cheaper to compute
wrong: Full-batch gradients are mathematically wrong
Mini-batches remove the need for a learning rate
Small batches give a lower final loss by design
qs.why: A sampled gradient is cheap and good enough; many cheap steps beat a few expensive exact ones.

cards: A convolutional layer slides small filters across an image. Each filter has k × k × C_in weights plus a bias, reused at every position.
Output size for input N, kernel k, padding p and stride s: (N + 2p − k)/s + 1.
Why share weights: an edge is an edge anywhere in the image. Sharing cuts parameters by orders of magnitude compared with a dense layer.
Stacking 3×3 layers grows the receptive field: two give 5×5, three give 7×7, with fewer weights than one big kernel.

wrong: It sees a larger area of the image than one 7×7 can
It needs no padding at all to keep the image the same size
It removes the need for any pooling layers
qs.why: 3 × 9C² = 27C² weights versus 49C², with an activation after each layer.

cards: Edge deployment fights memory and compute. A model’s weight memory is parameters × bytes per parameter: 4 for float32, 1 for int8.
Quantizing to int8 cuts memory 4× and often speeds inference on chips with integer units, usually costing under 1% accuracy if calibrated.
Why compute often limits more than memory: a conv layer’s multiply-accumulates are H_out × W_out × k² × C_in × C_out, far more than its weights.
Pruning removes small weights; distillation trains a small student to mimic a large teacher. Both trade a little accuracy for speed.
title: Deploying models on hardware

qs.why: 1 byte per parameter: 5 MB, a 4× reduction.

qs.q: A conv layer outputs 56×56, with a 3×3 kernel, 64 input and 64 output channels. How many millions of multiply-accumulates does it take?
A microcontroller has 256 kB of RAM and the int8 model needs 400 kB. Which step helps most directly?
qs.ans: Prune or distill to a smaller model
wrong: Convert the weights back to float32
Increase the batch size used at inference
Raise the learning rate and retrain
qs.why: The model must shrink. float32 makes it 4× bigger; batch size and learning rate don’t change weight memory.

qs.q: Rank these by weight memory for a 10-million-parameter model, most first.

demo.title: Fitting a model on a chip
demo.hint: Weight memory is parameters × bytes. Quantizing from float32 to int8 is a 4× cut. The flag shows whether the weights fit in the chip’s memory.

cards: Integral action sums error over time, so any steady error keeps pushing the output until the error is zero. It removes P-only offset.
Too much integral gain adds overshoot and oscillation: the integral keeps pushing after the error has already crossed zero.
Why windup happens: if the actuator saturates (a heater at 100%), the integral keeps growing. When the error flips, it takes ages to unwind.
Anti-windup clamps the integral, or stops integrating, while the output is saturated.
title: Integral action and windup

qs.q: A P-only temperature loop settles 2 °C below the setpoint. Which term removes that offset?
qs.ans: Integral
wrong: Derivative
A higher proportional gain alone
A feedforward on the sensor noise
qs.why: Only integral action keeps acting on a constant error until it reaches zero.

qs.q: A heater runs at 100% for 10 minutes to warm a cold tank, then overshoots badly. What is the most likely cause?
qs.ans: Integrator windup during saturation
wrong: The derivative gain is set too low
The sensor is mounted too close to the heater
The proportional gain is set too low
qs.why: The integral grew the whole time the heater was maxed out, then had to unwind past the setpoint.

qs.q: Ki = 0.5 per second, and an error of 4 units persists for 3 s. How much does the integral term add to the output?
What does a typical anti-windup scheme do?
qs.ans: Stops integrating while the output is saturated
wrong: Raises the integral gain while saturated
Turns off the proportional term while it is saturated
Resets the setpoint to the current value
qs.why: Freezing or clamping the integral keeps it from building up when the actuator can’t respond.

qs.q: For a well-damped loop, rank these integral gains by overshoot, most first.
qs.why: More integral action pushes harder after the error crosses zero.

demo.title: Windup after saturation
demo.hint: The longer the actuator sits at its limit, the more the integral stores up, and the bigger the overshoot when it finally unwinds. Clamping stops the build-up. Simplified illustration.

p.x: Integral action adds up the error over time: $∫e dt$.
While any steady error remains, the total keeps [[growing]] and pushes harder, until the error is zero.
It removes the offset that P control alone leaves.
The integral grows while the error is positive, so it is at its largest just as the error reaches zero.
So it keeps pushing after the error crosses zero. The output overshoots, and the integral must unwind through negative error.
Too much $K_i$: more overshoot and oscillation.

g.q: Raise the integral gain K_i a lot. The step response…
o: overshoots more
The large integral keeps pushing after the error crosses zero.
settles faster
The integral is at its peak when the error hits zero, so a bigger K_i pushes further past.

p.x: **Windup** starts when the actuator saturates: it is already at its limit, like a heater at 100 %.
When the error finally flips sign, the oversized integral takes a long time to unwind, and the output overshoots far.
**Anti-windup** limits the integral while the actuator is saturated. Two common ways:
**Clamping**: hold the integral at a set limit.
**Conditional integration**: stop integrating while the output is saturated.
The integral stays small, ready to act as soon as the actuator comes off its limit.

cards: Derivative action reacts to how fast the error changes, adding damping: it brakes the output before the error reaches zero.
But it amplifies noise. A sine of frequency ω has a derivative ω times larger, so high-frequency sensor noise gets boosted.
Why filter: real D terms pass the derivative through a low-pass filter, often with a corner 5–10 × the loop bandwidth.
Derivative on measurement, not error, avoids a huge kick when the setpoint jumps.
title: Derivative action and noise

qs.q: Sensor noise is a 0.01 V sine at 1000 rad/s. What is the amplitude of its derivative, in V/s?
qs.why: ω × A = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 V/s: tiny noise becomes a big derivative.

qs.q: A motor loop chatters and the drive gets hot after Kd is raised. What is the best fix?
qs.ans: Low-pass filter the derivative term
wrong: Raise Kd further for more damping
Remove the integral term entirely
Raise the sampling rate with no filter
qs.why: The derivative is amplifying sensor noise. Filtering keeps the damping at low frequencies and cuts the noise.

qs.q: Why compute the derivative on the measurement instead of on the error?
qs.ans: Setpoint steps don’t cause a kick
wrong: It removes sensor noise from the loop
It makes the integral term unnecessary
It doubles the damping it provides
qs.why: A setpoint step makes d(error)/dt huge for one sample. The measurement changes smoothly.

qs.q: What does derivative action add to a loop?
qs.ans: Damping, by opposing fast changes
wrong: Zero steady-state error
Higher gain at low frequency
A push that keeps growing while any error remains
qs.why: D responds to the rate of change, braking motion before it overshoots. Zero steady-state error and a push that grows while error remains are both integral action; higher low-frequency gain comes from P or I, not D.

qs.q: For a pure derivative, rank these noise frequencies by gain, highest first.
qs.why: Derivative gain grows in proportion to frequency.

demo.title: Derivative gain versus frequency
demo.hint: A pure derivative’s gain climbs forever with frequency. A filtered one levels off at the filter corner, so noise above it stops growing.

p.x: As the error falls fast toward zero, $de/dt$ is negative, so the D term pushes back.
It [[brakes]] the output before the error reaches zero: that is the added damping.
Derivative action amplifies **noise**.

p.cap: ω in rad/s: the derivative is ω times larger

p.x: Noise 1/100 of the signal becomes as big as the signal: high frequencies are boosted most.

g.q: Noise at 100 rad/s is 1/100 the size of a 1 rad/s signal. After differentiating, the noise is…
o: still 1/100 of the signal
Differentiating multiplies each sine by its own ω, so fast noise grows 100× more than the slow signal.
about as big as the signal

p.x: Real D terms pass the derivative through a **low-pass filter**.
Its corner is often 5–10 × the loop bandwidth: high enough to keep the braking, low enough to cut most noise.
When the setpoint jumps, the error jumps, and $de/dt$ spikes for an instant: a **derivative kick** to the actuator.

p.cap: y is the measured output; it can't jump, so no kick

p.x: Between setpoint changes $de/dt = −dy/dt$, so the damping is the same, without the kick.

g.q: Use −dy/dt instead of de/dt. Between setpoint jumps, the damping is…
o: the same
With r constant, de/dt = −dy/dt exactly.
weaker
y and e change at the same rate when r is constant, so the D term is identical there.

cards: A loop goes unstable when its open-loop gain is 1 (0 dB) at a phase of −180°: the feedback then reinforces itself.
Gain margin is how much gain can rise before that happens. Phase margin is how much extra phase lag the loop tolerates at the 0 dB crossover.
Why 45–60° phase margin: below about 30°, step responses ring with large overshoot; more margin is calmer but slower.
Time delay adds phase lag ωT that grows with frequency, which is why delays eat margin and limit bandwidth.
title: Gain and phase margin

qs.q: At the 0 dB crossover, the open-loop phase is −135°. What is the phase margin, in degrees?
At −180° phase, the open-loop gain is −12 dB. What is the gain margin, in dB?
qs.why: The gain could rise 12 dB, about 4×, before reaching 0 dB at −180°.

qs.q: A 10 ms delay sits in a loop that crosses over at 50 rad/s. How much phase lag does the delay add there, in degrees?
A loop with 15° phase margin is given a step. What response do you expect?
qs.ans: Heavy ringing and large overshoot
wrong: A smooth, slow rise with no overshoot
Exponential growth without bound
A response identical to 60° margin
qs.why: Low phase margin means a lightly damped closed loop: lots of oscillation before it settles.
qs.hint: Phase margin works like damping: the less margin, the more the closed loop rings. 15° is well below the 45–60° target.

qs.q: Rank these phase margins by step-response overshoot, most first.
qs.why: Overshoot falls as phase margin rises: roughly 50%, 30%, 15% and 2%.

demo.title: Delay eats phase margin
demo.hint: A delay adds lag ωT at crossover. Push the crossover higher or the delay longer, and the margin melts until the loop goes unstable.

p.x: Around the loop, a signal comes back scaled by the **open-loop gain** and shifted by its **phase**.
At −180°, the subtraction at the summing point flips sign: the returning signal [[reinforces]] the input.
If the gain there is also 1 (0 dB), the oscillation sustains itself: the loop is at the edge of instability.
Two margins say how far the loop is from that edge.

p.c: extra lag allowed, where gain = 0 dB

p.x: A 10 dB gain margin means the gain could rise about 3.2× before the loop oscillates.
For a standard second-order loop, phase margin sets the damping, and so the overshoot.
45–60° is the usual target. Below about 30° the step response rings; more margin is calmer but slower.

g.q: Phase margin drops from 60° to 30°. Step overshoot goes from about 9 % to…
o: about 18 %
That doubles overshoot as the margin halves. Overshoot grows much faster than that as damping falls.
about 40 %
30° of margin means ζ ≈ 0.27, and that overshoots about 40 %.

p.x: A time delay adds phase lag that grows [[in proportion to]] frequency, and leaves the gain unchanged.

p.cap: pure delay T in s, ω in rad/s, φ in radians

p.x: So a delay eats phase margin, and limits how fast (how high a bandwidth) the loop can be.

cards: A digital controller samples, computes and updates at a fixed rate. A zero-order hold behaves like a delay of about half a sample period.
Rule of thumb: sample 10–30 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth. Slower sampling eats phase margin and can destabilize the loop.

Why anti-alias filters: after sampling, noise faster than half the sample rate looks exactly like a slower wobble, and the loop reacts to it. No filter after sampling can separate the two, so filter before sampling.
Discrete PID: integral becomes a running sum × Δt, derivative a difference ÷ Δt. Both depend on a steady, known Δt.
title: Digital control and sampling

qs.q: A loop runs at 1 kHz. Treating the hold as half a sample of delay, what delay is that, in ms?
qs.why: Half of 1 ms = 0.5 ms.

qs.q: The closed-loop bandwidth is 20 Hz. Using 20× as the rule of thumb, what sample rate is needed, in Hz?
A loop crosses over at 100 rad/s and samples at 200 Hz, a 5 ms sample period. How much phase does the hold’s half-sample delay cost there, in degrees?
The control task’s timing jitters between 1 and 3 ms, but the code assumes Δt = 2 ms. What suffers most?
qs.ans: The derivative and integral terms
wrong: Only the proportional term
Only the sensor’s resolution
Nothing, since the average Δt is right
qs.why: I and D scale with Δt, so jitter makes them wrong every sample; D becomes especially noisy.

qs.q: For a 10 Hz bandwidth loop, rank these sample rates by phase lost to sampling, most first.
qs.why: Hold delay is half a period, so lag falls as the rate rises.

demo.title: Sample rate and lost phase
demo.hint: The hold acts like half a sample of delay. At 10× the crossover frequency it costs about 18°; at 30× only about 6°.

p.x: A digital controller runs the same cycle every sample period $T_s$.
A **zero-order hold** keeps $u$ constant until the next update. On average the output is half a period late, so the hold acts like a delay of about $T_s/2$.
Rule of thumb: sample 10–30 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth $ω_b$.

p.cap: hold modelled as a delay of T_s/2; φ in radians

p.x: Lost phase ≈ 180°/N when sampling N × the bandwidth: slower sampling eats phase margin.

g.q: Sample at only 5 × the bandwidth instead of 20 ×. The phase lost at ω_b…
o: stays about 9°
The hold's delay is T_s/2, and T_s is 4× longer, so the lag at the same ω is 4× more.
grows to about 36°
4× the sample period, 4× the delay, 4× the phase lag: 36°.

p.x: After sampling, noise faster than half the sample rate looks exactly like a slower wobble, and the loop reacts to it.
Example: sampled at 100 Hz, a 90 Hz ripple shows up as a 10 Hz wobble.
No filter after sampling can tell the two apart, so the anti-alias filter goes [[before]] the sampler.
In code, the integral becomes a running sum and the derivative a difference.
Both assume a steady, known $Δt$. If the timing jitters, I and D are wrong.

cards: Form controls limit a feature’s shape on its own, with no datum. Flatness puts a surface between two parallel planes a set distance apart.
Straightness limits a line element, or an axis, to a zone. Circularity and cylindricity do the same for round features.
Why form matters alongside size: a plate can be in size everywhere yet warped like a potato chip. Flatness catches that.
Rule #1: for a regular size feature, perfect form is required at MMC, so the size limits already cap the form error.
title: Flatness and straightness

qs.q: Which control needs no datum reference?
qs.ans: Flatness
wrong: Perpendicularity
Position
Parallelism
qs.why: Form controls such as flatness compare a feature with itself. Orientation and location need datums.

qs.q: A plate surface is measured at 12 points. The highest is +0.03 mm and the lowest −0.02 mm from a best-fit plane. What flatness does it achieve, in mm?
qs.why: Flatness is the zone width that contains all points: 0.03 − (−0.02) = 0.05 mm.

qs.q: A 10.00 ± 0.05 mm thick plate has no flatness callout. Under Rule #1, what is the largest flatness error allowed?
wrong: No limit at all
qs.why: The surfaces must stay within a perfect-form boundary at MMC (10.05). The full 0.10 mm size tolerance can be used up by form.

qs.q: A shaft passes size checks everywhere but won’t slide into a mating bore. Which control would have caught it?
qs.ans: Straightness of the axis
wrong: Flatness of one end face
Surface roughness Ra
Concentricity of the chamfer
qs.why: A bent shaft can be in size at every cross-section but exceed its envelope. Axis straightness limits the bend.

qs.q: Rank these flatness callouts by how hard they are to make, hardest first.
qs.why: Tighter zones need finer processes: lapping, grinding, milling, then as-cut.

demo.title: Flatness from measured points
demo.hint: Flatness is the gap between the two parallel planes that just enclose every point. One high spot widens the zone even if everything else is perfect.

p.x: **Form controls** limit a feature's shape on its own.
**Flatness**: every point of the surface lies between two parallel planes a set distance apart.
Form needs no datum: the two planes may tilt and shift to hug the surface as closely as they can.

g.q: A flatness callout needs a datum to measure from. True or false?
o: true
That's orientation, like parallelism. Flatness compares the surface only with itself, so the planes are free to tilt.
false
Flatness compares the surface only with itself. The enclosing planes tilt to fit it, so no datum is used.

p.x: **Straightness**: a line on the surface, or an axis, lies inside a zone.
**Circularity**: each cross-section lies between two concentric circles.
**Cylindricity**: the whole round surface lies between two coaxial cylinders.
A plate can be bent like a potato chip while its thickness stays the same everywhere.
Flatness checks the face against a plane, so it catches the warp. A sealing face may need flatness tighter than its size tolerance.

g.q: A caliper reads 10.00 mm at every spot on that plate. Is the face flat?
o: yes
A caliper measures thickness between two points. A bent plate of even thickness reads the same everywhere.
can't tell
Two-point readings only show thickness. Warp shows only when the face is checked against a plane, such as a surface plate.

p.x: **Rule #1** (ASME Y14.5): a regular feature of size must have perfect form at MMC.
A shaft Ø10.00–10.05 must pass through a perfect Ø10.05 ring, its MMC envelope. So its size limits [[also cap]] its form error.
ISO drawings don't assume this; there, the size needs an Ⓔ to get the same envelope.

cards: Orientation controls hold a feature at an angle to a datum: perpendicularity (90°), parallelism (0°) and angularity (any other angle).
The zone is two planes, or a cylinder for an axis, oriented exactly to the datum. They control tilt, not location.
Why tolerance in mm, not degrees: a 0.05 mm zone over a 100 mm face is a tighter angle than over 10 mm. The zone scales with the feature.
Angle equivalent: tilt ≈ zone / length radians. 0.05 mm over 100 mm is 0.0005 rad, about 0.03°.
title: Perpendicularity and parallelism

qs.q: A 0.05 mm perpendicularity zone applies to a face 50 mm tall. What is the largest tilt it allows, in degrees?
A face is perpendicular to datum A within 0.02 mm, but it sits 0.5 mm from its nominal location. Does it meet the perpendicularity callout?
qs.ans: Yes; orientation ignores location
wrong: No; it must also be located within 0.02 mm
No; location errors double the tilt reading
Only if datum A is a cylindrical surface
qs.why: Orientation controls float: the zone may sit anywhere, as long as it is oriented to the datum.

qs.q: Which control holds a hole’s axis at 30° to a datum face?
qs.ans: Angularity
wrong: Perpendicularity
Parallelism
Profile of a line
qs.why: Angularity is the general orientation control for any basic angle other than 0° and 90°.

qs.q: A 0.1 mm parallelism zone over a 200 mm long surface allows what tilt, in mm per meter?
qs.why: 0.1 mm over 0.2 m = 0.5 mm per meter.

qs.q: For a 0.05 mm zone, rank these feature lengths by the tilt angle allowed, largest first.
qs.why: Tilt ≈ zone/length, so shorter features allow more angle.

demo.title: Zone width and tilt angle
demo.hint: The same zone allows less angle on a longer feature. That is why GD&T specifies orientation as a width, not an angle.

p.x: **Orientation controls** hold a feature at an angle to a datum.
**Perpendicularity**: at 90°.
**Parallelism**: at 0°.
**Angularity**: at any other angle, given as a basic angle.
The zone is two parallel planes, or a cylinder for an axis, set at the exact angle to the datum.
It keeps that angle but may slide to wherever the feature is.
A perpendicular hole can still be in the wrong place: position or profile locates it.
Same 0.05 mm perpendicularity zone, on faces of different length.
Tilt ≈ zone ÷ length. A zone in mm scales with the feature, which is how a mating part feels the error.

g.q: On the 10 mm face, compared with the 100 mm face, the zone allows…
o: the same tilt
That would be true of a tolerance in degrees. A fixed width allows more angle over a shorter length.
10× more tilt
Tilt ≈ zone ÷ length, so a 10× shorter face may tilt 10× more.
10× less tilt
Backwards: the same width over a shorter length is a steeper angle, so more tilt fits.

p.cap: small angles, θ in radians

p.x: That's a slope of 1 mm per metre.

cards: Profile of a surface puts a complex surface inside a zone of uniform width around its true shape, defined by basic dimensions in CAD.
With datums it controls form, orientation, location and size together. Without datums it controls only form.
Why it’s popular: one callout replaces a pile of ± dimensions on curves, and it maps directly to a CMM comparing points to the CAD model.
By default the zone is split equally: a 0.4 profile means ±0.2 about the true surface. A U modifier can make it unequal.
title: Profile of a surface

qs.q: A surface has a 0.3 mm profile tolerance, equally disposed. How far may a point lie outside the true surface, in mm?
qs.why: Equal disposition splits the 0.3 zone into ±0.15.

qs.q: A profile callout references datums A, B and C. What does it control?
qs.ans: Form, orientation, location, size
wrong: Only the surface’s form error
Only its orientation to datum A
Only the surface finish and its flatness
qs.why: Fully referenced profile locks the zone to the datum frame, so it controls everything about the surface.

qs.q: Why is profile of a surface a good fit for a molded or cast freeform part?
qs.ans: It checks the whole surface against CAD at once
wrong: It needs no basic dimensions or CAD model at all
It ignores any form error inside the zone
It applies only to planar and round faces
qs.why: The CMM compares measured points to the model, and one zone width governs the whole curved surface.

qs.q: A CMM finds a point 0.12 mm outside nominal on a surface with a 0.2 mm profile, equally disposed. By how much is it out of tolerance, in mm?
qs.why: The zone allows ±0.10, so 0.12 is 0.02 mm out.

qs.q: Rank these controls by how much they govern, most first.
items: Profile of a surface to A, B and C
Profile of a surface with no datums
qs.why: Fully located profile, then form-only profile, then form controls on a plane, then on a single line.

demo.title: Profile zone check
demo.hint: Equal disposition splits the zone evenly about the true surface. Shift the deviation and see how much room is left on each side.

p.x: **Profile of a surface** puts a complex surface inside a zone of [[uniform width]] around its true shape.
The zone follows every curve, the same thickness everywhere, and every point of the real surface must lie in it.
Basic dimensions define the true shape, usually by pointing to the CAD model.
Profile can be called out with datums or without them.

p.c: form, tilt, location and size: the zone is locked to the datums
plain surface; the zone floats to fit it

g.q: On a plain surface, profile without datums controls…
o: only form
With nothing to locate it, the zone can move and tilt to fit the surface, so only the shape is checked.
form and location
Location needs something to measure from. Without datums the zone floats, so only shape is checked.

p.x: Why it's popular: one callout replaces a pile of ± dimensions on curves.
It maps straight onto a coordinate measuring machine (CMM), which compares measured points with the CAD surface.
A Ⓤ modifier makes the split unequal.
The number after Ⓤ is the part of the zone on the side that adds material. 0.4 Ⓤ 0.1: 0.1 mm there, 0.3 mm on the side that removes it.
0.4 Ⓤ 0.4 puts the whole zone on the material-adding side, as for a casting face that must always leave stock to machine.

cards: Circular runout is checked by spinning the part on its datum axis and reading an indicator on each cross-section. Total runout sweeps the whole surface at once.
Runout combines form, orientation and location error relative to the axis, which is what matters for things that spin.
Why it maps to vibration: an offset e spins up an unbalance force F = m e ω². Runout is a quick shop-floor proxy for that offset.
Full indicator movement for a pure offset e is 2e, since the surface swings e toward and e away from the indicator.
title: Runout and rotating parts

qs.q: A shaft journal is offset 0.01 mm from the datum axis, with perfect form. What runout does an indicator show, in mm?
qs.why: The surface swings ±0.01, so full indicator movement is 2e = 0.02 mm.

qs.q: A 2 kg rotor has its center of mass 0.05 mm off-axis and spins at 3000 rpm. What is the unbalance force, in N?
What is the difference between circular and total runout?
qs.ans: Total sweeps the whole surface in one reading
wrong: Total runout needs no datum axis at all
Circular runout also controls the diameter
They are identical; the names are interchangeable
qs.why: Circular checks each cross-section independently; total runout also catches taper and axial waviness.

qs.q: The rotor speed doubles. How does the unbalance force from the same offset change?
qs.ans: It rises 4 times
wrong: It doubles
It stays the same
It halves
qs.why: F = m e ω², so doubling ω quadruples the force.

qs.q: Rank these by unbalance force for a 1 kg rotor with 0.02 mm offset, highest first.
qs.why: Force grows with speed squared.

demo.title: Offset, runout and unbalance
demo.hint: Runout reads twice the offset. The unbalance force from that offset grows with the square of speed, so high-speed rotors need very tight runout.

p.x: Runout is checked by spinning the part on its datum axis against a dial indicator.
**Circular runout**: one reading at each cross-section, checked one section at a time.
**Total runout**: the indicator sweeps the whole surface while it spins, and every reading counts together.
A runout reading mixes three errors relative to the spin axis: out-of-round, tilt and offset.
The indicator can't tell them apart, so one reading gives the combined, worst-case wobble. Tilt shows fully only in total runout.
Runout checks the surface geometry a rotating part spins with. Balance also depends on how the mass is spread.

p.cap: rigid rotor, center of mass offset e from the spin axis

p.x: Twice the speed, four times the force: $F ∝ ω^2$. Runout is a quick shop-floor indicator of a geometric offset; mass spread matters too.

g.q: Spin the same rotor twice as fast. The unbalance force…
o: doubles
That treats F as proportional to ω. Speed is squared in F = m e ω².
quadruples
F = m e ω², so 2× the speed gives 2² = 4× the force.

p.x: A round surface offset by $e$ from the spin axis swings $e$ toward the indicator, then $e$ away. So the needle moves [[twice]] the offset.

p.cap: pure offset, perfectly round surface

cards: Tightening a bolt stretches it like a stiff spring. That tension, the preload, clamps the joint together.
Torque relates to preload by T = K F d, where d is the nominal diameter and K the nut factor: about 0.2 dry, 0.15 or less lubricated.
Why torque is a poor gauge: most torque goes into friction. A change in lubrication can shift preload by 30% or more at the same torque.
Typical target preload is about 75% of the proof load for reusable joints, so the bolt never loosens under service loads.
title: Bolt torque and preload

qs.q: An M10 bolt (d = 10 mm) needs 20 kN preload with K = 0.2. What torque is required, in N·m?
The same bolt is torqued to 40 N·m, but it is lubricated so K = 0.14. What preload results, in kN?
Why can lubricating threads without changing the torque spec be dangerous?
qs.ans: Preload rises and may yield the bolt
wrong: Preload falls and the joint loosens
Lubricant weakens the steel itself
Torque wrenches misread when the threads are oily
qs.why: Less friction means more of the torque becomes tension, so the bolt can be overstretched.

qs.q: Which method controls preload most accurately?
qs.ans: Measuring bolt stretch directly
wrong: Torque wrench on dry threads
Tightening by feel with a wrench
Torque wrench on oiled threads
qs.why: Stretch is proportional to tension, independent of friction. Torque methods typically scatter ±25%.

qs.q: For the same torque and bolt, rank these conditions by preload, highest first.
qs.why: F = T/(Kd), so lower K gives more preload.

demo.title: Torque, friction and preload
demo.hint: Same wrench setting, different friction: preload goes as 1/K. Lubricate without adjusting the spec and the bolt may pass its proof load.

p.x: Tightening the nut stretches the bolt elastically, like a stiff spring.
The stretched bolt pulls the parts together. Its initial tension is the **preload**.

vars: nut factor, an estimate of the effect of friction

p.x: For the same bolt and nut factor, torque rises [[in proportion]] to preload.

p.cap: Empirical estimate for a given thread and contact condition

p.x: Typical $K$ is about 0.20 dry and 0.15 or less lubricated. A 10 mm dry bolt at 20 kN needs about 40 N·m by this estimate.
Most tightening torque overcomes friction at the threads and under the turning nut or bolt head.
Lubrication lowers $K$. At the same torque, that raises preload.
Changing $K$ from 0.20 to 0.15 raises the estimated preload by about 33%.
If the stretch can be measured, it tracks tension in the elastic range without relying on a friction estimate.

g.q: Lubricate the threads but keep the torque and bolt size fixed. How does preload change?
o: It falls
Less friction leaves more of the applied torque available to stretch the bolt.
It rises
The lower nut factor gives more preload for the same torque.
It stays the same
Torque alone does not fix preload. The nut factor changes too.

p.x: The **proof load** is a specified test load the bolt must withstand without permanent stretch.
For a reusable joint, a common preload target is [[below]] the proof load.
Preload helps keep the parts clamped in service. Verify clamp force and bolt tension under service loads and allow for tightening scatter.

cards: Power through a shaft is P = Tω. At a fixed power, lower speed means higher torque, which is why gearboxes before a slow output get bigger shafts.
Torque is written T in shaft design, because τ is taken: τ is the shear stress the torque causes. At the surface of a solid round shaft, τ = 16T/(πd³).
Why diameter dominates: stress goes as 1/d³. A 26% larger diameter halves the stress.
Hollow shafts carry nearly as much torque with much less mass, because the core does little work.
title: Shafts in torsion

qs.q: A motor delivers 15 kW at a shaft speed of 150 rad/s. What is the shaft torque, in N·m?
qs.why: P = T·ω, so T = P/ω = 15,000 W ÷ 150 rad/s = 100 N·m. (150 rad/s is about 1430 rpm. Given rpm, convert first: ω = 2πn/60.)
qs.hint: Power = torque × angular speed, with P in watts and ω in rad/s.

qs.q: A solid 25 mm shaft carries 100 N·m. Its polar moment is J = πd⁴/32 = 38,350 mm⁴. What is the maximum shear stress, in MPa?
qs.hint: τ = T·r/J. Work in N·mm and mm so the answer comes out in N/mm², which is MPa.

qs.q: A shaft’s diameter is doubled. How does the shear stress change for the same torque?
qs.ans: It falls to 1/8
wrong: It falls to 1/2
It falls to 1/4
It falls to 1/16
qs.why: τ = T·r/J with r = d/2 and J = πd⁴/32, so τ = 16T/(πd³) ∝ 1/d³. Doubling d divides τ by 2³ = 8.
qs.hint: τ = T·r/J. J grows with d⁴ while r grows with d.

qs.q: A 10:1 reducer follows a motor. Which shaft must be thicker, ignoring losses?
qs.ans: The slow output shaft
wrong: The fast input shaft
Both need exactly the same size
Whichever is longer
qs.why: Same power at 1/10 the speed means 10× the torque on the output shaft.

qs.q: For 10 kW, rank these shaft speeds by torque, highest first.
qs.why: T = P/ω: about 955, 191, 64 and 27 N·m.

demo.title: Sizing a shaft
demo.hint: Torque comes from power over speed; stress from torque over d³. Slow the shaft down and you must grow it to keep the stress in check.

p.x: At equal power, the slower shaft carries more torque.

p.cap: Steady rotation

p.x: An ideal 10:1 reducer has one tenth the input speed at its output and ten times the torque. With other design limits equal, that favors a thicker output shaft.

g.q: A lossless speed reducer passes the same power through both shafts. Which carries more torque?
o: Fast input shaft
It turns faster. Less torque is needed there to transmit the same power.
Slow output shaft
Equal power at lower angular speed requires more torque.

vars: largest shear stress, at the rim

p.cap: Solid round shaft in elastic torsion

p.x: **Shear stress** measures force per area acting along a surface. In a shaft it grows from zero at the center to its peak at the rim.
At distance $r$ from the center, $τ = Tr/J$. The **polar moment** $J$ measures how far the section area lies from the axis.
Hold torque fixed on a solid round shaft. Its surface stress scales [[inversely]] with the cube of the diameter.

p.cap: Same torque, elastic torsion

p.x: Bore a hole through the middle of an elastic round shaft. Keep its outer diameter, material and allowed surface stress fixed.
The bore removes a larger share of the mass than of the torque capacity. The missing material was near the low-stress center.
Example: bore diameter is 60% of the outside diameter.

g.q: Which loses a larger fraction of its original value when the shaft is bored?
o: Mass per length
Removing the low-stress core saves mass with a smaller loss of torque capacity.
Torque capacity
That would favor the core. Material farther from the axis makes the larger contribution to torsion.

cards: Rolling bearings wear out by surface fatigue: after enough load cycles, small pits form on the races and rolling elements. The L10 life is the number of revolutions that 90% of a batch of identical bearings reaches or exceeds.
L10 = (C/P)ᵖ million revolutions, where C is the dynamic load rating, P the equivalent load, p = 3 for ball and 10/3 for roller bearings.
Why load matters so much: doubling the load on a ball bearing cuts its life by 2³ = 8.
Hours = L10 × 10⁶ / (60 × rpm). Typical targets: 20,000–40,000 h for industrial machines running full shifts.
title: Bearing life

qs.q: A ball bearing has C = 20 kN and carries P = 2 kN. What is L10, in millions of revolutions?
qs.why: (20/2)³ = 1000 million revolutions.

qs.q: A ball bearing with C = 20 kN carries P = 2 kN, so L10 = 1000 million revolutions. It runs at 1000 rpm. What is its L10 life in hours?
The load on a ball bearing rises by 26%. Roughly how does its life change?
qs.ans: It halves
wrong: It falls by 26%
It falls by about 13%
It falls to a quarter
qs.why: 1.26³ ≈ 2, so life falls by half.

qs.q: What does an L10 life of 20,000 h mean?
qs.ans: 90% of bearings last at least 20,000 h
wrong: Every bearing fails at exactly 20,000 h
The average bearing lasts 20,000 h
10% of bearings reach 20,000 h
qs.why: L10 is the life 90% exceed; the median life is several times longer.

qs.q: For a ball bearing with C = 30 kN, rank these loads by life, longest first.
qs.why: (C/P)³ gives 27,000, 3,375, 1,000 and 125 million revolutions.

demo.title: Load versus bearing life
demo.hint: Life falls with the cube of load for ball bearings, a bit faster for rollers. A modest overload costs a lot of life.

p.x: Repeated rolling contact can cause **surface fatigue**. Small pits form on the rolling elements or the tracks they run on.
Under the same operating conditions, 90% of comparable bearings are expected to last [[at least]] $L_{10}$ revolutions.
That makes $L_{10}$ the **basic rating life**. About 10% of the group is expected to fail from fatigue sooner.

vars: basic rating life in millions of turns
dynamic load rating listed by the maker
equivalent steady load for bearing life

p.cap: Basic fatigue rating at constant equivalent load

p.x: Use the same force units for $C$ and $P$. The exponent $p$ is 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings.
Keep the same ball bearing and increase its equivalent load $P$. The life calculation uses the cube of the load ratio.
About 26% more load halves the rating life of a ball bearing.
Doubling the load leaves only one eighth of the life, because the load ratio is cubed.

g.q: Equivalent load rises by about 26%. What happens to the rating life?
o: It drops by about a quarter
That treats the change as nearly linear. The load ratio enters cubed.
It drops by about half
Cubing the factor 1.26 gives about 2, and load is in the denominator.

p.x: Hours of rating life come from dividing the rated number of turns by turns per hour at constant speed.
For full-shift industrial service, a design may target 20,000–40,000 h. Choose the target for the machine's duty and maintenance plan.

cards: In a preloaded joint, an external load P is shared: the bolt takes C·P and the clamped parts take the rest, with C = kb/(kb + km).
Bolts are usually much less stiff than the clamped members, so C is often 0.2–0.3: the bolt sees only a small part of the external load.
Why that protects bolts in fatigue: the cyclic load on the bolt is C times the external swing, so a stiff joint and a slender bolt help.
The joint separates when the members’ share wipes out the preload: P_sep = Fi/(1 − C).
title: Bolted joint stiffness

qs.q: Bolt stiffness kb = 200 kN/mm and member stiffness km = 800 kN/mm. What is the joint constant C?
With C = 0.2, a 10 kN external load is applied to a joint preloaded to 20 kN. What is the bolt tension now, in kN?
With C = 0.2 and a 20 kN preload, at what external load does the joint separate, in kN?
Why does a gasket between the parts often hurt fatigue life?
qs.ans: It softens the members, raising the bolt’s share
wrong: It adds friction that raises the preload
It stiffens the bolt relative to the clamped parts
It reduces the external load on the joint
qs.why: A soft gasket lowers km, raising C, so more of each load cycle goes through the bolt.

qs.q: The bolt carries C × the external load, so a 10 kN load swing moves the bolt by C × 10 kN. Rank these joints by bolt load swing, largest first.
qs.why: Bolt swing = C × 10 kN: 0.6 → 6 kN, 0.4 → 4 kN, 0.25 → 2.5 kN, 0.1 → 1 kN. Bigger C, bigger share for the bolt.

demo.title: Load sharing in a bolted joint
demo.hint: The bolt sees only a share C of the external load until the joint separates; past that, it takes everything. Stiffer members keep C small.

vars: outside force pulling the joint apart
stiffness of the parts being clamped
fraction of added load seen by the bolt

p.cap: Linear elastic joint, parts still in contact

p.x: The bolt gains $CP$ in tension. The parts lose $(1 − C)P$ of their initial clamp force.
A **gasket** is a layer between parts that fills gaps to seal a joint. Consider adding a soft gasket while keeping the bolt stiffness fixed.
A soft gasket makes the clamped stack easier to compress. The bolt then takes a larger share of each added load.
In joints with clamped parts several times stiffer than the bolt, $C$ may be around 0.20–0.30.

g.q: What does the soft layer do to the bolt's share of an added load before the joint opens?
o: It raises the share
The clamped parts are less stiff, which reduces the denominator of the stiffness fraction.
It lowers the share
That would require stiffer clamped parts. A softer stack raises the bolt's share.

p.x: **Fatigue** is damage from repeated loading. For a joint that stays closed, the bolt's force swing is [[proportional]] to the outside force swing.

p.cap: Δ means change in force, with joint stiffnesses fixed

p.x: With $C = 0.20$, a 10 kN outside swing gives a 2.00 kN bolt swing.
Stiffer clamped parts or a more flexible bolt can reduce the bolt's force swing.
The joint starts to separate when the loss of clamp force consumes the initial clamp force $F_i$.

p.cap: Outside force at first separation, with constant C until opening

p.x: Take a preload of 20.0 kN and a bolt share $C = 0.20$.
Once the parts separate, the closed-joint load split no longer applies.

cards: Structures carry dead loads (their own weight), live loads (people, furniture, vehicles) and environmental loads (wind, snow, earthquakes).
A load path is the chain that carries load to the ground: slab → beam → girder → column → footing → soil. Every link must be strong enough.
Why tributary area: each beam carries the floor area halfway to its neighbors. Load on it = area pressure × spacing × span.
Office floors are often designed for about 2.4 kPa (50 psf) live load, plus partitions and dead load.
title: Loads and load paths

qs.q: Floor beams are spaced 3 m apart, span 6 m and carry 5 kPa total. What is the total load on one beam, in kN?
qs.why: Tributary area = 3 × 6 = 18 m², and 18 × 5 = 90 kN.

qs.q: Which is a live load?
qs.ans: People in an office
wrong: The concrete floor slab
The steel beams’ own weight
Permanent brick cladding
qs.why: Live loads move or change. Self-weight and permanent finishes are dead loads.

qs.q: A column is removed during renovation. What must happen to its load?
qs.ans: Another path must carry it to the ground
wrong: It spreads into the air around the floor
The floor slab absorbs it without change
It disappears once the column is gone
qs.why: Load has to reach the foundation. A transfer beam or new column must provide the path.

qs.q: A 1 m wide strip of floor carries 4 kPa over a 5 m span. What is the uniform load on the strip, in kN/m?
qs.why: 4 kN/m² × 1 m width = 4 kN/m along the span.

qs.q: Order the load path in a typical steel building, from where load starts to the ground.
qs.why: Load flows from the surface it lands on, down through progressively larger members to the soil.

demo.title: Tributary load on a beam
demo.hint: A beam picks up the floor halfway to each neighbor. Wider spacing means fewer, heavier beams; longer spans raise both load and bending.

p.x: A structure carries three kinds of load.
**Dead load**: the structure's own weight plus anything permanently fixed to it, such as floors, walls and finishes.
**Live load**: anything that moves or comes and goes: people, furniture, vehicles.
**Environmental loads** come from the site: wind $W$, snow $S$ and earthquakes $E$.

g.q: A car parked in a garage for months. Its weight counts as…
o: dead load
Dead load is only the permanent weight of the structure and what's fixed to it. A car can drive away, so it's live load however long it stays.
live load
It can move or be removed, so it's live load, even while it sits still.

p.x: A **load path** is the chain of members that carries a load down to the ground.
Each link, and each connection between links, must carry everything passed to it. One weak link breaks the path.

p.cap: equal spacing, uniform pressure

p.x: Codes set a minimum design live load for each use of a floor.
That's 50 psf, the weight of about 244 kg on each square meter.
The floor is designed for this plus partitions and its own dead load.

cards: A truss is made of straight members joined at pins, loaded only at the joints. Each member is then purely in tension or compression.
Method of joints: at each pin, forces must balance in x and y. Start at a joint with at most two unknown members.
Why triangles: a triangle can’t change shape without changing a member’s length, so it’s rigid. A square racks into a parallelogram.
A simple planar truss is stable and determinate when m = 2j − 3, with m members and j joints.
title: Trusses and triangles

qs.q: A planar truss has 7 joints. How many members make it simple and determinate?
A symmetric two-member truss holds 10 kN at its apex. Each member makes 30° with the horizontal. What is the force in each member, in kN?
qs.why: Vertical balance: 2F sin 30° = 10, so F = 10 kN, in compression.

qs.q: In a simple truss bridge with a load on the bottom chord, what is the top chord typically in?
qs.ans: Compression
wrong: Tension
Pure bending
Torsion
qs.why: Like a beam, the top of the truss shortens and the bottom stretches.

qs.q: Why do compression members in trusses often look thicker than tension members?
qs.ans: Compression members can buckle
wrong: Compression members carry larger forces
Tension members are made of steel cable only
Thicker members lower the truss’s weight
qs.why: Slender compression members fail by buckling well before material yield.

qs.q: For a 10 kN apex load on a symmetric two-member truss, rank these member angles from horizontal by member force, highest first.
qs.why: F = P/(2 sin θ): about 28.8, 14.6, 7.1 and 5.3 kN. Shallow trusses carry big forces.

demo.title: Shallow trusses carry big forces
demo.hint: Two members holding a load at their apex: as they flatten, each needs a larger force to supply the same vertical component.

p.x: An ideal **truss**: straight members joined by pins, with loads applied only at the joints.
Then each member carries only a force along its own length:
**Tension**: the member is pulled and stretches.
**Compression**: the member is pushed and shortens.
Load a member between its joints and it bends as well. That's why trusses take their loads at the joints.

g.q: Hang a load halfway along one member instead of at a joint. That member…
o: still only stretches or shortens
Pure tension or compression needs the loads at the pins. A load partway along pushes across the member, so it bends like a small beam.
bends as well
The load pushes across the member between its pins, so it carries bending on top of its axial force.

p.x: **Method of joints**: treat each pin as a point. Its forces must balance in both directions.

p.cap: each pin in static equilibrium

p.x: Two equations per joint solve two unknown member forces, so start at a joint with at most two.
Symmetric apex, members 30° above horizontal, 10 kN down. Vertical balance, both members in compression:
Three bars of fixed length fit together in only one shape, so a pinned triangle holds its shape.
A square with pinned corners racks into a parallelogram while all four sides keep their length.
Add one diagonal and the square becomes two triangles: rigid again.

p.cap: 3 support reactions, members arranged in triangles

p.x: Each joint gives 2 equations. 3 of the 2j equations find the support reactions; the rest find one force per member.
With [[fewer]] members than that, the truss can move like a mechanism. With more, it's indeterminate: balance alone can't find the forces.

cards: A slender column fails by bowing sideways at a load far below its crushing strength. Euler’s critical load: Pcr = π²EI/(KL)².
K sets the effective length: 1.0 pinned both ends, 0.5 fixed both ends, 2.0 for a flagpole fixed at the base and free at the top.
Why length is so powerful: Pcr goes as 1/L². Double the height and the buckling load falls to a quarter.
Buckle about the weak axis: use the smaller I. Bracing the weak axis at midheight halves that effective length.
title: Column buckling

qs.q: A pinned steel column has E = 200 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and L = 4 m. What is Pcr, in kN?
The same column is made fixed at both ends instead of pinned. How does Pcr change?
qs.ans: It rises 4 times
wrong: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
qs.why: K drops from 1 to 0.5, and Pcr ∝ 1/K², so 4×.

qs.q: A flagpole is fixed at the base and free at the top. What is its effective length factor K?
qs.why: It buckles like half of a pinned column twice as long.

qs.q: An I-beam column has I_x = 50 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and I_y = 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, with equal unbraced lengths. About which axis does it buckle?
qs.ans: The weak axis, using I_y
wrong: The strong axis, using I_x
Both axes buckle together
Neither; I-beams can’t buckle
qs.why: Buckling follows the lowest Pcr, set by the smaller I.

qs.q: For the same column, rank these end conditions by buckling load, highest first.
qs.why: Pcr ∝ 1/K²: factors of 4, about 2, 1 and 0.25.

demo.title: Euler buckling
demo.hint: Buckling load falls with the square of effective length. Fix the ends or brace midway and the same column carries several times more.

p.x: A slender column fails by bowing sideways at a load [[far below]] its crushing strength.

vars: second moment of area about the bending axis
effective-length factor, set by the ends

p.cap: straight elastic column, load on its axis

p.x: Steel, $E$ = 200 GPa, $I$ = 8×10^6 mm^4, pinned ends ($K$ = 1):
$KL$ is the effective length: a pinned-end column that long buckles at the same load.
Stiffer end restraint gives a [[shorter]] $KL$ and a higher $P_{cr}$.
Real fixed ends rotate a little, so design uses larger values: 0.65 fixed–fixed, 2.1 flagpole.
Same column section, material and ends: $E$, $I$ and $K$ fixed. Change only the length.
$P_{cr} ∝ 1/L^2$: length enters squared, while $E$ and $I$ enter only once.

g.q: Make the column twice as tall. Its buckling load…
o: halves
That treats P_{cr} as 1/L. Length is squared in Euler's formula, (KL)².
falls to a quarter
P_{cr} = π²EI/(KL)², so doubling L divides it by 2² = 4.
falls to an eighth
That would be 1/L³, like a cantilever's tip deflection. Euler's load goes as 1/L².

p.x: A column buckles about the axis with the smaller $I$: its weak axis. For a 100 × 200 mm bar:

p.c: 200 mm deep in the bending direction
100 mm deep in the bending direction

p.x: A brace that stops weak-axis sway at midheight [[halves]] that axis's effective length.
Weak-axis $P_{cr}$ rises 4×, matching the strong axis in this bar. The axis with the lower $P_{cr}$ governs.

cards: Limit state design multiplies loads up and strengths down. A common combination is 1.2D + 1.6L: dead load is known well, live load less so.
Resistance factors φ (for example 0.9 for steel bending) cover material and construction variability. Check φRn ≥ factored load effect.
Why combinations: maximum wind, snow and people rarely occur at once. Codes list several combinations; the worst governs.
Uplift checks use 0.9D: if dead weight is overestimated, wind lifting the roof is underestimated.
title: Load factors and combinations

qs.q: A beam carries a 20 kN·m dead-load moment and a 30 kN·m live-load moment. What is the factored moment using 1.2D + 1.6L, in kN·m?
A steel beam’s nominal moment capacity is 90 kN·m, with φ = 0.9. What is its design capacity, in kN·m?
qs.why: φMn = 0.9 × 90 = 81 kN·m, which exceeds 72, so it passes.

qs.q: Why does live load get a larger factor than dead load?
qs.ans: It is far less predictable
wrong: It is usually the larger of the two
It acts only for short periods
It produces tension, not compression
qs.why: Self-weight is calculated closely; occupancy loads vary a lot and can be misjudged.

qs.q: A light roof is checked for wind uplift. Why use 0.9D instead of 1.2D?
qs.ans: Less dead weight is the unsafe case
wrong: Wind codes require smaller factors
Roof dead load is known exactly
Uplift checks ignore the dead load entirely
qs.why: Dead weight resists uplift, so overestimating it is unconservative. 0.9 assumes a little less.

qs.q: With D = 10 and L = 10 (any units), rank these combinations by factored load, highest first.

demo.title: Which combination governs
demo.hint: With a big live load, 1.2D + 1.6L wins. When live load is tiny compared with dead load, 1.4D can govern instead.

p.x: Limit state design multiplies loads up and strengths down.

p.cap: D, L and U as the same effect, such as a bending moment

p.x: Dead load is known well from material weights; live load is less certain, so it gets the bigger factor.
For $D$ = 20 and $L$ = 30 kN·m:

g.q: Live load gets the bigger factor, 1.6 against 1.2, because it's…
o: less certain
Weights of concrete and steel are known well. How many people or how much furniture a floor will hold is not.
usually larger
Factors don't depend on which load is bigger; dead load is often the larger one. They reflect how uncertain each load is.

p.x: Resistance factors $φ$ scale strength down to cover variability in materials and construction.

p.cap: one check for each way the member can fail
vars: nominal strength, such as bending strength M_n

p.x: 81 ≥ 72, so this bending check is satisfied. Shear, deflection and the connections get their own checks.
Maximum wind, snow and people [[rarely]] occur at the same time.
So codes list several combinations, each with one load at its maximum and the others reduced. Check them all; the worst governs.
For $D$ = 20 and $L$ = 30 kN·m:
Here $1.2D + 1.6L$ governs. $1.4D$ takes over only when $L < D/8$.
Wind can lift a light roof. Its own dead weight is what holds it down.

p.cap: wind W acting upward, dead load D downward

p.x: Here dead load helps, so it's factored down: if its weight is overestimated, the uplift is underestimated.
Light roof: $D$ = 0.5 kPa down, wind 0.6 kPa up.
The connections must hold the roof down against that net uplift.

g.q: For this uplift check, the roof's dead load is factored…
o: up, like 1.2D
Factoring dead load up is cautious only when it adds to the load. Here it resists the wind, so a bigger D would hide the uplift.
down, like 0.9D
Dead load works against the wind here, so the cautious choice is to count less of it.

cards: General-purpose I/O pins can be set as outputs (drive high or low) or inputs (read a voltage as 1 or 0).
An unconnected input floats and reads noise. A pull-up resistor ties it to the supply, so it reads 1 until a button pulls it to ground.
Why 10 kΩ is common: it holds the line firmly while wasting little current, 3.3 V / 10 kΩ = 0.33 mA when pressed.
Output pins can only source or sink a few mA to tens of mA. Use a transistor for motors, relays and bright LEDs.
title: GPIO and pull resistors

qs.q: A 3.3 V pull-up of 10 kΩ goes to a button to ground. How much current flows while it’s pressed, in mA?
A button input reads random 1s and 0s when nobody touches it. What is missing?
qs.ans: A pull-up or pull-down resistor
wrong: A larger supply decoupling capacitor
A faster processor clock speed
A series resistor in the LED line
qs.why: Without a pull resistor, the input floats and picks up noise.

qs.q: An LED (2.0 V drop) runs from a 3.3 V pin at 5 mA. What series resistor is needed, in Ω?
qs.why: (3.3 − 2.0) / 0.005 = 260 Ω; 270 Ω is the nearest standard value above.

qs.q: A 12 V, 200 mA relay coil must be switched from a 3.3 V pin. What is the right approach?
qs.ans: Drive a transistor with a flyback diode
wrong: Wire the relay coil straight to the pin
Add a pull-up resistor to the coil
Power the coil from the 3.3 V rail
qs.why: The pin can’t supply 12 V or 200 mA. A transistor switches it, and the diode absorbs the coil’s turn-off spike.

qs.q: Rank these pull-up values by current wasted when the button is pressed, most first.
qs.why: I = V/R, so smaller resistors waste more current.

demo.title: Choosing a pull-up
demo.hint: Small pull-ups waste current when pressed; large ones are weak and pick up noise. 4.7–47 kΩ is the usual sweet spot.

p.x: General-purpose I/O (**GPIO**) pins are set in code as outputs or inputs.
An input reads 1 above its high threshold and 0 below its low threshold (both in the datasheet).
An unconnected input floats and reads noise. A **pull-up** resistor ties it to the supply.
Released, the pull-up holds the pin at 1. Pressed, the button pulls it to ground: 0.

g.q: Pull-up to 3.3 V, button to ground. Pressed, the pin reads…
o: That's the released state. Pressing connects the pin straight to ground.
The button shorts the pin to ground; the pull-up only lets a small current flow.

p.x: With the button pressed, the pull-up carries current from 3.3 V to ground:
1 kΩ wastes 10× the current. 1 MΩ wastes almost none but holds the line so weakly that noise and leakage can flip it. 10 kΩ sits between.
An output pin can source or sink only a few mA to tens of mA; the datasheet gives the limit.
Switch big loads with a transistor:
Use a logic-level MOSFET (rated $R_{DS(on)}$ at your pin voltage) and a diode across the motor to catch its inductive spike.

g.q: A small motor draws 500 mA. Drive it straight from a pin?
o: yes, at 3.3 V
The voltage doesn't fix it: 500 mA is many times a pin's limit.
no, use a transistor
500 mA is far over a pin's few-to-tens of mA. The pin switches a transistor, and the transistor carries the motor current.

cards: Pulse-width modulation switches a pin fully on and off quickly. The duty cycle is the fraction of each period it’s on.
A load that responds slowly, like a motor, heater or LED seen by the eye, behaves as if it got the average: V_avg = duty × V_supply.
Why switch instead of using a resistor: a switch is either fully on or off, so it wastes almost no power. A resistor burns the difference as heat.
Timer resolution sets the steps: a 10-bit timer gives 1024 duty levels.
title: PWM and duty cycle

qs.q: A 12 V supply is switched at 25% duty. What is the average voltage, in V?
A 1 kHz PWM signal is at 40% duty. How long is it high each period, in ms?
qs.why: Period = 1 ms; 40% of it is 0.4 ms.

qs.q: Why does PWM waste less power than a series resistor when dimming a motor?
qs.ans: The transistor is fully on or off, so it barely heats
wrong: PWM lowers the motor’s internal winding resistance
The pulses cancel the motor’s back EMF losses
PWM stores energy in the supply capacitor
qs.why: A transistor has nearly zero voltage across it when on and zero current when off, so its loss is tiny.

qs.q: A timer has 8-bit resolution. How many duty-cycle steps does it offer?
qs.why: 2⁸ = 256 steps.

qs.q: For a 5 V PWM signal, rank these duty cycles by average voltage, highest first.

demo.title: PWM duty cycle
demo.hint: The pin is either at the supply or at zero. The slow load sees the average, which is just the duty cycle times the supply.

p.x: **Pulse-width modulation (PWM)** switches a pin fully on and fully off, quickly.
The **duty cycle** $D$ is the fraction of each period the pin is on.
A load that responds slowly, like a motor, a heater or an LED seen by the eye, behaves as if it got the average.

p.cap: load much slower than one PWM period

g.q: 25 % duty on a 12 V supply. The motor acts as if it got…
o: 3 V
9 V
That's the off fraction. Duty cycle is the fraction of time on.
6 V
That's 50 % duty. At 25 % the pin is on a quarter of the time.

p.x: A switch is either fully on (no voltage across it) or fully off (no current), so it wastes [[almost no]] power.
Not quite zero: a little is lost in the switch's on-resistance and during each transition.
The timer's resolution sets how finely the duty cycle can be set.

p.cap: n-bit timer counting its full range

p.x: Each step is about 0.1 % duty.

cards: An analog-to-digital converter maps 0 to Vref onto integer codes. An n-bit ADC has 2ⁿ codes, so one step is Vref/2ⁿ.
Convert a reading back with V = code × Vref / 2ⁿ. A 12-bit ADC at 3.3 V has steps of about 0.8 mV.
Why scale signals to fill the range: a 0–1 V sensor on a 0–3.3 V ADC uses under a third of the codes, wasting resolution.
Signals above Vref clip, and above the supply can damage the pin. Use a divider or op-amp to scale them down.
title: ADC resolution and scaling

qs.q: A 10-bit ADC uses Vref = 5 V. What voltage is one step, in mV?
A 12-bit ADC with Vref = 3.3 V reads 2048. What voltage is that, in V?
A 0–10 V sensor must feed a 0–3.3 V ADC. What is the simplest fix?
qs.ans: A resistor divider of about 1/3
wrong: A pull-up resistor to 3.3 V
A higher-resolution ADC on the same pin
A larger series capacitor
qs.why: A divider scales 10 V to about 3.3 V. Without it the input clips or is damaged.

qs.q: A temperature sensor outputs 0–0.5 V into a 0–3.3 V, 10-bit ADC. How many codes does it actually use?
qs.ans: About 155
wrong: All 1024
About 512
About 31
qs.why: 0.5/3.3 × 1024 ≈ 155. Amplifying it by about 6 would use the full range.

qs.q: At Vref = 3.3 V, rank these ADCs by step size, finest first.
qs.why: Steps of about 0.05, 0.81, 3.2 and 12.9 mV.

demo.title: ADC quantization
demo.hint: Each extra bit halves the step. The stair-step is what the processor sees; the smooth line is the real signal. Fewer bits, bigger stairs.

p.x: An analog-to-digital converter maps 0 to $V_{ref}$ onto whole-number codes. An $n$-bit ADC has $2^n$ codes.

p.cap: ideal ADC, input between 0 and V_{ref}

g.q: Add 2 bits to an ADC. The step size…
o: halves
That's one extra bit. Each bit doubles the codes, so two bits make 4× as many.
drops to a quarter
2 more bits give 2² = 4× the codes over the same range, so each step is a quarter.

p.cap: some datasheets divide by 2ⁿ − 1; the difference is under one step

p.x: 12-bit ADC, $V_{ref}$ = 3.3 V, reading code 2,048:
A 0–1 V sensor on a 0–3.3 V ADC uses [[under a third]] of the codes, wasting resolution.
Amplify it 3× first (0–3 V) and it uses about 91 % of the codes.
Inputs above $V_{ref}$ clip: they all read the top code (4,095 at 12 bits).
Inputs above the supply can damage the pin. Scale them down first with a divider or an op-amp.
0–10 V signal, divider 22 kΩ over 10 kΩ:
Only 5 % under 3.3 V: use 1 % resistors so tolerance can't push it over.

cards: UART sends bytes as framed bits: 1 start bit, 8 data bits, usually 1 stop bit. That is 10 bits on the wire per byte.
Throughput = baud ÷ 10 bytes per second. At 115,200 baud that is 11,520 bytes/s.
Why clocks must match: each side times bits from its own clock. A combined mismatch over about 2–3% shifts the sampling point out of the bit by the end of a frame.
SPI and I²C share a clock line, so timing tolerance is far less of an issue. SPI is fastest; I²C needs only two wires.
title: Serial links and timing

qs.q: At 9600 baud with 8N1 framing, how many bytes per second can a UART send?
qs.why: 10 bits per byte: 9600/10 = 960 bytes/s.

qs.q: A 1 kB (1024 byte) message goes out at 115,200 baud, 8N1. How long does it take, in ms?
A UART link prints garbage characters. Both sides are set to 115,200. What is a likely cause?
qs.ans: One clock is several percent off
wrong: The cable is longer than about 10 cm
The data has too many zero bits
SPI is needed for any text
qs.why: Without a shared clock, a frequency error accumulates across the frame and bits are sampled wrong.

qs.q: Which bus needs only two wires and can address many devices?
qs.ans: I²C
wrong: SPI
Parallel GPIO
Analog voltage
qs.why: I²C uses clock and data lines with addresses. SPI needs a chip-select line per device.

qs.q: Rank these links by bytes per second, highest first.
qs.why: About 1.25 MB/s, 100 kB/s, 11.5 kB/s and 960 B/s.

demo.title: Baud rate and transfer time
demo.hint: Every byte costs 10 bit times with 8N1 framing. Doubling the baud rate halves the time; the start and stop bits are a fixed 20% overhead.

p.x: **UART** sends each byte as a framed burst of bits.
1 + 8 + 1 = 10 bits on the wire per byte, with the usual one stop bit.

g.q: How many bits go on the wire for each byte?
o: That's only the data. The start and stop bits frame every byte.
1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10.
There's a start bit and a stop bit, so 2 extra bits.

p.cap: 1 start, 8 data, 1 stop bit; no gaps between bytes

p.x: There's no shared clock: each side times bits from its own clock, starting at the start bit's edge.
The receiver samples each bit near its middle. A clock error adds up bit by bit.
A design rule with margin: near 5 %, the sample point drifts out of the last bits.

g.q: A small clock mismatch causes errors first at…
o: the start of the frame
Timing restarts at each start edge, so the first bits are still close to centre.
the end of the frame
The error grows with every bit, so the last bits drift furthest from centre.

p.x: SPI and I²C send a clock line with the data, so timing tolerance matters [[much less]].

p.c: clock, two data lines, chip select
clock and data, shared by many chips

p.x: SPI often runs at 10 MHz or more; I²C usually at 100 kHz to 1 MHz.

cards: A sketch’s degrees of freedom are its independent ways to move or change shape. Constraints remove those freedoms by specifying geometric relationships or dimensions.
A free point in a plane has two degrees of freedom: horizontal coordinate x and vertical coordinate y. A free circle has three: center coordinates x,y and radius r.
Constraining a point to a horizontal line fixes its vertical position but leaves horizontal motion. A constraint removes only the motion it actually prevents.
A circle centered at the origin still needs a radius or diameter dimension. Fixing its center removes two freedoms, leaving one size freedom.
title: Degrees of freedom

qs.q: A sketch point is constrained to a horizontal construction line but has no other constraints. What motion remains?
qs.ans: Sliding along the line
wrong: Moving perpendicular to the line
Rotating the construction line
Changing the point’s diameter
qs.why: The line fixes the point’s vertical coordinate. Its horizontal coordinate remains free.

qs.q: A free circle has its center constrained to the sketch origin. How many degrees of freedom remain?
qs.why: The center’s two coordinates are fixed, but the radius can still change.

qs.q: Which information fully defines an otherwise free circle in a planar sketch?
qs.ans: Its center position and radius
wrong: Its radius and circumference
Its area and diameter
Its center’s horizontal coordinate alone
qs.why: Two center coordinates and one size determine the circle. Radius and circumference describe the same size freedom and do not locate the center.

qs.q: Rank these geometric objects by remaining degrees of freedom, largest first. Assume no additional constraints.
items: A circle with free center and radius
A point free in the sketch plane
A point constrained to a fixed line
A point coincident with the fixed origin
qs.why: The remaining freedom counts are 3, 2, 1, and 0.

demo.title: A circle needs three parameters
demo.hint: A free planar circle needs two center coordinates and one radius. Constraining its center removes two freedoms; specifying its size removes the last. Counts assume independent, compatible constraints.

demoNeeded: Show a draggable circle. Center constraints disable translation; a radius constraint disables resizing. Display the remaining freedom count beside the geometry.

cards: Geometric relations express how features should behave together. Symmetry keeps paired geometry equally spaced around an axis; equal constraints preserve equal sizes without duplicating dimensions.
For hole centers symmetric about x = 0 with spacing p, their coordinates are xleft = −p/2 and xright = p/2. A centered plate of width W has edges at ±W/2.
Each hole’s center-to-edge distance is e = (W − p)/2. This relationship follows from splitting the unused width equally between both sides.
With W = 100 mm and p = 60 mm, hole centers are at ±30 mm and each center-to-edge distance is 20 mm.
title: Symmetry and geometric relations

qs.q: A centered plate has width W = 120 mm. Two hole centers are symmetric about x = 0 with spacing p = 80 mm. What is their center-to-edge distance e in mm?
qs.why: The right edge is at 60 mm and the right hole center at 40 mm. Their separation is 60 − 40 = 20 mm.

qs.q: A plate has width W = 100 mm and symmetric hole centers spaced p = 60 mm apart. Each hole has radius r = 5 mm. What material distance remains from either hole boundary to the nearest plate edge, in mm?
qs.why: Center-to-edge distance is (100 − 60)/2 = 20 mm. Subtracting the hole radius leaves 20 − 5 = 15 mm.

qs.q: A centered plate widens from 100 mm to 120 mm. Its symmetric holes must remain 20 mm from the nearest edge, measured to their centers. What should the new center spacing p be?
qs.ans: 80 mm
wrong: 60 mm
100 mm
40 mm
qs.why: p = W − 2e = 120 − 40 = 80 mm. Keeping the old 60 mm spacing would increase the edge distances.

qs.q: Two circles must remain equal in size when the design changes. Which constraint expresses that intent directly?
qs.ans: An equal-radius relation
wrong: Two independent radius dimensions with matching values
A tangent relation between their circumferences
A fixed center-to-center spacing
qs.why: An equality relation preserves the relationship during edits. Two initially equal dimensions can later diverge independently.

demo.title: Symmetric hole placement
demo.hint: Change plate width W or hole spacing p. Symmetry splits the unused width equally. Distances shown are measured to hole centers, not hole boundaries.

figNeeded: Draw a plate centered at x = 0, with width W, hole-center spacing p, and equal center-to-edge distances e. Label hole radius r separately.

cards: A redundant constraint repeats information already implied by other constraints. A conflicting constraint demands geometry incompatible with the existing requirements.
For ordered collinear points A, B, and C, lengths satisfy AC = AB + BC. Once AB and BC are fixed, AC is determined rather than independently adjustable.

A reference dimension reports a size without controlling it; SolidWorks calls it a driven dimension. The dimensions that do control the sketch are driving dimensions. A driven dimension lets you read a derived size without adding another equation to the sketch solver.
If AB = 30 mm and BC = 20 mm, AC must be 50 mm. Driving AC to 50 repeats information; driving it to 55 creates a conflict.
title: Redundant and conflicting constraints

qs.q: Ordered collinear points have AB = 35 mm and BC = 25 mm. A third driving dimension demands AC = 64 mm. By how many mm does that demand exceed the compatible value?
qs.why: The compatible value is AC = 35 + 25 = 60 mm. The demand exceeds it by 64 − 60 = 4 mm.

qs.q: A rectangle already has horizontal and vertical edge relations. A new 90° relation between adjacent edges adds what kind of information?
qs.ans: Redundant angular information
wrong: An independent size constraint
A conflicting rotation requirement
A reference for its absolute position
qs.why: Horizontal and vertical directions already imply perpendicularity. The extra angle repeats that relationship rather than locating or sizing the rectangle.

qs.q: AB and BC are driving dimensions on ordered collinear points. You want AC displayed while allowing it to follow edits to AB. What is the appropriate role for AC?
qs.ans: A reference (driven) dimension
wrong: A third driving dimension
A fixed relation on all three points
An equality constraint between AB and BC
qs.why: A reference (driven) dimension reports AC and follows AB and BC. Making AC a third driving dimension repeats what AB + BC already sets, which is redundant at best and conflicting after an edit. Fixing the points stops all edits; making AB = BC adds a rule nobody asked for.

qs.q: Two constraints on a point are x + y = 10 and 2x + 2y = 20. Why is the point not fully located?
qs.ans: The equations describe the same line
wrong: Two coordinate equations necessarily conflict
The second equation fixes only the point’s scale
A planar point requires three independent coordinates
qs.why: The second equation is twice the first, so it removes no additional freedom. The point can still move along the line.

demo.title: Compatible or conflicting lengths
demo.hint: AB and BC determine AC for ordered collinear points. Matching the requested AC repeats information; a nonzero mismatch means all three driving dimensions cannot be satisfied together.

cards: A fully constrained sketch can still have multiple geometric solutions. Dimensions may determine distances without specifying which side of a line a feature occupies.
An isosceles triangle with equal sides L and base b has apex height h = ±√[L² − (b/2)²]. Fix the base horizontally and center it at the origin.
The two signs represent mirrored solutions. At b = 2L they merge into a flat triangle; beyond that value, the requested lengths cannot form a triangle.
For the upper solution, dh/db = −b/(4h). As h approaches zero, small base changes cause large height changes, making nearly flat geometry sensitive.
With L = 50 mm and b = 60 mm, the apex can be at h = +40 mm or −40 mm. Design intent must select the intended side.
title: Branches and near-degenerate geometry

qs.q: An isosceles sketch has equal sides L = 50 mm and base b = 80 mm, so the apex height is h = √(50² − 40²) = 30 mm. For the upper solution, what is |dh/db| = b/(4h)?
qs.why: |dh/db| = 80/(4 × 30) = 0.6667: each extra mm of base lowers the apex by about 0.67 mm. Using h = 40 (half the base) instead of the height gives 0.5.

qs.q: A solver rebuilds a triangle below its base even though its dimensions match the previous triangle above the base. What was missing from the design intent?
qs.ans: A requirement selecting the apex side
wrong: A second dimension repeating the base length
An additional equal-length relation on the two sides
A tighter numerical display precision for dimensions
qs.why: Both mirrored triangles satisfy the same lengths. Repeating existing dimensions does not select one geometric branch.

qs.q: For fixed L, why does a nearly flat isosceles triangle become difficult to edit predictably?
qs.ans: Height becomes highly sensitive to base length
wrong: The equal-side constraint becomes independent twice
The triangle acquires unrestricted rigid translation
Its base length stops affecting the apex position
qs.why: |dh/db| = b/(4h) grows as h approaches zero. The geometry becomes sensitive even though the base remains fixed in position.

qs.q: With L = 50 mm and the upper apex selected, rank base lengths by sensitivity magnitude |dh/db|, largest first.
qs.why: Sensitivity b/[4√(L² − b²/4)] increases as the base approaches 2L = 100 mm.

demo.title: Two solutions approach a singular shape
demo.hint: Both curves satisfy equal sides L = 50 mm. As base length approaches 100 mm, the apex height becomes extremely sensitive. The slider stops short of the flat, singular configuration.

figNeeded: Draw both mirrored triangles with fixed horizontal base b, equal sides L, and signed apex heights ±h. Add a nearly flat case.

cards: Spindle speed counts tool revolutions per minute. Cutting speed describes how fast the cutting edge moves past the material. Larger tool diameters produce higher cutting speed at the same spindle speed.
For diameter D in mm and spindle speed n in revolutions per minute, cutting speed Vc = πDn/1000 in m/min.
Each revolution moves an edge through one circumference πD. Multiplying circumference by revolutions per minute gives edge travel per minute.
A 10 mm tool at 3000 revolutions per minute has Vc = π × 10 × 3000/1000 = 94.25 m/min.
title: Spindle and cutting speed

qs.q: What does cutting speed Vc describe in peripheral milling?
qs.ans: The cutting edge’s tangential speed
wrong: The table’s programmed travel speed
The number of teeth contacting each second
The axial distance removed per pass
qs.why: Cutting speed follows the rotating edge. Table travel is feed rate, a separate motion.

qs.q: A tool has D = 20 mm and n = 1500 revolutions per minute. What is Vc in m/min?
Tool diameter doubles while spindle speed n remains unchanged. How does cutting speed Vc change?
qs.ans: It doubles
wrong: It stays unchanged
It increases fourfold
It falls by half
qs.why: Vc is proportional to diameter. A doubled circumference travels twice as far during each revolution.
