qs.q: At the same spindle speed n, rank tool diameters by cutting speed Vc, largest first.
qs.why: Vc = πDn/1000, so cutting speed increases directly with D when n is fixed.

demo.title: Diameter changes edge speed
demo.hint: Spindle speed counts rotations; cutting speed measures edge travel. The model uses diameter in mm, spindle speed in revolutions per minute, and cutting speed in m/min.

cards: Feed per tooth measures the programmed advance associated with each tooth passage. It connects spindle rotation, tooth count, and machine feed rate.
Feed rate vf = fz zn, where fz is feed per tooth in mm/tooth, z tooth count, and n revolutions per minute. Then vf is in mm/min.
More tooth passages per minute require faster table motion to preserve the same advance per tooth. Feed per tooth is not necessarily the actual maximum chip thickness.
With fz = 0.05 mm/tooth, z = 4, and n = 3000 revolutions per minute, vf = 600 mm/min.
title: Feed per tooth

qs.q: A tool has z = 4 teeth and runs at n = 2500 revolutions per minute. With fz = 0.04 mm/tooth, how long does a 200 mm constant-feed move take in seconds?
A two-tooth tool runs at n = 3000 revolutions per minute and vf = 300 mm/min. A four-tooth replacement runs at 2000 revolutions per minute. What vf preserves the original fz, in mm/min?
qs.why: Original fz = 300/(2 × 3000) = 0.05 mm/tooth. New vf = 0.05 × 4 × 2000 = 400 mm/min.

qs.q: A four-tooth tool runs at 3000 revolutions per minute and 600 mm/min. What feed rate preserves fz when spindle speed falls to 1500 revolutions per minute?
qs.ans: 300 mm/min
wrong: 600 mm/min
1200 mm/min
150 mm/min
qs.why: Original fz = 600/(4 × 3000) = 0.05 mm/tooth. The new feed is 0.05 × 4 × 1500 = 300 mm/min.

qs.q: Rank these cases by programmed feed per tooth fz, largest first. All tools have z = 4 teeth.
qs.why: Using fz = vf/(zn) gives 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, and 0.025 mm/tooth.

demo.title: Coordinate feed and spindle speed
demo.hint: Increasing spindle speed or tooth count requires proportionally more feed to preserve fz. This is a kinematic relationship, not a material-specific cutting recommendation.

cards: Requested cutting conditions may exceed spindle or feed limits. Calculate actual spindle speed first, then calculate feed from that speed rather than from an unattainable request.
Required spindle speed is nreq = 1000Vc/(πD). With limit nmax, actual n = min(nreq,nmax). For target feed per tooth fz and z teeth, required feed is vf = fz zn.
If the machine caps feed below vf, actual feed per tooth falls. Conversely, capping spindle speed while retaining feed calculated from nreq increases actual feed per tooth.
For D = 10 mm and requested Vc = 200 m/min, nreq ≈ 6366 rev/min. A 5000 rev/min limit gives actual Vc ≈ 157.1 m/min.
title: Machine limits and actual feed

qs.q: A 10 mm tool requests Vc = 200 m/min, but nmax = 5000 revolutions per minute. For z = 4 and target fz = 0.05 mm/tooth, what feed should be paired with the capped speed, in mm/min?
A four-tooth tool was programmed for 6000 revolutions per minute and 1200 mm/min. Spindle speed is capped at 4000 revolutions per minute while feed stays unchanged. What is actual fz?
qs.ans: 0.075 mm/tooth
wrong: 0.050 mm/tooth
0.0333 mm/tooth
0.300 mm/tooth
qs.why: Actual fz = 1200/(4 × 4000) = 0.075 mm/tooth. Retaining the original 0.05 ignores the spindle-speed reduction.

qs.q: A six-tooth tool runs at 5000 revolutions per minute. Target fz is 0.04 mm/tooth, but actual feed is capped at 900 mm/min. What percentage of target fz is achieved?
qs.why: Required feed is 0.04 × 6 × 5000 = 1200 mm/min. The achieved fraction is 900/1200 = 0.75, or 75%.

qs.q: Order the dependent checks when setting feed from a cutting-speed target with a spindle limit.
items: Calculate nreq from Vc and D
Apply the spindle limit to obtain n
Calculate required feed from fz, z, and n
Check feed capability and resulting actual fz
qs.why: Feed depends on actual spindle speed. A feed limitation must then be checked because it can change the achieved advance per tooth.

demo.title: Spindle limits change the result
demo.hint: The tool diameter is fixed at 10 mm. Once the spindle limit is reached, requesting more cutting speed no longer increases actual cutting speed. Feed calculations must use actual spindle speed.

cards: A cutting operation must fit both available spindle power and torque. Passing a power check does not guarantee sufficient torque at low rotational speed.
For rectangular engagement, removal rate Q = ae ap vf/60 in mm³/s. Here ae is radial width in mm, ap axial depth in mm, and vf feed in mm/min.
A simplified cutting-power estimate is Pcut = uQ, where u is specific cutting energy in J/mm³. Spindle torque is T = Pcut/ω, with ω = 2πn/60 in rad/s.
At ae = 5 mm, ap = 2 mm, vf = 600 mm/min, and u = 2 J/mm³, Q = 100 mm³/s and Pcut = 200 W.

Specific cutting energy varies with material and cutting conditions. This model screens feasibility; it does not establish tool life, chatter stability, chip evacuation, or manufacturer-approved settings.
title: Power and torque constraints

qs.q: A cut has ae = 5 mm, ap = 2 mm, vf = 600 mm/min, and u = 2 J/mm³. At n = 300 revolutions per minute, what cutting torque T is required in N·m?
A cut requires 200 W at 300 revolutions per minute. The spindle can deliver 500 W but only 5 N·m at that speed. What limits feasibility?
qs.ans: Required torque exceeds available torque
wrong: Required power exceeds the 500 W rating
The wattage check establishes sufficient capacity
Converting speed to rad/s increases available torque
qs.why: Required torque is 200/(2π × 300/60) = 6.366 N·m, above 5 N·m. A sufficient power rating does not override the torque limit.

qs.q: A model allows Pcut = 300 W with u = 3 J/mm³, ae = 4 mm, and ap = 2 mm. What maximum feed vf follows from this power model, in mm/min?
qs.why: Qmax = Pcut/u = 100 mm³/s. Then vf = 60Q/(ae ap) = 6000/8 = 750 mm/min.

qs.q: A screening calculation assumes constant u. Feed vf and spindle speed n both double while ae and ap remain unchanged. What happens to the predicted cutting torque?
qs.ans: It stays unchanged
wrong: It doubles
It falls by half
It increases fourfold
qs.why: Removal rate and power double, but angular speed also doubles. Their ratio T = Pcut/ω stays unchanged under the constant-u assumption.

demo.title: Power is not torque
demo.hint: The fixed engagement is ae = 5 mm and ap = 2 mm, with specific cutting energy u = 2 J/mm³. For the same removal rate, lower spindle speed requires more torque.

cards: Generalization means performing well on new examples from the intended use setting. A model can fit its training examples closely without learning a relationship that transfers.
Training data fit model parameters. Validation data guide choices such as model complexity. Test data provide a final evaluation after those choices are fixed.
Overfitting occurs when a model captures accidental details of training data. Those details can reduce training error while making predictions on new examples worse.
If training error falls from 10 to 2 while validation error rises from 12 to 18, the improved training fit has not improved measured generalization.
title: Training and unseen examples

qs.q: Which dataset should guide the choice between candidate model complexities?
qs.ans: The validation dataset
wrong: The final test dataset
The training predictions alone
The deployment inputs without outcomes
qs.why: Validation data support model selection. Repeatedly choosing models from final test results turns the test set into another selection set.

qs.q: What term describes fitting accidental training details that fail to transfer to new examples?
qs.why: Overfitting improves agreement with training-specific variation rather than the transferable relationship.

qs.q: A more complex model lowers training error but raises validation error. What does this comparison suggest?
qs.ans: The added complexity is overfitting
wrong: The validation set should be used for fitting next
The lower training error proves better generalization
The evaluation metric must have reversed its direction
qs.why: The model fits training data better but performs worse on held-out examples. Training fit alone does not establish generalization.

qs.q: Order this evaluation workflow chronologically.
items: Separate training, validation, and test data
Choose a candidate using validation results
Evaluate the fixed choice on test data
qs.why: The test set remains outside the fitting and selection process so it can evaluate the chosen procedure.

demo.title: Better fit can generalize worse
demo.hint: These illustrative curves show training error falling while validation error eventually rises. They are a teaching model, not fitted experimental results. Try complexity 5, where validation error is lowest.

cards: Compare models using the same evaluation examples and metric. For classification, error rate is the number of incorrect predictions divided by the number evaluated.
If a group has errors E and examples N, its error rate is E/N. Pooling groups requires total errors divided by total examples, not an unweighted average of group percentages.
A small group should not receive the same influence as a much larger group when estimating error per example. Different weighting can be valid, but it answers a different question.
Groups with 2 errors among 20 examples and 18 among 180 give pooled error 20/200 = 10%.
title: Compare errors fairly

qs.q: Model A makes 6 validation errors among 40 examples and 14 among another 160. What is its pooled validation error percentage?
qs.why: Total errors are 6 + 14 = 20 across 40 + 160 = 200 examples. Error percentage is 100 × 20/200 = 10%.

qs.q: On the same 200 validation examples, model A makes 18 errors and model B makes 24. By how many percentage points is A’s error rate lower?
qs.ans: 3 percentage points
wrong: 6 percentage points
25 percentage points
12 percentage points
qs.why: A has 9% error and B has 12%, a difference of 3 percentage points. The 25% figure is the relative reduction, not the percentage-point difference.

qs.q: A dataset contains 1000 examples. You reserve 20% for testing, then 25% of the remaining examples for validation. How many examples remain for training?
qs.why: Testing uses 200, leaving 800. Validation uses 25% of 800 = 200, leaving 600 training examples.

qs.q: One validation group has 10 examples with 20% error; another has 90 examples with 0% error. What is pooled error per example?
qs.why: The groups contain 2 and 0 errors, respectively. Pooled error is 2/100 = 2%; averaging 20% and 0% equally gives the wrong weighting.

demo.title: Weight groups by their sizes
demo.hint: These fixed groups contain 20 and 180 examples. Compare pooled error per example with the unweighted mean of group error rates. The two estimates answer different weighting questions.

cards: Data leakage lets information unavailable at prediction time influence model development or evaluation. It can make measured performance look better than deployment performance.
Repeated observations from one machine, person, or part share information. If deployment targets new machines, split by machine before fitting rather than randomly splitting individual observations.

Fit preprocessing on training data only, then apply its learned transformation to validation data. Learning transformations from held-out observations lets those observations influence the pipeline being evaluated.

For ten machines with twenty observations each, reserving two entire machines gives forty test observations. A random forty-observation holdout does not necessarily test performance on unseen machines.
title: Leakage and grouped data

qs.q: A failure model will be deployed on previously unseen motors. Each training motor contributes hundreds of highly similar sensor windows. Which split best matches that deployment target?
qs.ans: Hold out entire motors
wrong: Randomly divide all windows between sets
Hold out every tenth window from each motor
Balance each motor equally across all sets
qs.why: Motor-level splitting tests transfer to new motors. Window-level splitting can place nearly identical operating signatures in both training and evaluation.

qs.q: A dataset has 12 machines, each providing 50 records. Three complete machines are reserved for testing. How many records remain available for training and validation?
qs.why: Holding out three machines leaves 12 − 3 = 9 machines. Their records total 9 × 50 = 450.

qs.q: A model predicts whether a part will fail before inspection. A feature records the repair code assigned after inspection. What is the primary problem?
qs.ans: The feature uses future outcome information
wrong: The feature is categorical rather than numerical
The feature requires more balanced sampling
The feature makes the model insufficiently complex
qs.why: The repair code is unavailable at the required prediction time and can reveal the outcome. Encoding it differently does not remove the leakage.

qs.q: Order a grouped evaluation pipeline for deployment on unseen machines.
items: Assign machines to training and held-out groups
Fit preprocessing using training records only
Train the model on transformed training records
Transform and evaluate the held-out records
qs.why: Machine separation precedes any learned preprocessing. Held-out records use the training transformation without participating in its fitting.

demo.title: Hold out machines, not just rows
demo.hint: There are ten machines with twenty records each. Holding out complete machines tests unseen-machine transfer. The bars count records; they do not claim that records from one machine are statistically independent.

demoNeeded: Show ten colored machine groups. Toggle between random row splitting and whole-machine splitting to reveal when the same machine appears on both sides.

cards: Repeatedly selecting the best validation result can fit the validation noise. The reported winner may look better than its true future performance even when every individual training run avoids leakage.

In a simplified model, each ineffective candidate independently has probability p of appearing successful by chance. Across m candidates, the probability of at least one apparent success is 1 − (1 − p)^m.

Nested cross-validation separates selection from evaluation. Inner splits choose settings within an outer training partition; the untouched outer test partition evaluates that complete selection procedure.
With p = 0.05 and m = 10 independent candidates, at least one chance success occurs with probability 1 − 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 40.13%. Real candidate results are often correlated.
Once outer results guide further tuning, they are no longer an untouched evaluation. Preserve a separate final test when the development process keeps adapting to reported results.
title: Selection bias and nested evaluation

qs.q: Under the independent-candidate teaching model, each of ten ineffective candidates has p = 0.05 probability of passing a validation threshold by chance. What is the probability of at least one pass, as a percentage?
qs.why: The probability of no passes is 0.95¹⁰. Its complement is 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = 0.4013, or 40.13%.

qs.q: A team chooses hyperparameters using all available data, then reports cross-validation scores with those settings fixed. What evaluation concern remains?
qs.ans: The settings already used the evaluation observations
wrong: Fixed settings prevent models from being retrained per fold
Cross-validation requires the same model parameters in every fold
Hyperparameter selection changes only computation time
qs.why: The observations influenced settings before being treated as held out. Nested evaluation repeats selection without access to each outer test partition.

qs.q: What does properly nested cross-validation primarily evaluate?
qs.ans: The training-and-selection procedure
wrong: One model fitted once on the entire dataset
The lowest inner-fold error among every candidate
The irreducible noise of the target variable
qs.why: Each outer fold evaluates a model selected using only its outer training partition. The result concerns the procedure, not one globally preselected fit.

qs.q: Order the steps within one outer fold of nested cross-validation.
items: Set aside the outer test partition
Compare settings using inner training-validation splits
Refit the selected setting on the outer training partition
Evaluate once on the outer test partition
qs.why: The outer test data remain outside both tuning and refitting, so their result evaluates the complete selection workflow.

demo.title: More chances to find a lucky winner
demo.hint: Each ineffective candidate independently passes a threshold with probability p. More candidates increase the chance of at least one misleading success. This is an illustrative independence model; real candidate results may be correlated.

readouts.label: Chance of at least one pass (%)

cards: A function packages instructions behind a callable name. Parameters are names in its definition; arguments are values supplied when calling it.
In Python, `return` sends a value back to the caller and ends that function call. Printing displays information but does not replace a returned value.
Returning values lets one calculation feed another. The caller can store, combine, or test the result without depending on text displayed on a screen.
For `def double(v): return 2*v`, the call `double(3)` returns 6. The parameter is v; the argument is 3.
title: Arguments and returned values

qs.q: In `def square(value):`, what is `value`?
qs.ans: A parameter
wrong: The returned result
A function call
The function’s name
qs.why: A parameter names an input inside the function definition. The actual value supplied by a call is an argument.

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def double(v):
    return 2 * v
print(double(3))
```
qs.why: The call supplies v = 3, so the returned value is 2 × 3 = 6.

qs.q: What does a Python function return when execution reaches its end without executing a return statement?
qs.ans: `None`
wrong: Its last printed value
Its first argument
qs.why: Python returns None implicitly. Displaying a value with print does not make it the return value.

qs.q: Order the execution of `result = double(3)` followed by `print(result)`.
items: Return the result to the caller
Store and then print the returned result
qs.why: The function computes and returns before the caller finishes assigning and using the result.

demo.title: A function maps input to output
demo.hint: This models double(v), which returns 2*v. The output is a value the caller can use, regardless of whether it is printed.

cards: Functions can be composed: one function’s returned value becomes another function’s argument. Evaluate the inner call before applying the outer function.
Python keyword arguments identify parameters by name. For `def scale(v, gain=2): return gain*v`, the call `scale(3, gain=4)` returns 12.
A default value supplies an omitted argument; it does not override an explicitly supplied value. Named arguments help distinguish inputs with different roles.
With scale’s default gain of 2, `scale(scale(3), gain=4)` first produces 6, then returns 24.
title: Composition and named arguments

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def scale(v, gain=2):
    return gain * v
print(scale(scale(3), gain=4))
```
qs.why: The inner call returns 2 × 3 = 6. The outer call uses gain = 4 and returns 4 × 6 = 24.
Offset keeps its default 1 while gain becomes 4. The result is 4 × (3 + 1) = 16.

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def add_bias(v):
    return v + 2

def square(v):
    return v * v
print(square(add_bias(3)))
```
qs.why: add_bias(3) returns 5. square then receives 5 and returns 25.

qs.q:
What does this Python code print?
```
def f(v):
    return v + 2

def g(v):
    return 3 * v
print(f(g(4)) - g(f(4)))
```
qs.why: f(g(4)) = 14, while g(f(4)) = 18. Their difference is −4; changing function order changes the result.

demo.title: Compose two scaling calls
demo.hint: The inner function multiplies its argument by 2. Its returned value enters an outer call with the selected gain. The default input 3 and outer gain 4 produce 24.

cards: Python passes object references into functions. Rebinding a parameter changes its local reference; mutating the referenced object can change what the caller observes.
For a list parameter a, `a.append(5)` changes the shared list. Assigning `a = [5]` binds the local name to a different list and does not rebind the caller’s variable.
Default arguments are evaluated when the function is defined. A mutable default list can therefore be reused across calls, accumulating state unexpectedly.
Use a default of None and create a new list inside the function when independent calls need independent storage. Copying a list is shallow: nested objects can remain shared.
title: Mutation and shared objects

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def modify(a):
    a.append(3)
    a = [9]

values = [1, 2]
modify(values)
print(len(values))
```
qs.why: append changes the caller’s list to [1, 2, 3]. Rebinding local a to [9] does not replace values.

qs.q:
What does this Python code print?
```
def collect(v, bag=[]):
    bag.append(v)
    return len(bag)

collect(4)
print(collect(7))
```
wrong: `None`
qs.why: Both calls reuse the same default list, so it contains two items. A fresh empty list is not created automatically for each call.

qs.q: Which function avoids sharing a default list between independent calls?
qs.ans: `def f(a=None):` followed by creating a list when a is None
wrong: `def f(a=[]):` followed by appending to a inside the function
`def f(a=list()):` followed by returning the modified list
`def f(a=[]):` followed by assigning a second local name to a
qs.why: A None sentinel allows construction during each call. Both [] and list() in a default expression are evaluated at function definition.

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
original = [[1], [2]]
copy = original.copy()
copy[0].append(9)
print(len(original[0]))
```
qs.why: The outer list is copied, but its inner lists remain shared. Appending through copy[0] changes original[0] to [1, 9].

demo.title: A reused default accumulates state
demo.hint: Each call appends one item. Reusing a mutable default grows one shared list; creating a fresh list per call leaves each returned list with one item. Compare the results as call count increases.

demoNeeded: Animate references from caller and parameter names to list objects. Contrast mutation, local rebinding, and shallow copying.

cards: A closure is a function that retains access to names from an enclosing function scope. The referenced values may be looked up when the closure runs rather than copied when it is created.
Python closures created in one loop can share the same loop-variable binding. After the loop finishes, calling each closure can therefore use the loop variable’s final value.
A default parameter such as `lambda i=i: i` evaluates the right-hand i when the function is created. For an immutable integer, this captures that iteration’s value.
Creating three zero-argument closures with `lambda: i` inside `for i in range(3)` and calling them after the loop produces 2, 2, 2. Their sum is 6.
Capturing a mutable object as a default preserves its reference, not a deep snapshot. Later mutation can still change what a stored callback observes.
title: Closures and binding time

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def make_functions():
    funcs = []
    for i in range(3):
        funcs.append(lambda: i)
    return funcs

funcs = make_functions()
print(sum(f() for f in funcs))
```
qs.why: All closures read the same enclosing i, whose final value is 2. The sum is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

qs.q: Inside a function, callbacks created by `lambda: i` should retain each loop iteration’s integer i. Which replacement does that?
qs.ans: `lambda i=i: i`
wrong: `lambda: int(i)`
`lambda: i + 0`
`lambda: [i][0]`
qs.why: The default argument is evaluated during creation. The other expressions still look up i when the callback runs.

qs.q:
What integer does this Python code print?
```
def make_functions():
    return [lambda i=i: i for i in range(4)]

funcs = make_functions()
print(funcs[1]() + funcs[3]())
```
qs.why: Each default captures its iteration’s integer. The selected callbacks return 1 and 3, giving 4.

qs.q:
What does this Python code print?
```
items = [1]
f = lambda saved=items: len(saved)
items.append(2)
print(f())
```
wrong: `None`
qs.why: The default captures the list reference, not a deep copy. Appending changes that same list, so the callback sees length 2.

demo.title: Late lookup versus captured integers
demo.hint: Create n callbacks for loop values 0 through n − 1, then call them after the loop. Late-bound callbacks all return n − 1; captured integer defaults return their individual iteration values.

cards: A permanent-magnet DC motor converts electrical input into rotation. Within a simple linear model, winding current produces electromagnetic torque.
Torque τ = kt I, where I is winding current and kt the torque constant in N·m/A. Torque is a turning effect; mechanical power also depends on rotational speed.
Magnetic forces on current-carrying conductors create the turning effect. Reversing current reverses electromagnetic torque when the motor’s magnetic field direction stays fixed.
With kt = 0.1 N·m/A and I = 2 A, electromagnetic torque is 0.2 N·m. Friction and other losses can reduce the torque available to an external load.
title: Current produces torque

qs.q: In the simple permanent-magnet DC motor model, which quantity directly determines electromagnetic torque?
qs.ans: Winding current
wrong: Rotor speed alone
Supply voltage alone
Winding resistance alone
qs.why: Torque follows τ = kt I. Voltage influences current through the circuit, but voltage alone does not specify torque.

qs.q: A motor has kt = 0.08 N·m/A and winding current I = 3 A. What electromagnetic torque τ is produced in N·m?
A permanent-magnet motor’s current reverses while its magnetic field remains fixed. What reverses directly?
qs.ans: Electromagnetic torque
wrong: The motor’s winding resistance
The permanent magnet’s polarity
The rotor’s position instantaneously
qs.why: Torque changes sign with current. Rotor motion responds over time because the rotor has inertia.

qs.q: For the same positive kt, rank these positive currents by electromagnetic torque, largest first.
qs.why: The linear model τ = kt I makes torque proportional to current.

demo.title: Torque follows current
demo.hint: The torque constant is fixed at 0.1 N·m/A. Reverse current to reverse torque. This is electromagnetic torque; friction, magnetic saturation, and thermal limits are excluded.

p.x: A permanent-magnet DC motor converts electrical input into rotation.
In a simple linear model, the winding current is what produces the electromagnetic torque.
Electromagnetic torque is [[proportional]] to winding current.

p.cap: linear motor model, fixed magnet field

p.x: Torque is a turning effect. Mechanical power also needs speed: $P = τω$.
The turning effect comes from magnetic forces on the current-carrying conductors in the winding.
Reverse the current and the torque reverses, as long as the magnet field keeps its direction: $τ = k_t I$ with $I$ negative.

g.q: Reverse the winding current, same permanent magnets. The torque…
o: reverses
Force on a conductor flips with the current direction when the field stays the same.
keeps its direction
The force depends on the current's direction. Only flipping both current and field would keep it.
drops to zero
Torque depends on the size of the current, which is unchanged. Only its sign flips.

p.x: That's the electromagnetic torque. Friction and other losses take some, so the load gets a little less.

cards: A rotating motor generates a back voltage that opposes the applied voltage during motoring. Faster rotation leaves less voltage to drive current through winding resistance.
At steady current, V = IR + keω. Here V is terminal voltage, R winding resistance, ke the back-voltage constant, and ω speed in rad/s.
Combine I = τ/kt with ω = (V − IR)/ke to estimate loaded speed. Increasing load torque requires more current and a larger resistive voltage drop.
With V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, ke = kt = 0.1 in compatible SI units, and τ = 0.2 N·m, I = 2 A and ω = 80 rad/s.
title: Back voltage and speed

qs.q: A motor has V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, kt = 0.1 N·m/A, and ke = 0.1 V·s/rad. At electromagnetic torque τ = 0.3 N·m, what steady speed ω follows in rad/s?
A motor has R = 1 Ω, ke = 0.05 V·s/rad, and kt = 0.05 N·m/A. What terminal voltage V is required for τ = 0.1 N·m at ω = 100 rad/s?
qs.why: I = 0.1/0.05 = 2 A. Required voltage is IR + keω = 2 × 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 7 V.

qs.q: At V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, ke = 0.1 V·s/rad, and ω = 100 rad/s, what current flows in the steady model?
qs.ans: 1 A
wrong: 6 A
5 A
qs.why: Back voltage is keω = 10 V. Current is (12 − 10)/2 = 1 A; 6 A incorrectly ignores rotation.

qs.q: At unchanged supply voltage, a motor’s load torque increases while it remains in the linear steady motoring regime. Why does speed fall?
qs.ans: Higher current increases the resistive voltage drop
wrong: The torque constant decreases in direct proportion to load
The back voltage must increase to supply more current
The winding resistance becomes zero under higher torque
qs.why: More torque requires more current. The larger IR drop leaves less back voltage keω, so steady speed decreases.

demo.title: Load torque reduces speed
demo.hint: Use V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, and ke = kt = 0.1 in compatible SI units. Friction and inductance are omitted. More torque needs more current and leaves less voltage for rotation.

p.x: A spinning motor generates a **back voltage** that opposes the applied voltage while it's motoring.
Faster rotation leaves [[less]] voltage to push current through the winding resistance.

p.cap: steady current, winding inductance ignored

p.x: The terminal voltage splits into a resistive drop and the back voltage. Solved for speed:
To estimate loaded speed, combine

p.cap: fixed terminal voltage, steady state

g.q: Load torque rises, same supply voltage. The speed…
o: drops
More torque needs more current, the IR drop grows, and less voltage is left for back voltage, so ω falls.
rises
More load needs more current, which takes voltage away from the back voltage. Speed falls.
stays the same
Only with R = 0. The IR drop grows with current and leaves less for k_e ω.

p.x: About 764 rpm.

cards: Motor torque accelerates the combined rotating inertia only after opposing load torque is supplied. A drive’s current limit therefore sets an acceleration limit.
Angular acceleration α = (kt I − τload)/J. Here J is total inertia referred to the motor shaft, τload opposing torque, kt torque constant, and I current.
Inertia resists changes in speed, not steady speed itself. With constant net torque, speed change is Δω = αt over elapsed time t.
A voltage-limited drive cannot sustain its current limit indefinitely as speed rises. At steady current Imax, the transition occurs near ω = (Vmax − ImaxR)/ke.
For kt = 0.1 N·m/A, I = 4 A, τload = 0.1 N·m, and J = 0.01 kg·m², α = 30 rad/s².
title: Acceleration and current limits

qs.q: A motor has kt = 0.1 N·m/A, current I = 4 A, opposing torque τload = 0.1 N·m, and J = 0.01 kg·m². If current stays constant, how long does a 60 rad/s speed increase take in seconds?
qs.why: Net torque is 0.4 − 0.1 = 0.3 N·m. Thus α = 0.3/0.01 = 30 rad/s² and t = 60/30 = 2 s.

qs.q: A drive has Vmax = 24 V and Imax = 4 A. The motor has R = 2 Ω and ke = 0.1 V·s/rad. At what speed ω does sustaining Imax require the full voltage, in rad/s?
qs.why: ω = (Vmax − ImaxR)/ke = (24 − 4 × 2)/0.1 = 160 rad/s.

qs.q: A current-limited motor accelerates an inertia J against constant load torque. J doubles while current and load torque stay unchanged. What happens to the time for the same speed increase?
qs.ans: It doubles
wrong: It stays unchanged
It increases fourfold
It falls by half
qs.why: Net torque stays fixed, so α is inversely proportional to J. Halving acceleration doubles the time for a fixed Δω.

qs.q: A motor has kt = 0.1 N·m/A and drive current limit Imax = 3 A. An opposing load requires 0.35 N·m at rest. What does the simple model predict?
qs.ans: The drive cannot produce positive net starting torque
wrong: More inertia will provide the missing starting torque
Back voltage will raise current above the configured limit
The load will accelerate once steady speed is reached
qs.why: Maximum motor torque is 0.1 × 3 = 0.3 N·m, below the 0.35 N·m opposition. Inertia cannot supply a sustained missing drive torque.

demo.title: Current sets acceleration
demo.hint: Torque constant is 0.1 N·m/A. The plot assumes the drive sustains selected current and that opposing torque stays constant. It excludes voltage saturation, friction variation, and the initial inductive current rise.

p.x: Motor torque first has to supply the opposing load torque. Only what's left over accelerates the rotating inertia.
A drive's current limit caps the motor torque ($τ = k_t I$).
So the current limit also sets an acceleration limit.

p.cap: rigid drive, J referred to the motor shaft
vars: total inertia at the motor shaft, kg·m²

p.x: The top of the fraction is the net torque: motor torque minus load torque.
Same net torque, twice the inertia: half the acceleration. $α ∝ 1/J$

g.q: Double $J$, same current and load. The acceleration…
o: halves
α = net torque / J, so twice J gives half α.
doubles
Inertia resists acceleration: J sits on the bottom of the fraction.
stays the same
Net torque is the same, but it now has twice the inertia to speed up.

p.x: Inertia resists [[changes in]] speed, not steady speed itself.

p.cap: constant net torque over time t

p.x: At steady speed, the motor only needs torque for the load and friction.
At low speed the drive can hold its current limit $I_{max}$. As speed rises, the back voltage $k_e ω$ grows until the drive runs out of voltage.

p.cap: steady current, winding inductance ignored

p.x: Faster than that, current and torque fall.

cards: A motor can generate electrical power when mechanical motion drives it. With positive shaft speed, negative electromagnetic torque opposes rotation and can convert mechanical power into electrical power.
Use V = IR + keω, with current I positive into the motor. Electrical input is Pelec = VI; electromagnetic mechanical output is Pmech = kt Iω.
With kt = ke in compatible SI units, Pelec = Pmech + I²R. Winding heat I²R remains positive even when electrical and mechanical power reverse direction.
Example: V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, ke = kt = 0.1, ω = 140 rad/s gives I = −1 A: 12 W returned, 2 W of winding heat.
Regeneration requires a drive and supply capable of accepting returned energy. Otherwise a rising bus voltage needs another energy path, such as a suitable braking circuit.
title: Regeneration and power flow

qs.q: A motor has V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, ke = 0.1 V·s/rad, and ω = 140 rad/s. Using current positive into the motor, what is electrical input power Pelec in W?
qs.why: I = (12 − 0.1 × 140)/2 = −1 A. Thus Pelec = VI = 12 × (−1) = −12 W, indicating returned electrical power.

qs.q: At ω = 140 rad/s, a motor has kt = 0.1 N·m/A, I = −1 A, and R = 2 Ω. Ignoring other losses, how much mechanical power enters the motor in W?
qs.why: Pmech = kt Iω = −14 W, so 14 W enters mechanically. Of that, I²R = 2 W becomes heat and 12 W can leave electrically.

qs.q: A drive commands regenerative braking into a DC supply that cannot absorb power. No braking resistor or other energy sink is provided. What electrical risk follows?
qs.ans: The DC bus voltage can rise
wrong: Winding resistance reverses sign during braking
Mechanical energy disappears when torque becomes negative
A current command guarantees the supply absorbs power
qs.why: Returned energy can charge the bus capacitance and raise voltage. Commanding negative torque does not create an energy-absorbing capability in the supply.

qs.q: A motor’s speed remains positive while current changes from +2 A to −2 A. Its winding resistance is unchanged. How does copper heating change?
qs.ans: It stays unchanged
wrong: It becomes negative
It falls to zero
It doubles
qs.why: Copper heating is I²R, so equal current magnitudes produce equal heating. Reversing current changes torque and power direction, not the sign of resistive loss.

demo.title: Cross from motoring into generation
demo.hint: V = 12 V, R = 2 Ω, and ke = kt = 0.1 in compatible SI units. Above 120 rad/s, current becomes negative. Assume a bidirectional drive and energy-absorbing supply; friction is excluded.

p.x: Driven by outside motion, a motor can [[generate]] electrical power.
With speed positive, negative electromagnetic torque opposes the rotation.
That braking torque turns mechanical power into electrical power.

p.cap: current I counted positive into the motor

p.x: Either one turns negative when power flows the other way.
Multiply $V = I R + k_e ω$ by $I$, with $k_e = k_t$ in SI units:
$I^2$ is positive either way: the winding heats even while power flows back.

g.q: Regenerating, the current is negative. Winding heat $I^2 R$ is…
o: still positive
Squaring removes the sign: (−1)² × 2 = +2 W.
negative
I² can't be negative. Electrical and mechanical power reverse; the heat doesn't.

p.lab: Motor driven faster by its load

p.x: The shaft puts in 14 W: 12 W goes back to the supply and 2 W heats the winding.
Regeneration only works if the drive and supply can accept the returned energy.
If nothing takes it, the bus voltage [[rises]], so it needs another path, such as a braking resistor circuit.

cards: Longitudinal static stability concerns the initial pitching tendency after an angle-of-attack disturbance. A stable response produces a moment tending to oppose that disturbance.
For a local teaching model, M = −kΔα. M is pitching moment, positive nose-up; Δα is angle-of-attack change in radians; k is restoring stiffness in N·m/rad.
With k > 0, a positive angle disturbance produces a negative, nose-down moment. With k < 0, the moment reinforces the disturbance instead.
For k = 10 N·m/rad and Δα = 0.1 rad, M = −1 N·m. This initial restoring tendency does not by itself establish that oscillations will decay.
title: Restoring pitch moments

qs.q: After a small increase in angle of attack, an aircraft develops a nose-down pitching moment. What does this indicate about its local static response?
qs.ans: A restoring tendency
wrong: A destabilizing tendency
Proof of zero oscillation
Proof of immediate return to trim
qs.why: The moment opposes the disturbance. It does not establish the full time history or whether oscillations decay.

qs.q: Using M = −kΔα with k = 10 N·m/rad and Δα = 0.1 rad, what is M in N·m?
qs.why: M = −10 × 0.1 = −1 N·m, a nose-down moment under the stated convention.

qs.q: In M = −kΔα, which sign of k gives a locally destabilizing response?
qs.ans: Negative
wrong: Positive
Zero
Either sign if the angle is small
qs.why: Negative k makes M have the same sign as Δα, reinforcing the disturbance. Zero k gives no restoring slope in this model.

qs.q: For the same positive Δα, rank these positive restoring stiffnesses by nose-down moment magnitude, largest first.
qs.why: |M| = kΔα for positive k and Δα. Larger stiffness produces a larger opposing moment.

demo.title: Does the moment restore or reinforce?
demo.hint: Positive moment is nose-up and positive disturbance increases angle of attack. Positive k gives a restoring slope; negative k reinforces the disturbance. This local model does not describe damping or complete aircraft motion.

figNeeded: Draw an aircraft with positive angle-of-attack disturbance Δα and a restoring nose-down moment M. Label the positive nose-up moment convention.

p.x: Disturb an aircraft's angle of attack, and it starts to pitch one way or the other.
**Static stability** is about that first tendency. A stable aircraft makes a pitching moment that opposes the disturbance.
Static stability only sets the first push. Whether the oscillations then die out depends on damping: dynamic stability.

g.q: True or false: a statically stable aircraft always settles back without growing oscillations.
o: True
That mixes static and dynamic stability. A restoring moment can overshoot; without enough damping the swings can grow.
False
Static stability is only the initial tendency. Damping decides whether the motion dies out.

vars: change in angle of attack, rad

p.x: In a stable aircraft the moment [[pushes back]] against the disturbance, so the model has a minus sign:

p.cap: small disturbances, linear teaching model

p.x: Take a positive disturbance: the nose pitches up, $Δα$ > 0.
Negative means nose-down: the moment opposes the disturbance. On its own that doesn't show the oscillations will decay.

cards: The neutral point is the center-of-gravity location giving zero local pitching-moment slope with angle of attack for the specified control condition. Forward center-of-gravity placement gives positive static margin.
Static margin SM = (xnp − xcg)/c. Positions xnp and xcg increase aft from the same reference; c is mean aerodynamic chord.
In a local fixed-control model, Cmα = −SM CLα. Cmα is pitching-moment coefficient slope and CLα lift-coefficient slope with angle of attack. Use the same angle units for both.
For c = 2 m, xnp = 1.2 m, and xcg = 1.0 m, SM = 0.1. If CLα = 5 rad⁻¹, Cmα = −0.5 rad⁻¹.
Moving the center of gravity aft reduces the lever arm responsible for restoring response. The neutral point depends on aircraft configuration and control assumptions.
title: Center of gravity margin

qs.q: An aircraft has c = 2 m, xnp = 1.2 m, xcg = 1.0 m, and CLα = 5 rad⁻¹. What is Cmα in rad⁻¹ under the stated fixed-control model?
An aircraft initially has SM = 0.15 and chord c = 200 mm. Its center of gravity moves aft by 20 mm while the neutral point stays fixed. With CLα = 5 rad⁻¹, what is the new Cmα in rad⁻¹?
qs.why: The margin decreases by 20/200 = 0.1, leaving SM = 0.05. Then Cmα = −0.05 × 5 = −0.25 rad⁻¹.

qs.q: For xnp = 1.2 m and c = 2 m, what is the aftmost xcg that preserves SM ≥ 0.1?
qs.why: xcg ≤ xnp − SM c = 1.2 − 0.1 × 2 = 1.0 m. Using 0.1 m directly ignores normalization by chord.

qs.q: With xnp = 1.2 m and c = 2 m fixed, rank center-of-gravity positions by static margin, largest first.
qs.why: The margins are 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, and 0. Moving aft reduces xnp − xcg.

demo.title: Move the center of gravity
demo.hint: The neutral point is fixed at 1.2 m, chord at 2 m, and CLα at 5 rad⁻¹. Move the center of gravity aft to reduce static margin and eventually reverse the moment slope.

figNeeded: Draw a chord reference with aft-increasing x, center of gravity xcg, neutral point xnp, and chord c. Label their separation and normalized static margin.

p.x: **Neutral point**: the center-of-gravity position where the pitch moment stops changing with angle of attack.
**Static margin**: how far the center of gravity sits ahead of the neutral point, as a fraction of chord.
Center of gravity ahead of the neutral point: positive static margin and a restoring moment. The neutral point is for a stated control condition, such as stick fixed.

g.q: Put the center of gravity ahead of the neutral point. The static margin is…
o: positive
Static margin measures how far the center of gravity sits ahead of the neutral point, so ahead is positive.
negative
Negative margin is a center of gravity behind the neutral point, where disturbances grow.

p.cap: both positions measured aft from the same reference

p.x: $SM$ = 0.1: the center of gravity is a tenth of a chord ahead of the neutral point.
More static margin, stiffer in pitch: the moment slope $C_{mα}$ gets [[more negative]].

p.cap: local fixed-control model; same angle units for both slopes
vars: slope of pitching-moment coefficient with α
slope of lift coefficient with α

p.x: Negative slope: more angle of attack brings a nose-down moment.
Moving the center of gravity aft shrinks the static margin. Same aircraft, $x_{np}$ = 1.2 m:
Aft of the neutral point the slope turns positive: a disturbance grows.
Where the neutral point sits depends on the configuration and on whether the controls are held fixed or left free.

g.q: Move the center of gravity to 1.3 m, behind the neutral point. The moment slope turns…
o: positive
SM = (1.2 − 1.3)/2 = −0.05, so C_mα = −SM·C_Lα = +0.25: the moment now reinforces a disturbance.
more negative
Moving the center of gravity aft cuts the static margin. Past the neutral point it goes negative and the slope flips sign.

cards: Pitch trim requires zero net pitching moment. A stable aircraft may still need elevator deflection to balance its moment at a particular lift coefficient.
Use the local model Cm = Cm0 − SM CL + Cδδ. Cm is moment coefficient, Cm0 its offset, SM static margin, CL lift coefficient, and δ elevator deflection.
Cδ is moment-coefficient change per unit elevator deflection. Here positive δ means trailing-edge down, angles use degrees, and Cδ is negative. Trim requires δ = (SM CL − Cm0)/Cδ.
With Cm0 = 0.02, SM = 0.1, CL = 0.5, and Cδ = −0.01 per degree, trim requires δ = −3°. Negative deflection supplies a nose-up contribution.
Elevator travel limits can prevent trim even when the static margin is positive. This linear model is local and excludes stall, large-deflection nonlinearities, and changes in control effectiveness.
title: Trim and elevator limits

qs.q: Using Cm = Cm0 − SM CL + Cδδ, take Cm0 = 0.02, SM = 0.1, CL = 0.5, and Cδ = −0.01 per degree. What elevator deflection δ trims the aircraft, in degrees?
An aircraft has Cm0 = 0.02, SM = 0.2, and Cδ = −0.01 per degree. Its most negative elevator deflection is δ = −10°. What maximum positive CL can be trimmed under this model?
qs.why: At δ = −10°, zero moment requires 0 = 0.02 − 0.2CL + 0.1. Thus CL = 0.12/0.2 = 0.6.

qs.q: For Cm0 = 0.02, SM = 0.2, CL = 0.8, and Cδ = −0.01 per degree, elevator travel stops at δ = −10°. What residual Cm remains?
qs.why: Cm = 0.02 − 0.2 × 0.8 + (−0.01)(−10) = −0.04. Required trim deflection is −14°, beyond the travel limit.

qs.q: At fixed positive CL, Cm0, and negative Cδ, increasing positive static margin changes required trim deflection how?
qs.ans: It requires more negative elevator
wrong: It removes the need for elevator deflection
It requires a more positive elevator angle
It leaves trim unchanged because stability is separate
qs.why: Increasing SM increases the nose-down term −SM CL. More negative δ provides the compensating nose-up moment under the stated sign convention.

demo.title: Find the trim deflection
demo.hint: Cm0 = 0.02 and Cδ = −0.01 per degree are fixed. The curve crosses zero at trim. A required deflection outside ±10° lies beyond the displayed travel range, even if static margin is positive.

p.x: **Trim** means zero net pitching moment, so the aircraft holds its pitch without being pushed nose-up or nose-down.
Stability and trim are separate. A stable aircraft can still need the elevator deflected to balance at a given lift coefficient.

g.q: True or false: a statically stable aircraft trims with the elevator in its neutral position.
o: True
That merges stability with trim. Stability is about the moment's slope; trim needs the moment itself to be zero, which usually takes some elevator.
False
Stability sets how the moment changes with α. Balancing it to zero at a given C_L usually takes some elevator.

vars: change in C_m per unit δ

p.cap: linear, small deflections

p.x: Trim means $C_m$ = 0.
Signs: positive $δ$ is trailing edge down, in degrees. That lifts the tail and pitches the nose down, so $C_δ$ is negative.
Set $C_m$ = 0 and solve for the elevator angle:

p.cap: linear model, angles in degrees

p.x: Negative: trailing edge up. That pushes the tail down and adds the nose-up moment needed.
The elevator only moves so far: say ±10°. Same aircraft, slowed down to $C_L$ = 1.4:
Past the stop, so it can't trim, even with positive static margin. This linear model also leaves out stall, large deflections and changes in elevator effectiveness.

g.q: With ±10° of elevator travel, can it trim at C_L = 1.4?
o: Yes, within the travel
The required angle grows with C_L: (0.1 × 1.4 − 0.02)/(−0.01) = −12°, past the −10° stop.
No, it runs out
It needs −12°, beyond the −10° stop. Positive static margin doesn't guarantee enough elevator.

cards: An aft tail can provide a balancing pitch moment through its force and lever arm. The needed force can also change the lift the wing must produce.
Tail-force magnitude Ft = qt St |CLt|. Here qt is local tail dynamic pressure, St tail area, and CLt tail lift coefficient. Its moment magnitude is Mt = Ft lt, with lever arm lt.
Local dynamic pressure qt = ρVt²/2 uses tail flow speed Vt and density ρ. Wake effects can make Vt differ from aircraft speed, reducing available control moment.
For a downward tail force in steady level flight, wing lift Lw = W + Ft, where W is weight. Pitch balance therefore does not by itself establish adequate wing stall margin.
With ρ = 1 kg/m³, Vt = 20 m/s, St = 0.5 m², |CLt|max = 1, and lt = 2 m, maximum tail moment is 200 N·m.
title: Tail authority and wing loading

qs.q: A tail has ρ = 1 kg/m³, Vt = 20 m/s, St = 0.5 m², and lt = 2 m. What |CLt| is needed to balance a moment magnitude of 150 N·m?
An aircraft weighs W = 1000 N and requires a downward tail force Ft = 100 N for trim. Wing dynamic pressure is qw = 250 Pa and wing area Sw = 4 m². What wing lift coefficient CLw is required?
qs.why: The wing must provide Lw = W + Ft = 1100 N. Thus CLw = Lw/(qwSw) = 1100/(250 × 4) = 1.1.

qs.q: Tail area, lever arm, density, and maximum |CLt| stay fixed. Wake interference reduces local tail speed to 80% of its previous value. What fraction of the previous maximum tail moment remains?
qs.why: Maximum tail moment scales with dynamic pressure and therefore Vt². The remaining fraction is 0.8² = 0.64; 0.36 is the lost fraction.

qs.q: At a flight condition, the wing can produce at most 1080 N before stall. Aircraft weight is 1000 N, and pitch trim requires 100 N of downward tail force. What does the combined check show?
qs.ans: Trim requires more wing lift than is available
wrong: The wing has 80 N of usable trim margin
The tail reduces required wing lift to 900 N
Pitch balance removes the need for a wing lift check
qs.why: Required wing lift is 1000 + 100 = 1100 N, exceeding 1080 N. Checking weight alone misses the additional lift required by tail downforce.

demo.title: Local flow sets tail authority
demo.hint: Density is 1 kg/m³, tail area 0.5 m², lever arm 2 m, and maximum |CLt| is 1. The selected speed is local tail speed, which may differ from aircraft speed in a wake.

figNeeded: Draw an aircraft with weight W downward at the center of gravity, wing lift Lw upward, and tail force Ft downward aft. Label tail lever arm lt, tail area St, and local tail flow Vt.

p.x: An aft tail balances pitch with a modest force on a long lever arm.
That force also counts in the vertical balance, so it changes how much lift the wing must make.

p.cap: l_t: lever arm from the center of gravity
V_t: local flow speed at the tail

p.x: A wing's or propeller's wake can change the airflow at the tail, so $V_t$ can differ from the aircraft's speed. With $ρ$ = 1 kg/m^3:
Moment goes with $V_t^2$: 30 % less speed, about half the control moment.

g.q: A wake slows the tail flow from 20 to 14 m/s. The most tail moment it can make…
o: about halves
q_t goes with V_t², and (14/20)² = 0.49.
drops 30 %
That's linear in speed. Dynamic pressure goes with V_t², so 0.7² ≈ 0.49.
stays the same
Tail force is q_t S_t |C_Lt|, and q_t falls with the local speed.

p.x: With the tail pushing down, the wing must make [[more lift than]] the weight:

p.cap: steady level flight, tail force downward

p.x: More wing lift means a higher $C_L$, closer to $C_{L,max}$. Balanced in pitch doesn't mean far from stall.

cards: In plain English: An ADC is the part that turns a real-world voltage into a number a computer can use.
An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) measures a voltage and reports it as a whole number, called a code.
Resolution is the number of bits, N. An N-bit ADC has 2^N codes: 12 bits gives 4096 codes, from 0 to 4095.
The reference voltage Vref sets the top of the scale. One step, the LSB, is Vref / 2^N. With 3.3 V and 12 bits, one LSB is about 0.8 mV.
Why steps? A number has finitely many values but a voltage does not, so every reading is rounded to the nearest step. Anything smaller than one LSB is invisible.
How it sounds at work: “What’s the LSB on that channel?” “It’s a 12-bit converter on a 3.3 volt reference.” “We’re railed at full scale.”
title: What an ADC does
plain: An ADC is the part that turns a real-world voltage into a number a computer can use.
talk: “What’s the LSB on that channel?”
“It’s a 12-bit converter on a 3.3 volt reference.”
“We’re railed at full scale.”

demo.title: Bits and step size
demo.hint: Each extra bit halves the step. Vref stretches or shrinks the whole scale.

qs.q: How many different codes can a 10-bit ADC report?
qs.why: 2^10 = 1024 codes, numbered 0 to 1023. 512 is 2^9, one bit short.

qs.q: A 12-bit ADC uses a 4.096 V reference. How big is one LSB?
qs.why: 4.096 V / 4096 codes = 0.001 V = 1 mV. That reference value is popular for exactly this reason.

qs.q: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: How many bits the converter has
The smallest voltage step it can report
The largest input it can convert
The voltage every code is measured against
qs.why: These four words describe almost any ADC in one sentence.

qs.q: “The converter can’t tell apart two voltages that are closer than about a millivolt.”
qs.ans: The LSB is about 1 mV.
wrong: The offset is about 1 mV.
The full scale is about 1 mV.
The noise floor is about 1 mV.
qs.why: The LSB is the step size. Offset is a constant shift, and noise is random wobble; neither is the step.

qs.q: “I’m reading 4095 no matter what I do.”
qs.ans: The input is at or above full scale
wrong: The input is stuck near zero volts
The converter has 4095 bits of noise
The sample rate is set too low
qs.why: 4095 is the top code of a 12-bit ADC. A reading pinned there means the voltage is at or past the reference.

cards: In plain English: Rounding every reading to the nearest step adds a small, unavoidable error, and more bits make it smaller.
Rounding to the nearest code leaves an error of up to ±½ LSB. This is quantization error, and no ideal ADC escapes it.
For a busy signal the error behaves like noise with an rms value of LSB / √12, about 0.29 LSB.
Best possible signal-to-noise ratio for a full-scale sine: SNR = 6.02·N + 1.76 dB. A 12-bit ADC tops out near 74 dB.
Why 6 dB per bit? Each bit halves the step, which halves the noise voltage, and half the voltage is −6.02 dB.
How it sounds at work: “We’re quantization-limited, a quieter amp won’t help.” “Six dB a bit, so that’s about two bits we’re missing.”
title: Quantization noise
plain: Rounding every reading to the nearest step adds a small, unavoidable error, and more bits make it smaller.
talk: “We’re quantization-limited, a quieter amp won’t help.”
“Six dB a bit, so that’s about two bits we’re missing.”

demo.title: Ideal SNR against bits
demo.hint: The line rises 6.02 dB per bit. No real converter sits above it.

qs.q: What is the ideal SNR of a 16-bit ADC for a full-scale sine?
A 10-bit ADC has a 5 V reference. What is the largest quantization error on one reading?
qs.why: LSB = 5 V / 1024 = 4.88 mV, and the worst rounding error is half of that. 1.41 mV is the rms value, LSB/√12.

qs.q: Going from 12 to 14 bits improves the ideal SNR by about how much?
qs.ans: 12 dB
wrong: 2 dB
6 dB
24 dB
qs.why: Each bit adds 6.02 dB, so two bits add about 12 dB. 6 dB is the gain from a single bit.

qs.q: One LSB is 1.2 mV. What is the rms quantization noise?
“We’re quantization-limited on this channel.”
qs.ans: The ADC step size sets the noise floor
wrong: The amplifier noise sets the noise floor
The sample rate is below Nyquist
The reference voltage is drifting
qs.why: If quantization dominates, only more bits or oversampling help. A quieter amplifier would change nothing.

cards: In plain English: If you measure too slowly, fast signals disguise themselves as slow ones, and you cannot tell afterwards.
Sampling at fs can only represent frequencies below fs/2, the Nyquist frequency.
Anything above fs/2 does not vanish. It folds back and appears at |f − k·fs| for the whole number k that lands it below fs/2. This impostor is an alias.
Why? Samples only record where the wave was at each instant. A 7 kHz and a 3 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz hit exactly the same points.
Once sampled, an alias is indistinguishable from real signal, so the fix must be analog: an anti-alias low-pass filter before the ADC.
How it sounds at work: “That spur isn’t real, it’s folding back.” “What’s the anti-alias corner?” “We’re sampling at ten times the bandwidth.”
title: Aliasing and Nyquist
plain: If you measure too slowly, fast signals disguise themselves as slow ones, and you cannot tell afterwards.
talk: “That spur isn’t real, it’s folding back.”
“What’s the anti-alias corner?”
“We’re sampling at ten times the bandwidth.”

demo.title: Where a tone lands
demo.hint: Sampling at 10 kHz. Push the input past 5 kHz and watch it fold back down.

qs.q: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear in the data?
qs.why: |7 − 10| = 3 kHz, which is below the 5 kHz Nyquist frequency.

qs.q: Where must an anti-alias filter go?
qs.ans: In the analog path, before the ADC
wrong: In firmware, right after the ADC
In the digital path, after decimation
On the reference pin of the ADC
qs.why: After sampling, an alias sits at a legitimate frequency and cannot be separated. It has to be removed before the sampler.

qs.q: 60 Hz mains hum leaks into a signal sampled at 50 Hz. Where does the hum show up?
qs.ans: 10 Hz
wrong: 60 Hz
25 Hz
110 Hz
qs.why: |60 − 50| = 10 Hz. 60 Hz cannot exist in data whose Nyquist frequency is 25 Hz.

qs.q: Put the signal chain in order, from the physical world to the data.
qs.why: Scale the signal, remove what would alias, freeze it, turn it into a code, then clean up digitally.

qs.q: “That 3 kHz spur isn’t real, it’s folding back.”
qs.ans: A tone above Nyquist is aliasing into the band
wrong: The amplifier is clipping at 3 kHz
The sensor resonates at exactly 3 kHz
The ADC is missing codes near 3 kHz
qs.why: “Folding” is aliasing. The real tone lives above fs/2 and has been mirrored down to 3 kHz.

cards: In plain English: There are a few different ways to build the chip that turns voltages into numbers, and each trades speed for precision differently.
A SAR converter runs a binary search: one comparison per bit. Typically 12 to 18 bits, up to a few million samples per second, and no memory of the last sample.
A sigma-delta converter samples far faster than needed with a crude 1-bit quantizer, then filters digitally. Typically 16 to 24 bits, but slow, and its filter takes time to settle.
A flash converter compares the input against every level at once using 2^N − 1 comparators. Fastest of all, but rarely above 8 bits.
Why the tradeoff? Precision needs either time (many careful steps) or hardware (many parallel parts). Each architecture spends a different one.
How it sounds at work: “Use a SAR if you’re muxing channels.” “It’s a delta-sigma, so mind the filter settling.” “Flash is overkill unless you’re in the gigasamples.”
title: SAR, sigma-delta, flash
plain: There are a few different ways to build the chip that turns voltages into numbers, and each trades speed for precision differently.
talk: “Use a SAR if you’re muxing channels.”
“It’s a delta-sigma, so mind the filter settling.”
“Flash is overkill unless you’re in the gigasamples.”

qs.q: How many comparators does an 8-bit flash ADC need?
qs.why: 2^8 − 1 = 255, one for every boundary between codes.

qs.q: A lab balance needs 24-bit readings ten times a second. Which architecture fits?
qs.ans: Sigma-delta
wrong: Flash
Pipeline
SAR
qs.why: Very high resolution at a low rate is the sigma-delta specialty. SAR converters top out near 18 to 20 bits.

qs.q: One ADC is switched rapidly between eight sensors. Why is a SAR usually preferred over a sigma-delta?
qs.ans: Each conversion is independent of the last one
wrong: It needs no reference voltage at all
It has far higher resolution per sample
Its input draws no current when switching
qs.why: A sigma-delta’s digital filter still holds the previous channel and needs several outputs to settle. A SAR starts fresh every time.

qs.q: Rank these by typical top sample rate, fastest first.
qs.why: Flash converts in one step, pipeline in a few staged steps, SAR in N steps, and sigma-delta needs many oversampled cycles per output.

qs.q: How many comparison steps does a 12-bit SAR take per conversion?
qs.why: A binary search settles one bit per step, so N bits take N steps.

qs.q: “It’s a delta-sigma, so mind the settling when you switch channels.”
qs.ans: Its digital filter needs several samples to clear
wrong: Its input capacitor needs time to discharge
Its reference needs a moment to warm up again
Its comparator needs a fresh calibration cycle
qs.why: The filter still holds data from the previous channel. The first few outputs after a switch are a blend and must be discarded.

cards: In plain English: The number of bits printed on the box is rarely the number of bits you can actually trust.
Real converters add noise and distortion. SINAD is the ratio of signal to everything else, noise plus distortion, in dB.
Effective number of bits: ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76) / 6.02. It is the resolution of an ideal ADC with the same SINAD.
SFDR, spurious-free dynamic range, is the gap between the signal and the largest single spur. It matters when one false tone would be mistaken for something real.
Slow converters quote noise two ways. Effective resolution uses rms noise; noise-free resolution uses peak-to-peak noise, about 6.6× larger, so it is about 2.7 bits lower.
Averaging helps because random noise partly cancels: oversampling by 4× and averaging gains one bit. It does nothing for distortion.
How it sounds at work: “It’s a 16-bit part but we get about 13.” “What’s the ENOB at our input frequency?” “Is that noise-free bits or effective bits?”
title: ENOB and real resolution
plain: The number of bits printed on the box is rarely the number of bits you can actually trust.
talk: “It’s a 16-bit part but we get about 13.”
“What’s the ENOB at our input frequency?”
“Is that noise-free bits or effective bits?”

qs.q: An ADC measures SINAD = 74 dB. What is its ENOB?
A 24-bit converter’s datasheet lists 21.5 bits of effective (rms) resolution. About how many noise-free bits is that?
qs.ans: 18.8 bits
wrong: 21.5 bits
24 bits
20.5 bits
qs.why: Peak-to-peak noise is about 6.6× the rms noise, and log2(6.6) ≈ 2.7 bits. 21.5 − 2.7 = 18.8.

qs.q: “The biggest false tone the converter creates is 90 dB below the real signal.”
qs.ans: SFDR is 90 dB.
wrong: SNR is 90 dB.
SINAD is 90 dB.
ENOB is 90 dB.
qs.why: SFDR measures the single largest spur. SNR and SINAD sum noise across the whole band.

qs.q: Noise is random and white. Oversampling by 16× and averaging gains about how many bits?
qs.ans: 2 bits
wrong: 4 bits
16 bits
1 bit
qs.why: Each 4× of oversampling halves the noise, which is one bit. 16× is two factors of four.

qs.q: “It’s a 16-bit part but we only get about 13 bits.”
qs.ans: Noise and distortion limit it to an ENOB of 13
wrong: Three of the output pins are disconnected
The reference is set to 13/16 of full scale
Firmware shifts each result right by 3
qs.why: The bottom bits still toggle, but they carry noise. ENOB says how many bits behave like an ideal converter’s.

cards: In plain English: A precise measuring chip is fussy about the circuit feeding it; get that wrong and the expensive precision is wasted.
A SAR input is a switch and a sampling capacitor. Each time the switch closes, the capacitor yanks charge from the source. This is charge kickback.
A small RC at the pin acts as a charge bucket: the capacitor supplies the gulp, the driver amplifier refills it before acquisition ends.
The input must settle within ½ LSB during acquisition. That takes (N + 1)·ln 2 time constants: about 9 τ for 12 bits and 11.8 τ for 16 bits.
Why C0G capacitors? X7R capacitance changes with voltage, so the filter corner moves with the signal and creates distortion. C0G stays put.
The reference pin is hit by the same kind of gulp on every bit trial. It needs a large capacitor right at the pin, or a buffer, or the top codes sag.
How it sounds at work: “Is the driver settling in the acquisition window?” “Put a C0G on the input, not X7R.” “The reference is drooping during the bit trials.”
title: Driving a SAR input
plain: A precise measuring chip is fussy about the circuit feeding it; get that wrong and the expensive precision is wasted.
talk: “Is the driver settling in the acquisition window?”
“Put a C0G on the input, not X7R.”
“The reference is drooping during the bit trials.”

qs.q: How many time constants does a 12-bit input need to settle within ½ LSB?
A 16-bit SAR has a 500 ns acquisition time. What is the largest input time constant that still settles to ½ LSB?
qs.ans: About 42 ns
wrong: About 72 ns
About 31 ns
About 500 ns
qs.why: 16 bits need 17 × ln 2 = 11.8 τ, and 500 / 11.8 = 42 ns. 31 ns comes from dividing by 16, which is over-cautious; 72 ns forgets most of the bits.

qs.q: Front-end notes for a 16-bit, 1 MSPS SAR channel. Which line should a reviewer flag?
lines: Reference: 10 µF ceramic placed at the REF pin
Driver: op-amp with 300 kHz gain-bandwidth
Input filter: 33 Ω in series, 2.2 nF C0G to ground
Layout: analog and digital return currents kept apart
qs.why: A 300 kHz amplifier cannot recover from kickback in a sub-microsecond acquisition window. Drivers for 1 MSPS SARs have tens of MHz of bandwidth.
qs.ans: Driver: op-amp with 300 kHz gain-bandwidth
wrong: Reference: 10 µF ceramic placed at the REF pin
Input filter: 33 Ω in series, 2.2 nF C0G to ground
Layout: analog and digital return currents kept apart

qs.q: Why is C0G preferred over X7R for the capacitor at a precision ADC input?
qs.ans: Its capacitance does not change with voltage
wrong: Its capacitance per volume is much higher
Its series resistance damps the kickback
Its leakage current cancels the input bias
qs.why: A voltage-dependent capacitor makes a signal-dependent filter, which shows up as harmonic distortion. X7R wins on density, not linearity.

qs.q: “The reference droops during conversion.”
qs.ans: The REF pin cannot supply charge fast enough
wrong: The reference voltage is set too low overall
The reference has too much thermal drift
The ADC is drawing power from the reference
qs.why: Each bit trial pulls a gulp of charge from REF. Without a big local capacitor or a buffer the voltage sags mid-conversion and bends the result.

cards: In plain English: Building a chip design is a pipeline: you describe the circuit in text, and tools turn it into real wiring.
Digital hardware is written as RTL, register-transfer level code (Verilog or VHDL). It describes registers and the logic between them, not instructions that run in order.
Synthesis turns RTL into a netlist: actual logic cells and the wires joining them. On an FPGA the cells are lookup tables (LUTs) and flip-flops.
Place and route picks a physical spot for every cell and a path for every wire. Only now are the real delays known.
Timing analysis checks every path against the clock. When all paths pass, timing is closed, and the tool writes a bitstream that configures the FPGA.
Why simulate first? A full build can take hours. Simulation finds logic bugs in seconds, before any of that.
How it sounds at work: “It passes in sim but we haven’t closed timing.” “Synthesis inferred a latch.” “I’ll kick off a build and flash the new bitstream.”
title: From code to bitstream
plain: Building a chip design is a pipeline: you describe the circuit in text, and tools turn it into real wiring.
talk: “It passes in sim but we haven’t closed timing.”
“Synthesis inferred a latch.”
“I’ll kick off a build and flash the new bitstream.”

qs.q: Put the FPGA build flow in order.
qs.why: Describe it, prove the logic, turn it into cells, give them places and wires, check the delays, then make the configuration file.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Code describing registers and the logic between them
A list of logic cells and their connections
A tiny memory that implements any small logic function
The file that configures the FPGA
qs.why: Each stage of the flow hands the next one of these.

qs.q: A 4-input LUT can implement any function of 4 inputs. How many bits of memory does it hold?
qs.why: Four inputs have 2^4 = 16 combinations, and the LUT stores one output bit for each.

qs.q: What does synthesis produce?
qs.ans: A netlist of logic cells
wrong: A bitstream for the device
A timing report for every path
A waveform of simulated signals
qs.why: Synthesis maps RTL to cells. The bitstream comes only after place and route.

qs.q: “We haven’t closed timing yet.”
qs.ans: Some paths are too slow for the target clock
wrong: The simulation has not finished running
The clock source has not been chosen
The build has not been scheduled yet
qs.why: Until every path meets its timing requirement, the design is not guaranteed to work at speed, even if it seems to on the bench.

cards: In plain English: Signals take time to travel through a chip, and the clock must tick slowly enough for them to arrive.
A flip-flop needs its input stable for a setup time before the clock edge and a hold time after it.
Between two flip-flops, data must make the trip in one clock period: T ≥ tcq + tlogic + tsetup. tcq is the clock-to-output delay of the launching flop.
Slack is the time to spare: required time minus arrival time. Positive slack passes. The shortest workable T gives fmax = 1 / T.
Why are hold problems different? Hold fails when data arrives too soon after the same edge. The clock period is not in that equation, so slowing the clock cannot fix it.
How it sounds at work: “Worst negative slack is minus 200 picoseconds.” “That’s a hold violation, slowing the clock won’t save you.” “Pipeline that path, it’s the critical one.”
title: Setup, hold and slack
plain: Signals take time to travel through a chip, and the clock must tick slowly enough for them to arrive.
talk: “Worst negative slack is minus 200 picoseconds.”
“That’s a hold violation, slowing the clock won’t save you.”
“Pipeline that path, it’s the critical one.”

demo.title: How fast can it clock?
demo.hint: Logic delay dominates. Halve it by adding a pipeline register and fmax nearly doubles.

qs.q: tcq = 0.4 ns, logic delay = 4.2 ns, tsetup = 0.4 ns. What is fmax?
The clock period is 10 ns. Data, including setup time, needs 8.7 ns. What is the slack?
qs.why: 10 − 8.7 = +1.3 ns to spare.

qs.q: A path has a hold violation. Which change can fix it?
qs.ans: Add delay to the data path
wrong: Lower the clock frequency
Remove logic from the data path
Raise the clock frequency
qs.why: Hold fails because data arrives too early. Slowing the clock is the tempting answer, but the period does not appear in the hold check.

qs.q: At a 100 MHz target, the worst setup slack is −0.3 ns. Roughly how fast can this design run as is?
qs.ans: 97 MHz
wrong: 103 MHz
70 MHz
99.7 MHz
qs.why: The slowest path needs 10 + 0.3 = 10.3 ns, and 1 / 10.3 ns = 97.1 MHz.

qs.q: “Worst negative slack is minus 200 picoseconds.”
qs.ans: The slowest path misses its deadline by 0.2 ns
wrong: The fastest path has 0.2 ns of spare time
The clock arrives 0.2 ns early at every flop
The design can run 200 ps faster than asked
qs.why: Negative slack means late. WNS is the single worst path, the one that sets the speed limit.

cards: In plain English: When two parts of a chip run on different clocks, handing data between them safely takes special care.
If a flip-flop’s input changes inside its setup and hold window, the output can hover between 0 and 1 for a while. This is metastability.
Signals from another clock domain will eventually land in that window. You cannot prevent it, only give it time to resolve.
For one bit, use a synchronizer: two flip-flops in a row on the receiving clock. The first may go metastable; it has a full period to settle before the second samples it.
Why not synchronize a bus bit by bit? Each bit resolves on its own, so some arrive a cycle later than others and the receiver reads a value that never existed.
For multi-bit data, cross a Gray-coded count (one bit changes per step), or use an asynchronous FIFO or a handshake.
How it sounds at work: “Is that signal synchronized into this domain?” “Don’t double-flop a bus.” “Run the CDC checker before you call it done.”
title: Crossing clock domains
plain: When two parts of a chip run on different clocks, handing data between them safely takes special care.
talk: “Is that signal synchronized into this domain?”
“Don’t double-flop a bus.”
“Run the CDC checker before you call it done.”

qs.q: An 8-bit binary counter crosses to another clock domain through a two-flop synchronizer on each bit. What goes wrong?
qs.ans: Bits can arrive on different cycles
wrong: Every bit arrives two cycles late
The synchronizers consume too much area
The counter loses its reset value
qs.why: A uniform two-cycle delay would be harmless. The danger is that bits changing together are captured apart, producing a count that was never sent.

qs.q: A binary counter steps from 011 to 100. How many bits change at once?
qs.why: All three bits flip, so a badly timed capture could read any of eight values. In Gray code the same step changes one bit.

qs.q: Notes from a clock-domain-crossing review. Which line is the problem?
lines: Button input passes through a two-flop synchronizer
FIFO read and write pointers cross in Gray code
12-bit sample bus is double-registered bit by bit into the 100 MHz domain
Reset asserts asynchronously and releases synchronously
qs.why: A multi-bit value cannot be synchronized one bit at a time. It needs a FIFO, a handshake, or a valid flag that is synchronized while the data is held steady.
qs.ans: 12-bit sample bus is double-registered bit by bit into the 100 MHz domain
wrong: Button input passes through a two-flop synchronizer
FIFO read and write pointers cross in Gray code
Reset asserts asynchronously and releases synchronously

qs.q: Giving a synchronizer twice as long to resolve changes its mean time between failures how?
qs.ans: It grows exponentially
wrong: It doubles
It quadruples
It stays about the same
qs.why: The chance of still being metastable decays exponentially with time, so a little extra settling time buys an enormous improvement.

qs.q: “That flop can go metastable.”
qs.ans: Its input may change right at the clock edge
wrong: Its clock input is not connected
Its output drives too many loads
Its reset is stuck in the active state
qs.why: Metastability comes from violating setup or hold. The output may sit at an in-between voltage before falling to 0 or 1.

cards: In plain English: Measuring anything with a computer takes the same four steps: sense it, clean it up, turn it into numbers, store it.
A sensor, or transducer, turns a physical quantity such as temperature, force or pressure into an electrical signal.
That raw signal is usually tiny and noisy. Signal conditioning amplifies it, filters it and protects the electronics.
An ADC then samples the conditioned voltage and turns each sample into a number. Software scales the numbers back into physical units.
Why so many stages? Each one fixes a different mismatch: physics to volts, small to large, continuous to discrete, raw counts to meaning.
How it sounds at work: “Channel 3 is railed.” “What’s the sample rate on the strain channels?” “Is that raw counts or engineering units?”
title: The measurement chain
plain: Measuring anything with a computer takes the same four steps: sense it, clean it up, turn it into numbers, store it.
talk: “Channel 3 is railed.”
“What’s the sample rate on the strain channels?”
“Is that raw counts or engineering units?”

qs.q: Put the measurement chain in order, starting from the physical world.
qs.why: Sense, clean up, digitize, convert the counts to physical units, then save.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal
Power fed to a sensor so it can produce a signal
One measurement path into the system
How many readings are taken each second
qs.why: These are the nouns of every data acquisition conversation.

qs.q: A type K thermocouple makes about 41 µV per °C. Over a 100 °C span, what must happen before a 0 to 3.3 V ADC can use it well?
qs.ans: Amplify it by several hundred
wrong: Attenuate it by several hundred
Sample it several hundred times faster
Filter it with a high-pass filter
qs.why: 100 °C gives only about 4 mV. Without gain it would cover a handful of ADC codes.

qs.q: “We take a thousand readings every second.”
qs.ans: We sample at 1 kHz.
wrong: We have 1 kHz of bandwidth.
We resolve down to 1 kHz.
We log at 1 kilobit per second.
qs.why: Readings per second is the sample rate. Bandwidth is the range of signal frequencies, at most half the sample rate.

qs.q: “Channel 3 is railed.”
qs.ans: Its reading is stuck at the range limit
wrong: Its cable is mounted on the DIN rail
Its reading is perfectly steady
Its sample rate is at the maximum
qs.why: “Railed” means stuck at the highest or lowest value the electronics can produce. The real signal is somewhere beyond it, and that data is lost.

cards: In plain English: Measure too slowly and you miss things; too fast and you drown in data. Picking the rate is a real decision.
Nyquist says sample at more than twice the highest frequency present. That is the minimum to avoid aliasing, not enough to see the wave’s shape.
To see shape, peaks and timing in the time domain, sample at about 10× the highest frequency of interest.
Data volume = channels × bytes per sample × sample rate × time. Eight 16-bit channels at 1 kHz fill 57.6 MB an hour.
A multiplexed system shares one ADC, so channels are read one after another and the per-channel rate is the total rate divided by the channel count.
Why does that matter? The channels are not captured at the same instant. Comparing phase or timing between them needs simultaneous sampling: one ADC per channel.
How it sounds at work: “Is that aggregate or per-channel?” “We need simultaneous sampling on the accelerometers.” “Ten times the bandwidth is my rule of thumb.”
title: Choosing a sample rate
plain: Measure too slowly and you miss things; too fast and you drown in data. Picking the rate is a real decision.
talk: “Is that aggregate or per-channel?”
“We need simultaneous sampling on the accelerometers.”
“Ten times the bandwidth is my rule of thumb.”

qs.q: Eight channels of 16-bit data at 1 kHz each are logged for one hour. How much data is that?
You want to see the shape of a 100 Hz vibration waveform on screen. Which sample rate is a sensible choice?
qs.ans: 1 kHz
wrong: 200 Hz
100 Hz
210 Hz
qs.why: About 10× gives ten points per cycle. 210 Hz satisfies Nyquist but draws a jagged, misleading wave.

qs.q: A multiplexed DAQ card runs at 100 kS/s in total across 4 channels. What is the rate per channel?
qs.why: 100 kS/s shared among 4 channels is 25 kS/s each.

qs.q: Two accelerometers are read by a multiplexed ADC. What error does this add when comparing them?
qs.ans: A time skew that looks like phase shift
wrong: A gain mismatch between the two
A DC offset on the second channel
A doubling of the noise floor
