qs.why: The second channel is sampled slightly later than the first. At high frequencies that delay is a significant fraction of a cycle.

qs.q: “We need simultaneous sampling on these channels.”
qs.ans: All channels must be captured at once
wrong: All channels must use the same gain
All channels must share one ADC
All channels must log to the same file
qs.why: Simultaneous sampling uses an ADC or sample-and-hold per channel so the timing relationship between signals is preserved.

cards: In plain English: A sensor’s signal is often thousands of times too small, so it gets magnified to fit the measuring device.
An ADC’s codes are spread across its full input range. A signal that fills only a sliver of the range uses only a sliver of the codes.
Choose gain so the largest expected signal nearly fills the range: gain ≈ ADC range / sensor span. A 0 to 20 mV sensor into a 0 to 2.5 V ADC wants a gain of 125.
Too much gain is worse than too little, because the peaks hit the limit and clip, and clipped data is gone for good. Leave headroom.
An instrumentation amplifier amplifies the difference between two wires and rejects voltage common to both. Its common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) says how well: 80 dB means 10,000 to 1.
How it sounds at work: “We’re only using the bottom tenth of the range.” “Leave some headroom, it’ll clip on transients.” “What’s the CMRR at 60 hertz?”
title: Gain and range
plain: A sensor’s signal is often thousands of times too small, so it gets magnified to fit the measuring device.
talk: “We’re only using the bottom tenth of the range.”
“Leave some headroom, it’ll clip on transients.”
“What’s the CMRR at 60 hertz?”

qs.q: A sensor outputs 0 to 10 mV. The ADC accepts 0 to 3.0 V. What gain fills the range exactly?
A 0 to 10 mV signal goes straight into a 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V range, with no amplifier. About how many codes does it use?
qs.ans: About 12
wrong: About 124
About 41
About 330
qs.why: One LSB is 3.3 V / 4096 = 0.81 mV, and 10 mV / 0.81 mV ≈ 12 codes. 41 forgets to divide by the reference.

qs.q: An amplifier has a CMRR of 80 dB. With 1 V of common-mode voltage, what input error does it cause?
qs.why: 80 dB is a ratio of 10,000. 1 V / 10,000 = 100 µV, as if that much signal were added at the input.

qs.q: What happens if the gain is set too high?
qs.ans: Peaks clip at the limit of the range
wrong: Noise rises above the signal level
Resolution drops below one LSB
The sample rate has to be reduced
qs.why: Gain raises signal and input noise together, so their ratio holds. The real damage is saturation: flat-topped data with the peaks missing.

qs.q: “We’re only using the bottom tenth of the ADC range.”
qs.ans: The signal is too small, so resolution is wasted
wrong: The signal is too large, so peaks are clipped
The reference is ten times too small
The sample rate is a tenth of what it should be
qs.why: Using a tenth of the range throws away more than three bits. More gain ahead of the ADC gets them back.

cards: In plain English: To measure a tiny stretch in metal, engineers use a clever circuit that only reacts to change.
A strain gauge is a resistor that changes value when stretched: ΔR / R = GF · ε. The gauge factor GF is about 2, and ε is strain.
The change is minute. At 1000 µε, a 350 Ω gauge moves by 0.7 Ω, just 0.2%.
A Wheatstone bridge puts the gauge with three matching resistors. Balanced, its output is zero, so only the change appears. One active gauge gives Vo ≈ Vex · GF · ε / 4.
Why not just measure the resistance? You would be hunting a 0.2% change riding on a huge baseline. The bridge subtracts the baseline before amplifying.
Two active gauges (half bridge) double the output and four (full bridge) quadruple it, while cancelling temperature effects.
How it sounds at work: “Is it a quarter, half or full bridge?” “Let’s go ratiometric so excitation drift drops out.” “It’s a 2 millivolt per volt load cell.”
title: Bridges and strain gauges
plain: To measure a tiny stretch in metal, engineers use a clever circuit that only reacts to change.
talk: “Is it a quarter, half or full bridge?”
“Let’s go ratiometric so excitation drift drops out.”
“It’s a 2 millivolt per volt load cell.”

demo.title: Quarter-bridge output
demo.hint: With GF = 2. Even large strain produces only millivolts.

qs.q: Quarter bridge, Vex = 10 V, GF = 2, strain = 500 µε. What is the output?
A 350 Ω gauge with GF = 2 sees 1000 µε. By how much does its resistance change?
Compared with a quarter bridge at the same strain, a full bridge gives how much output?
wrong: The same
qs.why: Four active gauges each contribute. 2× is the half bridge.

qs.q: Why use a bridge instead of measuring the gauge’s resistance directly?
qs.ans: It cancels the large unchanging baseline
wrong: It raises the gauge factor of the gauge
It removes the need for any amplifier
It makes the gauge immune to all noise
qs.why: The bridge outputs only the change. An amplifier is still needed, but now it can amplify millivolts of pure signal.

qs.q: “Let’s go ratiometric.”
qs.ans: Use the excitation voltage as the ADC reference
wrong: Use a ratio of two gauges as the output
Use a resistor divider on the bridge output
Use the ADC reference as the amplifier gain
qs.why: Bridge output is proportional to excitation. If the ADC measures against that same voltage, any drift in it cancels out.

cards: In plain English: “Zero volts” is not the same everywhere in a building, and that difference sneaks into measurements as hum.
Ground is not one voltage. Current flowing in ground wiring means two “grounds” a few metres apart can differ by millivolts to volts.
Connect two grounded boxes with a signal cable and you close a ground loop. Current flows in the cable’s ground, and its voltage drop adds to your signal, usually as 50 or 60 Hz hum.
A differential input measures between two signal wires and ignores what both share. It is the standard cure, along with isolation.
Twisting the pair makes interference hit both wires equally. For low-frequency sensor wiring, ground the cable shield at one end only, so the shield cannot carry loop current.
Why does single-ended fail? It measures the signal against local ground, so any ground difference is indistinguishable from signal.
How it sounds at work: “That 60 hertz is a ground loop.” “Go differential on that channel.” “Where’s the shield terminated?”
title: Ground loops and hum
plain: “Zero volts” is not the same everywhere in a building, and that difference sneaks into measurements as hum.
talk: “That 60 hertz is a ground loop.”
“Go differential on that channel.”
“Where’s the shield terminated?”

qs.q: A sensor is grounded at a machine and its DAQ is grounded at a wall outlet 20 m away. The single-ended reading shows 60 Hz hum. What is the likely cause?
qs.ans: A voltage between the two grounds
wrong: A sample rate below 120 Hz
An ADC reference that is too low
A thermocouple wired backwards
qs.why: The two grounds differ, current flows in the signal return, and the drop adds to the reading at mains frequency.

qs.q: A ground loop drives 2 A through a cable shield with 50 mΩ of resistance. What error voltage does that create?
qs.why: V = I · R = 2 A × 0.05 Ω = 0.1 V = 100 mV. That can dwarf a sensor signal.

qs.q: Wiring notes for a low-level, low-frequency sensor. Which line invites trouble?
lines: Signal runs on a twisted pair
Shield bonded to chassis at the sensor and at the DAQ
Input configured as differential
Cable routed away from the motor drive leads
qs.why: Grounding the shield at both ends closes a loop through it. For low-frequency signals, bond it at one end.
qs.ans: Shield bonded to chassis at the sensor and at the DAQ
wrong: Signal runs on a twisted pair
Input configured as differential
Cable routed away from the motor drive leads

qs.q: “The two boxes disagree about what zero volts is.”
qs.ans: There’s a ground potential difference.
wrong: There’s a common-mode rejection.
There’s a floating reference.
There’s crosstalk between them.
qs.why: Different ground voltages are a ground potential difference. Common-mode rejection is the ability to ignore it.

qs.q: Which change best removes ground-loop hum from a measurement?
qs.ans: Measure differentially or isolate the input
wrong: Add a second ground wire in parallel
Increase the gain ahead of the ADC
Sample faster and average the readings
qs.why: A second ground wire only shrinks the error. Differential or isolated inputs stop the ground difference from being measured at all.

cards: In plain English: Factories send sensor readings as a small electric current because current survives long wires better than voltage.
Industrial sensors often signal with current: 4 mA means the bottom of the range and 20 mA the top. The 16 mA in between is the span.
Why current? In a series loop the same current flows everywhere, so resistance in hundreds of metres of wire does not change the reading. A voltage signal would sag.
Why start at 4, not 0? A “live zero”. A reading of 0 mA can only mean a fault such as a broken wire, never a real measurement.
At the receiver, a precision resistor turns current back into voltage. 250 Ω gives 1 to 5 V.
How it sounds at work: “It’s a two-wire, loop-powered transmitter.” “We’re reading 3.6 milliamps, that’s a sensor fault.” “Drop it across a 250 ohm shunt.”
title: The 4–20 mA loop
plain: Factories send sensor readings as a small electric current because current survives long wires better than voltage.
talk: “It’s a two-wire, loop-powered transmitter.”
“We’re reading 3.6 milliamps, that’s a sensor fault.”
“Drop it across a 250 ohm shunt.”

qs.q: A 4–20 mA signal reads 12 mA. What percentage of the range is that?
qs.why: (12 − 4) / 16 = 0.5. The tempting slip is 12 / 20 = 60%, which ignores the live zero.

qs.q: A 0 to 10 bar pressure transmitter outputs 16 mA. What is the pressure?
The receiver reads 0 mA from a 4–20 mA transmitter. What does that mean?
qs.ans: The loop is open or unpowered
wrong: The measurement is at zero
The measurement is below range
The transmitter is saturated high
qs.why: Zero on the scale is 4 mA. A true 0 mA means no current can flow: a broken wire, a dead supply or a dead transmitter.

qs.q: Why does a 300 m cable not spoil a 4–20 mA reading?
qs.ans: Current is the same all along a series loop
wrong: Long cables have very little resistance
The transmitter raises its output to match
Current signals travel faster than voltage
qs.why: The transmitter regulates loop current. Wire resistance costs supply voltage, not accuracy, as long as the supply has enough to spare.

qs.q: What voltage appears across a 250 Ω receiver resistor at 20 mA?
qs.why: 0.020 A × 250 Ω = 5 V. At 4 mA it is 1 V, hence “1 to 5 volts”.

qs.q: “We’re reading 3.6 milliamps on that loop.”
qs.ans: The transmitter is reporting a fault
wrong: The measurement is slightly negative
The loop wire is broken somewhere
The receiver resistor is too small
qs.why: Below 4 mA is outside the valid range. Many transmitters deliberately pull the loop to about 3.6 mA to flag an internal fault; a broken wire would read 0 mA.

cards: In plain English: A design review is a meeting where other engineers hunt for problems in your design before it gets built.
A design review puts a design in front of engineers who did not create it. Their job is to find problems; the presenter’s job is to let them.
Why bother? A mistake caught on paper costs an afternoon. The same mistake caught after parts are made can cost months.
Reviews come in a sequence. The preliminary design review (PDR) asks: is this the right approach? The critical design review (CDR) asks: is the design finished enough to build?
Before testing comes a test readiness review (TRR): are we ready to test, and do we know what passing looks like?
Findings leave the room as action items: each one a task with an owner and a due date.
How it sounds at work: “We got dinged at CDR.” “That’s an action item, who owns it?” “Are we through PDR yet?”
title: PDR, CDR and friends
plain: A design review is a meeting where other engineers hunt for problems in your design before it gets built.
talk: “We got dinged at CDR.”
“That’s an action item, who owns it?”
“Are we through PDR yet?”

qs.q: Put these reviews in the order they happen.
qs.why: Agree what it must do, choose an approach, finish the design, then confirm readiness to test.

qs.q: Match each item to the question it answers.
pairs: Is the design ready to build?
Who fixes this, and by when?
qs.why: Each review is a gate with one main question.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of a design review?
qs.ans: To find problems while they are cheap to fix
wrong: To show management that work is on schedule
To decide which engineer made each mistake
To get signatures so that parts can be ordered
qs.why: Approval is a by-product. A review that finds nothing has usually not looked hard enough.

qs.q: “Someone has to go fix that and report back by Friday.”
qs.ans: That’s an action item, due Friday.
wrong: That’s a requirement, due Friday.
That’s a waiver, due Friday.
That’s a milestone, due Friday.
qs.why: An action item is a task with an owner and a date. A waiver is permission not to meet a requirement.

qs.q: “We got dinged at CDR.”
qs.ans: Reviewers found problems that must be fixed
wrong: Reviewers approved the design early
Reviewers cancelled the review meeting
Reviewers asked for a lower-cost design
qs.why: “Dinged” means findings were raised. The team leaves with action items to close before the design can move on.

cards: In plain English: Engineers write rules for what a product must do, and a few small words in those rules carry legal weight.
A requirement is a statement the product must satisfy. By convention “shall” marks a binding requirement, “should” a goal, and “will” a statement of fact or intent.
TBD, to be determined, means nobody knows the value yet. TBR, to be resolved or reviewed, means a value is proposed but not yet confirmed.
Every requirement needs a verification method: test (measure it), analysis (calculate or simulate it), inspection (examine it) or demonstration (operate it and watch).
Why so strict? A requirement is a contract between teams. “Fast” or “easy to use” cannot be passed or failed, so it will be argued about at the worst possible time.
How it sounds at work: “Is that a shall or a should?” “There are still twelve TBDs in the spec.” “How do we verify that, test or analysis?”
title: Shall, should, TBD
plain: Engineers write rules for what a product must do, and a few small words in those rules carry legal weight.
talk: “Is that a shall or a should?”
“There are still twelve TBDs in the spec.”
“How do we verify that, test or analysis?”

qs.q: Which sentence is a binding requirement?
qs.ans: The pump shall deliver 2 L/min.
wrong: The pump should deliver 2 L/min.
The pump will deliver 2 L/min.
The pump may deliver 2 L/min.
qs.why: “Shall” is the contract word. “Will” reads as strong but by convention only states a fact or intention.

qs.q: A spec says “Mass shall be less than 2.0 kg (TBR)”. What does TBR tell you?
qs.ans: 2.0 kg is proposed but not yet confirmed
wrong: 2.0 kg is final and has been verified
The mass has not been estimated at all
The requirement has been formally waived
qs.why: TBR flags a number that exists but is still under review. A completely unknown value would be TBD.

qs.q: Match each verification method to how it is done.
pairs: Measure it with instruments under set conditions
Show it by calculation or simulation
Examine the item or its drawings
Operate it and watch it work
qs.why: Roughly from most to least effort. Demonstration shows that it works without detailed measurement.

qs.q: Four draft requirements. Which one cannot be verified as written?
lines: The board shall draw less than 150 mA at 3.3 V
The enclosure shall survive a 1 m drop onto concrete
The interface shall be easy to use
The logger shall record at 1 kHz ± 1%
qs.why: “Easy to use” has no pass or fail. A verifiable version names a measure, such as a task completed by new users within a set time.
qs.ans: The interface shall be easy to use
wrong: The board shall draw less than 150 mA at 3.3 V
The enclosure shall survive a 1 m drop onto concrete
The logger shall record at 1 kHz ± 1%

qs.q: “There are still twelve TBDs in the spec.”
qs.ans: Twelve required values have not been decided
wrong: Twelve requirements have failed their tests
Twelve requirements have been deleted
Twelve values are proposed and under review
qs.why: TBD means undetermined. Proposed-but-unconfirmed values would be TBRs.

cards: In plain English: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a weighing scale whose readings jump around, and why.
The design: a load cell rated 2 mV/V, excited from the 5 V USB rail, wired straight into a microcontroller’s 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference. Readings jump by whole kilograms.
Finding 1. Full-scale output is 2 mV/V × 5 V = 10 mV. One LSB is 0.81 mV, so the entire scale spans about 12 codes.

Finding 2. Excitation comes from noisy USB power while the ADC measures against a separate 3.3 V. That matters because bridge output scales with excitation: any wobble on the 5 V looks exactly like a change in weight.
Finding 3. Nothing limits bandwidth ahead of the ADC, so mains hum and switching noise alias straight into the readings.
The fix reviewers asked for: a 24-bit sigma-delta bridge converter with a built-in amplifier, using the excitation voltage as its reference.
How it sounds at work: “Your excitation and your reference aren’t tracking.” “You’ve got twelve counts across full scale.” “Use a bridge ADC and make it ratiometric.”
title: Case: the jittery scale
plain: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a weighing scale whose readings jump around, and why.
talk: “Your excitation and your reference aren’t tracking.”
“You’ve got twelve counts across full scale.”
“Use a bridge ADC and make it ratiometric.”

qs.q: A 2 mV/V load cell is excited with 5 V. What is its output at full load?
qs.why: 2 mV per volt of excitation × 5 V = 10 mV.

qs.q: With a 12-bit ADC and a 3.3 V reference, about how many codes does that 10 mV span?
qs.why: LSB = 3300 mV / 4096 = 0.806 mV. 10 / 0.806 ≈ 12.4 codes for the whole scale.

qs.q: The original design notes. Which line is the root of the “drifts with USB noise” complaint?
lines: Load cell: 350 Ω full bridge, 2 mV/V
Excitation: 5 V taken from the USB supply
ADC reference: internal 3.3 V regulator
Firmware: averages 16 readings per output
qs.why: Bridge output scales with excitation. Feeding it from a noisy rail that the ADC does not measure against turns supply noise into apparent weight.
qs.ans: Excitation: 5 V taken from the USB supply
wrong: Load cell: 350 Ω full bridge, 2 mV/V
ADC reference: internal 3.3 V regulator
Firmware: averages 16 readings per output

qs.q: Which single change fixes the most?
qs.ans: A bridge-input sigma-delta ADC referenced to the excitation
wrong: A 16-bit SAR ADC wired the same way as before
Averaging 256 readings instead of 16 in firmware
A sample rate raised from 100 Hz to 10 kHz
qs.why: It adds gain, resolution, filtering and ratiometric operation together. A 16-bit SAR alone still gives about 200 codes and keeps the supply-noise problem.

qs.q: “Your excitation and your reference aren’t tracking.”
qs.ans: Supply drift shows up as a false change in reading
wrong: The two voltages are routed on different layers
The bridge is wired with reversed polarity
The reference is larger than the excitation
qs.why: If both came from the same voltage, any drift would scale signal and reference together and cancel. Separate sources do not cancel.

cards: In plain English: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a metal bracket that cracked in testing, and what reviewers saw.
The design: a machined 6061-T6 aluminium bracket holding a sensor. It passed a static load check with a factor of 3, then cracked after two hours of vibration testing.
Finding 1. The crack began at a sharp inside corner. A sudden change in shape concentrates stress; the local stress is Kt times the nominal stress, and for a sharp corner Kt is 3 or more.
Why did static analysis miss it? Ductile metal yields locally and forgives a stress concentration under one steady load. Under millions of vibration cycles, fatigue starts exactly there.
Finding 2. One mounting hole sat 4 mm from the edge with a 4.5 mm diameter. A common rule keeps the hole centre at least 2 diameters from an edge.
Finding 3. A cosmetic face carried a ±0.01 mm tolerance. Nothing touched it. Tight tolerances cost money and should exist only where function needs them.
How it sounds at work: “It initiated at the stress riser.” “Put a radius in that corner.” “Do you really need ten microns on that face?”
title: Case: the cracked bracket
plain: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a metal bracket that cracked in testing, and what reviewers saw.
talk: “It initiated at the stress riser.”
“Put a radius in that corner.”
“Do you really need ten microns on that face?”

qs.q: Nominal stress at a corner is 40 MPa and the stress concentration factor Kt is 3. What is the local peak stress?
qs.why: Peak stress = Kt × nominal = 3 × 40 = 120 MPa.

qs.q: The bracket passed a static check with a factor of 3 but cracked in vibration. Why?
qs.ans: Fatigue starts at local stress peaks
wrong: Vibration loads exceed any static load
Aluminium weakens as it gets warmer
Static checks apply only to steel parts
qs.why: Static strength depends on average stress across the section. Fatigue life depends on the local peak, which the sharp corner tripled.

qs.q: Notes on the bracket drawing. Which line caused the failure?
lines: Material: 6061-T6 aluminium
Inside corners: sharp, R0 max
Mounting holes: Ø4.5 through, centres 9 mm from the edge
Break all outside edges 0.2 max
qs.why: A sharp inside corner is a stress concentration. A fillet radius there spreads the load and can extend fatigue life many times over.
qs.ans: Inside corners: sharp, R0 max
wrong: Material: 6061-T6 aluminium
Mounting holes: Ø4.5 through, centres 9 mm from the edge
Break all outside edges 0.2 max

qs.q: “The crack began where the shape changes suddenly.”
qs.ans: It initiated at a stress concentration.
wrong: It initiated at the neutral axis.
It initiated at the yield point.
It initiated at a datum feature.
qs.why: A stress concentration, or stress riser, is a local peak caused by geometry. The neutral axis is where bending stress is zero.

qs.q: “Do you really need ten microns on that face?”
qs.ans: The tolerance is tighter than the function needs
wrong: The tolerance is too loose to assemble
The face needs a finer surface finish
The face is too small to be machined
qs.why: Tight tolerances mean slower machining, more inspection and more scrap. The question asks the designer to justify the cost or loosen it.

cards: In plain English: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a data recorder that quietly lost data, and how reviewers caught it.
The design: a logger samples at 1 kHz in a timer interrupt, pushes each sample into a 64-entry buffer, and the main loop writes them to an SD card. Field data has gaps nobody noticed for weeks.
Finding 1. SD cards occasionally stall for 200 ms or more while they reorganize internally. A 64-sample buffer at 1 kHz covers only 64 ms.
Finding 2. When the buffer filled, the code overwrote the oldest samples without a word. Losing data is bad; losing it silently is worse, because the file still looks fine.
Finding 3. The main loop read a 32-bit sample counter that the interrupt updates. On an 8-bit processor that read takes several instructions, and the interrupt can strike between them.
Why did testing miss it? Average write time was 2 ms. Designs fail on the worst case, not the average.
How it sounds at work: “What’s your worst-case latency on the card write?” “Is that read atomic?” “Count your overruns, don’t hide them.”
title: Case: the missing samples
plain: A walk through a real-shaped design mistake: a data recorder that quietly lost data, and how reviewers caught it.
talk: “What’s your worst-case latency on the card write?”
“Is that read atomic?”
“Count your overruns, don’t hide them.”

qs.q: At 1 kHz, how long can a 64-sample buffer absorb a stalled write?
qs.why: 64 samples at 1 ms each is 64 ms.

qs.q: What is the minimum buffer size, in samples, to ride out a 200 ms stall at 1 kHz?
qs.why: 200 ms × 1 sample/ms = 200 samples. A real design adds generous margin on top.

qs.q: The firmware design notes. Which line should a reviewer reject?
lines: Timer interrupt triggers a sample every 1 ms
Interrupt reads the ADC and pushes to a ring buffer
When the buffer is full, overwrite the oldest sample
Main loop writes to the card in 512-byte blocks
qs.why: Silent overwrite hides data loss. At the least, count overruns and record them in the file so the gap is visible.
qs.ans: When the buffer is full, overwrite the oldest sample
wrong: Timer interrupt triggers a sample every 1 ms
Interrupt reads the ADC and pushes to a ring buffer
Main loop writes to the card in 512-byte blocks

qs.q: Why can the main loop read a corrupt 32-bit counter on an 8-bit processor?
qs.ans: The interrupt can update it mid-read
wrong: The counter overflows after 255 counts
The compiler stores it in the wrong order
The processor cannot hold 32-bit values
qs.why: The read takes four separate byte loads. If the interrupt fires between them, the result mixes old and new bytes.

qs.q: “What’s your worst-case latency on the card write?”
qs.ans: The longest a write can ever stall
wrong: The typical time a write takes
The delay before the first write
The time to mount the card at boot
qs.why: Buffers must be sized for the longest stall, not the average. A design that works 99.9% of the time still drops data daily at 1 kHz.

cards: In plain English: Engineers deliberately build things stronger than needed, and they have precise words for how much extra.
Factor of safety is capability divided by demand. A part that can take 300 MPa and sees 120 MPa has a factor of safety of 2.5.
Margin of safety is what is left after a required factor: MS = allowable / (load × required factor) − 1. Zero means exactly enough; negative means it fails the requirement.
Derating is the same idea for components: use a part well below its rating. A common rule runs ceramic capacitors at no more than half their rated voltage.
Why margin? Loads are estimates, materials vary and models are wrong in small ways. Margin is how you pay for what you do not know.
How it sounds at work: “Margin went negative on that joint.” “We derate caps fifty percent on voltage.” “What factor are we holding on yield?”
title: Margin and derating
plain: Engineers deliberately build things stronger than needed, and they have precise words for how much extra.
talk: “Margin went negative on that joint.”
“We derate caps fifty percent on voltage.”
“What factor are we holding on yield?”

qs.q: A material yields at 300 MPa and the working stress is 120 MPa. What is the factor of safety?
Allowable stress is 300 MPa, applied stress is 100 MPa, and the required factor is 1.5. What is the margin of safety?
qs.why: 300 / (100 × 1.5) − 1 = 1.0. +2.0 forgets the required factor, and 3.0 is the plain factor of safety.

qs.q: Capacitors are derated to 50% of rated voltage. What is the highest working voltage for a 16 V part?
“We run the part well below its maximum on purpose, so it lasts.”
qs.ans: We derate it.
wrong: We qualify it.
We burn it in.
We overdrive it.
qs.why: Derating is operating below a rating for reliability. Burn-in is running parts early to weed out weak ones.

qs.q: “Margin went negative on that joint.”
qs.ans: It no longer meets its required safety factor
wrong: It has more strength than it needs
It will certainly break in service
It has been removed from the design
qs.why: Negative margin means load times the required factor exceeds the allowable. It fails on paper; it may not break, but it cannot ship as is.

cards: In plain English: Engineers have spoken shorthand for sizes and ratios, and it sounds like nonsense until someone explains it.
A “thou” or “mil” is one thousandth of an inch: 0.001 in, or 25.4 µm. Sheet thickness, PCB traces and machining cuts are all quoted this way.
In a machine shop, a “tenth” is not 0.1 of anything obvious. It is a tenth of a thou: 0.0001 in, about 2.5 µm.
A micron is a micrometre: 0.001 mm. A human hair is roughly 70 microns across.
Decibels compress ratios. For voltage, 20 dB is 10×, and 40 dB is 100×. For power, 3 dB is 2×, so “down 3 dB” means half the power.
Why the shorthand? These numbers are said hundreds of times a day. “Hold it to two tenths” is quicker than “plus or minus two ten-thousandths of an inch”.
How it sounds at work: “Take another five thou off.” “Hold that bore to a couple of tenths.” “We’re down 3 dB at the corner.”
title: Numbers out loud
plain: Engineers have spoken shorthand for sizes and ratios, and it sounds like nonsense until someone explains it.
talk: “Take another five thou off.”
“Hold that bore to a couple of tenths.”
“We’re down 3 dB at the corner.”

qs.q: How many millimetres is 5 thou?
A machinist says “hold it to a couple of tenths”. What tolerance is that?
qs.ans: 0.0002 inch
wrong: 0.2 inch
0.02 inch
0.2 mm
qs.why: A shop “tenth” is a tenth of a thousandth of an inch. Two of them is 0.0002 in, about 5 µm.

qs.q: A voltage gain of 40 dB is a ratio of how many times?
qs.why: For voltage, ratio = 10^(dB/20) = 10^2 = 100.

qs.q: Match the spoken unit to its size.
qs.why: A mil is not a millimetre, which is the classic mix-up: a mil is about 1/40 of one.

qs.q: A signal is “down 3 dB”. What has happened to its power?
qs.ans: It has halved
wrong: It has dropped by 3%
It has dropped to a third
It has dropped to a tenth
qs.why: 10·log10(0.5) = −3.01 dB. A tenth of the power would be −10 dB.

qs.q: “Shave another five thousandths of an inch off it.”
qs.ans: Take another five thou off.
wrong: Take another five tenths off.
Take another five microns off.
Take another five points off.
qs.why: A thou is a thousandth of an inch. Five tenths would be only 0.0005 in, and five microns is smaller still.

cards: In plain English: “Engineer” covers very different jobs. Here is what each kind actually spends the day doing.
Mechanical engineers own the physical object: its shape, strength, heat, moving parts and how it gets manufactured.
Electrical engineers own the circuits: the boards, the power, and the signals running between chips.
Firmware engineers write the code that lives inside the device itself and talks directly to the hardware.
Systems engineers own the big picture: the requirements, and the agreements about how each team’s piece connects to the others.
Test engineers prove it works, mostly by trying hard to make it fail, because customers will. A new board’s first power-up, getting each part working in turn, is called bring-up.
How it sounds at work: “I spent all day in bring-up.” “We’re blocked on the vendor.” “That’s an interface problem, ask systems.”
title: Who does what
plain: “Engineer” covers very different jobs. Here is what each kind actually spends the day doing.
talk: “I spent all day in bring-up.”
“We’re blocked on the vendor.”
“That’s an interface problem, ask systems.”

qs.q: Match each engineer to what they own.
pairs: The physical parts and how they are made
The code running inside the device
The proof that it all works
qs.why: Most hardware products need all four, and they talk to each other constantly.

qs.q: What does a systems engineer mainly own?
qs.ans: Requirements and how the pieces connect
wrong: Computer systems and office networks
Detailed drawings of every part
Factory equipment and assembly lines
qs.why: Despite the name, it is not IT. Systems engineers keep separate teams building toward one coherent product.

qs.q: “I spent all day in bring-up.”
qs.ans: Powering up a new board for the first time
wrong: Raising a problem with their manager
Lifting equipment onto a test stand
Presenting a design to reviewers
qs.why: Bring-up is the first power-on of new hardware: checking each part step by step. It is slow, tense and rarely goes smoothly.

qs.q: “We’re blocked on the vendor.”
qs.ans: A supplier must deliver before work can continue
wrong: A supplier has been banned from the project
A supplier is visiting the office this week
A supplier has raised its prices sharply
qs.why: “Blocked” means unable to proceed. The cause here is something an outside company owes them.

qs.q: “The new circuit boards arrived and we’re turning them on for the first time.”
qs.ans: We’re doing board bring-up.
wrong: We’re doing a design review.
We’re doing a board respin.
We’re doing a regression run.
qs.why: A respin is a redesign of the board. A regression run re-checks that old features still work.

cards: In plain English: Five words engineers use constantly, explained so you can follow the story of their day.
The spec, short for specification, is the written list of what the product must do. “In spec” is good. “Out of spec” is a problem.
Tolerance is how far from perfect a part is allowed to be. Because nothing can be made exactly, every dimension comes with a permitted error.
Margin is the spare room between what is needed and what the design can take. Engineers sleep better with margin.
A rev, short for revision, is a numbered version of a design. Rev A is the first; rev B fixes what rev A got wrong.
Root cause is the real underlying reason something failed, as opposed to the symptom. Finding it can take days and is a genuine victory.
How it sounds at work: “It’s out of spec.” “We finally found root cause.” “That’s fixed in rev C.”
title: Dinner-table decoder
plain: Five words engineers use constantly, explained so you can follow the story of their day.
talk: “It’s out of spec.”
“We finally found root cause.”
“That’s fixed in rev C.”

qs.q: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The written list of what it must do
How far off a part is allowed to be
Spare room beyond what is needed
A numbered version of a design
qs.why: With these four words you can follow most hardware stories.

qs.q: “The first units came back out of spec.”
qs.ans: They failed to meet a written requirement
wrong: They arrived later than was promised
They cost more than was budgeted
They were shipped without documents
qs.why: Out of spec means a measured value fell outside what the specification allows.

qs.q: “We finally found root cause.”
qs.ans: They know the real reason for the failure
wrong: They know which person made the error
They have a temporary workaround
They have restarted the investigation
qs.why: Root cause is the underlying reason, not blame and not a patch. It usually means a real fix is now possible.

qs.q: “We have 20% margin on power.” What does that mean?
qs.ans: The supply can give 20% more than needed
wrong: The design uses 20% of the available power
The power is 20% above the allowed limit
The power bill came in 20% under budget
qs.why: Margin is headroom. Demand could grow by a fifth before the supply ran out.

qs.q: “We changed the design, so this is the second version of the board.”
qs.ans: This is rev B of the board.
wrong: This is spec B of the board.
This is lot B of the board.
This is tier B of the board.
qs.why: Revisions are lettered or numbered versions of a design. A lot is one manufacturing batch of the same design.

cards: In plain English: A machine has its own preferred shaking rate, which may differ from how fast its motor turns.
A natural frequency belongs to a vibration mode: a particular pattern of motion. A real machine can have several modes; a single mass on one spring has one.
For a linear mass-spring model, fn = √(k/m)/(2π). Here fn is natural frequency in Hz, k is spring stiffness in N/m, and m is moving mass in kg.
Forcing frequency is how often a repeated load acts, in Hz. One load cycle per revolution at 1200 rpm produces forcing at 20 Hz.

Why it happens: near resonance, repeated forcing transfers energy efficiently into a mode. Damping dissipates energy and limits steady response; natural frequency alone does not specify vibration amplitude.
In this model, quadrupling stiffness doubles natural frequency. Quadrupling mass halves it. State the relevant mode and forcing source when proposing a resonance fix.
title: Natural frequency and forcing frequency
plain: A machine has its own preferred shaking rate, which may differ from how fast its motor turns.
demoNeeded: Show a mass-spring response versus forcing frequency with sliders for mass, stiffness, and damping; label natural frequency and the response maximum separately.

qs.q: “The bracket wants to shake at 30 cycles per second, even though the motor turns at a different rate.”
qs.ans: 30 Hz is the bracket’s natural frequency.
wrong: The motor forces the bracket at 30 Hz.
The bracket’s damping is 30 Hz.
30 Hz is the motor’s critical speed.
qs.why: Natural frequency belongs to the bracket’s mode. “The motor forces it at 30 Hz” confuses it with the excitation, which the speaker says is different. Damping isn’t measured in hertz. A critical speed belongs to the rotating shaft, not the bracket.

qs.q: “Check the once-per-rev against that bracket mode.”
qs.ans: Compare rotation frequency with the bracket's natural frequency.
wrong: Compare rotation acceleration with the bracket's natural frequency.
Compare blade-passing frequency with the bracket's natural frequency.
Compare rotation frequency with the bracket's damping coefficient.
qs.why: Once-per-rev means one excitation cycle per shaft revolution. The distractors substitute acceleration, blade-passing excitation, or a damping coefficient for the quantities being compared.

qs.q: A linear mass-spring model has stiffness 18000 N/m and mass 2.00 kg. Using fn = √(k/m)/(2π), where k is stiffness and m is mass, find natural frequency.
qs.why: √(18000/2.00) = 94.87 rad/s. Dividing by 2π gives 15.10 Hz; reporting 94.87 Hz would confuse angular and cyclic frequency.

qs.q: For a linear mass-spring model, natural frequency fn = √(k/m)/(2π), with stiffness k in N/m and mass m in kg. What happens when k becomes four times larger and m stays fixed?
qs.ans: Natural frequency doubles.
wrong: Natural frequency becomes fourfold.
Natural frequency becomes half.
Natural frequency remains unchanged.
qs.why: The square root makes √4 = 2. Fourfold drops the square root; half reverses the stiffness dependence; unchanged incorrectly treats frequency as independent of stiffness.

qs.q: Follow this calculation workflow for a motor's once-per-revolution excitation.
items: Read the shaft speed in rpm
Label the result as forcing frequency in Hz
Compare with the relevant structural natural frequency
qs.why: Dividing revolutions per minute by 60 gives revolutions per second. For once-per-revolution loading, that is the excitation frequency to compare with a mode.

qs.q: Review these assumptions for a bracket vibration calculation. Which line is flawed?
lines: Represent the first bracket mode with one equivalent mass and spring
Use stiffness in N/m and equivalent mass in kg
Convert once-per-revolution excitation from rpm to Hz by dividing by 60
Set the bracket's natural frequency equal to motor speed for every operating condition
qs.why: This confuses a structural property with an applied excitation. Motor speed can change without changing the bracket's mass or stiffness.
qs.ans: Set the bracket's natural frequency equal to motor speed for every operating condition
wrong: Represent the first bracket mode with one equivalent mass and spring
Use stiffness in N/m and equivalent mass in kg
Convert once-per-revolution excitation from rpm to Hz by dividing by 60

p.x: Tap a machine bracket and let it vibrate freely. Its own preferred rate of shaking is its **natural frequency**.
That rate [[can differ]] from the rate at which the motor shakes it.
One rate belongs to the bracket. The other comes from whatever is driving it.
A **mode** is a particular pattern of vibration, with its own natural frequency.
A mass that can only slide back and forth on one spring has one vibration mode.
With two linked masses, they can move together or against each other. Different patterns can have different natural frequencies.

g.q: If a second linked mass can move independently, how many modes can the system have?
o: Still only one
That would be true if the masses had to move together.
More than one
The two masses can move in different patterns, each with its own frequency.

p.cap: One mass, a linear spring, and no damping

p.x: Use $k = 18,000$ N/m and $m = 2.00$ kg. The square root gives radians per second, so divide by $2π$ radians per cycle.
**Forcing frequency** is how often a load repeats. Measure it in hertz (cycles per second).
A once-per-revolution load repeats one time per turn. For a shaft turning at 1200 rpm, divide by 60 seconds per minute.
**Resonance** is the large response that can occur when forcing is near a natural frequency.
A repeated force transfers energy [[more efficiently]] to the mode near resonance.
**Damping** removes vibration energy. It limits the steady shaking even when the force keeps adding energy.
Natural frequency tells you where to look for resonance. The forcing and damping also set how much the part moves.
Consider the same linear mass–spring model. Change just the spring or just the mass.
Name the mode and the repeated load before proposing a fix. Check whether the change moves their frequencies farther apart.

g.q: With mass fixed, what happens to natural frequency if stiffness quadruples?
o: Quadruples
That uses a linear rule. Frequency follows the square root of stiffness.
Doubles
With the mass fixed, frequency scales by the square root of four.
Halves
That is what happens when mass quadruples with stiffness fixed.

cards: In plain English: How quickly shaking dies away tells you how strongly a system dissipates vibration energy.
A ring-down is free motion after the driving force stops. For one underdamped linear mode, damping ratio ζ is dimensionless and lies between zero and one.
Why it happens: viscous damping removes mechanical energy during motion. Successive same-direction displacement peaks shrink by a constant ratio when one linear mode dominates.
Logarithmic decrement δ = ln(x1/x2)/n. Here δ is dimensionless; x1 and x2 are positive same-direction peak amplitudes in m, separated by n complete cycles, a dimensionless count.
For this model, ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²). Use natural logarithms. Count intervals between peaks, not the number of peaks you marked.
Reject intervals contaminated by ongoing forcing, beating, clipping, or the noise floor. Otherwise the amplitude ratio can describe measurement artifacts instead of damping.
title: Estimate damping from ring-down
plain: How quickly shaking dies away tells you how strongly a system dissipates vibration energy.
figNeeded: Plot an underdamped ring-down with six positive peaks, mark the first and sixth amplitudes, and show the five complete periods between them.

qs.q: “Use peaks on the same side, five cycles apart.”
qs.ans: Compare same-direction peaks separated by five periods.
wrong: Compare opposite-direction peaks separated by five half-periods.
Compare adjacent same-direction peaks using five as divisor.
Compare five successive same-direction peaks across five periods.
qs.why: Same-direction peaks recur once per full cycle. Opposite extrema introduce half-cycle counting; adjacent peaks span one cycle; five successive peaks span four intervals.

qs.q: “After we stop pushing it, each swing is smaller because the system loses mechanical energy.”
qs.ans: The free response decays through damping.
wrong: The forcing frequency decays through damping.
The spring stiffness decays through damping.
The moving mass decays through damping.
qs.why: Damping dissipates energy and reduces free-response amplitude. It does not inherently reduce an external forcing frequency, spring stiffness, or moving mass.

qs.q: In a single-mode viscous ring-down, same-direction amplitudes fall from 8.00 mm to 2.00 mm over five complete cycles. Calculate δ = ln(x1/x2)/n, the dimensionless logarithmic decrement.
qs.why: ln(8.00/2.00)/5 = 0.2773. The matching amplitude units cancel; using log base 10 or forgetting the five-cycle divisor gives a different result.

qs.q: For an underdamped viscous mode with dimensionless logarithmic decrement δ = 0.2773, calculate dimensionless damping ratio ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²).
qs.why: 0.2773/√(4π² + 0.2773²) = 0.04409, or 4.409% of critical damping. The requested answer is the ratio, not the percentage.

qs.q: Order this ring-down analysis workflow.
items: Record motion after removing the excitation
Select two clean same-direction peaks and count full cycles between them
Calculate the natural logarithm of their amplitude ratio per cycle
Convert logarithmic decrement to damping ratio
qs.why: A valid free-decay interval comes first. Peak amplitudes and cycle count determine decrement, which then determines damping ratio for the assumed model.

qs.q: Review this damping measurement plan. Which line is flawed?
lines: Remove the forcing before selecting the analysis interval
Choose a response dominated by one mode
Use peak amplitudes well above the measurement noise
Count five consecutive same-direction peaks as five complete cycles
qs.why: Five consecutive same-direction peaks contain four cycle intervals. Dividing by five would underestimate decrement and damping.
qs.ans: Count five consecutive same-direction peaks as five complete cycles
wrong: Remove the forcing before selecting the analysis interval
Choose a response dominated by one mode
Use peak amplitudes well above the measurement noise

p.x: Give a flexible part a push and let go. Watch how quickly its swings get smaller.
Decay tells you how strongly **damping** drains the energy of the vibration.
A **ring-down** is the free motion after the driving force stops.
The **damping ratio** is damping divided by the critical amount at which free oscillations stop. It has no units.
A linear mode still rings while it decays if the ratio is [[between]] zero and one. That is **underdamped** motion.

p.cap: Underdamped motion

p.x: A **viscous damper** pushes against motion with a force proportional to speed. It turns mechanical energy into heat.
Compare successive peaks on the same side of the rest position. That measures one full cycle each time.
With one linear mode and viscous damping, each peak is the same fraction of the peak one cycle before it.

g.q: How does each peak compare with the preceding peak on the same side?
o: Same fraction each time
A single mode has an exponentially decaying envelope.
Same drop each time
A fixed drop would make the envelope a straight line. Viscous free decay gives a fixed fraction.

p.x: **Logarithmic decrement** $δ$ measures the decay per cycle. Use heights $x_a$ and $x_b$ from an earlier and a later peak on the same side of rest.

p.cap: One linear viscous mode. Use matching height units. n counts full cycles. ln is natural log.
Underdamped linear mode with viscous damping

p.x: Count the intervals between peaks. Both results are unitless. Keep extra digits until the final step.
Two nearby modes can sometimes add and sometimes cancel. The resulting rise and fall is called **beating**.
Reject peaks that grow again during free decay. Their changing heights can reflect beating.
Also reject peaks while forcing continues, when the recorder cuts off the tops (**clipping**), or when the signal is as small as the noise.

g.q: Some peaks grow again after forcing stops. For a one-mode damping estimate, do you…
o: Keep the interval
That treats peaks from different patterns as though they all belong to one freely decaying mode.
Reject the interval
The peak ratio can reflect beating instead of damping.

cards: In plain English: Soft mounts can reduce vibration reaching a machine, but they can also amplify motion at some speeds.
For a linear mass-spring-damper under sinusoidal base motion, TR is absolute mass-displacement amplitude divided by base-displacement amplitude. TR is dimensionless; below one means isolation.
Define r = f/fn, dimensionless frequency ratio. Excitation frequency f and undamped natural frequency fn are in Hz. Damping ratio ζ is dimensionless.
TR = √[(1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)]. This assumes one mode, viscous damping, and steady sinusoidal motion.
Why it happens: above r = √2, inertia limits how closely the mass follows its base. Softer mounts lower natural frequency but require more travel under load.
More damping reduces resonant amplification but increases transmissibility at fixed r above √2. Check startup motion, available travel, and rigid bypasses through pipes or cables.
title: Select isolation mounts
plain: Soft mounts can reduce vibration reaching a machine, but they can also amplify motion at some speeds.

demo.title: Base isolation
demo.hint: Below r = √2 the mount amplifies motion; above it, it isolates. Damping tames the peak but costs isolation at high r.

qs.q: “The cable bundle is shorting out the isolators.”
qs.ans: The bundle creates a stiff vibration bypass.
wrong: The bundle increases the isolators' viscous damping.
The bundle reduces the supported equipment's mass.
The bundle changes the commanded excitation frequency.
qs.why: Here ‘shorting out’ means a parallel mechanical transmission path. It does not establish increased viscous damping, reduced mass, or a changed drive command.

qs.q: “The machine moves only one fifth as far as its vibrating support at this test frequency.”
qs.ans: Displacement transmissibility is 0.20 at this frequency.
wrong: Displacement damping ratio is 0.20 at this frequency.
Displacement frequency ratio is 0.20 at this frequency.
Displacement isolation efficiency is 0.20 at this frequency.
qs.why: The response-to-input amplitude ratio is transmissibility. Damping and frequency ratios describe different quantities; amplitude isolation efficiency would be 0.80, not 0.20.

qs.q: A linear base-excited isolator has dimensionless frequency ratio r = 3.00 and damping ratio ζ = 0.100. Find TR = √[(1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)].
qs.why: The numerator is 1.36 and denominator is 64.36. √(1.36/64.36) = 0.1454; omitting the square root would return the squared amplitude ratio.

qs.q: For a linear viscously damped isolator under sinusoidal base motion, hold frequency ratio r = excitation frequency/natural frequency at 3.00. What does increasing damping do to absolute displacement transmissibility?
qs.ans: It increases transmitted motion.
wrong: It decreases transmitted motion.
It leaves transmitted motion unchanged.
It changes only transmitted phase.
qs.why: At fixed r above √2, more viscous damping increases this transmissibility. Decrease incorrectly extends the resonance benefit; unchanged ignores damping; phase-only ignores the amplitude effect.

qs.q: Order this mount-selection workflow before releasing a design.
items: Specify operating excitation frequencies and supported load
Select candidate stiffness and damping for the target isolation
Check startup travel and mechanical bypass paths
Verify the installed response against acceptance limits
qs.why: Input conditions determine the candidate mount. Transient motion and parallel stiffness can invalidate steady-state predictions, so installed verification closes the selection.

qs.q: Review a single-mode isolation design note. Which line should be flagged?
lines: Define transmissibility using absolute machine displacement divided by base displacement
Evaluate isolation at each relevant operating frequency
Check hose and cable stiffness across the mounts
Increase viscous damping to reduce transmissibility at every frequency
qs.why: More damping does not improve isolation everywhere. It controls resonance but raises transmissibility in the isolation region for this model.
qs.ans: Increase viscous damping to reduce transmissibility at every frequency
wrong: Define transmissibility using absolute machine displacement divided by base displacement
Evaluate isolation at each relevant operating frequency
Check hose and cable stiffness across the mounts

p.x: A soft mount can keep a vibrating base from shaking the machine it supports. That reduction in motion is **isolation**.
At some speeds, the same mount can [[amplify]] the motion.
Near a natural frequency, a small motion of the base can make the machine move farther than the base.
For a sinusoidally moving base, **transmissibility** $TR$ compares the size of the machine's motion with the size of the base motion.

vars: machine amplitude from a fixed reference
base amplitude from the same reference
p.cap: Use the same units for both amplitudes

p.x: $TR < 1$ means isolation. $TR > 1$ means amplification. At $TR = 1$, the amplitudes match.
If the machine moves a fifth as far as the base, $TR = 0.200$.
The **frequency ratio** $r$ is greater than one when the excitation frequency is [[higher than]] the natural frequency.

vars: damping ratio, a fraction of critical damping

p.cap: The hertz cancel, so r is unitless.

p.x: Use one linear mass–spring–damper mode with steady sinusoidal base motion. A viscous damper resists motion in proportion to relative speed.
The machine moves less than its base when $r > √{2}$. Inertia, the resistance of the mass to a change in motion, keeps it from following the base closely.
Softer mounts lower the natural frequency, so $r$ rises at the same forcing frequency.
Allow more travel under the load. A softer spring compresses farther under the same weight.

g.q: Keep the machine mass fixed and choose softer mounts. What happens to its natural frequency?
o: It falls
A softer spring restores the mass less strongly, so it oscillates more slowly.
It rises
The frequency ratio can rise because the natural frequency in the denominator falls.

p.x: More damping lowers the steady response peak near resonance. During startup, forcing may pass through that region.
At fixed $r > √{2}$, more damping transmits more motion because the damper couples the machine to the base.
Check startup travel and look for stiff bypasses such as pipes or cables that carry vibration around the mounts. Verify the installed motion.

g.q: Hold $r$ fixed above $√{2}$. With more damping, what happens to transmissibility?
o: It rises
The damper transmits more of the base motion to the isolated mass.
It falls
That extends the resonance benefit into the isolation region, where the effect reverses.

cards: In plain English: A rotating shaft can shake strongly when its rotation excites one of its bending modes.
A lateral critical speed occurs when rotational excitation interacts resonantly with a lateral rotor mode. Once-per-revolution unbalance is a common excitation, but not the only possible source.
For a simplified non-gyroscopic rotor, Nc = 60fn. Critical speed Nc is in rpm; undamped lateral natural frequency fn is in Hz. This estimates the once-per-revolution crossing.
Why it happens: rotating unbalance applies a repeating lateral force. Near a rotor mode, the shaft and supports respond strongly unless damping and excitation levels limit the motion.
Bearing stiffness, support flexibility, temperature, and gyroscopic effects can move critical speeds. A rigid-bearing calculation does not establish the installed machine's operating separation.

Specify separation using a stated denominator and operating range. Above-critical operation can be intentional, but startup crossings require a verified transient response and an approved operating procedure.
title: Critical shaft speed and support stiffness
plain: A rotating shaft can shake strongly when its rotation excites one of its bending modes.
figNeeded: Show a Campbell diagram with modal frequency versus shaft speed and once-per-revolution excitation, marking crossings and the operating speed band.

qs.q: “The pedestal flexibility pulled the first critical down.”
qs.ans: Support compliance lowered the first critical speed.
wrong: Support damping lowered the shaft's commanded speed.
Support compliance lowered the rotor's unbalance mass.
Support stiffness increased the first bending frequency.
qs.why: Added compliance can lower the installed mode frequency and associated critical speed. The other answers confuse modal behavior with speed control, unbalance, or the opposite stiffness change.

qs.q: “The machine runs faster than its first bending resonance, and we have checked the startup crossing.”
qs.ans: It operates supercritically with a verified crossing.
wrong: It operates subcritically with a verified crossing.
It operates critically at every steady running speed.
It operates without any lateral bending vibration modes.
qs.why: Supercritical means above the relevant critical speed. Subcritical means below; continuous critical operation confuses a crossing with steady speed; modes do not disappear above resonance.

qs.q: A simplified non-gyroscopic rotor has effective lateral stiffness 200000 N/m and modal mass 5.00 kg. Estimate its once-per-revolution critical speed using Nc = 60√(k/m)/(2π).
qs.why: √(200000/5.00) = 200 rad/s. Multiplication by 60/(2π) gives 1910 rpm. This idealized estimate excludes speed-dependent bearing and gyroscopic effects.

qs.q: A predicted critical speed is 2400 rpm and maximum operating speed is 1800 rpm. The project defines separation as (critical speed − maximum operating speed)/maximum operating speed. Give the dimensionless ratio.
qs.why: (2400 − 1800)/1800 = 0.3333. Dividing by critical speed instead gives 0.2500; that uses a different definition.

qs.q: Order this workflow for assessing a rotor's critical-speed separation.
items: Define the operating speed range and excitation orders
Predict rotor modes using representative bearings and supports
Compare predicted crossings with the operating range and uncertainty
Validate the response and resolve unacceptable crossings
qs.why: Excitation and boundary conditions determine the relevant crossings. Comparing nominal values alone misses model uncertainty and installed behavior.

qs.q: Review the release notes for a rotor installation. Which line is flawed?
lines: Include pedestal flexibility in the lateral model
State the denominator used for critical-speed separation
Account for the bearing properties expected at operating temperature
Accept the installed critical speed solely from a rigid-support shaft model
qs.why: The last line treats an ideal boundary condition as installed validation. Real support compliance and bearing properties can shift the critical speed.
qs.ans: Accept the installed critical speed solely from a rigid-support shaft model
wrong: Include pedestal flexibility in the lateral model
State the denominator used for critical-speed separation
Account for the bearing properties expected at operating temperature

p.x: A rotating shaft can bend and vibrate sideways. This sideways motion is called **lateral** vibration.
A **bending mode** is a characteristic shape in which the shaft and its supports vibrate together.
Rotation can excite a bending mode and make the shaft shake.
A bending mode has a **natural frequency**: the rate at which it oscillates freely.
At a **lateral critical speed**, a repeating force excites resonance as its frequency [[matches]] a sideways mode’s frequency.
Uneven mass around the axis produces a force once per turn. Other sources can repeat a different number of times per turn, called their **excitation order**.
Use the lateral natural frequency $f_n$ in Hz to estimate the critical speed $N_c$ in rpm.

p.cap: One force cycle per turn, no gyroscopic effects

p.x: Uneven mass applies a rotating sideways force that repeatedly drives the shaft and supports.
If the forcing frequency is near a natural frequency, successive pushes can build a large response.
Damping dissipates vibration energy. Near resonance, more damping gives a [[smaller]] response for the same forcing.
The installed rotor rests on bearings and pedestals. A pedestal is the base that supports a bearing.
Support **compliance** is how easily the support deflects under load. Added compliance can lower the first bending frequency and its critical speed.
For one mode with negligible gyroscopic effects, use stiffness $k$ of 200 kN/m and effective mass $m$ of 5.00 kg.
Use bearing properties at operating temperature and account for gyroscopic effects from shaft spin in the installed model.

g.q: In a simple rotor model, if the pedestals get more flexible at the same effective mass, how does the first critical speed tend to change?
o: It falls
Softer supports reduce the restoring stiffness for sideways motion.
It rises
That is the trend for stiffer supports at the same effective mass.

p.x: Compare predicted crossings and their uncertainty with the full running speed range. State the denominator for any separation ratio.
For a critical at 2400 rpm and a running maximum of 1800 rpm, the gap is 0.3333 times that maximum.
Running above a critical is **supercritical**. Running below it is **subcritical**.
A startup crossing needs a verified transient response (motion while speed changes) and an approved operating procedure.

g.q: The rotor starts from rest and runs supercritically. When must you verify the crossing response?
o: During startup
Speed passes through the critical on the way to the running range.
Only at steady speed
A steady test above the critical misses the crossing on the way up.

cards: In plain English: Balancing adds or removes material in the right locations to reduce rotating forces and couples.
Unbalance U = me, where U is in kg·m, m is eccentric mass in kg, and e is its distance from the rotation axis in m. Angular position also matters.
Unbalance-force amplitude Fu = Uω². Here Fu is in N and angular speed ω is in rad/s. Doubling speed quadruples force for unchanged unbalance.
Why it happens: eccentric mass requires centripetal acceleration. Its rotating force excites the supports; measured vibration also depends on the machine's dynamic response.
For a known single-plane unbalance, correction mass mc = U/rc. Here mc is in kg and correction radius rc is in m. Added correction mass goes opposite the known unbalance vector.
Equal opposite unbalances in separated axial planes can form a couple despite zero net unbalance force. Use two-plane balancing when both resultant unbalance and couple require correction.
title: Unbalance vectors and correction planes
plain: Balancing adds or removes material in the right locations to reduce rotating forces and couples.
figNeeded: Contrast one unbalance vector in a disk with equal opposite unbalance vectors in two separated axial planes, labeling the resulting rotating couple.

qs.q: “It passes the static check, but we've still got a couple.”
qs.ans: Opposed unbalances form a rotating couple.
wrong: Aligned unbalances remain in a single axial plane.
The rotation speed has become twice the test speed.
The rotor's total mass has become twice the target.
qs.why: A static check can miss couple unbalance: opposing vectors at different axial positions. Aligned single-plane vectors create resultant unbalance; speed and total mass changes do not define a couple.

qs.q: “The offset mass stayed the same, but doubling the shaft speed made its rotating force four times larger.”
qs.ans: Unbalance force scales with speed squared.
wrong: Unbalance force scales directly with speed.
Unbalance force scales with the square root of speed.
Unbalance force scales inversely with speed squared.
qs.why: Centripetal acceleration is proportional to angular speed squared. The distractors replace the squared law with linear, square-root, or inverse-square dependence.

qs.q: A known single-plane unbalance comes from 12.0 g at radius 40.0 mm. What added correction mass is needed at radius 60.0 mm, opposite the known unbalance?
qs.why: Balance mass-radius products: 12.0 × 40.0 = mc × 60.0, giving mc = 8.000 g. Matching units allow this calculation directly in g and mm.

qs.q: An unbalance magnitude U = 0.000480 kg·m rotates at 3000 rpm. Find rotating-force amplitude Fu = Uω², using angular speed ω = 2π × rpm/60 in rad/s.
qs.why: Angular speed is 314.159 rad/s. Force is 0.000480 × 314.159² = 47.37 N; using 50 revolutions/s without 2π underestimates it.

qs.q: Order this known-unbalance correction calculation, assuming one-plane correction is appropriate.
items: Determine the magnitude and angle of the known unbalance vector
Divide unbalance magnitude by correction radius to find added mass
Place the added mass opposite the unbalance and verify the result
qs.why: The radius sets the required correction mass. Opposing the known unbalance vector cancels it ideally; verification checks installation and model assumptions.

qs.q: Review this rigid-rotor balance plan. Which line is flawed?
lines: Record correction radius and angular reference
Distinguish a single-plane resultant from a separated-plane couple
Verify residual vibration after the correction
Place correction mass opposite measured vibration phase without determining the rotor response
qs.why: Measured vibration phase includes the machine's transfer response. It is not automatically the heavy-spot angle; a calibrated influence method or equivalent validated relation is needed.
qs.ans: Place correction mass opposite measured vibration phase without determining the rotor response
wrong: Record correction radius and angular reference
Distinguish a single-plane resultant from a separated-plane couple
Verify residual vibration after the correction

p.x: If the rotor’s mass is offset from the shaft axis, rotation can tug on the bearings.
Balancing adjusts the distribution of mass to [[reduce]] those rotating loads.
Where you add or remove material matters, both around the shaft and along it.
The same mass gives [[more]] unbalance farther from the axis.

p.cap: Magnitude for one offset mass. For the vector, also record its angle around the shaft.
Fixed unbalance, steady rotation

p.x: Doubling speed gives four times the force. At 3000 rpm, 50.0 turns/s times $2π$ rad per turn gives about 314 rad/s.

p.l: At that speed, from the unbalance above

g.q: If you double angular speed and keep the same unbalance, what happens to the rotating force?
o: It quadruples
Speed enters as a square, so doubling it multiplies force by four.
It doubles
That would follow from a linear relation. Each speed factor doubles in the square.

p.x: Keeping off-axis mass on a circle requires inward acceleration. The rotor exerts a matching rotating force on its supports.
**Phase** marks where a vibration cycle is relative to a reference mark on the rotor. The bearings and supports can shift that phase.
Use a measured or validated response to relate the vibration phase to the unbalance angle.

g.q: Can you identify the heavy spot from the measured vibration’s timing alone?
o: Yes, directly
That assumes the sensor motion follows the force with no phase shift.
No, you need the response
The machine changes the motion’s magnitude and timing relative to the force.

p.x: A **correction plane** is a slice along the shaft where a weight can be fitted. Here one plane suffices and the unbalance vector is known.

p.cap: Add the mass opposite the known unbalance angle

p.x: Use 60.0 mm radius and the unbalance from earlier. Verify vibration after fitting the correction.
Equal, opposite forces in separate planes form a **couple**: they rock the rotor end to end with no net push.
Use two planes when correcting both net unbalance and a couple.

cards: In plain English: A balancing trial measures how each correction location affects both ends of a rotor.
An influence coefficient relates a known trial unbalance to the change in measured vibration. Use amplitude and phase, represented as a complex vector, at a fixed speed and sensor configuration.
Why it happens: each correction plane can affect both bearings. Two-plane balancing must solve their coupled responses; independent amplitude-only adjustments discard phase and cross-coupling.
Record the baseline, then test each trial plane separately against that baseline. Remove the first trial before the second unless the calculation explicitly accounts for retained trial unbalance.

Nearly dependent influence responses make the correction calculation sensitive to measurement noise. Check trial response, phase repeatability, sensor setup, and correction-plane suitability before trusting a large computed correction.

Accept results using specified locations, speed, load, units, amplitude convention, and limits. An RMS velocity limit cannot be compared directly with peak displacement; a low-speed balance does not establish flexible-rotor performance.
title: Two-plane influence balancing and acceptance
plain: A balancing trial measures how each correction location affects both ends of a rotor.
figNeeded: Show two axial correction planes and two bearing sensors, with arrows indicating that either plane can influence both sensors.

qs.q: “Those two influence columns are almost dependent.”
qs.ans: The correction solution is sensitive to measurement errors.
wrong: The correction solution is independent of measurement errors.
The two correction planes affect only their nearest bearings.
The measured phase angles can be omitted from the calculation.
qs.why: Nearly dependent columns make inversion ill-conditioned. Independence reverses that result; local-only response ignores coupling; dropping phase loses necessary vector information.

qs.q: “Adding the trial weight near the drive end changed vibration at both bearings.”
qs.ans: The trial plane influences both measurement locations.
wrong: The trial plane influences only its nearest measurement location.
The trial plane proves the original unbalance lies at that end.
The trial plane proves both bearings have identical dynamic stiffness.
qs.why: The observation establishes cross-coupled response. It does not localize the original unbalance, prove identical supports, or justify a nearest-bearing-only model.

qs.q: For the special case of collinear signed responses, corrections x and y in g produce bearing changes: A = 2x + y and B = x + 2y, in µm. Required changes are A = −3.00 µm and B = 0.00 µm. Find x and y.
qs.why: From x + 2y = 0, x = −2y; substitution gives y = 1 and x = −2. The alternatives ignore cross-coupling, reverse the correction sign, or swap the planes. Negative means the opposite angular direction.

qs.q: For a pure sinusoidal vibration, RMS velocity equals peak velocity divided by √2. A measured peak velocity is 4.00 mm/s. What is RMS velocity?
qs.why: 4.00/√2 = 2.828 mm/s. This conversion requires a sinusoid; it is not a general conversion for arbitrary vibration waveforms.

qs.q: Order this two-plane trial workflow; the specified method compares each trial with the original baseline.
items: Measure baseline amplitude and phase at both bearings
Add the first-plane trial and measure both bearings
Remove the first trial, add the second-plane trial, and measure both bearings
Remove trials and compute and install the coupled correction
Measure both bearings again under the specified acceptance conditions
qs.why: Separate trials identify each plane's influence relative to the same baseline. Removing trial masses prevents them from becoming unintended permanent corrections.

qs.q: Review a final balance report with a contractual RMS velocity limit. Which line is flawed?
lines: Report measurement locations and sensor directions
Compare peak displacement directly with the RMS velocity limit
Confirm trial masses were removed or explicitly included in final corrections
Record the post-correction measurement at each required location
qs.why: Peak displacement and RMS velocity differ in both physical quantity and amplitude convention. A valid comparison requires matching quantities and conventions, with waveform and frequency information for any conversion.
qs.ans: Compare peak displacement directly with the RMS velocity limit
wrong: Report measurement locations and sensor directions
Confirm trial masses were removed or explicitly included in final corrections
Record the post-correction measurement at each required location

p.x: A **correction plane** is a location along the shaft where you can add balance weight.
For a trial, add a known mass at a known radius and angle in one plane.
Measure how the trial changes the vibration at each end of the rotor.
A complex vibration vector stores **amplitude** (size) and **phase** (angle from a shaft mark).
At fixed speed and sensor setup, an **influence coefficient** is the vibration change [[divided by]] the trial unbalance.
At fixed radii, the coefficients below are 1 or 2 µm/g. Use signed masses $x$ and $y$ in grams for changes $A = −3.00$ µm and $B = 0$ µm.
Either plane can change both bearing readings. This is **cross-coupling**.
Solve both responses together and keep their phase as well as their amplitude.
The **baseline** is the original reading at each bearing. Record amplitude and phase before adding a trial.
For a common baseline, measure each trial by itself. Remove the first before the second unless the calculation accounts for it.
Remove trial weights before installing the computed correction, or include their effect in the final correction.

g.q: Both trials will be compared with the original baseline. What should you do with the first trial weight before measuring the second?
o: Remove it
That isolates the vibration change due to the second plane.
Leave it
Without accounting for it, the second reading would include both trials.

p.x: An **influence column** is one plane’s set of coefficients across the sensors. Two columns are nearly dependent if one looks like a scaled and phase-shifted copy of the other.
Similar response patterns make the planes hard to distinguish. Small measurement errors can then produce large changes in the calculated weights.
Check trial signal size, phase repeatability, sensor placement and correction-plane choice before trusting a large result.

g.q: If the planes produce nearly the same pattern at the sensors, how do small measurement errors affect the calculated correction?
o: They can have a large effect
The calculation can trade one plane’s correction against the other.
They have little effect
Similar response patterns make the planes harder to tell apart, which magnifies error.

p.x: Record each required sensor location and direction, speed and load. Match the limit’s units and use the [[same]] amplitude convention.
**Peak** is the largest magnitude. **RMS** is the square root of the mean square. A peak displacement is a different quantity from RMS velocity.

p.cap: Velocity for pure sinusoidal vibration only

p.x: A low-speed balance alone cannot establish how a flexible rotor responds at operating speed.

cards: In plain English: A function is a rule that turns each input number into exactly one output number.
A function is a rule: put a number in, get one number out. f(x) = 2x + 1 means double the input, then add 1. So f(3) = 2·3 + 1 = 7.
f(x) is read “f of x.” The letter in the brackets is the input. f(5) means: replace every x in the rule with 5 and work it out.
Engineers use functions constantly: deflection as a function of load, temperature as a function of time. The input is what you set; the output is what you get.
A graph shows every input–output pair at once. Find the input on the horizontal axis, go straight up or down to the curve, and read its height: that is the output.
Why it matters: one input never gives two outputs. That is what makes a function useful for prediction: choose the input and the output is decided.
title: Functions: inputs and outputs
plain: A function is a rule that turns each input number into exactly one output number.

qs.q: f(x) = 2x + 1. What is f(3)?
qs.why: Replace x with 3: 2·3 + 1 = 7. Answering 6 forgets the + 1; answering 9 adds before doubling.

qs.q: f(x) = x² − 4. What is f(5)?
qs.why: 5² = 25, then 25 − 4 = 21. Answering 6 doubles 5 instead of squaring it; answering 1 subtracts before squaring.

qs.q: g(t) = 20 + 5t gives a part's temperature in °C, t minutes after the heater turns on. What does g(4) = 40 tell you?
qs.ans: After 4 minutes the part is at 40 °C
wrong: After 40 minutes the part is at 4 °C
It warms by 40 °C every 4 minutes
The part started out at 40 °C
qs.why: The input (4) is the time and the output (40) is the temperature. Swapping them mixes up input and output. The warming rate is 5 °C per minute, and the starting temperature is g(0) = 20 °C.

qs.q: Which rule is not a function of x, because one input gives two outputs?
qs.ans: y = ±√x
wrong: y = x²
qs.why: y = ±√x gives both 2 and −2 for x = 4. y = x² sends two inputs (2 and −2) to the same output, which is allowed. A constant like y = 3 gives every input the same output, also allowed. y = 2x − 7 is an ordinary straight line.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The number you put in, x
The number you get out, f(x)
The output when the input is 3
The set of plotted input–output pairs
qs.why: Input goes in, output comes out, f(3) names one specific output, and a graph shows all the pairs at once.

qs.q: “However much load you put on the shelf decides how far it sags.”
qs.ans: Deflection is a function of load.
wrong: Load is a function of deflection.
Deflection is equal to load.
Deflection and load are independent.
qs.why: Load is what you choose (the input) and sag, or deflection, is the result (the output), so deflection is a function of load. Reversing them swaps input and output; “equal to” claims the numbers match; “independent” says load has no effect at all.

p.x: A **function** assigns an output to each allowed input.
Each input has [[exactly one]] output.
Two different inputs can share an output.
In $f(x)=2x+1$, $x$ is the input. Double it, then add one.
Read $f(x)$ as “$f$ of $x$.” The parentheses tell you which input to use.
Replace every $x$ in the rule with $5$, then calculate.

g.q: What does $f(5)$ ask you to do?
o: Use 5 as the input
Replace every x by 5.
Multiply f by 5
The parentheses indicate evaluation.

p.x: A beam model can give deflection as an output for a specified load.
A heating model can give temperature as an output for a specified time.
Find the [[input]] on the horizontal axis.
Follow a vertical line to the curve.
Read the output from the vertical axis.
Consider a rule that gives the input $4$ two outputs, $2$ and $−2$.
No. One input with two outputs breaks the rule. Repeated outputs across different inputs are fine.

g.q: Can this rule still be a function?
o: Yes
Sharing outputs is allowed, but here one input has two outputs.
No
A function gives each input exactly one output.

cards: In plain English: Before calculating, check which inputs a formula actually allows, including inputs fed in from another formula.
A function gives one output for each allowed input. Its domain is the set of allowed inputs; its range is the set of outputs it actually produces.
Three real-number rules: a denominator can't be 0, a square root needs an input ≥ 0, and a logarithm needs an input > 0. So √0 is fine but ln 0 is not.
Composition f(g(x)) means: compute g(x) first, then feed that number into f. Read it from the inside out.
Domain of f(g(x)): x must be allowed in g, and g(x) must be allowed in f. With f(u) = ln u and g(x) = x − 3, you need x − 3 > 0, so x > 3.

The ranges never have to match. Example: f(u) = √u and g(x) = x − 4. g can give negative outputs, and √ can’t take those, but that doesn’t stop you composing them: you just keep the x values where x − 4 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 4.
title: Domains and composition
plain: Before calculating, check which inputs a formula actually allows, including inputs fed in from another formula.

qs.q: Over the real numbers, what is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 2)?
qs.ans: All real x except x = 2
wrong: All real x except x = 0
