cards: In plain English: Local derivative information builds polynomial approximations.
A Taylor polynomial uses derivatives at a center divided by factorials. A Maclaurin polynomial is centered at zero.
For dimensionless x, exp(x) begins 1+x+x²/2+x³/6. Truncation produces an approximation, not an identity for all inputs.
Why it happens: the factorial coefficients make the polynomial match successive derivatives at the expansion point.
title: Taylor and Maclaurin polynomials
plain: Local derivative information builds polynomial approximations.

qs.q: “The quadratic coefficient needs the factorial.”
qs.ans: Divide the second derivative by two factorial.
wrong: Use the second derivative unchanged as its coefficient.
Multiply the second derivative by two factorial.
Divide the function value instead of its second derivative.
qs.why: The Taylor coefficient uses the corresponding derivative divided by its factorial, not an unscaled, multiplied, or wrong-order value.

qs.q: Evaluate the degree-three Maclaurin polynomial 1+x+x²/2+x³/6 for exp(x) at dimensionless x=0.2.
qs.why: Substitution gives 1.221333…, rounded to 1.221.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Polynomial matching derivatives at a center
Product of positive integers up to an index
qs.why: Taylor polynomial means polynomial matching derivatives at a center. Maclaurin polynomial means taylor polynomial centered at zero. Factorial means product of positive integers up to an index.

qs.q: Which Taylor setup is flawed?
lines: Choose an expansion center
Use derivatives evaluated at that center
Divide each derivative by its order factorial
Use the second derivative directly as the quadratic coefficient
qs.why: The quadratic coefficient is the second derivative divided by 2!.
qs.ans: Use the second derivative directly as the quadratic coefficient
wrong: Choose an expansion center
Use derivatives evaluated at that center
Divide each derivative by its order factorial

cards: In plain English: An approximation needs an error estimate as well as a formula.
A Lagrange remainder bound uses a bound on the next derivative throughout the interval between the center and evaluation point.
Matching many derivatives locally does not automatically prove that an infinite Taylor series equals the original function.
Why it happens: equality with the infinite series requires the remainder to tend to zero, not merely the existence of every derivative.
title: Taylor remainder and validity
plain: An approximation needs an error estimate as well as a formula.

qs.q: “The derivative bound must cover the whole connecting interval.”
qs.ans: Use a valid maximum bound along that interval.
wrong: Use only the derivative value at the center always.
Assume all smooth functions equal their Taylor series.
Treat the next coefficient alone as the error everywhere.
qs.why: A point value is not a uniform bound; smoothness alone does not imply analyticity; displacement factors also matter.

qs.q: For dimensionless x, approximate sin(x) by x at x=0.1. Using the degree-two Taylor polynomial x and |sin third derivative|≤1, bound the absolute error by |x|³/6.
Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Difference between the function and its polynomial
Valid upper magnitude bound over an interval
Function equal locally to its convergent power series
qs.why: Remainder means difference between the function and its polynomial. Derivative bound means valid upper magnitude bound over an interval. Analytic function means function equal locally to its convergent power series.

qs.q: Order a Taylor error bound.
items: Identify the polynomial degree and next derivative
Bound that derivative over the connecting interval
Multiply by displacement power and divide by the required factorial
qs.why: The bound must apply throughout the interval used by the remainder theorem.

cards: In plain English: Within convergence ranges, series can simplify differentiation, integration, and limits.
Inside a power series radius, termwise differentiation and integration are valid and preserve the radius. Endpoint behavior can change.
Leading nonzero powers often determine limits of ratios near the expansion center. Retain enough terms to survive cancellation.
Why it happens: local convergence controls the infinite operations, while cancellation can remove the apparently dominant contribution.
title: Series operations and local limits
plain: Within convergence ranges, series can simplify differentiation, integration, and limits.

qs.q: “The constant and linear terms canceled; keep the quadratic.”
qs.ans: Retain the first surviving nonzero order.
wrong: Stop at the canceled linear approximation anyway.
Treat cancellation as proof the entire function vanishes.
Use the highest written power regardless of lower survivors.
qs.why: Truncating too early, confusing local cancellation with identity, or choosing the wrong leading order gives incorrect limits.

qs.q: For dimensionless x, find lim as x→0 of [exp(x)−1−x]/x².
qs.why: The numerator begins x²/2, so the ratio tends to 1/2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Termwise differentiation means differentiating each power-series term. Leading order means lowest surviving nonzero power locally. Cancellation means removal of equal opposing terms.

qs.q: Which series manipulation is flawed?
lines: Work inside the convergence radius
Recheck endpoints after termwise integration
Retain enough terms after cancellation
Assume endpoint convergence is unchanged after differentiation
qs.why: Differentiation preserves the radius but can change convergence at its endpoints.
qs.ans: Assume endpoint convergence is unchanged after differentiation
wrong: Work inside the convergence radius
Recheck endpoints after termwise integration
Retain enough terms after cancellation

cards: In plain English: A path can be described by how both coordinates depend on a parameter.
Parametric coordinates x(t) and y(t) define a path. Where x′(t) is nonzero, dy/dx=y′(t)/x′(t).
For a second derivative with respect to x, differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide again by x′(t). All variables here are dimensionless.
Why it happens: the parameter rate must be converted into an x-rate using the chain rule.
title: Parametric derivatives
plain: A path can be described by how both coordinates depend on a parameter.

qs.q: “Divide by the horizontal parameter rate.”
qs.ans: Convert the parameter derivative into an x-derivative.
wrong: Use the vertical parameter derivative alone for dy/dx.
Multiply both coordinate rates to obtain dy/dx.
Divide the horizontal rate by the vertical rate instead.
qs.why: These alternatives omit, multiply, or invert the conversion factor.

qs.q: For dimensionless x(t)=t² and y(t)=t³, find dy/dx at t=2.
qs.why: The ratio is 3t²/(2t)=3t/2, giving 3.

qs.q: A dimensionless parametric curve has dx/dt=2 and dy/dt=6 at a point. What is dy/dx there?
qs.why: Divide vertical rate by horizontal rate. Twelve multiplies the rates; one third inverts them; six ignores the horizontal conversion.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Coordinate rate with respect to the parameter
qs.why: Parameter means independent variable tracing a path. Parametric derivative means coordinate rate with respect to the parameter. dy/dx means vertical change per horizontal change.

qs.q: Order a parametric derivative calculation.
items: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter
Check that the horizontal derivative is nonzero
Divide the vertical rate by the horizontal rate
qs.why: The quotient converts parameter changes to coordinate changes.

cards: In plain English: Path length depends on motion along the path, including repeated traversal.
Parametric arc length integrates the norm of the coordinate derivative. The speed is nonnegative even when a coordinate decreases.
A parameter interval can trace the same geometric segment more than once. The integral counts all traversed distance.
Why it happens: speed accumulates local distance rather than net displacement, so reversals do not cancel.
title: Parametric length and traversal
plain: Path length depends on motion along the path, including repeated traversal.

qs.q: “That interval traces the circle twice.”
qs.ans: The length integral counts both traversals.
wrong: The length integral automatically removes repeated traversal.
Opposite coordinate changes cancel all traveled distance.
The net endpoint displacement always equals path length.
qs.why: Length accumulates traversal; it does not deduplicate paths or reduce to displacement.

qs.q: For dimensionless x(t)=3cos(t), y(t)=3sin(t), find arc length for 0≤t≤π.
qs.why: Speed is constantly 3, giving length 3π.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Speed means norm of the parameter velocity. Traversal means passage along a path. Displacement means difference between endpoint positions.

qs.q: Which path-length note is flawed?
lines: Integrate the norm of the derivative
Check how many times the parameter traces the path
Keep speed nonnegative
Replace path length by endpoint displacement for every path
qs.why: Endpoint displacement ignores curvature and reversals.
qs.ans: Replace path length by endpoint displacement for every path
wrong: Integrate the norm of the derivative
Check how many times the parameter traces the path
Keep speed nonnegative

cards: In plain English: Polar descriptions use distance and angle, with a different area element.
Polar coordinates satisfy x=r cos(θ), y=r sin(θ). Here r is a dimensionless radial coordinate and θ is in radians.
Polar area over a non-overlapping sweep integrates r²/2 with respect to angle. Check intersections and traversal before assigning bounds.
Why it happens: a thin sector has area one half radius squared times its small angle.
title: Polar coordinates and area
plain: Polar descriptions use distance and angle, with a different area element.

qs.q: “The sector area needs the squared radius.”
qs.ans: Integrate one half the radius squared over angle.
wrong: Integrate radius alone over angle for sector area.
Integrate circumference alone over angle for sector area.
Square the final angle integral instead of its radius.
qs.why: The sector geometry requires r²/2, not length quantities or a squared final integral.

qs.q: A dimensionless polar region has 0≤r≤2 and 0≤θ≤π/2. Find its area.
qs.why: The sector area is (1/2)(4)(π/2)=π.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Region swept by a radial segment
qs.why: Polar radius means radial coordinate. Polar angle means angular coordinate in radians. Sector means region swept by a radial segment.

qs.q: Order a polar area calculation.
items: Square the radial boundary and divide by two
qs.why: The sector element gives the area without double counting.

figNeeded: Show a polar sector with radius, angle increment, and its small area element.

cards: In plain English: A polar formula needs coordinate conversion before its tangent is interpreted.
Polar tangent calculations differentiate x=r cos(θ) and y=r sin(θ) with respect to angle, then form their derivative ratio.
A focus-based conic can use r=p/(1+e cos(θ)), where p is a positive dimensionless scale and e is dimensionless eccentricity.
Why it happens: changing angle changes both radius and direction, so differentiating radius alone does not describe the Cartesian tangent.
title: Polar tangents and conic geometry
plain: A polar formula needs coordinate conversion before its tangent is interpreted.

qs.q: “Radial change is not the Cartesian tangent by itself.”
qs.ans: Differentiate both converted Cartesian coordinates.
wrong: Use dr/dθ directly as every Cartesian tangent slope.
Keep radius fixed even when its formula varies.
Ignore the angle derivatives of sine and cosine.
qs.why: All three alternatives omit part of the coordinate dependence.

qs.q: For dimensionless r=6/(1+0.5cos(θ)), evaluate r at θ=0.
qs.why: At zero, cosine is one, so r=6/1.5=4.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Reference point used in a conic definition
Tangent obtained from angle-dependent Cartesian coordinates
qs.why: Eccentricity means dimensionless conic-shape parameter. Focus means reference point used in a conic definition. Polar tangent means tangent obtained from angle-dependent cartesian coordinates.

qs.q: Which polar tangent step is flawed?
lines: Convert both coordinates
Differentiate both with respect to angle
Check where the horizontal derivative vanishes
Use the radial derivative alone as dy/dx
qs.why: The tangent includes changes in direction as well as radius.
qs.ans: Use the radial derivative alone as dy/dx
wrong: Convert both coordinates
Differentiate both with respect to angle
Check where the horizontal derivative vanishes

cards: In plain English: Vectors combine size with direction.
A vector is represented by components in a chosen basis. Its Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of squared orthonormal components.
A unit vector has norm one. Normalize a nonzero vector by dividing every component by its norm.
Why it happens: orthogonal components combine through the Pythagorean theorem rather than by simply adding their magnitudes.
title: Vector components and norms
plain: Vectors combine size with direction.

qs.q: “Normalize the direction before using it.”
qs.ans: Divide the nonzero vector by its norm.
wrong: Divide the vector by the sum of its components.
Multiply the vector by its norm instead.
Set every component equal to one instead.
qs.why: Component sums are not norms; multiplication scales up; all-one components change direction.

qs.q: Find the Euclidean norm of the dimensionless vector (2,−3,6).
qs.why: The squared norm is 4+9+36=49, so the norm is 7.

qs.q: A dimensionless vector has orthonormal components (3,4). What is its Euclidean norm?
qs.why: The norm is √(9+16)=5. Seven sums magnitudes, twenty-five omits the square root, and one confuses the vector with its normalized direction.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Component means coordinate in a chosen basis. Norm means vector magnitude. Unit vector means vector of norm one.

qs.q: Order vector normalization.
items: Compute the sum of squared orthonormal components
Take its square root and check it is nonzero
Divide each component by that norm
qs.why: Normalization preserves direction while setting magnitude to one.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for vector components and norms, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **vector** describes a displacement or another quantity with direction and size.
Its **components** are the signed amounts along the chosen axes. Its **norm** is its length.
A **basis** is a set of directions used to build every vector. An **orthonormal** basis uses unit directions that are mutually [[perpendicular]].

p.cap: x, y and z are the components of v along perpendicular unit axes.

p.x: A **unit vector** has length one. To find the unit vector $u$ pointing along a nonzero vector $v$, divide all its components by the same length.

p.cap: v must have nonzero length.

p.x: Walk $3$ units east, then $4$ units north.
The straight-line distance is $5$ units. The two legs meet at a right angle.

g.q: How far are you from the start?
o: 5 units
The two perpendicular legs are squared and added before taking the root.
7 units
Adding the legs gives the distance walked around the corner.
25 units
That is the squared distance. Take its square root.

cards: In plain English: A dot product measures alignment and extracts a directional component.
The Euclidean dot product sums matching component products in an orthonormal basis. Zero dot product means perpendicular nonzero vectors.
Scalar projection onto a unit direction is the dot product with that direction. Projection onto a nonunit vector requires normalization.
Why it happens: perpendicular components contribute nothing to change along the selected direction.
title: Dot products and projections
plain: A dot product measures alignment and extracts a directional component.

qs.q: “You forgot to normalize the projection direction.”
qs.ans: Use a unit direction for scalar projection.
wrong: Use the raw direction regardless of its magnitude.
Use the cross product magnitude for scalar projection.
Add the component sums instead of taking a dot product.
qs.why: These alternatives introduce scaling, measure perpendicular area, or use an unrelated operation.

qs.q: For dimensionless vectors a=(1,2,3) and b=(4,−1,2), calculate a·b.
qs.why: Matching products sum to 4−2+6=8.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Perpendicular in the specified inner product
Signed component along a unit direction
qs.why: Dot product means scalar measure of vector alignment. Orthogonal means perpendicular in the specified inner product. Scalar projection means signed component along a unit direction.

qs.q: Which projection statement is flawed?
lines: Choose the projection direction
Normalize it for scalar projection
Use matching-coordinate products
Treat a raw nonunit dot product as the scalar projection
qs.why: A nonunit direction multiplies the projection by its norm.
qs.ans: Treat a raw nonunit dot product as the scalar projection
wrong: Choose the projection direction
Normalize it for scalar projection
Use matching-coordinate products

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for dot products and projections, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **dot product** combines two vectors into one number that measures alignment.
A **projection** extracts the part of a vector along a chosen direction. The scalar projection gives the signed length of that part.
Nonzero vectors with zero dot product are [[perpendicular]].

p.cap: In the plane, use the components along x and y. Add the matching z product in space.

p.x: **Orthogonal** means perpendicular in this dot product.
Project $a$ onto direction $b$. First form the unit vector $u$ by dividing the nonzero $b$ by its length.

p.cap: b specifies the direction.
Signed scalar projection. Multiply by u for the projected vector.

p.x: A cart moves east and north. You measure the eastward part of its displacement.
Adding a purely northward displacement leaves the eastward projection unchanged.
Only the component parallel to the chosen direction enters the dot product.

g.q: Add another displacement due north. What happens to the eastward projection?
o: It increases
The overall displacement can grow without adding any eastward component.
It stays the same
North is perpendicular to east, so its eastward component is zero.

cards: In plain English: Normals encode the orientation of planes.
In three dimensions, a cross product is perpendicular to both input vectors and follows the right-hand rule. Its magnitude is their parallelogram area.
A plane can be specified by a point and a nonzero normal. A line can be specified by a point and direction.
Why it happens: displacement within a plane has zero dot product with its normal, turning a geometric condition into a linear equation.
title: Cross products, lines, and planes
plain: Normals encode the orientation of planes.

qs.q: “Those two spanning directions give the plane normal.”
qs.ans: Take their cross product if they are independent.
wrong: Take their dot product to obtain a normal vector.
Add the two directions to obtain a perpendicular vector.
Use their cross product even when they are parallel.
qs.why: A dot product is scalar, a sum is generally in-plane, and parallel vectors give a zero cross product.

qs.q: Find the z-component of the cross product (1,0,0)×(0,3,0). All components are dimensionless.
qs.why: The right-hand cross product points along positive z with magnitude 3.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Oriented perpendicular vector in three dimensions
Vector perpendicular to a surface or plane
Zero normal dot product with in-plane displacement
qs.why: Cross product means oriented perpendicular vector in three dimensions. Normal means vector perpendicular to a surface or plane. Plane equation means zero normal dot product with in-plane displacement.

qs.q: Order a plane construction from three noncollinear points.
items: Form two displacement vectors from one point
Cross them to obtain a nonzero normal
Set the normal dot displacement from the chosen point equal to zero
qs.why: Noncollinearity ensures the normal is nonzero.

figNeeded: Show two plane-spanning vectors, their right-hand normal, and a point on the plane.

p.x: A **plane** is a flat surface that extends without bound.
Its **normal** is a nonzero vector perpendicular to the surface. It tells you the plane’s orientation.
Given three points that don’t lie on one line, form two displacements from the same point. Their cross product, introduced next, gives a normal.
The **cross product** has length equal to the parallelogram area. Parallel inputs give zero. Swapping the inputs reverses the vector.

p.cap: In right-handed axes, subscripts pick components.

p.x: A line needs a point and a nonzero vector pointing [[along]] the line.
Starting from the given point, move any signed multiple of the direction vector.
A plane also needs a point. Its nonzero normal sticks straight out of it.
Let $p$ be a point in the plane, $r$ a candidate point and $n$ its nonzero normal.
A move by $n$ leaves the plane because it adds a displacement perpendicular to the plane.

p.cap: Only points r in the plane pass this test.

g.q: Starting at p, move by the vector n. Where do you land?
o: Off the plane
A nonzero normal displacement adds a positive term to the normal dot product.
In the plane
To stay in the plane, the displacement must be perpendicular to the normal.

cards: In plain English: A moving point can change speed, direction, or both.
A space curve uses a vector-valued position function. Its first derivative is parameter velocity and the velocity norm is speed.
Curvature measures turning per unit arc length. A circle has curvature equal to the reciprocal of its radius.
Why it happens: acceleration can change the velocity direction even when its magnitude stays constant.
title: Space curves, curvature, and motion
plain: A moving point can change speed, direction, or both.

qs.q: “Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration.”
qs.ans: Direction changes can produce normal acceleration.
wrong: A constant velocity magnitude fixes its direction too.
Acceleration can only change the velocity magnitude.
A curved path always requires increasing speed.
qs.why: Velocity has direction as well as magnitude; turning does not require speeding up.

qs.q: A circle has dimensionless radius 4. What is its curvature?
qs.why: Circle curvature is reciprocal radius, so it is 0.25.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Turning rate per unit arc length
qs.why: Velocity means derivative of position. Curvature means turning rate per unit arc length. Normal acceleration means acceleration component changing motion direction.

qs.q: Which motion statement is flawed?
lines: Differentiate position for velocity
Use velocity norm for speed
Distinguish tangential and normal acceleration
Infer zero acceleration from constant speed alone
qs.why: Circular motion at constant speed has nonzero normal acceleration.
qs.ans: Infer zero acceleration from constant speed alone
wrong: Differentiate position for velocity
Use velocity norm for speed
Distinguish tangential and normal acceleration

figNeeded: Show tangent and normal directions along a space curve and a local osculating circle.

p.x: **Velocity** describes how fast and in what direction a point moves.
**Speed** is just the length of the velocity. A point can turn while keeping the same speed.
A **space curve** gives position $r(t)$. Velocity is its rate of change [[with respect to time]].

p.cap: For differentiable position r and time t. Speed is the length of v.

p.x: **Arc length** is distance measured along the curve. **Curvature** $κ$ measures how quickly the tangent direction turns per unit of that distance.

p.cap: For a circle of radius R, at any point.

p.x: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity. A point travels around a circle at constant nonzero speed.
Acceleration is nonzero because the velocity keeps turning.
For steady circular motion, the acceleration points inward. This is **normal acceleration**: the component perpendicular to velocity that changes its direction.

g.q: Is the acceleration zero?
o: Yes, it is zero
Constant speed fixes the length of velocity. Its direction still changes.
No, it is nonzero
A change of direction is a change in velocity.

cards: In plain English: Agreement along a few paths does not establish agreement along every path.
A multivariable limit must be the same along all approaches within the domain. Different path limits disprove existence.
Checking finitely many paths can fail to detect a problematic curved approach. Continuity still requires the limit to equal the point value.
Why it happens: two or more independent input directions allow infinitely many approach paths.
title: Multivariable limits and continuity
plain: Agreement along a few paths does not establish agreement along every path.

qs.q: “Both axes agree, but that is not a proof.”
qs.ans: Other approach paths may produce different values.
wrong: Two matching axis limits always prove the full limit.
Only straight-line approaches matter in several variables.
The assigned point value determines every path limit.
qs.why: Finite path checks, excluding curves, and substituting the point value do not establish a multivariable limit.

qs.q: For dimensionless f(x,y)=xy/(x²+y²), evaluate its limit at the origin along y=x.
qs.why: Along y=x with x≠0, the expression is x²/(2x²)=1/2.

qs.q: Two paths approaching a point give different limits for a scalar function. What follows?
qs.ans: The full limit does not exist.
wrong: The full limit is their arithmetic average.
The full limit equals the larger path limit.
The full limit equals the assigned point value.
qs.why: A full limit must agree along every path. Averaging, choosing the larger limit, or using the point value does not repair path dependence.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Common limit over all allowed approaches
Nearby limit equals the point value
qs.why: Path limit means limit along one approach curve. Multivariable limit means common limit over all allowed approaches. Continuity means nearby limit equals the point value.

qs.q: Which limit proof is flawed?
lines: Use unequal path limits to disprove existence
Check the domain near the point
Use a bound covering all paths to prove a limit
Use agreement along two axes as sufficient proof
qs.why: A third path can disagree despite matching axis limits.
qs.ans: Use agreement along two axes as sufficient proof
wrong: Use unequal path limits to disprove existence
Check the domain near the point
Use a bound covering all paths to prove a limit

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for multivariable limits and continuity, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **limit** is the value the output approaches as the inputs approach a point.
Test approaches through the **domain**, the set of allowed inputs. The value at the point plays no role.
If the outputs approach [[different]] values on two paths, the limit fails to exist.
A limit must have one value that works for every approach.
Near the origin, divide $x^2y$ by $x^4+y^2$. The result is zero on both axes away from the origin.
On the curve $y=x^2$, the numerator is $x^4$ and the denominator is $2x^4$. This gives $1/2$.
These two approaches give different values, so the limit fails to exist. **Continuity** requires a limit equal to the value at the point.

g.q: What value do you get along y = x² away from the origin?
o: Substitution makes the denominator twice the numerator.
Zero applies on the axes. Here both coordinates are nonzero.
The denominator has two equal x⁴ terms.

p.x: Infinitely many straight and curved paths can approach the same point.
To prove a limit, control the output error for every nearby input using its distance from the point.

cards: In plain English: A gradient combines sensitivities to independent inputs.
A partial derivative changes one input while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects first partial derivatives into a vector.
The gradient points toward steepest local increase under the Euclidean metric when it is nonzero.
Why it happens: the directional derivative is the gradient dot a unit direction, maximized when the vectors align.
title: Partial derivatives and the gradient
plain: A gradient combines sensitivities to independent inputs.

qs.q: “Hold the other independent inputs fixed.”
qs.ans: Calculate a partial derivative with respect to this input.
wrong: Vary every independent input at the same rate instead.
Differentiate only the sum of all input coordinates.
Treat the selected input as constant during differentiation.
qs.why: Partial differentiation isolates one input; coordinated changes are a total derivative, and freezing the selected input removes its effect.

qs.q: For dimensionless f(x,y)=x²y+3y, calculate ∂f/∂x at (2,4).
qs.why: Holding y fixed gives 2xy, which is 16 at (2,4).

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Sensitivity to one input with others fixed
qs.why: Partial derivative means sensitivity to one input with others fixed. Gradient means vector of first partial derivatives. Level set means inputs producing one constant output.

qs.q: Order a gradient calculation.
items: Differentiate with respect to each while fixing the others
Assemble the derivatives in coordinate order
qs.why: The coordinate order determines how the gradient aligns with directions.

demoNeeded: Show a surface and level contours with the gradient at a movable point.

p.x: A **sensitivity** is a rate of output change as an input varies.
For a scalar function, which gives one number, each input can have its own sensitivity.
A **partial derivative** varies one input while holding the others [[fixed]].

p.cap: For f(x,y), f_x varies x alone and f_y varies y alone.

p.x: The **gradient** collects those first derivatives in a vector.
For a differentiable function, a nonzero gradient points toward the steepest local increase per unit distance.
A **level set** contains inputs with the same output. The gradient is perpendicular to the tangent of a level curve wherever that tangent exists.
A **directional derivative** measures the rate per unit distance in a direction given by a unit vector $u$.

p.cap: For differentiable f at the point.

p.x: The zero gradient gives no first-order change. For a nonzero gradient the rate is greatest when $u$ points along it.

g.q: If the gradient is zero, what is the rate along a unit direction?
o: Zero in every direction
The dot product with the zero vector is zero.
Positive in some direction
An increase here must come from changes beyond first order.

cards: In plain English: A local multivariable model combines all first-order input changes.
The directional derivative along a unit vector is its dot product with the gradient. A nonunit direction measures a scaled parameter rate instead.
A differentiable scalar function is locally approximated by its value plus gradient dot input displacement. Existence of partial derivatives alone does not ensure differentiability.
Why it happens: differentiability means one linear model captures every sufficiently small direction with a smaller-order residual.
title: Directional derivatives and tangent planes
plain: A local multivariable model combines all first-order input changes.

qs.q: “Partials exist, but the total linear approximation still needs justification.”
qs.ans: Partial derivatives alone do not ensure differentiability.
wrong: Every existing pair of partial derivatives proves differentiability.
Differentiability requires all partial derivatives to vanish.
A tangent model ignores all but one coordinate change.
qs.why: Partial existence is weaker than differentiability; zero derivatives are unnecessary and all inputs contribute.

qs.q: At a dimensionless point, gradient=(3,4) and unit direction=(0,1). Find the directional derivative.
qs.why: The dot product is 4.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Rate along a specified unit direction
Existence of a valid total linear approximation
qs.why: Directional derivative means rate along a specified unit direction. Tangent plane means first-order local graph approximation. Differentiability means existence of a valid total linear approximation.

qs.q: Which directional-rate calculation is flawed?
lines: Evaluate the gradient at the point
Normalize a nonzero direction
Take the gradient dot the unit direction
Use an arbitrary nonunit direction while claiming rate per unit distance

For a piecewise smooth path $r(t)$, the derivative gives the directed motion per unit increase in the path parameter $t$.
For a scalar integrand, weight it by the length of that derivative. For work, take the dot product of the field with the derivative.
Traverse the same path backward through the same scalar and vector fields.
Reversing the path reverses the sign of work. The scalar integral against arc length is unchanged.

g.q: What happens to the work integral?
o: It changes sign
Each little directed displacement reverses.
It stays the same
That is true for the scalar integral against length.

p.x: A small step has the same length both ways, but its displacement points in the [[opposite]] direction on the return trip.
The length weight stays the same. The dot product with the directed step changes sign.

cards: In plain English: Some work integrals depend only on endpoints.
A conservative field is the gradient of a scalar potential. Its line integral equals final potential minus initial potential.
Path independence implies zero circulation around closed paths in the relevant domain. Domain restrictions matter.
Why it happens: along a path, the gradient dot path derivative is the ordinary derivative of the potential by the chain rule.
title: Conservative fields and potentials
plain: Some work integrals depend only on endpoints.

qs.q: “Use the potential difference instead of tracing the entire path.”
qs.ans: Evaluate final potential minus initial potential.
wrong: Evaluate the potential only at the final endpoint.
Integrate the potential itself against arc length instead.
Ignore whether the field is actually conservative.
qs.why: The endpoint theorem needs a valid potential and both endpoint values; it is not a scalar arc-length integral.

qs.q: A dimensionless potential is φ(x,y)=x²+y². Find the work of its gradient from (1,0) to (2,1).
qs.why: Potential difference is 5−1=4.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Scalar function whose gradient gives the field
Work integral around a closed curve
qs.why: Potential means scalar function whose gradient gives the field. Path independence means integral depends only on endpoints. Closed-path circulation means work integral around a closed curve.

qs.q: Which endpoint-theorem use is flawed?
lines: Verify a potential for the field
Keep endpoints inside the relevant domain
Subtract initial potential from final potential
Apply the theorem to every vector field without checking a potential
qs.why: General vector fields need not have path-independent integrals.
qs.ans: Apply the theorem to every vector field without checking a potential
wrong: Verify a potential for the field
Keep endpoints inside the relevant domain
Subtract initial potential from final potential

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for conservative fields and potentials, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An **endpoint** is the start or finish of a path. Work is **path independent** on a domain when all paths there with the same ordered endpoints have the same work.
A function of position can store all the information you need to calculate that work.
A **conservative field** $F$ is the gradient of a scalar **potential** $φ$. Its work from $A$ to $B$ depends [[only on the endpoints]].

p.cap: For a piecewise smooth path inside the domain of the potential.

p.x: Compute the final potential minus the initial potential.
A **closed path** returns to its starting point. **Circulation** is work around such a path.
Closed paths in the domain have zero circulation because both endpoints are the same point.
Check that the potential is defined everywhere on the path.

g.q: What circulation can a conservative field give on a closed path in its domain?
o: Zero
The two endpoint potential values cancel.
A nonzero value
That could happen only if the field does not have a single potential on the path’s domain.

p.x: Along the path $r(t)$, the potential becomes a function of the path parameter $t$.

p.cap: By the chain rule, evaluated at r(t) on each smooth part.

p.x: Integrate this ordinary derivative over the path parameter to get the potential change.

cards: In plain English: A planar boundary circulation can be computed from what happens throughout its interior.
Green’s theorem relates positively oriented planar boundary circulation to the double integral of the field’s scalar curl over the enclosed region.
The field must satisfy the theorem’s smoothness and domain requirements throughout the region. Inner boundaries have opposite orientation to outer boundaries.
Why it happens: circulation along shared interior edges cancels, leaving only boundary contributions.
title: Green’s theorem
plain: A planar boundary circulation can be computed from what happens throughout its interior.

qs.q: “The inner hole boundary runs the other way.”
qs.ans: Orient inner boundaries clockwise for positive orientation.
wrong: Orient every boundary counterclockwise regardless of holes.
Omit all inner boundary contributions automatically.
Reverse the outer boundary but keep the same integral sign.
qs.why: Positive orientation keeps the region on the left, forcing inner boundaries to reverse relative to outer ones.

qs.q: For dimensionless F=(−y/2,x/2), scalar curl is 1. Find counterclockwise circulation around the unit circle using Green’s theorem.
qs.why: Integrate curl 1 over the unit disk: the result is its area π.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Traversal keeping the region on the left
Planar derivative difference measuring circulation density
Relation between planar boundary circulation and interior curl
qs.why: Positive planar orientation means traversal keeping the region on the left. Scalar curl means planar derivative difference measuring circulation density. Green’s theorem means relation between planar boundary circulation and interior curl.

qs.q: Order a Green’s theorem calculation.
items: Check the region, orientation, and field regularity
qs.why: Domain and orientation checks precede the conversion.

figNeeded: Show positive outer and inner boundary orientations for a planar region with a hole.

p.x: **Circulation** measures how much a vector field pushes along an oriented closed curve. Orientation is the direction you travel.
**Green’s theorem** moves the calculation from a plane region’s boundary to its interior.
Write the field’s horizontal and vertical components as $P$ and $Q$. **Scalar curl** measures local counterclockwise circulation per unit area.

p.cap: Q_x differentiates Q along x. P_y differentiates P along y.

p.x: Add the scalar curl over the plane region.
The result is the circulation along the oriented boundary shown.
Require continuous first partial derivatives throughout an open neighborhood of the region and its piecewise smooth boundary.
A positive boundary keeps the region on your left, so its inner and outer loops go in [[opposite]] senses.
Travel counterclockwise around the outside and clockwise around holes.
Imagine splitting the region into adjacent patches and adding their boundary circulations.
Shared edges cancel because the patches traverse them in opposite directions. Only the region’s boundary remains.

g.q: What happens to contributions on a shared edge?
o: They cancel
The edge is traversed in opposite directions by its two patches.
They add in the same direction
That would count the shared edge twice with the same orientation.

cards: In plain English: A local derivative test does not always establish global path independence.
A smooth conservative field is curl-free. A curl-free field on a simply connected open domain is conservative under standard hypotheses.
A hole can prevent a closed curve from shrinking inside the domain, allowing nonzero circulation despite zero local curl.
Why it happens: local derivative information cannot detect every global topological obstruction.
title: Curl-free fields and domain holes
plain: A local derivative test does not always establish global path independence.

qs.q: “Zero curl is not enough on this punctured domain.”
qs.ans: Check domain topology and closed-loop circulation.
wrong: Declare a global potential from zero curl alone everywhere.
Fill the missing point without checking the field singularity.
Treat every closed path as contractible in the domain.
qs.why: These alternatives omit the topological and domain assumptions needed for the converse.

qs.q: For dimensionless F=(−y/(x²+y²),x/(x²+y²)), its dot product with the unit-circle tangent parameter derivative is 1. Find circulation for angle 0 to 2π.
qs.why: The parameter integral of 1 over [0,2π] is 2π, although the field is curl-free away from the origin.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Every closed loop can shrink within the domain
Global domain feature preventing a local conclusion from extending
qs.why: Curl-free means zero local curl. Simply connected means every closed loop can shrink within the domain. Topological obstruction means global domain feature preventing a local conclusion from extending.

qs.q: Which potential-field conclusion is flawed?
lines: Check the field domain
Look for excluded singularities
Distinguish local curl from global circulation
Infer a global potential from zero curl on any punctured domain
qs.why: The missing point can support nonzero circulation around it.
qs.ans: Infer a global potential from zero curl on any punctured domain
wrong: Check the field domain
Look for excluded singularities
Distinguish local curl from global circulation

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for curl-free fields and domain holes, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A field’s **curl** measures local circulation. Zero curl rules out a local spin detected by first derivatives.
**Path independence** is a global statement: every pair of paths with the same endpoints gives the same work.
A smooth **conservative** field is a gradient, so it has zero curl.
**Simply connected** means the domain is path-connected and each closed loop can be shrunk to a point [[within]] it.
On a simply connected open domain, the converse holds: a continuously differentiable field with zero curl is conservative.
Consider a curl-free field on the plane with the origin removed. A closed path winds around that missing point.
A hole can allow nonzero circulation even when curl vanishes everywhere the field is defined.

g.q: Can this path have nonzero circulation?
o: Yes, it can
The missing point blocks contraction, so local zero curl need not imply zero work around the loop.
No, it cannot
Zero curl gives the global conclusion only with additional domain conditions.

p.x: For a loop around a hole, filling its interior can require points where the field is undefined.
A local derivative test never measures what happens at those missing points. Check the domain before inferring a potential.

cards: In plain English: Flux counts how strongly a field passes through an oriented surface.
A parameterized surface uses two independent parameters. Crossing its tangent vectors gives an oriented area vector.
Scalar surface area uses the cross-product norm. Flux uses the field dot the oriented area vector, preserving normal direction.
Why it happens: only the field component normal to a surface passes through it; tangential components contribute no flux.
title: Surface parameterization and flux
plain: Flux counts how strongly a field passes through an oriented surface.

qs.q: “The cross-product order reversed the normal.”
qs.ans: Reverse the flux sign when orientation reverses.
wrong: Keep the flux unchanged for every normal reversal.
Replace oriented area by its norm in every flux integral.
Use only the tangential field component for flux.
qs.why: These errors discard orientation or project onto the wrong direction.

qs.q: A dimensionless constant field (0,0,3) crosses an upward-oriented flat region of area 2. Find its flux.
qs.why: Normal field component 3 times area 2 gives flux 6.

qs.q: A surface flux integral uses a chosen unit normal. What happens when only that normal is reversed?
qs.ans: The flux sign reverses.
wrong: The flux remains unchanged.
The flux magnitude doubles.
The field magnitude reverses sign.
qs.why: The normal projection changes sign. Magnitude of the field stays nonnegative; geometry is not doubled and orientation cannot be ignored.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Integral of normal field component over a surface
Oriented normal scaled by local area
qs.why: Flux means integral of normal field component over a surface. Area vector means oriented normal scaled by local area. Parameterization means coordinates describing the surface.

qs.q: Order a parameterized flux integral.
items: Choose a surface parameterization and required orientation
Form the correctly oriented tangent cross product
Dot the field with that area vector and integrate
qs.why: The cross product supplies both scale and orientation.

figNeeded: Show two surface tangents, their oriented cross product, and normal field projection.

p.x: **Flux** measures how strongly a field passes through a surface.
An **oriented** surface has a chosen normal direction, perpendicular to its tangent plane. Flow along that normal contributes positive flux.
A **parameterization** gives each surface point as a position vector depending on two parameters.
Vary one parameter at a time to get two tangent vectors. At a regular patch they are independent, so their cross product gives a nonzero oriented area vector.
For scalar area, use the [[length]] of the area vector. The length is independent of the chosen normal.
For flux, dot the field with the oriented area vector instead. Reversing the normal changes the sign of that dot product.
Imagine a sheet in a moving fluid. The fluid velocity at the sheet lies entirely in the local tangent plane.
Only the normal part of the field passes through the surface. A tangent field contributes zero flux.

g.q: What is the local flux through the sheet?
o: Zero
The flow runs along the sheet and its normal component is zero.
Nonzero
Motion along the sheet does not pass through it.

cards: In plain English: Net outward flux through a closed boundary equals interior source accumulation.
The divergence theorem equates outward flux through a closed surface with the volume integral of divergence, assuming sufficient smoothness.
Divergence is the sum of each vector component’s derivative along its own coordinate. Open surfaces need closure or another method.
Why it happens: flux across neighboring interior faces cancels; only the external boundary remains.
title: Divergence theorem
plain: Net outward flux through a closed boundary equals interior source accumulation.

qs.q: “Close the surface before applying the divergence theorem.”
qs.ans: Include the missing boundary and its flux.
wrong: Apply the closed-surface theorem directly to any open patch.
Set the missing-face flux to zero without calculation.
Use inward normals while retaining the outward-flux sign.
qs.why: Closure and orientation are required; an omitted face need not have zero flux.

qs.q: For dimensionless F=(x,y,z), divergence is 3. Find outward flux through a closed surface enclosing volume 2.
qs.why: The volume integral is constant divergence 3 times volume 2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Local net source strength per volume
Flux using normals directed out of the volume
qs.why: Divergence means local net source strength per volume. Closed surface means complete boundary of a volume. Outward flux means flux using normals directed out of the volume.

qs.q: Which divergence-theorem note is flawed?
lines: Use a closed boundary
Use outward normals
Check field regularity in the volume
Ignore a singularity inside the volume because the boundary is smooth
qs.why: Interior field regularity matters even when the boundary itself is smooth.
qs.ans: Ignore a singularity inside the volume because the boundary is smooth
wrong: Use a closed boundary
Use outward normals
Check field regularity in the volume

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for divergence theorem, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **closed surface** bounds a solid without an open edge. The outward normal points away from that solid.
**Divergence** measures local net outflow per unit volume, positive for a net source and negative for a net sink.
The **divergence theorem** equates the net outward flux of a field through a closed boundary to divergence integrated over the [[interior]].
Use the theorem for a piecewise smooth closed boundary with a field whose first partial derivatives are continuous on a neighborhood of the solid.
The volume integral sums the source and sink contributions throughout the solid.
Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be the field components along $x$, $y$ and $z$. The subscripts denote partial derivatives.

p.cap: Each derivative varies its indicated coordinate alone.

p.x: For an open surface, compute flux directly or close it with extra pieces. Subtract their flux using the outward orientation, then match the requested normal.

g.q: Which derivative belongs to the x component in the divergence sum?
o: Differentiate it along x
Divergence compares flow through the pair of faces normal to the component’s axis.
Differentiate it along y
That is a sideways change and does not give the net flow through the x faces.

p.x: Divide the solid into little volumes. Each shared face has opposite outward normals for its two neighbors.
Their flux contributions cancel. Only flux through the outer boundary survives the sum.

cards: In plain English: Boundary circulation and surface curl describe the same oriented accumulation.
Stokes’ theorem equates boundary circulation with surface flux of curl. Boundary and normal orientations must match the right-hand rule.
Any suitable spanning surface with the same oriented boundary can be used if the field is regular on the required surface.
Why it happens: local interior circulations cancel on shared edges, leaving the circulation around the boundary.
title: Stokes’ theorem
plain: Boundary circulation and surface curl describe the same oriented accumulation.

qs.q: “Choose the easier spanning surface with the same boundary.”
qs.ans: Preserve orientation and regularity.
wrong: Use any surface even with a different boundary instead.
Reverse the normal without changing circulation sign.
Ignore field singularities on the replacement surface.
qs.why: Surface substitution must preserve the boundary, orientation, and theorem hypotheses.

qs.q: A dimensionless curl field is constant (0,0,2). Find its flux through an upward flat disk of radius 1, hence the matching circulation.
qs.why: Normal curl 2 times disk area π gives 2π.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Surface whose boundary is the given curve
Equality of boundary circulation and surface curl flux
qs.why: Curl means vector measuring local circulation density. Spanning surface means surface whose boundary is the given curve. Stokes’ theorem means equality of boundary circulation and surface curl flux.

qs.q: Order a Stokes calculation.
items: Match its normal to the boundary orientation
Integrate normal curl over that surface
qs.why: The right-hand orientation links the two sides of the theorem.

figNeeded: Show an oriented loop and two spanning surfaces with matching right-hand normals.

p.x: **Circulation** is the work of a field along an oriented closed curve. **Curl** is the vector that measures local circulation about different axes.
Surface flux of curl counts the part of that local rotation along the surface normal.
**Stokes’ theorem** equates circulation around a surface boundary with the flux of curl through the surface.
Use an oriented piecewise smooth surface and a field with continuous first derivatives near it. Match the boundary to the normal by the right-hand rule.
A **spanning surface** has the given curve as its boundary. Two suitable surfaces span the same oriented curve. Their curl fluxes are equal and nonzero. Now reverse the normal on just one surface.
Reversing just one normal negates that surface’s curl flux. The fluxes now have opposite signs.

g.q: How do their curl fluxes compare now?
o: They have opposite signs
Reversing a normal negates its flux and reverses its boundary direction.
They still agree
They agreed when both surfaces induced the same boundary direction.

p.x: When adding the circulations of neighboring patches, a shared edge is traversed in [[opposite]] directions.
The interior edges cancel in pairs. Only circulation around the surface boundary remains.

cards: In plain English: The boundary type determines which integral theorem can simplify a problem.
Use Green for planar closed curves, Stokes for oriented curve boundaries of surfaces, and divergence for closed surfaces enclosing volumes.
Conservative-field endpoint evaluation is different: it replaces a path integral by a potential difference when a valid potential exists.
Why it happens: each theorem connects an integral to a boundary one dimension lower, with different geometry and regularity requirements.
title: Choosing an integral theorem
plain: The boundary type determines which integral theorem can simplify a problem.

qs.q: “This is a closed-surface flux problem, not a circulation problem.”
qs.ans: Consider divergence and the enclosed volume.
wrong: Use a potential difference between arbitrary surface points.
Use planar circulation without checking surface geometry.
Use Stokes directly on flux of the original field.
qs.why: Endpoint and circulation theorems do not directly replace general closed-surface flux; Stokes concerns curl flux.

qs.q: For dimensionless F=(2x,3y,4z), find its divergence.
qs.why: Differentiate each component in its own coordinate: 2+3+4=9.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Boundary circulation and surface curl flux
qs.why: Green means planar circulation and area curl. Stokes means boundary circulation and surface curl flux. Divergence theorem means closed-surface flux and volume divergence.

qs.q: Which theorem-selection note is flawed?
lines: Identify whether the integrand is work or flux
Identify whether the boundary is closed
Check orientation and singularities
Select a theorem solely because its name appears in the problem
qs.why: The integral type, geometry, and hypotheses determine applicability.
qs.ans: Select a theorem solely because its name appears in the problem
wrong: Identify whether the integrand is work or flux
Identify whether the boundary is closed
Check orientation and singularities

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for choosing an integral theorem, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Identify the object you are integrating over and how it is oriented before selecting a theorem.
A closed curve may bound a plane region or a surface in space. A closed surface can bound a volume.
For **Green’s theorem**, use a plane region and its positively oriented boundary. For **Stokes’ theorem**, match an oriented surface to its boundary curve.
For the **divergence theorem**, use a [[closed]] surface with outward normals and the volume that it encloses.
In each case check that the field has continuous first derivatives on the region or surface required by the theorem.
Suppose a vector field is the gradient of a continuously differentiable scalar **potential**. The path is piecewise smooth, lies in the domain of that potential, and may be open.
Use the final potential minus the initial potential. The path can be open.

g.q: How can you find the work without integrating along the path?
o: Subtract endpoint potentials
The derivative of the potential along the path is the work integrand.
Use the curl across a spanning surface
Stokes relates a surface to its full boundary. An open path alone is not that boundary.

p.x: Each boundary theorem trades a boundary integral for an integral one dimension higher. The geometry and the orientations determine the direction of the trade.
For volume source accumulation, form divergence from the field components $P$, $Q$ and $R$. A subscript indicates the coordinate that varies.

p.cap: For F with components along x, y and z.

cards: In plain English: A differential equation specifies how a quantity changes rather than just what it equals.
The order of a differential equation is its highest derivative order. An initial-value problem adds values at one independent-variable location.
Linear equations contain the unknown function and its derivatives only to first power, without products between them. Coefficients may depend on the independent variable.
Why it happens: derivative information leaves constants undetermined; appropriate initial data select a solution when existence and uniqueness conditions hold.
title: Models, order, and initial conditions
plain: A differential equation specifies how a quantity changes rather than just what it equals.

qs.q: “The initial condition selects one trajectory.”
qs.ans: It fixes a member of the solution family.
wrong: It changes the differential equation’s derivative order.
It guarantees uniqueness without any regularity assumptions.
It makes every nonlinear equation become linear.
qs.why: Initial data do not change order or linearity, and uniqueness still needs hypotheses.

qs.q: For dimensionless y′=2y and y(0)=3, find y at t=ln(2).
qs.why: The solution is 3exp(2t), giving 3×4=12.

qs.q: For an ordinary differential equation, what defines its order?
qs.ans: Its highest derivative order.
wrong: Its largest coefficient magnitude.
Its highest polynomial power of the unknown.
Its total number of written terms.
qs.why: Order concerns derivatives. Coefficient size, nonlinear degree, and term count are separate properties.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Highest derivative order in the equation
Specified state at one input location
Equation linear in the unknown and its derivatives
qs.why: Order means highest derivative order in the equation. Initial condition means specified state at one input location. Linear equation means equation linear in the unknown and its derivatives.

qs.q: Order an initial-value solution check.
items: Substitute the candidate into the differential equation
State the interval where the solution and equation are defined
qs.why: A valid solution must satisfy both dynamics and initial data.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for models, order, and initial conditions, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: The unknown function gives the value of a quantity at each input $t$. Time is one possible input.
The derivative gives the instantaneous [[rate of change]] of $y$ with respect to $t$.
A differential equation relates derivatives to other quantities. It might say the rate is proportional to the current value.
In $y″ = y^2$, the double prime means differentiate $y$ twice with respect to the input. The power means multiply $y$ by itself.
The equation is **second order**. Order counts how many times the highest derivative differentiates $y$.
An **initial condition** specifies the value of $y$ or a derivative at one input value. An **initial-value problem** combines the equation with such data.

g.q: What is the order of $y″ = y^2$?
o: First order
There is one derivative term, but that term differentiates twice.
Second order
The highest derivative is the second derivative, $y″$.
Fourth order
The exponent on $y$ is a power. It adds no derivatives.

p.x: In a **linear** differential equation, $y$ and its derivatives can be multiplied by coefficients and added. The coefficients may depend on the input $t$.

p.cap: g is a given function of t

p.x: A power such as $y^2$, or a product such as $y y′$, makes an equation nonlinear.
For the dimensionless equation $y′ = 2y$, the family is $y = C exp(2t)$. Here $C$ is any constant and $exp$ is the exponential function.
The derivative is $2C exp(2t)$, so the family satisfies the equation for all real $t$. Since $exp(0) = 1$, imposing $y(0) = 3$ gives $C = 3$.
Evaluate at $t = ln(2)$, where $ln$ is the natural logarithm, the inverse of $exp$.
Initial data select one trajectory when the problem has a unique solution.

cards: In plain English: Some equations separate into an input integral and an output integral.
A separable first-order equation factors into a function of the input times a function of the unknown. Move the unknown-dependent factor to its own side before integrating.
Check constant equilibrium solutions before dividing by an unknown-dependent factor. Logistic growth has equilibria at zero and its carrying capacity.
Why it happens: division by a factor that can vanish can remove valid constant solutions.
title: Separation, equilibria, and logistic growth
plain: Some equations separate into an input integral and an output integral.

qs.q: “You divided out an equilibrium.”
qs.ans: Check zero factors before separating variables.
wrong: Discard every constant solution from a differential equation.
Assume a divided-out factor can never vanish.
Add an arbitrary constant function as a solution automatically.
qs.why: The original equation, not the divided form, decides which constant solutions are valid.

qs.q: For dimensionless logistic y′=y(1−y/10), calculate the rate at y=2.
qs.why: The rate is 2(0.8)=1.6.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Equation whose input and output factors can be separated
Nonzero saturation level in the logistic model
qs.why: Separable equation means equation whose input and output factors can be separated. Equilibrium means constant solution with zero rate. Carrying capacity means nonzero saturation level in the logistic model.

qs.q: Which separation step is flawed?
lines: Identify equilibrium factors
Separate where division is valid
Integrate both sides
Discard all solutions where the divided factor vanishes
qs.why: Some divided-out values are valid equilibria of the original equation.
qs.ans: Discard all solutions where the divided factor vanishes
wrong: Identify equilibrium factors
Separate where division is valid
Integrate both sides

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for separation, equilibria, and logistic growth, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **separable** equation writes the rate as an input factor times an output factor. Here $t$ is the input, $y$ is the output, and $dy/dt$ (or $y′$) is its rate.
In $dy/dt = t(1+y)$, keep $t$ with $dt$. Divide by $1+y$ to put the $y$ factor with $dy$.

p.cap: where 1+y is nonzero

g.q: In $dy/dt = t(1+y)$, which factor stays with $dt$ after separation?
o: That factor depends on the output $y$, so it belongs with $dy$.
The factor $t$ depends only on the input and stays with $dt$.

p.x: Check zeros of the output factor before dividing. Then integrate each side [[separately]].
On an interval where the divided factor is nonzero, integrate the output side with respect to $y$ and the input side with respect to $t$. Include a constant of integration.
An **equilibrium** is a constant solution with zero rate. In logistic growth, the rate includes a factor that falls as $y$ approaches its **carrying capacity**, the nonzero saturation level.

p.cap: dimensionless example with carrying capacity 10

p.x: At $y = 0$ the first factor vanishes. At $y = 10$ the second vanishes. Both constant functions solve the original equation.
Try $y′ = ty$ with $y(0) = 1$. Plugging in $t = 0$ gives a zero rate at the starting point.
The solution is flat at the starting point. A constant $y = 1$ would also need zero rate at nearby times, but the right side would be $t$.
Dividing by an output factor can hide a constant solution. Check each zero of that factor in the original equation for a whole interval.

g.q: Does the zero rate at the start make $y = 1$ an equilibrium?
o: Yes, it stays at 1.
The rate must stay zero throughout an interval. Zero rate at a single point is insufficient.
No, only the starting slope is zero.
At other times the rate evaluated at $y = 1$ is $t$, so $y$ cannot stay at 1.

cards: In plain English: A carefully chosen multiplier turns a linear first-order equation into a product derivative.
Write the normalized equation as y′+p(t)y=q(t). Here all quantities are dimensionless and the prime denotes differentiation with respect to t.
An integrating factor is exp(∫p(t)dt). Multiplying the entire equation makes its left side the derivative of the factor times y.
Why it happens: the factor’s derivative supplies exactly the missing product-rule term.
title: Linear equations and integrating factors
plain: A carefully chosen multiplier turns a linear first-order equation into a product derivative.

qs.q: “Multiply the entire equation by the integrating factor.”
qs.ans: Turn the left side into a product derivative.
wrong: Multiply only the derivative term by that factor.
Multiply only the forcing term by that factor.
Use the negative exponent without checking the normalized sign.
qs.why: Partial multiplication changes the equation; the exponent sign follows the normalized coefficient.

qs.q: Solve dimensionless y′+2y=6 with y(0)=1. Evaluate y at t=ln(2)/2.
qs.why: The solution is y=3−2exp(−2t); the exponential is 1/2 at this time.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Equation with unit coefficient on the highest derivative
Specified input term independent of the unknown
qs.why: Integrating factor means multiplier producing a product derivative. Normalized equation means equation with unit coefficient on the highest derivative. Forcing means specified input term independent of the unknown.

qs.q: Order the integrating-factor method.
items: Normalize the coefficient of the derivative
Compute the exponential of the coefficient integral
Multiply the whole equation and integrate its product derivative
qs.why: Normalization determines the correct coefficient and sign.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for linear equations and integrating factors, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A first-order linear equation can have both a derivative term and a term proportional to the unknown.
A carefully chosen multiplier turns their sum into the derivative of [[a product]].
That multiplier is the **integrating factor**. Once the left side is a single derivative, integrate to recover the product.
Here $t$ is the input and $y′$ means $dy/dt$. To **normalize**, divide every term by the coefficient of $y′$ where that coefficient is nonzero.

p.cap: normalized form for dimensionless variables
vars: forcing, a given input independent of y

p.x: Dividing $2y′ − 4y = 6$ by $2$ gives $y′ − 2y = 3$. The coefficient $p(t)$ is $−2$.

g.q: After normalizing $2y′ − 4y = 6$, what is $p(t)$?
o: That is the coefficient before dividing the whole equation by 2.
Division by positive 2 keeps the negative sign.
Dividing the $y$ coefficient by 2 gives $−4/2 = −2$.

p.x: On an interval where the normalized coefficient $p(t)$ is continuous, build the integrating factor $μ$ by exponentiating an antiderivative of $p$.

p.cap: choose any one antiderivative of p

p.x: Multiply [[every term]] of $y′ + p(t)y = q(t)$ by $μ$. Since $μ′ = p(t)μ$, the product rule combines the two terms on the left.

p.cap: after multiplying both sides

p.x: Solve $y′ + 2y = 6$ with $y(0) = 1$. The integrating factor is $μ = exp(2t)$ because an antiderivative of $2$ is $2t$.
Multiply by $μ$ to get $(μy)′ = 6μ$. Integration gives $μy = 3μ + C$, where $C$ is a constant.
At $t = 0$, $μ = 1$ and $y = 1$, so $C = −2$. Divide by $μ$ to get $y = 3 − 2 exp(−2t)$.

cards: In plain English: Equation structure determines which transformation is valid.
An exact differential equation is the differential of a potential function; its solutions follow constant-potential sets.
A Bernoulli equation can become linear after a power substitution, with special zero solutions checked separately. Local uniqueness follows under suitable continuity and local Lipschitz conditions.
Why it happens: a valid substitution preserves dependencies, but singular transformations or insufficient regularity can lose solutions or uniqueness.
title: Exact equations, substitutions, and uniqueness
plain: Equation structure determines which transformation is valid.

qs.q: “The substitution is singular at zero.”
qs.ans: Check zero solutions in the original equation.
wrong: Assume the transformed equation covers every original input.
Assume singular substitution proves zero is impossible.
Declare uniqueness merely because a formula was obtained.
qs.why: Transformations can exclude valid solutions and a formula alone does not establish uniqueness.

qs.q: The exact dimensionless equation 2x dx+2y dy=0 has x²+y²=C. With x=3,y=4, find C.
qs.why: Substitution gives C=9+16=25.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Equation arising as a potential differential
Power transformation of a Bernoulli equation
One solution near the initial point under stated hypotheses
qs.why: Exact equation means equation arising as a potential differential. Bernoulli substitution means power transformation of a bernoulli equation. Local uniqueness means one solution near the initial point under stated hypotheses.

qs.q: Which existence claim is flawed?
lines: Check where the equation is defined
Check assumptions near the initial state
Check excluded cases after substitution
Assume continuity of the right side alone always guarantees uniqueness
qs.why: Continuity supports existence in common theorems, but uniqueness needs stronger conditions.
qs.ans: Assume continuity of the right side alone always guarantees uniqueness
wrong: Check where the equation is defined
Check assumptions near the initial state
Check excluded cases after substitution
