p.x: A **substitution** changes the variables or the way an equation is written. Here $t$ is the input and $y$ is the unknown. Can you recover $y$ from the new expression?
Both a positive and a negative value square to the same positive number. Squaring can lose information about the sign.
Inspect what a transformation preserves before using it to solve the equation.

g.q: If $y^2 = t$ for $t > 0$, which signs of $y$ are possible?
o: Only positive
The positive square root is one candidate. Its negative also squares to $t$.
Only negative
The negative root is one candidate. The positive root also squares to $t$.
Positive or negative
Squaring either sign of the square root gives the same $t$.

p.x: An **exact** equation has the form $dF = 0$. The differential $dF$ is the total change to first order in the **potential**, a single function $F$ of the variables.

Along a solution the potential stays constant, $F = C$. In the dimensionless example $2x dx + 2y dy = 0$, the potential is $F = x^2 + y^2$. Differentiate with respect to each coordinate while holding the other fixed to get $2x$ and $2y$.
The point $x = 3$, $y = 4$ fixes which constant-potential curve the solution follows.

p.cap: p and q depend only on the input; n is a constant other than 0 or 1

p.x: On an interval where the powers and their derivatives are defined and $y ≠ 0$, use the new unknown $u = y^{1−n}$.
The transformed equation is [[linear]]. The chain rule gives $u′ = (1−n)y^{−n}y′$.

p.cap: on the interval where the substitution is valid

p.x: If a substitution divides by $y$ or uses a power undefined at zero, test $y = 0$ in the original equation.
For $y′ = f(t,y)$, continuity of the right side $f$ near the starting point ensures local **existence**. A solution passes through that point on a short input interval.

For local **uniqueness**, a standard sufficient extra condition is that $f$ is locally Lipschitz in $y$. Near the initial point, differences in $f$ at the same $t$ are bounded by a fixed multiple of differences in $y$.
With these conditions there is exactly one solution near the starting point. Continuity alone can allow several.

cards: In plain English: Constant-coefficient equations turn exponential trial solutions into algebra.
For a linear constant-coefficient homogeneous equation, substituting an exponential turns derivatives into powers of its exponent rate.
Distinct real roots give independent exponentials; a repeated root needs a parameter-times-exponential solution; complex conjugate roots give exponential sine and cosine forms.
Why it happens: repeated roots cannot supply two independent copies of the same exponential, so an additional independent form is required.
title: Characteristic roots and homogeneous solutions
plain: Constant-coefficient equations turn exponential trial solutions into algebra.

qs.q: “That repeated root needs the extra time factor.”
qs.ans: Use a parameter-times-exponential second solution.
wrong: Use the same exponential twice with different constants.
Remove one initial condition because the root repeats.
Replace the repeated root by two arbitrary distinct roots.
qs.why: Duplicate solutions are dependent; the equation order and roots cannot be changed to compensate.

qs.q: For dimensionless y″−3y′+2y=0, find the larger characteristic root.
qs.why: The polynomial factors as (r−1)(r−2), so the larger root is 2.

qs.q: A constant-coefficient second-order homogeneous equation has a repeated real characteristic root r. Which pair is independent?
qs.ans: exp(rt) and t exp(rt)
wrong: exp(rt) and 2 exp(rt)
exp(rt) and −exp(rt)
t exp(rt) and 3t exp(rt)
qs.why: Multiplying one solution by t supplies the repeated-root companion. Each alternative pair contains only scalar multiples and is dependent.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Exponential rate solving the characteristic polynomial
Root occurring with multiplicity greater than one
qs.why: Characteristic root means exponential rate solving the characteristic polynomial. Homogeneous solution means solution with zero forcing. Repeated root means root occurring with multiplicity greater than one.

qs.q: Order a constant-coefficient homogeneous solution.
items: Fit constants using the initial data
qs.why: Multiplicity determines the independent basis functions.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for characteristic roots and homogeneous solutions, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A linear second-order equation adds terms in the unknown $y$, its first derivative $y′$ and its second derivative $y″$. Primes mean derivatives with respect to time $t$.
The equation is **homogeneous** when the forcing, the input on the right, is [[zero]].
For constant coefficients $a$, $b$ and $c$, with $a ≠ 0$, it has this form:

p.cap: fixed coefficients, no external input

p.x: Try $y = exp(rt)$, where $r$ is the trial rate. Differentiating once multiplies by $r$. Differentiating twice multiplies by $r^2$.

p.cap: after dividing out the nonzero exponential

p.x: A **characteristic root** is a rate $r$ that makes this polynomial zero. For $y″ − 3y′ + 2y = 0$, factor it like this:

p.cap: roots are 1 and 2 in this dimensionless example

p.x: Two distinct real roots give two **independent** exponentials. Neither is a constant multiple of the other.
A **repeated** root occurs more than once. With a repeated real root $r$, the independent pair is $exp(rt)$ and $t exp(rt)$.
Complex roots come in a conjugate pair: same real part $α$, opposite imaginary parts $±β$. Use a common envelope $exp(αt)$.
Multiply that envelope by $cos(βt)$ and $sin(βt)$ to get the two real solutions.

g.q: A real root $r$ repeats. Which function gives a second direction alongside $exp(rt)$?
o: $2 exp(rt)$
A fixed multiplier just rescales the same function.
$t exp(rt)$
The ratio to the first exponential is t, so it varies with time.

p.x: Suppose you give two copies of the same exponential separate constant weights.
Those weights appear only as their sum. There is just one freely adjustable coefficient.
Use an independent pair so both starting values, $y(0)$ and $y′(0)$, can be fitted.

g.q: How many independent weights do the two copies actually give you?
o: One weight
Only the sum of the weights changes the resulting exponential.
Two weights
Changing one weight and undoing that change in the other leaves the result identical.

cards: In plain English: A forced response combines a homogeneous family with one forced solution.
For a linear equation, the general solution is a homogeneous solution plus any one particular solution.

Undetermined coefficients guesses a forcing-related form when coefficients and forcing permit it. Overlap with the homogeneous solution requires multiplying the guess by sufficient powers of the independent variable.
Why it happens: the difference of any two particular solutions satisfies the homogeneous equation.
title: Particular solutions and superposition
plain: A forced response combines a homogeneous family with one forced solution.

qs.q: “The trial particular solution duplicates a homogeneous mode.”
qs.ans: Multiply the trial by enough powers of the input.
wrong: Keep the duplicate trial and divide its coefficient by zero.
Delete the homogeneous mode from the general solution.
Assume the forcing has no response because of the overlap.
qs.why: Overlap requires an independent trial form, not a singular coefficient or deletion of valid dynamics.

qs.q: For dimensionless y″+4y=8, find a constant particular solution.
qs.why: A constant has zero second derivative, leaving 4y=8.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One solution of the forced equation
Particular guess duplicating a homogeneous solution
qs.why: Particular solution means one solution of the forced equation. Superposition means addition of compatible linear responses. Trial overlap means particular guess duplicating a homogeneous solution.

qs.q: Which forced-solution claim is flawed?
lines: Find one valid particular solution
Retain the homogeneous family
Check trial overlap
Use linear superposition for every nonlinear equation
qs.why: Superposition generally fails for nonlinear equations.
qs.ans: Use linear superposition for every nonlinear equation
wrong: Find one valid particular solution
Retain the homogeneous family
Check trial overlap

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for particular solutions and superposition, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **particular solution** is any one function that solves the equation with its given input, also called forcing.
The **homogeneous family** is all the solutions obtained with the input set to zero.
Keep the same forcing and vary the freely adjustable part to match the starting values.
For a linear equation, [[add]] one particular solution to the homogeneous family to obtain the full family. This is **superposition**.

p.cap: linear equation with fixed forcing

p.x: For the dimensionless equation $y″ + 4y = 8$, try a constant. Its second derivative $y″$ is zero.
**Undetermined coefficients** tries a form like the forcing, then solves for its unknown weights. Use it with constant coefficients and inputs such as polynomials, exponentials or sinusoids.
If the trial overlaps a homogeneous mode, multiply the trial by a power of time. The power equals the multiplicity of the overlapping root.
For a simple root (one copy), one factor of $t$ moves the trial outside the homogeneous family.

g.q: The forcing is $exp(t)$ and its rate is a simple root. Which trial can work? $A$ is a weight to fit.
o: $A exp(t)$
The differential equation sends that homogeneous mode to zero for any A.
$A t exp(t)$
The extra factor of t makes differentiation produce a term proportional to the input.

p.x: Take two particular solutions of the same linear equation with the same input. To find how they differ, [[subtract]] one from the other.
The two copies of the input cancel. Their difference satisfies the zero-input equation.
Each choice of particular solution gives the same full family once all homogeneous solutions are included.

cards: In plain English: Forced oscillations combine startup behavior with ongoing excitation.
Damping removes energy from an oscillatory system. A stable transient decays, leaving a steady forced response when the input persists.
Undamped sinusoidal forcing at the natural frequency can cause secular growth. Damping changes the response and limits steady resonance amplification in the linear model.
Why it happens: resonant forcing can repeatedly add energy in phase with motion, while damping dissipates it.
title: Damping, resonance, and transient response
plain: Forced oscillations combine startup behavior with ongoing excitation.

qs.q: “Separate the decaying transient from the steady response.”
qs.ans: Separate initial and persistent forced motion.
wrong: Discard the forcing when describing the final response.
Assume every transient vanishes instantaneously at startup.
Assume resonance requires zero damping in every system.
qs.why: The long-time response retains forcing; transients take time to decay, and damped resonance remains possible.

qs.q: For dimensionless y″+4y=0, find the angular natural frequency.
qs.why: The standard coefficient is angular frequency squared, so its value is 2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Term with growth multiplying an oscillatory or modal factor
qs.why: Transient means response associated with initial adjustment. Steady forced response means persistent response to ongoing excitation. Secular term means term with growth multiplying an oscillatory or modal factor.

qs.q: Order a linear forced-response analysis.
items: Apply initial conditions to the total response
qs.why: Initial data apply to the sum, not just the homogeneous part.

demoNeeded: Compare undamped resonant growth with damped forced oscillations and transient decay.

p.x: A **transient** is the part of the motion that adjusts to the initial conditions. The **steady forced response** is the part sustained by a continuing input.
For a linear model, find the free motion with zero input and one particular response to the input.
Match the initial position and velocity to the sum, then separate the decaying and persistent parts if the system is stable.
**Damping** takes mechanical energy out of the oscillation. A viscous damper pushes against the velocity.
With stable damped motion, the transient [[decays]] after startup.
The free part tends to zero. If a sinusoidal input keeps driving the system, its steady oscillation remains.
The **angular natural frequency** $ω_0$ is the oscillation rate with no damping and no forcing. Time is $t$ and $y″$ is the second time derivative of $y$.

p.cap: undamped free motion

p.x: If the coefficient of $y$ is $4$ in a dimensionless equation, match it to $ω_0^2$.
Drive an undamped system at its natural frequency and the amplitude can grow with time. A growing factor multiplying an oscillation is a **secular term**.
Resonant forcing can add energy cycle after cycle when its push is in step with the velocity.
With positive damping, amplitude approaches a finite steady value under constant-amplitude sinusoidal forcing. The damper dissipates the energy added over each steady cycle.
A damped linear oscillator can still have a resonance peak. Its steady amplitude stays finite.

g.q: Add positive damping to a linear oscillator driven at its undamped natural frequency. What happens to the amplitude over time?
o: It grows without bound.
That needs the undamped case. Energy loss grows as the motion grows.
It settles to a finite value.
Dissipation balances the input energy over each steady cycle.

cards: In plain English: Known independent homogeneous solutions can construct responses to more general forcing.
Variation of parameters replaces homogeneous constants by functions and solves for their derivatives.
The Wronskian determinant tests independence for solutions of a regular linear equation. A nonzero value at one point implies independence throughout the regular interval.
Why it happens: independent homogeneous solutions form directions that can be combined with varying weights to reproduce forcing.
title: Variation of parameters and independence
plain: Known independent homogeneous solutions can construct responses to more general forcing.

qs.q: “The fundamental solutions must be independent.”
qs.ans: Check a nonzero Wronskian on the regular interval.
wrong: Use two identical solutions with different names instead.
Assume any two arbitrary functions solve the homogeneous equation.
Treat a zero Wronskian for arbitrary functions as a universal dependence proof.
qs.why: The method needs actual independent solutions; Wronskian equivalences require the linear-ODE setting.

qs.q: For dimensionless homogeneous solutions y1=exp(t), y2=exp(2t), evaluate W=y1 y2′−y1′ y2 at t=0.
qs.why: At zero the values are both 1 and derivatives are 1 and 2, giving W=1.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Determinant formed from functions and their derivatives
Independent homogeneous solutions spanning the family
Forcing method using variable homogeneous weights
qs.why: Wronskian means determinant formed from functions and their derivatives. Fundamental solutions means independent homogeneous solutions spanning the family. Variation of parameters means forcing method using variable homogeneous weights.

qs.q: Which variation-of-parameters setup is flawed?
lines: Normalize the differential equation
Use homogeneous solutions on a regular interval
Check their independence
Use the same homogeneous solution twice as a fundamental pair
qs.why: A dependent pair cannot span the second-order homogeneous solution space.
qs.ans: Use the same homogeneous solution twice as a fundamental pair
wrong: Normalize the differential equation
Use homogeneous solutions on a regular interval
Check their independence

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for variation of parameters and independence, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Two **fundamental solutions** $y_1$ and $y_2$ solve the zero-input equation. They are independent, so constant weights can combine them to make any homogeneous solution.
First **normalize** the forced equation: divide by the coefficient of the highest derivative so that coefficient becomes one.
Work on a **regular interval**, where that division is valid and the resulting coefficients and input are continuous.
**Variation of parameters** lets the weights $u_1$ and $u_2$ in a homogeneous combination [[vary with time]].

p.cap: normalized linear equation with forcing

p.x: Primes are time derivatives. Solve for the weight derivatives using input $f(t)$, then integrate the weights.
The **Wronskian** $W$ is a determinant that compares the function values and slopes of the pair. A prime is a time derivative.

p.cap: two solutions of the same regular homogeneous equation

p.x: To test the pair, try $y_1 = exp(t)$ and $y_2 = exp(2t)$ at $t = 0$.
A regular interval may contain points where an individual solution crosses zero. The method needs the pair to supply two independent directions for matching the forcing.
You can start at any point in that interval if the pair has a nonzero Wronskian at one point. The determinant stays nonzero throughout.
This guarantee uses two solutions of the same regular linear homogeneous equation. A zero determinant at a point can occur for arbitrary independent functions.

g.q: Your fundamental pair has a nonzero Wronskian at one point. Where can you start matching the forcing?
o: Only at the checked point.
For this equation the determinant stays nonzero as you move along the interval.
Anywhere in that regular interval.
Regular linear evolution preserves the pair's independence throughout that interval.

cards: In plain English: A transform turns differentiation into algebra while carrying initial conditions.
The unilateral Laplace transform integrates a function times a decaying exponential over nonnegative input time, where the integral converges.
The transform of a first derivative is transform variable times the function transform minus its initial value.
Why it happens: integration by parts transfers the derivative to the exponential kernel and leaves an initial boundary term.
title: Laplace transforms and initial values
plain: A transform turns differentiation into algebra while carrying initial conditions.

qs.q: “The initial-value term is missing from the transform.”
qs.ans: Retain the boundary contribution from differentiation.
wrong: Set every initial value to zero without justification.
Transform derivatives by multiplying only and ignoring boundaries.
Add the initial value with the wrong sign automatically.
qs.why: The unilateral derivative transform includes a specific subtractive initial term.

qs.q: For dimensionless transform variable s=2, evaluate the Laplace transform 1/s of the constant function 1.
qs.why: The transform is 1/s for positive s, giving 1/2.

qs.q: For unilateral Laplace transforms, Y(s) denotes the transform of y(t). What is the transform of y′(t)?
qs.ans: sY(s)−y(0)
wrong: sY(s)+y(0)
sY(s)
qs.why: Integration by parts gives the subtractive initial boundary term. The alternatives reverse its sign, omit it, or use an integration-like division.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Integral representation using a decaying exponential kernel
Variable replacing the original independent variable
qs.why: Laplace transform means integral representation using a decaying exponential kernel. Transform variable means variable replacing the original independent variable. Initial boundary term means initial-value contribution in derivative transforms.

qs.q: Order a Laplace initial-value solution.
items: Transform the equation including initial terms
Solve algebraically for the unknown transform
qs.why: Initial conditions are built into the transformed algebra.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for laplace transforms and initial values, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An initial-value problem gives a differential equation and starting values. The **Laplace transform** replaces each time function with an integral representation.
For a linear equation with constant coefficients, solve [[algebraically]] for the transform.
To **invert** is to recover the original function of time from its transform.
**Unilateral** means the integral uses only nonnegative time. For real positive $s$, the exponential weight decays.

p.cap: where the integral converges

p.x: For $y(t) = 1$ and real $s > 0$, the integral gives $Y(s) = 1/s$. In dimensionless time, $s = 2$ gives $0.500$.
To transform the first derivative $y′(t)$, take $Y(s)$ times $s$ and include a term from the starting value $y(0)$. The symbol $ℒ$ means take the transform.

p.cap: both transforms converge and the upper endpoint term vanishes

p.x: The starting value appears with a minus sign.

g.q: The upper endpoint contributes zero. How does the starting value enter the derivative transform?
o: It is added.
The endpoint at the start is the lower endpoint, so it is subtracted.
It is subtracted.
An endpoint difference is upper minus lower. At the start the exponential weight is one.

p.x: Integration by parts moves the derivative from $y(t)$ to the exponential weight $e^{−st}$, also called the **kernel**.
The derivative of the weight brings down $−s$. The minus sign in integration by parts changes this to the $+sY(s)$ term.
The **initial boundary term** comes from subtracting the lower endpoint. The weight there is one, so the term is $−y(0)$.

cards: In plain English: A delayed input must shift both its activation and its internal time.
A unit step switches from zero to one at its activation point. A shifted response often includes a step multiplied by a function of shifted time.
The time-delay transform rule uses the function evaluated at time minus the delay, not an unshifted copy.
Why it happens: a delayed process starts its internal clock when it activates.
title: Steps, shifts, and piecewise forcing
plain: A delayed input must shift both its activation and its internal time.

qs.q: “Shift the waveform as well as the step.”
qs.ans: Use elapsed time since activation inside the function.
wrong: Use the original time inside every delayed waveform.
Shift only the amplitude and leave activation unchanged.
Remove the step because the waveform was shifted.
qs.why: A delay changes activation and internal time; neither amplitude changes nor an ungated shift represents it generally.

qs.q: For dimensionless g(t)=u(t−2)(t−2)², where u is the unit step, evaluate g(5).
qs.why: The step is active and elapsed time is 3, giving 9.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Function activating at a specified input
Shift of activation and internal time
Input described by different formulas on different intervals
qs.why: Unit step means function activating at a specified input. Delay means shift of activation and internal time. Piecewise forcing means input described by different formulas on different intervals.

qs.q: Which delayed-input expression is flawed for a quadratic starting from zero at t=2?
lines: Use a step activated at two
Use elapsed time t−2 inside the quadratic
Keep the input zero before activation
Use u(t−2)t² as the delayed zero-start quadratic
qs.why: At activation that expression jumps to four instead of beginning at zero.
qs.ans: Use u(t−2)t² as the delayed zero-start quadratic
wrong: Use a step activated at two
Use elapsed time t−2 inside the quadratic
Keep the input zero before activation

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for steps, shifts, and piecewise forcing, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A forcing is an input to a differential equation. If the input changes rule when a switch flips, describe it [[piece by piece]].
**Piecewise forcing** uses a different formula on each time interval. Before a delayed input starts, its contribution is zero.
When the delayed input starts, read its waveform by elapsed time since activation.
The **unit step** $u$ is zero before its argument reaches zero and one after. Use $u(t−a)$ to place the switch at delay $a$ on the time axis $t$.
For an original waveform $f$, multiply $f(t−a)$ by the step to turn it off before activation.
At transform variable $s$, let $F(s)$ represent the original $f(t)$ and $G(s)$ the waveform after delay $a$.
In transform space, a delay [[multiplies]] the original transform by an exponential factor.

p.cap: for a nonnegative delay $a$ and a convergent transform

p.x: The step starts the input at $t = a$. The argument $t−a$ starts the waveform's clock there.
Consider a dimensionless quadratic input $g(t)$ meant to start from zero when $t = 2$. Someone writes $u(t−2)t^2$.
The unshifted square makes the input jump to $4$ as the step switches on. Shift the clock inside the square too.

p.cap: zero before the switch, elapsed time inside the square

g.q: Just after the switch, what value does the expression with the unshifted square approach?
o: The value would approach zero if the square used elapsed time. Here the square still uses clock time.
The step is one just after it activates, and clock time tends to two.

cards: In plain English: A linear system’s response to arbitrary input can be assembled from its response to brief impulses.
An ideal impulse has unit integral and represents a concentrated input in the distributional sense; it is not an ordinary finite-height function.
For a causal linear time-invariant system with zero initial state, convolution combines the impulse response with the input history.
Why it happens: linearity adds responses to individual input pieces, and time invariance shifts each piece’s response.
title: Impulses and convolution
plain: A linear system’s response to arbitrary input can be assembled from its response to brief impulses.

qs.q: “Use convolution for the zero-state response.”
qs.ans: Combine delayed impulse responses weighted by the input.
wrong: Multiply input and impulse response pointwise instead.
Ignore the earlier input history entirely.
Apply the same convolution rule to every nonlinear system.
qs.why: Convolution accumulates history; pointwise multiplication and unrestricted nonlinear use are different operations.

qs.q: For dimensionless h(t)=exp(−t) and unit-step input, the zero-state response is 1−exp(−t). Evaluate it at t=ln(2).
qs.why: The exponential is 1/2, so the response is 1/2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Zero-state response to a unit impulse
qs.why: Impulse response means zero-state response to a unit impulse. Convolution means history-weighted superposition integral. Zero-state response means response with zero initial state.

qs.q: Order a convolution setup for a causal linear time-invariant system.
items: Identify the impulse response and input
Shift the impulse response by the integration variable
Multiply by the input history and integrate over the causal interval
qs.why: Superposition accumulates the contribution of every earlier input piece.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for impulses and convolution, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: The **initial state** is the set of starting values needed to predict the system's motion. A **zero-state response** starts with all of them at zero.
An **impulse response** is the zero-state response to a unit impulse, an input concentrated at an instant with area one.
For a linear system, responses to separate input contributions can be [[added together]].
Add two inputs and you get the sum of their individual responses.
Approximate the impulse by a short rectangular pulse. Keep its area at one while making its width $w$ smaller.

p.cap: rectangular pulse with unit area

p.x: Halving the width doubles the height. In the zero-width limit the ideal impulse is a **distribution**, an object defined through integrals rather than a finite height at one point.

g.q: Keeping area fixed, what happens to the pulse height if you halve its width?
o: It halves.
Height and width multiply to give area. Halving both would shrink the area.
It doubles.
Height must double to offset the width being cut in half.

p.x: **Causal** means no response before the input. **Time-invariant** means delaying an input delays its response by the same amount.

p.cap: causal, linear, time-invariant system starting at rest

p.x: **Convolution** adds up responses weighted by past inputs.
Time invariance lets you shift the same response to every input time. Linearity lets you scale and add all those responses. That sum is called **superposition**.
With a unit step, every past contribution has weight one. Integrating the shifted exponential gives $y(t) = 1−e^{−t}$.

cards: In plain English: Transform-domain formulas describe input-output behavior under stated initial conditions.
A transfer function is output transform divided by input transform for a linear time-invariant model with zero initial conditions.
Poles correspond to denominator roots after algebraic cancellation in the input-output representation. Hidden internal modes can remain despite cancellation.
Why it happens: an unobservable or uncontrollable internal mode may disappear from one input-output transfer without disappearing from the state dynamics.
title: Transfer functions, poles, and cancellation
plain: Transform-domain formulas describe input-output behavior under stated initial conditions.

qs.q: “The canceled pole does not prove the internal mode is harmless.”
qs.ans: Check internal dynamics as well as the transfer function.
wrong: Assume every canceled mode has vanished from the system.
Infer internal stability from one reduced transfer alone always.
Treat a canceled unstable mode as a stable pole automatically.
qs.why: Algebraic cancellation can hide internal behavior rather than remove or stabilize it.

qs.q: For dimensionless transfer H(s)=2/(s+4), find the zero-frequency gain H(0).
qs.why: Substitution gives 2/4=0.5.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Singularity associated with a denominator root
Behavior present in the underlying state dynamics
qs.why: Transfer function means zero-state input-output transform ratio. Pole means singularity associated with a denominator root. Internal mode means behavior present in the underlying state dynamics.

qs.q: Which transfer-function claim is flawed?

Check denominator roots

Check denominator roots
Distinguish internal and input-output behavior

p.x: A model maps an input to an output. The **transform domain** describes both using their Laplace transforms.
For a linear, time-invariant model starting at rest, the input and output transforms are connected [[algebraically]].
Multiply the input transform by a function of the transform variable to get the output transform.

p.x: The **zero-frequency gain** is $H(0)$ when it is finite. Take the dimensionless example $H(s) = 2/(s+4)$.
A **pole** is a point where a transfer function grows without bound nearby. To locate poles of a ratio of polynomials, check its denominator roots.
In a dimensionless example, the numerator is $s−1$ and the denominator is $(s−1)(s+2)$. They share a factor.
Cancel the shared factor first. Only the remaining denominator root is a pole of this input-output transfer.

p.cap: the remaining pole is at $s = −2$

g.q: Which denominator root survives as a pole of this transfer?
o: The numerator shares the factor that vanishes here, so it cancels.
The factor that vanishes here has no matching numerator factor.

p.x: An **internal mode** is a natural pattern of growth, decay or oscillation in the system's state.
A mode is **uncontrollable** from an input if that input cannot excite it. It is **unobservable** from an output if its motion never shows in that output.
Either condition can hide a mode from the transfer. A hidden mode can still grow from an initial disturbance in the state.
Check the state dynamics for internal stability: do all natural responses to small initial disturbances stay small?

cards: In plain English: Higher-order equations can be rewritten as coupled first-order equations.
A state contains enough information to determine future evolution with the input. Introduce successive derivatives as separate state components.
A scalar second-order equation typically becomes two first-order equations. The state dimension differs from the number of measured outputs.
Why it happens: storing the function and its first derivative allows the highest derivative law to advance both quantities.
title: First-order state systems
plain: Higher-order equations can be rewritten as coupled first-order equations.

qs.q: “Position alone is not the full second-order state.”
qs.ans: Include velocity as another state component.
wrong: Replace velocity by an arbitrary output label.
Assume one measured output means one state always.
Remove a state because two equations are inconvenient.
qs.why: State information is determined by dynamics, not output count or notation convenience.

qs.q: For dimensionless y″+3y′+2y=0, let x1=y and x2=y′. At x1=1,x2=2, find x2′.
qs.why: The second state equation is x2′=−3x2−2x1, giving −8.

qs.q: For a scalar second-order equation, which standard two-component state retains both initial data?
qs.ans: The function and its first derivative.
wrong: The function listed twice as separate coordinates.
The first derivative listed twice as separate coordinates.
The function and an arbitrary constant label.
qs.why: Function and first derivative provide independent initial data. Duplicates or an unrelated label do not encode the required state.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: First-order evolution law for state variables
qs.why: State means information sufficient for future evolution. State dimension means number of independent state coordinates. State equation means first-order evolution law for state variables.

qs.q: Order a second-order-to-state conversion.
items: Define the first state as the original function
Define the second state as its derivative
Write the two first-order derivative equations
qs.why: The original second derivative supplies the second state equation.

p.x: The **order** of a differential equation is the highest derivative it contains. A first-order equation uses only first derivatives and undifferentiated quantities.
Each rate now has a first-order equation. The equations are **coupled** when one rate depends on another state component, a coordinate of the state.
A **state** is the set of quantities you need to [[predict]] what happens next, given the model and the input.
Take the original function and its successive derivatives up to, but excluding, the highest one. Each becomes a **state component**, one coordinate of the state.
A **state equation** gives a component's rate of change from the current state, time and any input.
**State dimension** counts independent state coordinates. A **measured output** is a quantity you observe, such as the position of a cart.
Measuring only position can leave velocity unobserved. A second-order model uses both position and velocity, giving two first-order equations.

g.q: A moving cart has one position sensor. Can its state have more coordinates than its measured output?
o: Yes, the state can be larger.
The sensor reports position. Velocity can still be needed to predict motion.
No, the dimensions must match.
The number of sensor readings doesn't determine how many quantities the model needs.

p.x: Let $y$ be a dimensionless position, $x_1=y$ and $x_2=y′$. A prime means a derivative with respect to time.

p.cap: dimensionless model, no input
the second rate is $x_2′ = −3x_2 − 2x_1$

cards: In plain English: Linear systems evolve as combinations of modes.
An eigenvector of a constant state matrix identifies a direction with exponential evolution at its eigenvalue rate.
All eigenvalues with negative real parts imply asymptotic stability for a finite-dimensional continuous-time linear system. Zero real parts require further analysis.
Why it happens: the real part controls exponential growth or decay; imaginary parts create oscillation.
title: Eigenmodes and linear stability
plain: Linear systems evolve as combinations of modes.

qs.q: “Negative real parts make the modes decay.”
qs.ans: All linear modes decay asymptotically.
wrong: Positive imaginary parts alone force exponential growth.
Zero real parts always guarantee asymptotic decay.
Negative real parts imply every state is identically zero.
qs.why: Oscillation is not growth, zero real parts are inconclusive for decay, and stable states may still have transients.

qs.q: For dimensionless diagonal system x′=diag(−2,−5)x, find the slower-decaying mode’s positive time constant.
qs.why: The slower rate is −2, corresponding to exp(−2t) and time constant 1/2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: State pattern evolving at an eigenvalue rate
Part controlling exponential envelope growth or decay
qs.why: Eigenmode means state pattern evolving at an eigenvalue rate. Real part means part controlling exponential envelope growth or decay. Asymptotic stability means nearby states converge to equilibrium.

qs.q: Which linear stability claim is flawed?
lines: Inspect eigenvalue real parts
Distinguish oscillation from growth
Check zero-real-part cases separately
Declare asymptotic stability whenever all real parts are nonpositive
qs.why: Zero real parts can produce persistent or growing motion, especially with defective modes.
qs.ans: Declare asymptotic stability whenever all real parts are nonpositive
wrong: Inspect eigenvalue real parts
Distinguish oscillation from growth
Check zero-real-part cases separately

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for eigenmodes and linear stability, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **mode** is a natural pattern of motion. In a linear system without input, adding solutions gives another solution.

p.cap: constant coefficients, no input
vars: state vector, the list of state coordinates

p.x: If you can build any initial state by adding scaled modes, evolve those modes separately and add their results.
An **eigenvector** $v$ is a nonzero vector that $A$ scales by a single number, its **eigenvalue** $λ$.

p.cap: for an eigenvector of the constant state matrix

p.x: An **eigenmode** starting at $v$ evolves by scaling that vector [[exponentially]].

p.cap: time $t$ measured from the start, with no input

p.x: The **real part** of a complex number is its component without the imaginary unit $i$, where $i^2=−1$. For a real number, it is the whole number.
An equilibrium is a state that stays fixed. It is **asymptotically stable** if nearby starts stay close and converge to it.
When every eigenvalue has a negative real part, the zero state is asymptotically stable. Any positive real part gives instability.
If no real parts are positive but one is zero, not every nearby start decays to zero. Check whether motion persists or grows.

g.q: A constant-matrix system has no input. Every eigenvalue has negative real part. What happens near zero?
o: The state converges to zero.
Every mode decays. Oscillations or polynomial factors from repeated roots do not prevent eventual decay.
The state keeps moving away.
This confuses negative real parts with positive ones. Negative real parts make the exponential envelope shrink.

p.x: The real part of a mode's eigenvalue sets its exponential growth or decay. The imaginary part gives the rate of oscillation, if present.
A decaying mode's **time constant** $τ$ is how long its exponential envelope takes to fall to $exp(−1)$ of its starting amplitude.

p.cap: real eigenvalue $λ<0$; time and rate dimensionless here

g.q: For two modes with real eigenvalues −2 and −5, which takes longer to reach the same fraction of its starting amplitude?
o: The −2 mode
The decay rate has smaller magnitude, so the time constant is larger.
The −5 mode
The more negative rate makes the exponential fall faster.

cards: In plain English: A local matrix model can describe behavior near an equilibrium.
An equilibrium makes every state derivative zero. The Jacobian of the vector field gives a local linearization there.
If the linearization is hyperbolic, eigenvalue real parts classify local stability. Zero real parts make the linearized test inconclusive.
Why it happens: nonzero exponential growth or decay dominates higher-order terms locally, while neutral directions leave those terms decisive.
title: Nonlinear equilibria and linearization
plain: A local matrix model can describe behavior near an equilibrium.

qs.q: “The zero eigenvalue makes this linearized verdict inconclusive.”
qs.ans: Analyze higher-order terms or use another method.
wrong: Declare asymptotic stability from the zero eigenvalue alone.
Declare instability from the zero eigenvalue alone.
Delete the neutral direction from the original dynamics.
qs.why: Neutral linear behavior does not determine nonlinear stability, and the state direction still exists.

qs.q: For dimensionless y′=y−y², evaluate the derivative of the right side at equilibrium y=1.
qs.why: The derivative is 1−2y, equal to −1; this equilibrium is locally attracting.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Equilibrium with no zero-real-part linearized eigenvalues
qs.why: Equilibrium means state with zero evolution rate. Linearization means jacobian-based local approximation. Hyperbolic equilibrium means equilibrium with no zero-real-part linearized eigenvalues.

qs.q: Order nonlinear equilibrium analysis.
items: Solve for states with zero derivative
Evaluate the Jacobian at each equilibrium
Classify nonneutral eigenvalues and investigate neutral cases
qs.why: The local test is applied separately at each equilibrium.

demoNeeded: Show a nonlinear phase portrait beside its local linearization at a selected equilibrium.

p.x: A **nonlinear** state equation can have rates that curve with the state, so one constant matrix cannot describe the whole system.
An **equilibrium** is a state where every rate is zero. A linear model there describes the motion of [[nearby]] states.
This approximation uses the slopes at that equilibrium. Farther away, the slopes can change enough to give different motion.
The **vector field** gives the rate at each state. Its **Jacobian** is the matrix of slopes of each rate with respect to each state coordinate.
Evaluating those slopes at an equilibrium gives the **linearization**, a first-order model for a small displacement from that equilibrium.

p.cap: one dimensionless state $y$ with rate $y′=F(y)$; $F(1)=0$

p.x: Here $F′$ is the slope with respect to $y$. The negative slope makes a small displacement decay.
For smooth rates, examine the eigenvalues of the Jacobian at the equilibrium. The equilibrium is **hyperbolic** if none has zero real part.
One positive real part makes the equilibrium unstable. Decay in other directions cannot remove the growing direction.
If all real parts are negative, small displacements decay back to the equilibrium: it is locally asymptotically stable.

g.q: Near an equilibrium, one linear mode grows exponentially and the others decay. Is the nonlinear equilibrium stable?
o: It is stable.
Decay in most directions is insufficient. A growing direction lets some nearby states leave.
It is unstable.
The growing mode dominates small displacements along that direction.

p.x: A **neutral direction** has zero eigenvalue real part, so its linear mode gives no exponential growth or decay.
With a neutral direction and no positive real parts, the linearized stability test is [[inconclusive]].
Both rates below have zero slope at the equilibrium $y=0$, but the higher powers of $y$ drive opposite motion.

cards: In plain English: A matrix exponential propagates an entire linear state.
The matrix exponential solves homogeneous constant-matrix state equations. It is a matrix power series, not elementwise exponentiation.
A forced solution adds a convolution-like matrix integral to the propagated initial state.
Why it happens: differentiating the matrix power series reproduces multiplication by the state matrix.
title: Matrix exponentials and forced systems
plain: A matrix exponential propagates an entire linear state.

qs.q: “That must be a matrix exponential, not elementwise exp.”
qs.ans: Use the matrix power-series operator.
wrong: Exponentiate each matrix entry independently in every case.
Apply the scalar exponential only to the determinant.
Replace the exponential by the matrix multiplied by time.
qs.why: Entrywise exponentiation, determinant substitution, and first-order truncation do not generally solve the system exactly.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=diag(−1,−2), find the first diagonal entry of exp(A t) at t=ln(2).
qs.why: Diagonal matrices exponentiate their diagonal entries, giving exp(−t)=1/2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Power-series exponential of a square matrix
Map propagating a linear homogeneous state
qs.why: Matrix exponential means power-series exponential of a square matrix. State transition means map propagating a linear homogeneous state. Forced response integral means accumulated propagated input contributions.

qs.q: Which state-propagation claim is flawed?
lines: Use a square state matrix
Propagate the initial state
Include input history for a forced response
Use elementwise exponentiation for every nondiagonal matrix
qs.why: General matrix powers couple entries, so elementwise exponentiation is incorrect.
qs.ans: Use elementwise exponentiation for every nondiagonal matrix
wrong: Use a square state matrix
Propagate the initial state
Include input history for a forced response

p.x: The **matrix exponential** maps the whole initial state through time when the state matrix is constant and there is no input.

vars: constant square matrix of rate coefficients

p.cap: starts at time zero, with $x′=Ax$

p.x: The **state transition** is the map $exp(At)$ that propagates the initial state.
The scalar exponential has a **power series**, an infinite sum built from successive powers. A square matrix $B$ can take the scalar's place, even with nonzero entries off its main diagonal.
Build powers by **matrix multiplication**. Exponentiating entries separately skips the coupling between coordinates.

p.cap: $B=At$; $I$ is the identity matrix, which leaves a vector unchanged

p.x: Each positive power is divided by the factorial of its exponent: multiply the positive integers up to that exponent.

g.q: How should you build the matrix powers in that series?
o: Power each entry separately.
That loses the products between entries that describe how coordinates are coupled.
Multiply the matrix by itself.
Each higher power is the previous matrix power times the original matrix.

p.x: A **forced** system has rate $Ax+u(t)$, with constant $A$. Input $u(s)$ at time $s$ propagates for $t−s$.
Find the state by [[adding]] the input response to the propagated initial state.
Integrate $g(s)$ from $0$ to $t$ to get the input response $r(t)$.

p.cap: $x_0$ is the state at time zero

p.x: Differentiate $exp(At)$ term by term. Each time power drops by one, leaving a factor of $A$ times the original series.

p.cap: constant state matrix $A$

cards: In plain English: Numerical solvers advance a differential equation using sampled rates.
Forward Euler adds step size times the current derivative to the current state. Its global error is first order under suitable regularity.
Runge–Kutta methods sample several intermediate rates. Classical RK4 has fourth-order global accuracy for sufficiently smooth problems with suitable steps.
Why it happens: extra rate samples capture variation across the step that a single initial derivative misses.
title: Euler and Runge–Kutta stepping
plain: Numerical solvers advance a differential equation using sampled rates.

qs.q: “The rate changes significantly within this step.”
qs.ans: Use a smaller step or a suitable higher-order method.
wrong: Assume the first sampled derivative stays exact throughout.
Increase the step until the changing rate disappears.
Treat formal accuracy order as a guarantee for every step.
qs.why: A varying rate invalidates the constant-rate approximation; large steps and formal order alone do not ensure accuracy.

qs.q: For dimensionless y′=y, start at y=1 and take one forward Euler step of size 0.1. Find the next y.
qs.why: Euler gives ynew=1+0.1(1)=1.1.

qs.q: Forward Euler for y′=f(t,y) uses step h from current (t,y). Which update is correct?
qs.ans: ynew=y+h f(t,y)
wrong: ynew=y−h f(t,y)
ynew=h f(t,y)
ynew=y+f(t,y)/h
qs.why: Euler adds the local rate times the step. The distractors reverse time direction, drop the old value, or invert the step scaling.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One-step update using the initial rate
Step method combining intermediate rate samples
Accumulated solution error over the interval
qs.why: Forward Euler means one-step update using the initial rate. Runge–Kutta method means step method combining intermediate rate samples. Global error means accumulated solution error over the interval.

qs.q: Order one forward Euler step.
items: Evaluate the derivative at the current state
Multiply by the chosen step size
Add that increment to the current state
qs.why: Euler extrapolates using the initial local rate.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for euler and runge–kutta stepping, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A differential equation can give you a rate of change even when you don't have a formula for the state.
A numerical solver samples that rate to [[estimate]] the state at the next time.
Use the new state to start the next step. The steps build an approximate solution.
**Forward Euler** uses the rate $f(t,y)$ at the current time $t$ and state $y$. Let $h$ be the step size.

p.cap: use the rate at the start of the step

p.x: Try the dimensionless equation $y′ = y$, starting at $y = 1$ with $h = 0.1$.
**Global error** is the gap from the exact solution after many steps. Euler is first order: for a smooth problem on a fixed interval, small enough steps give error that scales with $h$.
Multistage **Runge–Kutta** methods combine rate samples from several stages within a step. Classical **RK4** uses four stages.
For a smooth problem on the same time interval, RK4's global error falls faster as the step shrinks.
Euler's global error scales with $h$ and RK4's with $h^4$ when steps are sufficiently small and rounding is negligible.

g.q: As you halve already small steps, which method's global error shrinks by a larger factor?
o: Euler
Euler samples the initial rate only. For small steps its global error scales with the first power of the step size.
RK4
The fourth power of the step size shrinks faster than the first power.

p.x: Suppose the true rate of a state keeps rising during a forward time step. Euler carries the starting rate across the entire step.
The starting rate is below all later rates, so Euler predicts a smaller change than the true one.
More samples can capture how the rate changes within a step. With Euler you can shorten the step so its single rate stays representative.

g.q: How does this one Euler step compare with the true change?
o: It underestimates the change
The initial rate is below the average rate over the step.
It overestimates the change
That would happen if the starting rate were above the average, as with a rate that keeps falling.

cards: In plain English: A solver can need small steps for stability even when the visible solution changes slowly.
Adaptive solvers estimate local error and adjust step size against absolute and relative tolerances.
Stiff equations contain rapidly decaying modes that can impose severe explicit-method stability restrictions. Implicit methods can permit larger stable steps.
Why it happens: numerical amplification can grow a mode that the true differential equation damps. Accuracy and stability are separate requirements.
title: Adaptive steps and stiffness
plain: A solver can need small steps for stability even when the visible solution changes slowly.

qs.q: “The fast mode is gone physically but still limits explicit steps.”
qs.ans: This is a stiffness-related stability restriction.
wrong: The disappearing mode removes every numerical stability limit.
Tighter error tolerance always eliminates stiffness itself.
Any stable implicit step is automatically accurate.
qs.why: The discrete method still sees fast modes; tolerances do not alter the equation, and stability does not imply accuracy.

qs.q: For dimensionless y′=−10y, forward Euler has multiplier 1−10h. At h=0.15, find the multiplier.
qs.why: The multiplier is −0.5, whose magnitude is below one, so this test mode decays numerically.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Fast modes severely restricting explicit stable steps
Allowed error scale near small states
Allowed error scaled to state magnitude
qs.why: Stiffness means fast modes severely restricting explicit stable steps. Absolute tolerance means allowed error scale near small states. Relative tolerance means allowed error scaled to state magnitude.

qs.q: Which solver claim is flawed?
lines: Check stability as well as accuracy
Use tolerances appropriate to variable scales
Consider implicit methods for stiff systems
Assume an implicit method permits arbitrarily large accurate steps
qs.why: Implicit stability advantages do not remove accuracy requirements.
qs.ans: Assume an implicit method permits arbitrarily large accurate steps
wrong: Check stability as well as accuracy
Use tolerances appropriate to variable scales
Consider implicit methods for stiff systems

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for adaptive steps and stiffness, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: One solution can have both a slow trend and a **fast mode**, a component that decays much faster than the rest.
Even after the fast mode nearly disappears, an **explicit method** can still need short steps to keep errors in that mode from growing. Explicit methods use rates from values already known.
**Stability** here means a decaying component also decays in the numerical update.

g.q: Only the slow trend is visible now. Can the fast component still place a limit on the step?
o: Yes, it can still limit steps
A small error can put some of that fast component back into the computed solution.
No, the limit disappears
The fast rate remains in the differential equation even after its contribution to the true solution is tiny.

p.x: An **adaptive solver** estimates the error made in one proposed step. That estimate is the **local error**.
The **absolute tolerance** sets an error scale near zero. The contribution from **relative tolerance** [[grows with]] the magnitude of the state.
For a larger state, the same allowed fraction gives a larger allowed error.
If the estimated error is too large for the combined allowance, the solver retries with a smaller step.
An equation is **stiff** when fast decay forces an explicit method to use much smaller steps for stability than the slow trend needs for accuracy.
Many implicit methods allow [[larger]] stable steps on stiff problems.

p.c: evaluate rates using values already known
solve for a new state that also enters the rate

p.x: A suitable implicit update can damp the fast mode even at a step size that makes an explicit update unstable. Check the accuracy separately.
For the dimensionless decay law $y′ = −10y$, each Euler step multiplies the current state $y$ by a fixed factor.

p.cap: forward Euler for this decay law

p.x: This step flips the sign and halves the magnitude. If $|m| > 1$, the step would instead amplify a mode the equation damps.
A stable step can still distort the solution. Here the exact decay stays the same sign.

cards: In plain English: Local series can solve equations that lack simple elementary formulas.
At an ordinary point, a power-series trial yields a recurrence for its coefficients after substitution.
At certain regular singular points, Frobenius uses a leading power times a series. Its leading exponent satisfies an indicial equation.
Why it happens: equating coefficients of equal powers makes the differential equation hold order by order.
title: Power-series solutions and Frobenius
plain: Local series can solve equations that lack simple elementary formulas.

qs.q: “Match equal powers before reading off the recurrence.”
qs.ans: Align series indices before comparing coefficients.
wrong: Compare coefficients attached to different powers directly.
Assume every singular point supports ordinary Taylor series.
Discard initial coefficients without using the initial data.
qs.why: Index mismatch, ignoring singular structure, and deleting free data corrupt the recurrence.

qs.q: For dimensionless y′=y with y(0)=1, power-series coefficients satisfy a_(n+1)=a_n/(n+1). Find a3.
qs.why: Starting with a0=1 gives a1=1, a2=1/2, and a3=1/6.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Point with regular normalized equation coefficients
Equation determining a Frobenius leading exponent
qs.why: Recurrence means rule relating successive series coefficients. Ordinary point means point with regular normalized equation coefficients. Indicial equation means equation determining a frobenius leading exponent.

qs.q: Order a local series solution.
items: Choose the appropriate series form for the point
Substitute the series and align equal powers
Derive coefficient relations and apply initial data
qs.why: The point type determines the series form and the coefficient equations.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for power-series solutions and frobenius, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Some differential equations have no solution formula in elementary functions such as polynomials, exponentials or sines.
A **power series** adds terms that are successive powers of the distance from a chosen point, each multiplied by a coefficient.
When the series converges, it can describe the solution [[near]] that point.
The distance from the chosen point matters. The series can stop converging farther away.
For a linear equation, first divide by the coefficient of the highest derivative. This is the **normalized** equation.
At an **ordinary point**, the normalized coefficients have convergent power series there. Try a power series for the solution as well.
The resulting rule relating series coefficients is a **recurrence**. Use the initial data to set the starting coefficients.

At a **regular singular point**, some normalized coefficients fail to have a power series there. For a second-order equation at the origin, multiplying the coefficient of $y′$ by $x$ and the coefficient of $y$ by $x^2$ restores power series for both.

p.cap: near a regular singular point at the origin, on the positive side

p.x: The lowest power in the substituted equation gives the **indicial equation** for $r$. It can allow fractional exponents.

g.q: What can the equation for the leading exponent allow?
o: Only whole-number exponents
The ordinary series has whole-number powers, but the separate leading power is set by the differential equation.
Fractional exponents too
The lowest-power balance can give a fractional root. The series multiplying that power still uses whole-number powers.

p.x: For dimensionless $y′ = y$ with $y(0) = 1$, let $a_n$ be the coefficient of $x^n$ in $y$.
Differentiation lowers each power by one. Shift the derivative's index so both sides use $x^n$, then match its coefficients.

p.cap: $n$ is a nonnegative whole number. $a_0 = 1$ gives $a_1 = 1$.

cards: In plain English: Conditions at different locations can require solving for an unknown initial slope.
A boundary-value problem specifies conditions at more than one independent-variable location. It can have no solution, one solution, or multiple solutions.
Shooting guesses missing initial data, integrates an initial-value problem, and adjusts the guess to satisfy the far boundary.
Why it happens: the far-boundary mismatch becomes a root-finding problem in the unknown initial data.
title: Boundary-value problems and shooting
plain: Conditions at different locations can require solving for an unknown initial slope.

qs.q: “Use the end mismatch to adjust the starting slope.”
qs.ans: Solve a boundary residual in the shooting parameter.
wrong: Replace the far boundary by the initial value silently.
Assume every boundary problem has exactly one solution.
Change the differential equation to force the final value.
qs.why: Shooting adjusts missing data, not the required boundaries or governing equation; uniqueness is not automatic.

qs.q: For dimensionless y″=0 with y(0)=1 and y(2)=5, find the constant slope.
qs.why: The linear solution has slope (5−1)/(2−0)=2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Conditions imposed at different input locations
qs.why: Boundary-value problem means conditions imposed at different input locations. Shooting parameter means guessed missing initial datum. Boundary residual means mismatch at a required boundary.

qs.q: Which shooting statement is flawed?
lines: Guess the missing initial datum
Integrate to the far boundary
Adjust using the boundary residual
Assume shooting is well-conditioned for every boundary problem
qs.why: Small initial-data errors can amplify strongly, making shooting ill-conditioned.
qs.ans: Assume shooting is well-conditioned for every boundary problem
wrong: Guess the missing initial datum
Integrate to the far boundary
Adjust using the boundary residual

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for boundary-value problems and shooting, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An **initial-value problem** gives the needed conditions at one starting location.
A **boundary-value problem** gives conditions at [[different locations]] in the independent variable.
You might know a beam's displacement at both ends while its slope at the first end is unknown.
A boundary condition at the far end tests which starting slopes give a solution that meets both ends.
There may be no suitable starting slope, exactly one, or several. The equation and the boundary data determine which case you have.

g.q: Can several starting slopes satisfy the same boundary conditions?
o: Yes, they can
Different solution curves starting at the same value can reach the same target.
No, a target fixes one slope
A unique solution for each full set of starting data does not guarantee a unique slope that hits a target.

p.x: In **shooting**, the **shooting parameter** is the missing starting value you guess, such as the initial slope.
Integrate the equation as an initial-value problem for that guess. Subtract the required far-end value from the value you reach.
That difference is the **boundary residual**. Use it to adjust the guess until the residual is near zero.
Zero second derivative gives a constant slope $s$. Over the distance from $0$ to $2$, the solution ends at $1 + 2s$.
Shooting can be **ill-conditioned** on other equations. A tiny error in the starting value can grow into a large error at the far end.

cards: In plain English: Periodic signals can be assembled from independent sine and cosine components.
A Fourier series expands a periodic function in harmonically related sine and cosine modes. Orthogonality isolates coefficients by integration over a period.
Under standard convergence conditions, a jump is represented by the average of its one-sided limits. Oscillatory overshoot near jumps need not vanish in height.
Why it happens: orthogonal modes cancel in cross-products, so each projection extracts its own contribution.
branch: Fourier methods and partial differential equations
title: Fourier series and orthogonality
plain: Periodic signals can be assembled from independent sine and cosine components.

qs.q: “Project onto the harmonic over a full period.”
qs.ans: Use orthogonality to isolate its coefficient.
wrong: Read a coefficient from one arbitrary signal sample.
Integrate over any partial interval with unchanged normalization.
Assume every Fourier sum equals the assigned jump value.
qs.why: One sample and truncated periods lose orthogonality; jump convergence depends on one-sided limits.

qs.q: A dimensionless periodic signal is f(x)=3cos(x)+2sin(2x). What is its cos(x) Fourier coefficient under the usual sine-cosine convention?
qs.why: The coefficient multiplying cos(x) is 3; orthogonality removes the other harmonic.

qs.q: For a real Fourier series, how is a harmonic coefficient isolated under the appropriate full-period inner product?
qs.ans: Project onto the matching harmonic.
wrong: Read one arbitrary sample of the signal instead.
Sum all harmonic frequencies without weighting.
Use only the maximum value of the whole signal.
qs.why: Orthogonality isolates a harmonic through projection. One sample, frequency sums, and the overall maximum do not determine its coefficient.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Integer multiple of a fundamental frequency
Projection weight of a harmonic mode
Zero cross-mode inner product over the specified period
qs.why: Harmonic means integer multiple of a fundamental frequency. Fourier coefficient means projection weight of a harmonic mode. Orthogonality means zero cross-mode inner product over the specified period.

qs.q: Order a Fourier coefficient calculation.
items: Choose the matching basis mode and period
Integrate the signal times that mode over the period
Divide by the mode’s squared norm
qs.why: Normalization converts projection inner product into a coefficient.

figNeeded: Show Fourier approximations near a jump with the limiting midpoint and Gibbs overshoot marked.
br: Fourier methods and partial differential equations

p.x: A **periodic** signal repeats after a fixed time or distance, called its period. Its fundamental frequency is one cycle per period.
A **Fourier series** builds the signal from a constant and sine and cosine patterns called harmonics.
Their frequencies are [[whole-number multiples]] of the fundamental.
The first harmonic completes one cycle per period. The next completes two, then three, and so on.
A **Fourier coefficient** is the weight of one mode.
To isolate it, project onto that mode over a full period.
A **one-sided limit** is the level approached from one side. Suppose a piecewise smooth signal approaches 2 from the left and 6 from the right.
The series approaches **4** at the jump, whatever value the signal is assigned at that point.
Adding harmonics squeezes the ripples closer to the jump. Their peak overshoot need not shrink to zero. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.
To project $3cos(x)+2sin(2x)$ onto $cos(x)$, multiply by $cos(x)$ and integrate over $0$ to $2π$. Here $x$ is the dimensionless phase.
An **inner product** here is the integral of a product. These modes are **orthogonal**: their cross-product integrates to zero.
The integral against cosine is $3π$. Divide by the cosine’s **squared norm**, its integral against itself.
Cosine squared averages one half over a period of $2π$, so its integral is $π$.

g.q: What is the integral of $cos^2(x)$ over one period?
o: That is the period length. The integrand averages one half across it.
Cosine squared averages one half, so its integral is half the period.
Cosine integrates to zero over a period. Squaring makes every contribution nonnegative.

cards: In plain English: Boundary conditions select which spatial patterns a differential equation allows.
Separation of variables tries a product of functions of separate coordinates. Dividing by the product can produce a shared separation constant.
Homogeneous boundary conditions select eigenvalues and spatial eigenfunctions. Sturm–Liouville problems provide orthogonality under an appropriate weight.
Why it happens: a relation between independent variables can hold throughout the domain only when the separated expressions equal compatible constants.
branch: Fourier methods and partial differential equations
title: Separation of variables and eigenvalue boundaries
plain: Boundary conditions select which spatial patterns a differential equation allows.

qs.q: “The boundary conditions quantize the admissible modes.”
qs.ans: Only selected eigenvalues satisfy both boundaries.
wrong: Every separation constant satisfies every boundary condition.
Boundary conditions determine only the overall amplitude.
Orthogonality always uses an unweighted integral regardless of the operator.
qs.why: Boundary compatibility restricts eigenvalues, and the operator determines the correct inner-product weight.

qs.q: For dimensionless X″+λX=0 on 0<x<π with X(0)=X(π)=0, find the smallest positive eigenvalue λ.
qs.why: The modes are sin(nx) with positive integers n and eigenvalues n²; the smallest is 1.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Constant linking independently varying separated expressions
Nonzero function satisfying an operator eigenproblem and boundaries
Weight defining the operator’s orthogonality relation
qs.why: Separation constant means constant linking independently varying separated expressions. Eigenfunction means nonzero function satisfying an operator eigenproblem and boundaries. Sturm–Liouville weight means weight defining the operator’s orthogonality relation.

qs.q: Which separated-mode claim is flawed?
lines: Impose both boundary conditions
Exclude the trivial zero eigenfunction
Check admissible eigenvalues
Accept every separation constant without checking the boundaries
qs.why: Most separation constants do not support a nonzero function satisfying both boundaries.
qs.ans: Accept every separation constant without checking the boundaries
wrong: Impose both boundary conditions
Exclude the trivial zero eigenfunction
Check admissible eigenvalues

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for separation of variables and eigenvalue boundaries, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.
br: Fourier methods and partial differential equations

p.x: A **boundary condition** specifies what the solution does at an edge. Consider a string held by pins at both ends. A pin keeps that endpoint from moving.
The **displacement** must be zero at both ends. The string can still leave a pin at an angle, so its slope can be nonzero there.

g.q: Which quantity must be zero at both pins?
o: displacement
Each pin holds the endpoint at its original position.
slope
A pin can hold one point fixed while the string leaves it at an angle.

p.x: For a solution $u(x,t)$ that depends on position $x$ and time $t$, try a spatial factor $X$ and a time factor $T$.
In **separation of variables**, the factors are [[multiplied together]].

p.cap: when the equation allows product separation

p.x: Substitute and divide by the product where it is nonzero. The aim is to put all position dependence on one side and all time dependence on the other.
**Homogeneous** means zero boundary data. Try $X″+λX=0$ with $X(0)=X(π)=0$.
For positive $λ$, the first endpoint leaves a sine shape. The second requires $sin(√{λ}π)=0$.

p.cap: dimensionless x, n a positive integer

p.x: An allowed $λ$ is an **eigenvalue**. Its nonzero shape is an **eigenfunction**. The smallest $λ$ is 1.
In a **Sturm–Liouville** spatial problem, modes with different eigenvalues have zero weighted product integral. The equation sets the weight.
After separating, suppose an expression in position alone equals an expression in time alone throughout the interval and time range.
Hold time fixed and vary position. The time expression is fixed, so the position expression must stay [[unchanged]].
Each position gives the same value at that fixed time. Holding position fixed gives the same argument for time.
Both expressions equal a shared **separation constant**. The spatial boundaries can restrict its allowed values.

cards: In plain English: Diffusion smooths spatial differences by damping fine-scale patterns faster.
The one-dimensional heat equation relates time rate to spatial second derivative with positive diffusivity.
A sine spatial mode decays exponentially at a rate proportional to its squared spatial wave number. Initial data determine the mode amplitudes.
Why it happens: short-wavelength variations have larger second derivatives, driving faster smoothing.
branch: Fourier methods and partial differential equations
title: Heat equation and diffusion modes
plain: Diffusion smooths spatial differences by damping fine-scale patterns faster.

qs.q: “Higher spatial modes decay faster under diffusion.”
qs.ans: Their decay rates grow with wave number squared.
wrong: Their decay rates are independent of spatial frequency.
Their amplitudes grow exponentially for positive diffusivity.
Only the fundamental spatial mode is allowed to decay.
qs.why: The second derivative supplies the squared wave-number factor and a negative modal sign.

qs.q: For dimensionless diffusion with diffusivity 1, a mode sin(3x) has amplitude exp(−9t). Evaluate its amplitude at t=ln(2)/9.
qs.why: Substitution gives exp(−ln 2)=1/2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Fixed spatial pattern with a changing amplitude
qs.why: Diffusivity means coefficient setting diffusion rate. Spatial mode means fixed spatial pattern with a changing amplitude. Diffusion means evolution smoothing spatial variation.

qs.q: Order a separated heat-equation solution.
items: Find spatial modes satisfying the boundary conditions
Expand the initial condition in those modes
qs.why: Each initial mode evolves with its own diffusion rate.

demoNeeded: Animate low and high sine modes decaying under the heat equation.
br: Fourier methods and partial differential equations

p.x: **Diffusion** is the smoothing of a spatial difference, such as a warmer patch in a rod spreading heat into cooler surroundings.
A **spatial mode** is a fixed shape with a changing strength, called its amplitude. A wavy temperature pattern can be built by adding modes.
With no heat source, diffusion damps short-wavelength modes faster than broad ones.
In a uniform rod with no heat source, the time rate of temperature change is [[proportional]] to the spatial curvature.

p.cap: one spatial dimension, constant α > 0
vars: thermal diffusivity, setting the rate of smoothing

p.x: At a rounded temperature peak, the curvature is negative, so that spot cools.
For a sine mode $sin(kx)$, the wave number $k$ sets how tightly the waves fit along position $x$. Consider two allowed modes in the same rod.
The decay rate is $αk^2$, so doubling $k$ quadruples it.

p.cap: constant diffusivity α, zero-temperature endpoints

p.x: Find the modes that fit the boundaries, find their rates, then expand the starting temperature in those modes to get their initial amplitudes.

g.q: At the same diffusivity, doubling the wave number changes the decay rate by what factor?
o: This counts only one spatial derivative. Curvature brings in the wave number twice.
The rate scales with wave number squared, so doubling gives a factor of four.

p.x: Two spatial derivatives of $sin(3x)$ give $−9sin(3x)$. That large negative curvature factor gives a fast decay rate.

cards: In plain English: Oscillation and equilibrium require different governing equations and data.
The wave equation relates a second time derivative to spatial curvature and supports propagating or standing waves.
Laplace’s equation sets the spatial Laplacian to zero and describes many steady equilibrium fields. Boundary data, not two time-initial conditions, determine its boundary-value problem.
Why it happens: inertia stores and exchanges energy in waves, while Laplace models an equilibrium balance without a time-evolution term.
branch: Fourier methods and partial differential equations
title: Wave and Laplace equations
plain: Oscillation and equilibrium require different governing equations and data.

qs.q: “This is an equilibrium boundary problem, not a time-marching wave problem.”
qs.ans: Use the spatial Laplace equation with boundary data.
wrong: Specify initial displacement and velocity as the only data.
Use a time second derivative to define every equilibrium field.
Assume harmonic fields must be spatially constant everywhere.
qs.why: Steady harmonic fields need boundary information and can vary spatially without time dynamics.

qs.q: For dimensionless u(x,y)=x²−y², evaluate the Laplacian u_xx+u_yy.
qs.why: The second derivatives are 2 and −2, so their sum is zero.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Sum of pure second spatial derivatives
qs.why: Wave equation means evolution equation supporting inertial propagation. Laplacian means sum of pure second spatial derivatives. Harmonic function means function with zero laplacian.

qs.q: Which PDE classification is flawed?
lines: Distinguish first- and second-order time evolution
Check the spatial domain and boundaries
Recognize Laplace’s equation as a steady spatial relation
Assume every zero-Laplacian function is constant on every domain
qs.why: For example x²−y² is harmonic but nonconstant.
qs.ans: Assume every zero-Laplacian function is constant on every domain
wrong: Distinguish first- and second-order time evolution
Check the spatial domain and boundaries
Recognize Laplace’s equation as a steady spatial relation

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for wave and laplace equations, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.
br: Fourier methods and partial differential equations

p.x: A **partial differential equation** relates derivatives of a field, a quantity that depends on several variables.

p.c: A disturbed string moves in time
A source-free plate has reached a steady temperature

p.x: First decide whether the field is evolving or already in balance. That tells you what kinds of data to specify.
A stretched string has displacement $u$ at position $x$ and time $t$. Its curvature sets its acceleration in the ideal small-motion model.

p.cap: uniform string, no damping or forcing

p.x: Give the starting displacement and velocity as well as the string’s boundary conditions.
A pulse can travel along the string. Opposing waves can form a standing pattern.

g.q: Alongside starting displacement, which starting rate must you specify?
o: velocity
A second-order time equation needs both displacement and its time derivative.
acceleration
The equation already gives acceleration from the starting shape’s curvature.

p.x: The **Laplacian** is the [[sum]] of the second derivatives along the individual spatial axes.

p.cap: two spatial dimensions, steady and source-free

p.x: A field with zero Laplacian is **harmonic**. To find the field in a region, prescribe suitable boundary data, such as its value all along the edge.
In a wave, inertia allows energy to pass between motion and deformation. Laplace’s equation has no time term. It balances spatial curvatures.
Test that balance for the dimensionless field $u=x^2−y^2$.
The field is harmonic even though it varies with position. The two curvatures cancel.

g.q: For this field, what is the sum of the two curvatures?
o: That treats both terms as negative. The x² curvature is positive.
The +2 and −2 curvatures cancel.
That treats both terms as positive. The −y² curvature is negative.
