cards: In plain English: A matrix describes how input coordinates combine into output coordinates.
A matrix with m rows and n columns maps n-component input vectors to m-component output vectors. Here m and n are dimensionless positive integer counts.
Each output is the dot product of one row with the input. The columns show where the coordinate basis vectors go.
Why it happens: linearity combines basis-vector images using the input coordinates as weights.
title: Matrix shapes and linear maps
plain: A matrix describes how input coordinates combine into output coordinates.

qs.q: “The input dimension must match the column count.”
qs.ans: Use one input component for each matrix column.
wrong: Use one input component for each matrix row instead.
Ignore dimensions whenever all entries are numerical.
Require every linear map to have a square matrix.
qs.why: Rows count outputs, dimensions remain essential, and rectangular maps are valid.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=[[1,2],[3,4]] and x=(2,1), find the first component of Ax.
qs.why: The first row dot x is 1(2)+2(1)=4.

qs.q: A matrix has 3 rows and 5 columns and multiplies a column vector. How many components must that input vector have?
qs.why: The input dimension equals the column count. Three counts outputs, eight adds dimensions, and fifteen counts matrix entries.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Row count means number of output coordinates. Column count means number of input coordinates. Matrix-vector product means weighted combination of matrix columns.

qs.q: Order a matrix-vector product.
items: Check that input length matches the column count
Take each row’s dot product with the input
qs.why: The result has one component per row.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for matrix shapes and linear maps, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A matrix lists the numbers used by a **linear map**. Such a map preserves addition and scaling.
Each **column** gives the output from selecting its input coordinate alone and setting the others to zero.

g.q: Which part gives the output when just one input coordinate is set to one?
o: One column
A single input coordinate weights one full column.
One row
A row produces a single output coordinate.

p.x: A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns acts on an input with [[as many]] components as there are columns.
The input has $n$ components. The output has $m$, one for each row.
To find one output, multiply each row entry by the matching input entry.
Add the pairwise products to get the **dot product** of the row and the input.

g.q: How do you combine the resulting products to get a dot product?
o: Multiply them
The entries were already multiplied in pairs, and those contributions must be summed.
Add them
Each matched pair contributes additively to this output.

p.x: A **coordinate basis vector** has a single entry equal to one, with the rest zero.
The **image** of a vector is its output. Weight each basis vector's image by its input coordinate, then add the results.

cards: In plain English: Row operations simplify a system without changing its solutions.
Valid elementary row operations swap rows, multiply a row by a nonzero scalar, or add a multiple of one row to another.
An augmented matrix includes the right-hand side. Apply every row operation to that side too.
Why it happens: these operations replace equations by reversible combinations, preserving their common solution set.
title: Elimination and row operations
plain: Row operations simplify a system without changing its solutions.

qs.q: “Apply the operation to the augmented column too.”
qs.ans: Transform both coefficients and right-hand side.
wrong: Transform coefficients but leave the right-hand side fixed.
Transform only the right-hand side and keep all coefficients.
Multiply a row by zero to simplify it without changing solutions.
qs.why: Partial operations change the equations; multiplying by zero is not reversible.

qs.q: Solve dimensionless x+y=5 and x−y=1. What is x?
qs.why: Adding the equations gives 2x=6, so x=3.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Coefficients together with the right-hand side
Leading nonzero entry used in elimination
qs.why: Augmented matrix means coefficients together with the right-hand side. Row operation means reversible elementary equation transformation. Pivot means leading nonzero entry used in elimination.

qs.q: Which elimination step is flawed?
lines: Apply operations to the full augmented row
Use nonzero row scalings
Swap rows when needed
Scale a row by zero and claim an equivalent system
qs.why: Zero scaling destroys information and can enlarge the solution set.
qs.ans: Scale a row by zero and claim an equivalent system
wrong: Apply operations to the full augmented row
Use nonzero row scalings
Swap rows when needed

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for elimination and row operations, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: In **elimination**, simplify the equations while keeping the same solutions. A **pivot** is the leading coefficient used to clear entries below it.
Scaling by zero can erase a constraint. A valid row operation can be undone.

g.q: What happens if you multiply one row by zero?
o: You can lose a constraint
The old row cannot be recovered from a row of zeros.
All constraints are preserved
Scaling preserves an equation only when the scale is nonzero.

p.x: Swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one row to another.
To undo these steps, swap back, divide by the multiplier, or subtract the same multiple.
The right-hand side changes [[along with]] the coefficients during an operation.
An **augmented matrix** stores that right-hand side as an extra column, so apply the row operation to the whole row.
Equations can be replaced by reversible combinations of one another.
Every old solution satisfies the new equations. Reversing the operations shows that every new solution satisfies the old ones.

cards: In plain English: The reduced system reveals whether solutions exist and whether they are unique.
A row with all-zero coefficients and nonzero right-hand side makes a system inconsistent.
In a consistent system, nonpivot variables are free. A pivot in every variable column gives uniqueness.
Why it happens: a missing pivot leaves an input degree of freedom unconstrained by independent equations.
title: Consistency, pivots, and free variables
plain: The reduced system reveals whether solutions exist and whether they are unique.

qs.q: “There is a free variable, so this consistent system is not unique.”
qs.ans: At least one parameter remains in the solution.
wrong: A free variable makes every system inconsistent automatically.
A pivot-free variable must always equal zero only.
Consistency guarantees uniqueness regardless of pivot count.
qs.why: Free variables produce families in a consistent system; zero is only one possible choice.

qs.q: A consistent dimensionless linear system has 5 unknowns and coefficient rank 3. How many free variables are there?
qs.why: The count is unknowns minus pivots: 5−3=2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Variable not fixed by a pivot equation
qs.why: Consistent means has at least one solution. Free variable means variable not fixed by a pivot equation. Unique solution means exactly one allowed solution.

qs.q: Order a reduced-system interpretation.
items: Identify pivot and nonpivot variable columns
Describe the solution with any free parameters
qs.why: Consistency must be established before discussing solution freedom.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for consistency, pivots, and free variables, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A system is **consistent** if it has at least one solution. Row reduction makes that easier to check.
A **pivot** is the leading nonzero coefficient in a nonzero row of the reduced coefficient matrix.
Suppose a reduced equation has zero for every coefficient but a nonzero right-hand side.
That row is a contradiction. The system is **inconsistent**, meaning there is no common solution.

g.q: How many solutions satisfy that equation?
o: None
The left side is zero for every input.
Exactly one
No choice of a variable can change a left side with all-zero coefficients.
Infinitely many
A row of zeros permits all inputs only when the right side is also zero.

p.x: In a consistent system, a variable without a pivot can vary [[freely]].
Choose those free variables first. The pivot equations then determine the pivot variables.
**Rank** counts the coefficient pivots. Subtract it from the number of variables to count free variables.
Each free choice is an unconstrained **degree of freedom**. A consistent system is unique when there are no free choices.

cards: In plain English: Matrix multiplication represents ordered application of transformations.
For a composition, the rightmost matrix acts first. Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative.
The inner dimensions must agree. The product’s outer dimensions specify its output shape.
Why it happens: intermediate output coordinates from the first map become input coordinates for the second.
title: Matrix products and composition
plain: Matrix multiplication represents ordered application of transformations.

qs.q: “The order of the transforms matters.”
qs.ans: Apply the rightmost matrix first.
wrong: Swap the matrices freely because their sizes match.
Multiply matching entries to compose general linear maps.
Apply the leftmost matrix first in the usual column-vector convention.
qs.why: Equal sizes do not imply commutativity; entrywise products are different, and column-vector composition acts from the right.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=[[1,1],[0,1]] and B=[[2,0],[0,3]], find entry (1,2) of AB using one-based indices.
qs.why: Row 1 of A dotted with column 2 of B gives 3.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Changing order can change the result
qs.why: Composition means successive application of maps. Associativity means regrouping products without changing order. Noncommutativity means changing order can change the result.

qs.q: Which matrix-product statement is flawed?
lines: Check inner dimensions
Apply the rightmost map first
Keep transformation order explicit
Assume AB=BA whenever both products exist
qs.why: Both products can exist and still differ.
qs.ans: Assume AB=BA whenever both products exist
wrong: Check inner dimensions
Apply the rightmost map first
Keep transformation order explicit

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for matrix products and composition, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: **Composition** means applying maps in succession. The product $AB$ acts on a column vector. The letters $A$ and $B$ name the two maps.
The rightmost map $B$ acts first. Map $A$ takes its output as input.

g.q: Which map acts first?
o: Rightmost map
The vector is multiplied by B before A acts on the result.
Leftmost map
A is written first but acts on the intermediate result.

p.x: **Associative** means you can regroup three compatible factors without changing their order or the result.
**Commutative** would mean you could swap factors. Matrix products generally change when you swap them.
The inner dimensions must be [[equal]].
The column count of the left matrix must match the row count of the right matrix. The outer counts give the product shape.
To find one product entry, pick a row from the left matrix and a column from the right.
Take their dot product. Its paired entries run over the intermediate coordinates.

cards: In plain English: A basis describes a space without redundant directions.
The span of vectors contains all their linear combinations. Independence means no nontrivial combination gives zero.
A basis is an independent spanning set. Its size is the dimension of the space.
Why it happens: dependent vectors add no new direction, so they do not increase the set of representable vectors.
title: Span, independence, and bases
plain: A basis describes a space without redundant directions.

qs.q: “That new column is already in the span.”
qs.ans: It adds no independent direction.
wrong: It increases dimension merely because another vector was listed.
It makes every existing vector become zero.
It proves the entire set cannot span any space.
qs.why: A redundant vector does not increase dimension or destroy the span.

qs.q: In dimensionless R³, what is the dimension of the span of (1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,0)?
qs.why: The third vector is the sum of the first two, leaving two independent directions.

qs.q: A set already spans a vector space. Adding a vector in that span changes its dimension by how much?
qs.why: A redundant vector adds no independent direction. Counting the new entry, subtracting a direction, or adding two confuses list size with span dimension.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Only the zero coefficient combination produces zero
qs.why: Span means set of all linear combinations. Independence means only the zero coefficient combination produces zero. Basis means independent spanning set.

qs.q: Order a basis extraction from matrix columns.
items: Row-reduce to identify pivot column indices
Select those columns from the original matrix
Confirm they span the original column space independently
qs.why: Original pivot columns, not altered reduced columns, form a basis for the original column space.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for span, independence, and bases, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A vector's **linear combination** with other vectors is a sum of those vectors with chosen weights. Their **span** is the set of all such sums.
The span stays the same. The new vector's weight just changes the weights on the old vectors.

g.q: If you add a vector already in the span, what happens to that span?
o: It grows
Adding a vector expands the span only when it lies outside the old span.
It stays the same
The added vector can be replaced by a combination of the old ones.

p.x: Vectors are **independent** if the only weighted sum that gives zero uses all-zero weights.
If some nonzero choice of weights gives zero, the vectors are **dependent**. One can be written as a combination of the others.
A basis must be [[both]] independent and spanning.
Its vectors cover the space with no redundant directions. The number of basis vectors is the **dimension**.
To extract a basis from a list, put the vectors into columns and find pivots by row reduction.
Keep the corresponding columns from the original matrix. They span the same space as the original list and are independent.

cards: In plain English: Null-space directions can change an input without changing its output.
The null space consists of vectors sent to zero by a linear map. It is a subspace of the input space.
Every solution of a consistent system equals one particular solution plus a null-space vector.
Why it happens: adding a zero-output direction leaves the mapped right-hand side unchanged.
title: Null space and solution families
plain: Null-space directions can change an input without changing its output.

qs.q: “Move within the null space and the output stays fixed.”
qs.ans: Add a homogeneous solution to the particular solution.
wrong: Add any arbitrary input vector without checking its image.
Add a right-hand-side vector directly regardless of dimension.
Assume every null-space vector is the zero vector.
qs.why: Only zero-image directions preserve output; dimensions still matter and null spaces may be nontrivial.

qs.q: For dimensionless matrix A=[[1,2]], the null vector (x,1) satisfies A(x,1)=0. Find x.
qs.why: The equation is x+2=0, so x=−2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One input mapped to the required output
Linear system with zero right-hand side
qs.why: Null space means input vectors mapped to zero. Particular solution means one input mapped to the required output. Homogeneous system means linear system with zero right-hand side.

qs.q: Which null-space claim is flawed?
lines: Solve the homogeneous system
Parameterize free variables
Add null vectors to a particular solution
Assume null-space vectors can have arbitrary nonzero output
qs.why: A null-space vector has zero output by definition.
qs.ans: Assume null-space vectors can have arbitrary nonzero output
wrong: Solve the homogeneous system
Parameterize free variables
Add null vectors to a particular solution

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for null space and solution families, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: The **null space** consists of inputs that the map sends to zero. The map adds outputs when you add inputs.
The output stays fixed. The added direction contributes nothing to it.

g.q: If you add a null-space vector to an input, what happens to its output?
o: It stays fixed
The added input contributes zero to the output.
It becomes zero
Only the added direction is known to have zero output.

p.x: The null space solves the **homogeneous system**, whose right-hand side is zero.
It is a **subspace** of the input space: it contains zero and stays closed under addition and scaling.
A **particular solution** is any one input with the requested output. You can move [[within]] the null space to find other solutions.
Add any null-space vector to that particular solution. The output remains the requested one.
Two solutions with the same output have a difference that maps to zero.
This is why particular solution plus null-space vector describes every solution of a consistent system.

cards: In plain English: Rank counts output directions while nullity counts invisible input directions.
Rank is the dimension of the column space. Nullity is the dimension of the null space; together they equal the number of columns.
The row space is orthogonal to the null space. The column space is orthogonal to the left null space under Euclidean inner products.
Why it happens: a null vector has zero dot product with every row, so every row combination is also perpendicular to it.
title: Rank-nullity and fundamental spaces
plain: Rank counts output directions while nullity counts invisible input directions.

qs.q: “Rank and nullity must add to the input dimension.”
qs.ans: Use the matrix column count in rank-nullity.
wrong: Use the matrix row count regardless of shape instead.
Add rank to the number of measured right-hand sides.
Assume rank must equal nullity for every rectangular matrix.
qs.why: The domain dimension controls rank-nullity; output size and right-hand-side count are different quantities.

qs.q: A dimensionless 4-by-7 matrix has rank 3. Find its nullity.
qs.why: The input dimension is 7, so nullity is 7−3=4.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Vectors annihilated by the matrix transpose
qs.why: Rank means dimension of the matrix image. Nullity means dimension of the null space. Left null space means vectors annihilated by the matrix transpose.

qs.q: Order a rank-nullity check.
items: Determine the rank from independent pivots
qs.why: The resulting nullity counts unconstrained input directions.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for rank-nullity and fundamental spaces, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: The **column space** is the span of the columns. It contains all reachable outputs.
Its dimension is the **rank**. The **nullity** is the dimension of the space of inputs that map to zero.
Rank counts pivot variables. Nullity counts free variables in the zero-output system.
Rank plus nullity equals the column count, the number of input coordinates.

g.q: Which matrix count equals rank plus nullity?
o: Row count
Rows index output coordinates, not the full list of input variables.
Column count
Every column represents either a pivot variable or a free variable.

p.x: The **row space** contains combinations of rows. It is [[perpendicular]] to the null space under the ordinary dot product.
A null vector has zero dot product with each row, so it also has zero dot product with any row combination.
The **left null space** contains output-space vectors sent to zero by the transpose, which swaps rows and columns.
Each such vector is perpendicular to every column, and therefore to the whole column space.

cards: In plain English: The same vector can have different coordinate lists in different bases.
A coordinate vector gives coefficients relative to a chosen basis. It is not the geometric vector independent of that basis.
A basis matrix with basis vectors as columns maps basis coordinates to standard coordinates. Reversing that map requires solving a system.
Why it happens: basis coordinates are weights in a linear combination of basis vectors.
title: Coordinates and change of basis
plain: The same vector can have different coordinate lists in different bases.

qs.q: “Those are coordinates in the new basis.”
qs.ans: Map them through the new basis matrix.
wrong: Read them as standard coordinates without conversion.
Transpose the basis matrix as an inverse in every case.
Change the geometric vector whenever its coordinates change.
qs.why: Coordinate lists depend on basis; transpose is inverse only for orthogonal basis matrices, and a representation change need not move the vector.

qs.q: A dimensionless basis is b1=(1,1), b2=(1,−1). A vector has basis coordinates (3,2). Find its standard first coordinate.
qs.why: The standard vector is 3b1+2b2=(5,1).

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Coefficients relative to a specified basis
Matrix with basis vectors as columns
qs.why: Basis coordinates means coefficients relative to a specified basis. Basis matrix means matrix with basis vectors as columns. Change of basis means conversion between coordinate representations.

qs.q: Which coordinate conversion is flawed?
lines: State the source and destination bases
Use basis vectors as matrix columns
Solve for coordinates when converting back
Use a transpose as the inverse of every basis matrix
qs.why: A general invertible basis matrix need not be orthogonal.
qs.ans: Use a transpose as the inverse of every basis matrix
wrong: State the source and destination bases
Use basis vectors as matrix columns
Solve for coordinates when converting back

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for coordinates and change of basis, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A coordinate list gives weights on the vectors of a chosen basis.
The coordinate list can change even though the geometric vector stays fixed.

g.q: When you change bases while keeping the same vector, what can change?
o: The coordinate list
The same vector can be built from different weights on different basis vectors.
The geometric vector
Changing the basis describes the same vector using a different list.

p.x: Basis coordinates are weights used to [[combine]] the basis vectors.
For a **change of basis**, convert between lists for the same vector. Stack the new basis vectors as columns. Multiplying by this basis matrix yields the vector in standard coordinates.
Start with a vector in standard coordinates. You know the columns of the new basis matrix.
Solve the system with the basis matrix as the coefficient matrix. The unknowns are the new weights.

g.q: How do you find the weights for this new basis?
o: Multiply by the basis matrix
Multiplication by the basis matrix goes from basis weights to standard coordinates.
Solve for them
The weights must reproduce the supplied vector as a combination of the columns.

p.x: An **orthonormal** basis uses mutually perpendicular unit vectors.
For an orthonormal basis matrix, swapping rows and columns gives its inverse. A general basis needs a solve.

cards: In plain English: A determinant measures signed volume scaling for a square transformation.
A determinant is defined for square matrices. Its magnitude gives volume scaling; its sign records orientation reversal in real spaces.
A zero determinant means the square map collapses dimension and is not invertible.
Why it happens: dependent output directions span zero full-dimensional volume.
title: Determinants and volume scaling
plain: A determinant measures signed volume scaling for a square transformation.

qs.q: “The determinant is negative, so orientation flips.”
qs.ans: Volume magnitude scales by its absolute value.
wrong: The physical volume itself becomes negative instead.
The transformation must be singular whenever the sign is negative.
The determinant magnitude measures every vector length change equally.
qs.why: Sign describes orientation, not negative volume or singularity; volume scaling is not uniform length scaling.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=[[2,1],[3,4]], find det(A).
qs.why: The two-by-two determinant is 2×4−1×3=5.

qs.q: For a real square matrix with determinant −3, what is its unsigned volume scaling factor?
qs.why: Volume magnitude uses the absolute determinant. Negative three retains orientation sign; one third uses the inverse; nine squares the scale.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Signed volume scale of a square map
qs.why: Determinant means signed volume scale of a square map. Singular matrix means square matrix without an inverse. Orientation reversal means handedness change under a map.

qs.q: Order a two-by-two determinant calculation.
items: Subtract the second product from the first
qs.why: The subtraction records oriented area scaling.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for determinants and volume scaling, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A determinant is a single signed number for a square matrix.
Its absolute value measures the factor by which the map scales full-dimensional volume.
Volume scaling ignores sign. **Orientation** describes the handedness of an ordered set of axes.
A negative determinant reverses orientation. A positive one preserves it.

g.q: What does a negative determinant do to orientation?
o: Reverses it
A negative sign means the transformed axes have opposite handedness.
Preserves it
Preserved orientation corresponds to a positive sign.

p.x: A zero determinant means the map [[collapses]] full-dimensional volume.
The columns are dependent and their span has fewer dimensions than the input space. The square map is **singular**, meaning it has no inverse.
For a square matrix with top row $a,b$ and bottom row $c,d$, $D$ denotes its determinant.

p.cap: square matrix with two rows

p.x: Multiply down each diagonal. Subtract the opposite-diagonal product from the main-diagonal product.

cards: In plain English: An inverse undoes a nonsingular square map, but explicit inversion is often unnecessary.
A matrix inverse exists for a square full-rank matrix. Multiplying by the inverse reverses the map.
Numerical linear solves generally use factorizations rather than explicitly forming an inverse. One factorization can solve several right-hand sides.
Why it happens: factorization exploits elimination structure and usually avoids unnecessary computation and error from forming the full inverse.
title: Inverse maps and solving systems
plain: An inverse undoes a nonsingular square map, but explicit inversion is often unnecessary.

qs.q: “Solve the system; do not form the inverse just to multiply it.”
qs.ans: Use a suitable matrix factorization and back solves.
wrong: Divide corresponding matrix entries into the vector instead.
Take reciprocals of all matrix entries as an inverse.
Assume every rectangular matrix has a two-sided inverse.
qs.why: Entrywise division is not inversion; a two-sided inverse requires square nonsingularity.

qs.q: For dimensionless diagonal A=diag(2,5), solve Ax=(6,10). What is x2?
qs.why: The second equation is 5x2=10, giving x2=2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Map undoing a nonsingular square transformation
qs.why: Inverse means map undoing a nonsingular square transformation. Factorization means decomposition into easier matrix factors. Back substitution means solution of an upper-triangular system.

qs.q: Which inverse statement is flawed?
lines: Check square full rank for a two-sided inverse
Prefer a solve for a single right-hand side
Reuse suitable factors for multiple right-hand sides
Construct a general inverse by taking each entry’s reciprocal
qs.why: A matrix inverse must undo the full coupled map, not individual entries.
qs.ans: Construct a general inverse by taking each entry’s reciprocal
wrong: Check square full rank for a two-sided inverse
Prefer a solve for a single right-hand side
Reuse suitable factors for multiple right-hand sides

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for inverse maps and solving systems, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A square map has **full rank** when it reaches every output direction.
For every output there is exactly one input. The inverse takes that output back to the input.

g.q: How many inputs give a specified output for a square full-rank map?
o: None
Full rank means every output is reachable.
Infinitely many
Multiple inputs would require a nonzero null-space direction.
Exactly one
Full rank in a square matrix leaves no null-space freedom.

p.x: A square matrix with an inverse is **nonsingular**. Multiplying the matrix and its inverse in either order gives the identity map.
A diagonal matrix with nonzero diagonal entries is undone by reciprocating those entries. That shortcut does not apply entry by entry to a general matrix.
A **factorization** writes a matrix as a product of simpler matrices that are easy to solve with.
For several right-hand sides, [[reuse]] the same factors.
Each right-hand side needs new solves with the factors. The coefficient matrix and its factors stay the same.
Elimination yields triangular systems. An upper-triangular system has zeros below its diagonal.
Start with the last equation and work upward, substituting each known value. This is **back substitution**.

g.q: Where do you start solving an upper-triangular system?
o: At the last equation
The last equation has only the last unknown left.
At the first equation
Earlier equations can still contain unknowns from later columns.

cards: In plain English: Reordering equations can make elimination more reliable.
LU factorization stores elimination in lower- and upper-triangular factors. With row pivoting, a permutation matrix records the reordered equations.
Partial pivoting selects a large-magnitude candidate in the active column. It reduces dangerous division by tiny pivots but is not a universal cure for conditioning.
Why it happens: small pivots can magnify roundoff during elimination even when a better row is available.
title: LU factorization and pivoting
plain: Reordering equations can make elimination more reliable.

qs.q: “Swap to a safer pivot and apply the same permutation to the right side.”
qs.ans: Keep the permutation consistent throughout the solve.
wrong: Swap coefficient rows while leaving the right side unchanged.
Assume pivoting removes all sensitivity in the original problem.
Divide by a zero pivot to preserve the original row order.
qs.why: Inconsistent permutations change the system; conditioning is intrinsic, and zero division is invalid.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=[[2,1],[4,3]], eliminate entry (2,1) without pivoting. What multiplier subtracts row 1 from row 2?
qs.why: The multiplier is 4/2=2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Recorded reordering of rows or columns
Reordering to select a usable elimination pivot
qs.why: LU factors means lower- and upper-triangular elimination factors. Permutation means recorded reordering of rows or columns. Pivoting means reordering to select a usable elimination pivot.

qs.q: Order an LU-based solve with row permutation.
items: Apply the factorization’s row permutation to the right side
qs.why: The permutation must match the factorization convention.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for lu factorization and pivoting, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **pivot** is the entry used as a divisor to compute an elimination multiplier. Partial pivoting can swap in a different row.
Choose an entry of largest absolute value among the remaining rows in the active column.

g.q: Which candidate does partial pivoting use in the current column?
o: Smallest absolute value
A tiny divisor can make the multiplier unnecessarily large.
Largest absolute value
This avoids dividing by a smaller available entry.

p.x: In **LU factorization**, the lower-triangular factor $L$ stores elimination multipliers. The upper-triangular factor $U$ stores the resulting coefficients.
A lower-triangular matrix has zeros above the diagonal. An upper-triangular one has zeros below it.
A **permutation matrix** records the swaps. Apply them to the right-hand side [[in the same order]] as to the coefficient rows.
Then solve with the lower factor, followed by the upper factor.
To clear an entry, divide it by the pivot and subtract that multiple of the pivot row.
Small pivots can produce large multipliers, magnifying rounding errors. Pivoting helps with elimination but cannot undo the map's inherent sensitivity.

cards: In plain English: A small equation mismatch does not always mean a small solution error.
A residual is the right-hand side minus the matrix times the computed solution. Forward error compares the computed solution with the exact one.
A large condition number means small input perturbations can produce large relative output changes in adverse directions.
Why it happens: a nearly collapsed direction makes distinct inputs produce almost indistinguishable outputs.
title: Condition numbers and residuals
plain: A small equation mismatch does not always mean a small solution error.

qs.q: “The residual is small, but the system is ill-conditioned.”
qs.ans: The solution can still have substantial forward error.
wrong: A small residual always proves a small relative solution error.
Conditioning describes only how fast the solver executes.
A zero determinant is required for any sensitivity at all.
qs.why: Residual and forward error differ; conditioning concerns sensitivity and can be poor before exact singularity.

qs.q: For dimensionless diagonal A=diag(1,0.01), find its Euclidean condition number.
qs.why: The singular-value ratio is 1/0.01=100.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Equation mismatch for the computed solution
qs.why: Residual means equation mismatch for the computed solution. Forward error means difference from the exact solution. Condition number means measure of relative perturbation sensitivity.

qs.q: Which numerical report is flawed?
lines: Report a scaled residual
Consider the condition number
Distinguish backward and forward error
Conclude high solution accuracy from residual size alone for any matrix
qs.why: Ill-conditioning can amplify a small backward error into large forward error.
qs.ans: Conclude high solution accuracy from residual size alone for any matrix
wrong: Report a scaled residual
Consider the condition number
Distinguish backward and forward error

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for condition numbers and residuals, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Imagine a square map that almost flattens one direction. Moving far along that direction hardly changes the output.
A small output mismatch can hide a large input error when the map nearly flattens a direction.

g.q: Can a small output mismatch coexist with a large input error?
o: Yes
An input error in the nearly flattened direction barely shows in the output.
No
That would require the map to preserve lengths well in every direction.

p.x: The **residual** is the observed right-hand side minus the output predicted by the computed solution.
**Forward error** compares the computed solution with the exact one. **Backward error** asks how little the data must change to make the computed solution exact.
For an invertible matrix in Euclidean geometry, $κ$ is its condition number. The quantities $σ_{max}$ and $σ_{min}$ are its largest and smallest stretches of unit vectors.

p.cap: invertible matrix

p.x: A large ratio permits large relative solution changes from small relative changes to the right-hand side.
The output barely responds to inputs along a [[weakly stretched]] direction.
A substantially wrong input in that direction can still fit the equations closely. Report the residual together with conditioning information.

cards: In plain English: Some directions keep their orientation under a linear map.
An eigenvector is nonzero and maps to a scalar multiple of itself. The scalar is its eigenvalue.
Eigenvalues can be zero, negative, or complex. A zero eigenvalue makes a square matrix singular.
Why it happens: the transformation preserves the one-dimensional subspace spanned by an eigenvector, even if it reverses or scales it.
title: Eigenpairs and invariant directions
plain: Some directions keep their orientation under a linear map.

qs.q: “The zero vector is not an eigenvector.”
qs.ans: An eigenvector must define a nonzero direction.
wrong: The zero vector uniquely identifies every eigenvalue.
An eigenvector must always have positive components.
An eigenvalue must always be a positive real number.
qs.why: Zero gives no direction; signs and complex values are allowed.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=diag(2,5), vector v=(0,3) is an eigenvector. Find its eigenvalue.
A candidate eigenvector v satisfies Av=λv. Which additional condition is part of the definition?
qs.ans: The vector v is nonzero.
wrong: The eigenvalue λ is always positive.
Every component of v is nonzero.
The matrix A is always symmetric.
qs.why: Only the vector as a whole must be nonzero. Eigenvalues need not be positive, components may vanish, and nonsymmetric matrices also have eigenvectors.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Nonzero vector mapped to a multiple of itself
qs.why: Eigenvector means nonzero vector mapped to a multiple of itself. Eigenvalue means scale factor for an eigenvector. Invariant subspace means subspace mapped into itself.

qs.q: Order an eigenpair verification.
items: Check the candidate vector is nonzero
Compare the result with the proposed eigenvalue times the vector
qs.why: The eigenpair equation must hold component by component.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for eigenpairs and invariant directions, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A square map can mix coordinates. Some nonzero vectors map to multiples of themselves.
That line is an **invariant subspace**. Every point on it maps back to the line, possibly to zero.
For square matrix $A$, a nonzero vector $v$ with this property is an **eigenvector**. The multiplier $λ$ is its **eigenvalue**.

p.cap: square map, nonzero vector

p.x: Compute the image and verify the same multiplier works in every component.
An eigenvalue can be positive, negative, or zero. Over complex coordinates it can also be complex.
A negative eigenvalue reverses the direction of a real eigenvector while keeping its line invariant.

g.q: For a real eigenvector with a negative eigenvalue, where does its image point?
o: In the original direction
A positive multiplier would preserve the arrow's direction.
In the opposite direction
Multiplying by a negative real number reverses the arrow.

p.x: A zero eigenvalue sends a nonzero vector to zero, so the map is [[not invertible]].
The zero input has zero output too. An inverse could not distinguish the two inputs.

cards: In plain English: A full eigenvector basis can separate a transformation into independent scalar actions.
A matrix is diagonalizable when it has a basis of eigenvectors. The eigenvector matrix converts between modal and original coordinates.
Repeated eigenvalues do not automatically prevent diagonalization; sufficient independent eigenvectors are what matter.
Why it happens: in an eigenvector basis, each coordinate evolves independently by its eigenvalue factor.
title: Diagonalization and matrix powers
plain: A full eigenvector basis can separate a transformation into independent scalar actions.

qs.q: “A repeated eigenvalue is not enough to call it defective.”
qs.ans: Count its independent eigenvectors.
wrong: Declare every repeated-root matrix nondiagonalizable immediately.
Assume algebraic multiplicity always equals geometric multiplicity.
Use identical eigenvectors as separate basis columns.
qs.why: Repeated roots may still have a full eigenspace; duplicate vectors do not supply a basis.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=diag(2,3), find the second diagonal entry of A³.
qs.why: Diagonal powers act entrywise on the diagonal, giving 3³=27.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Representation in a complete eigenvector basis
Root multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial
qs.why: Diagonalization means representation in a complete eigenvector basis. Algebraic multiplicity means root multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial. Geometric multiplicity means dimension of the eigenspace.

qs.q: Which diagonalization claim is flawed?
lines: Find eigenvalues and eigenspaces
Count independent eigenvectors
Check that the eigenvector matrix is invertible
Declare diagonalizability solely from having listed the required number of roots with multiplicity
qs.why: A complete root list does not ensure a complete eigenvector basis.
qs.ans: Declare diagonalizability solely from having listed the required number of roots with multiplicity
wrong: Find eigenvalues and eigenspaces
Count independent eigenvectors
Check that the eigenvector matrix is invertible

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for diagonalization and matrix powers, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An **eigenbasis** is a full basis made from eigenvectors.
In an eigenbasis each coordinate is scaled on its own. The axes do not mix.

g.q: In this basis, can one coordinate feed into a different coordinate when the map acts?
o: No
An eigenvector maps to a multiple of itself, with no component in any other basis direction.
Yes
Mixing between coordinates is possible in a general basis, not in an eigenbasis.

p.x: A matrix is **diagonalizable** if it has an eigenbasis. The matrix of eigenvectors as columns maps eigenbasis coordinates to original coordinates.
The diagonal matrix of eigenvalues acts on eigenbasis coordinates, also called **modal coordinates**.
Repeated eigenvalues are [[compatible]] with diagonalization.

**Algebraic multiplicity** counts repeats as a root of the polynomial used to find eigenvalues. **Geometric multiplicity** is the dimension of the **eigenspace**, made of the associated eigenvectors and zero.
A positive integer matrix power repeats the same map. In an eigenbasis each application multiplies a coordinate by its own eigenvalue.
The factors multiply. Raise each eigenvalue to the desired power, then convert back to original coordinates.

g.q: How do the successive scale factors combine?
o: They add
No separate outputs are being summed. The same coordinate is scaled repeatedly.
They multiply
Each application scales the result of the preceding application.

cards: In plain English: Rotation and shear-like modal coupling require more than distinct real eigenvectors.
Real matrices can have complex eigenpairs in conjugate pairs. Their real dynamics can combine rotation with growth or decay.
A defective matrix lacks a full eigenvector basis. Generalized eigenvectors and Jordan blocks describe its remaining structure.
Why it happens: repeated roots can preserve fewer independent directions than their algebraic multiplicity suggests.
title: Complex modes and defective matrices
plain: Rotation and shear-like modal coupling require more than distinct real eigenvectors.

qs.q: “The Jordan coupling adds a polynomial time factor.”
qs.ans: Generalized modes supplement the missing eigenvectors.
wrong: A defective matrix has no eigenvalues at all.
Every repeated eigenvalue creates two independent ordinary eigenvectors.
Complex eigenvalues imply complex-valued physical states are mandatory.
qs.why: Defectiveness concerns missing eigenvectors; conjugate modes can combine into real states.

qs.q: For dimensionless A=[[1,1],[0,1]], find the upper-right entry of A³.
qs.why: Writing A=I+N with N²=0 gives A³=I+3N.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Complex values with opposite imaginary parts
Matrix lacking a complete eigenvector basis
qs.why: Conjugate pair means complex values with opposite imaginary parts. Defective matrix means matrix lacking a complete eigenvector basis. Generalized eigenvector means vector extending an eigenvector chain.

qs.q: Order a repeated-eigenvalue diagnosis.
items: Find the dimension of the eigenspace
Compare multiplicities and identify any eigenvector deficit
qs.why: A deficit requires generalized modal structure rather than diagonalization.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for complex modes and defective matrices, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: For a real matrix, a nonreal eigenvalue comes with its **complex conjugate**, obtained by flipping the sign of its imaginary part.
Conjugating the corresponding eigenvector gives an eigenvector for that partner.
A conjugate pair can describe rotation in a real plane. The eigenvalue magnitude scales the mode amplitude each step in modal coordinates.
The mode decays because each step shrinks it, even while the direction rotates.

g.q: If that magnitude is below one, what happens to the mode under repeated steps?
o: It decays
Every step multiplies its size by the same factor below one.
It grows
Growth requires a magnitude above one.
It keeps its size
An unchanged size requires unit magnitude.

p.x: A **defective** matrix has [[too few]] independent eigenvectors to form a basis in the field being used.
To step down an eigenvector chain, take the image of a vector and subtract the eigenvalue times that vector.
A **generalized eigenvector** reaches an ordinary eigenvector after repeating this step.
**Algebraic multiplicity** counts how many times a root repeats. Compare it with the number of independent eigenvectors for that root.
The **eigenspace** contains those eigenvectors and zero. A **Jordan block** places the eigenvalue on the diagonal and links chain members just above it.
For a nonzero eigenvalue, repeated action can multiply its powers by a polynomial in the step count. A block with eigenvalue zero eventually gives zero.

cards: In plain English: Real symmetric matrices have orthogonal modal directions and real curvature values.
A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenvector basis. Its quadratic form measures direction-dependent curvature or energy.
Positive definiteness means all eigenvalues are positive. Positive semidefiniteness allows zero eigenvalues.
Why it happens: orthogonal eigen-coordinates reduce the quadratic form to a sum of eigenvalue-weighted squared coordinates.
title: Symmetric spectra and quadratic forms
plain: Real symmetric matrices have orthogonal modal directions and real curvature values.

qs.q: “Zero eigenvalues make it semidefinite, not strictly definite.”
qs.ans: Some nonzero directions can have zero quadratic value.
wrong: Every nonzero direction must have strictly positive value.
A zero eigenvalue forces every quadratic value negative.
A symmetric matrix can never have a zero eigenvalue.
qs.why: Semidefinite forms allow flat directions; zero eigenvalues do not imply negativity or violate symmetry.

qs.q: For dimensionless Q=diag(2,3) and x=(1,2), calculate xᵀQx.
qs.why: The quadratic form is 2(1²)+3(2²)=14.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Scalar formed by vector-transpose matrix vector
Nonnegative quadratic value for every vector
qs.why: Symmetric matrix means matrix equal to its transpose. Quadratic form means scalar formed by vector-transpose matrix vector. Positive semidefinite means nonnegative quadratic value for every vector.

qs.q: Which symmetric-matrix claim is flawed?
lines: Use an orthonormal eigenbasis
Inspect eigenvalue signs for definiteness
Allow zero eigenvalues in semidefinite forms
Declare positive definiteness when one eigenvalue is zero
qs.why: Strict positive definiteness requires every eigenvalue to be positive.
qs.ans: Declare positive definiteness when one eigenvalue is zero
wrong: Use an orthonormal eigenbasis
Inspect eigenvalue signs for definiteness
Allow zero eigenvalues in semidefinite forms

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for symmetric spectra and quadratic forms, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **symmetric** real matrix equals its transpose, so swapping its rows and columns leaves it unchanged.
Its eigenvalues are real. It has a basis of unit eigenvectors that are mutually perpendicular.
A **quadratic form** is a scalar built from a vector $x$ and a matrix $Q$. The superscript $T$ turns a column into a row.

p.cap: real symmetric matrix

p.x: For the symmetric form here, each eigenvalue gives its weight along one eigenvector. These weights can represent curvature or energy in a model.
A **positive definite** form is positive for every nonzero input. A **positive semidefinite** form is nonnegative for every input.
The form is semidefinite only. The zero-eigenvalue direction prevents strict positivity.
Positive semidefiniteness needs all eigenvalues to be nonnegative. Positive definiteness needs them all to be positive.

g.q: If every eigenvalue is nonnegative but one is zero, which describes the form?
o: Strictly positive definite
Strict positivity excludes zero along any nonzero direction.
Semidefinite only
The zero-eigenvalue direction gives a zero value even for a nonzero vector.

p.x: In orthonormal eigenvector coordinates, the quadratic form splits into a sum of [[separate]] contributions.
Square each coordinate and multiply by its eigenvalue. Then add the weighted squares, with no cross terms.

cards: In plain English: Projection finds the closest representable component in a chosen geometry.
An inner product defines lengths and angles. Euclidean orthogonal projection minimizes squared Euclidean distance to a subspace.
The residual from an orthogonal projection is perpendicular to the target subspace.
Why it happens: any remaining in-subspace residual component could be removed to reduce squared distance.
title: Inner products and orthogonal projection
plain: Projection finds the closest representable component in a chosen geometry.

qs.q: “The projection residual must be perpendicular to the subspace.”
qs.ans: Check orthogonality to every spanning direction.
wrong: Check only that the residual has small positive components.
Require the residual itself to lie in the target subspace.
Assume any decomposition into two vectors is orthogonal.
qs.why: Component signs do not test orthogonality; a nonzero in-subspace residual is removable, and arbitrary decompositions need not be perpendicular.

qs.q: Project dimensionless b=(3,4) onto the x-axis. What is the norm of the residual?
qs.why: The projection is (3,0), leaving residual (0,4) of norm 4.

qs.q: For Euclidean orthogonal projection onto a subspace, where must the residual lie?
qs.ans: In the subspace’s orthogonal complement.
wrong: In the target subspace itself in every case.
In an arbitrary direction unrelated to the subspace.
In the same direction as every spanning vector.
qs.why: The residual is perpendicular to all representable directions; otherwise an additional projection would reduce the error.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Perpendicularity of projection error to the subspace
qs.why: Inner product means operation defining geometric alignment. Projection means closest component in a subspace. Residual orthogonality means perpendicularity of projection error to the subspace.

qs.q: Order projection onto a nonzero vector.
items: Compute the target dot the spanning vector
Divide by the spanning vector’s squared norm
Multiply the spanning vector by that coefficient
qs.why: The normalization accounts for a nonunit spanning vector.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for inner products and orthogonal projection, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An **inner product** is a rule for computing lengths and angles. In ordinary Euclidean geometry it is the dot product.
The **orthogonal projection** is the closest point in the target subspace by Euclidean distance.
To project vector $b$ onto the line through nonzero vector $u$, let $c$ denote the weight on $u$. A dot denotes dot product.

p.cap: nonzero line direction

p.x: The projected vector is $cu$. Subtract it from $b$ to get the residual.
The target is a subspace, so you can move along any of its directions from the projected point.
The residual is perpendicular to every direction in the subspace. It lies in the **orthogonal complement**.

g.q: At the closest point, how is the residual oriented relative to the subspace?
o: Perpendicular
A component in the subspace could still be removed by moving toward the input.
Parallel
A parallel residual would let you keep moving toward the input along the subspace.

p.x: If a residual still has a component in the target subspace, following that component makes the distance [[smaller]].
Moving within the subspace cannot remove a perpendicular component. Any extra in-subspace displacement adds squared distance.

cards: In plain English: Independent directions can be converted into orthonormal directions without changing their span.
Gram–Schmidt subtracts projections onto earlier orthonormal directions, then normalizes the remainder.
QR factorization writes a matrix as an orthonormal-column factor times an upper-triangular factor. Stable numerical implementations often use Householder transformations.
Why it happens: subtracting earlier components removes redundancy in direction while preserving the growing span.
title: Gram–Schmidt and QR
plain: Independent directions can be converted into orthonormal directions without changing their span.

qs.q: “Remove earlier projections before normalizing this column.”
qs.ans: Normalize only the orthogonal remainder.
wrong: Normalize the raw column and assume it becomes orthogonal.
Add earlier projections instead of subtracting them.
Divide by a zero remainder when the column is dependent.
qs.why: Normalization changes length, not angle; adding retains overlap, and zero remainder signals dependence.

qs.q: Orthogonalize dimensionless v=(1,1) against q=(1,0). What is the second component of the normalized remainder?
qs.why: Subtract (1,0), leaving (0,1), already unit length.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Component left after removing earlier projections
qs.why: Orthonormal means mutually perpendicular with unit lengths. QR factorization means orthonormal-column times triangular decomposition. Orthogonal remainder means component left after removing earlier projections.

qs.q: Which orthogonalization step is flawed?
lines: Subtract projections onto previous basis directions
Check remainder magnitude
Normalize a nonzero remainder
Assume normalizing vectors alone makes them mutually perpendicular
qs.why: Length normalization does not change the angle between vectors.
qs.ans: Assume normalizing vectors alone makes them mutually perpendicular
wrong: Subtract projections onto previous basis directions
Check remainder magnitude
Normalize a nonzero remainder

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for gram–schmidt and qr, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: To make an **orthonormal** list, aim for mutually perpendicular vectors of unit length.
Subtract the projection onto the earlier direction. Resizing alone cannot remove it.

g.q: Which action removes the component along an earlier unit direction?
o: Divide by its length
That changes the length while keeping the same direction.
Subtract its projection
This removes exactly the component in the earlier direction.

p.x: In **Gram–Schmidt**, remove projections onto all earlier orthonormal directions [[before]] normalizing.
The remainder is perpendicular to the earlier vectors. Divide it by its own length to make a unit vector.
For a matrix with independent columns, **QR factorization** writes it as $QR$. The columns of $Q$ are orthonormal. The factor $R$ is upper triangular, with zeros below its diagonal.
A **Householder transformation** reflects vectors across a plane. Numerical QR often uses these reflections to zero entries while limiting rounding error.
Rescale the unit vector to recover the original remainder. Add back the projections to recover the original column.
So the new and old lists span the same space at each step. Independent inputs ensure a nonzero remainder.

cards: In plain English: An inconsistent system can still have a best approximate fit.
Least squares minimizes the squared residual norm. At a minimizer, the residual is orthogonal to the matrix column space.
Normal equations express this orthogonality. QR or SVD often avoid the conditioning penalty of explicitly forming the transpose-times-matrix product.
Why it happens: changing coefficients can improve only residual components within the column space.
title: Least squares and normal equations
plain: An inconsistent system can still have a best approximate fit.

qs.q: “The residual should be orthogonal to every model column.”
qs.ans: Check the transpose-times-residual condition.
wrong: Require every residual component to be zero in all fits.
Require the coefficient vector to be orthogonal to the data.
Assume the smallest coefficient norm alone defines every least-squares fit.
qs.why: An inconsistent model leaves residuals; coefficient orthogonality and minimum norm are different criteria.

qs.q: Fit one dimensionless constant c to data 1,2,6 by minimizing (c−1)²+(c−2)²+(c−6)². Find c.
qs.why: The minimizing constant is the mean, (1+2+6)/3=3.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Output pattern associated with one coefficient
qs.why: Least squares means minimization of squared residual norm. Normal equations means equations enforcing column-space residual orthogonality. Model column means output pattern associated with one coefficient.

qs.q: Order a linear least-squares fit.
items: Build the model matrix and data vector
Solve the least-squares problem with a suitable factorization
qs.why: A fitted coefficient vector alone does not establish model adequacy.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for least squares and normal equations, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: An inconsistent system has no exact solution. Candidate predictions can miss the data above or below.
**Least squares** minimizes the sum of squared mismatches, also called the squared residual norm.

g.q: Which score prevents opposite mismatches from canceling?
o: The sum of squared mismatches
Squaring counts mismatches of either sign and penalizes larger ones.
The signed sum of mismatches
Positive and negative mismatches can cancel without a close fit.

p.x: The **residual** is the data minus the prediction. Each model column is the output pattern for one coefficient. The columns span all achievable predictions.
At a minimizer the prediction is the orthogonal projection of the data onto this column space.
Let $A$ be the model matrix and $r$ the residual. Transposing $A$ makes each column into a row.

p.cap: ordinary least squares, at a minimizer

p.x: Every model column has zero dot product with the residual.
Changing coefficients only moves the prediction [[within]] the column space.
The perpendicular residual cannot be reduced that way. QR and SVD can solve the fit without forming $A^T A$, which squares the Euclidean condition number for a full-column-rank matrix.

cards: In plain English: Different measurement quality should change how residuals are penalized.
Weighted least squares assigns different importance to residuals. Independent measurement errors with known variances motivate inverse-variance weights.
Correlated errors require a covariance-aware metric. A good numerical fit does not prove the model captures the correct physics.
Why it happens: unreliable directions should contribute less to the fitted objective than precisely measured ones under the assumed error model.
title: Weighted fits and model sensitivity
plain: Different measurement quality should change how residuals are penalized.

qs.q: “Use inverse variance, not inverse standard deviation, for these weights.”
qs.ans: Square the uncertainty scale before taking its reciprocal.
wrong: Use the standard deviation itself as a larger-is-better weight.
Use inverse standard deviation as the quadratic weight always.
Ignore correlations even when the error model includes them.
qs.why: Quadratic residual weights use inverse variance; covariance matters when errors correlate.

qs.q: Two independent dimensionless measurements are 2 with variance 1 and 8 with variance 4. Find their inverse-variance weighted constant estimate.
qs.why: Weights are 1 and 1/4; the estimate is (2+2)/(1.25)=3.2.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Weight means coefficient penalizing a squared residual. Inverse variance means precision-based weight for independent errors. Covariance means joint variation between error components.

qs.q: Which weighted-fit note is flawed?
lines: State the error model
Use inverse variances for independent known-variance errors
Account for covariance when relevant
Treat a small fitting residual as proof of a physically correct model
qs.why: A flexible or misspecified model can fit observed data closely without representing the underlying mechanism.
qs.ans: Treat a small fitting residual as proof of a physically correct model
wrong: State the error model
Use inverse variances for independent known-variance errors
Account for covariance when relevant

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for weighted fits and model sensitivity, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Two independent sensors measure the same quantity but have different known **variances**, the expected squared spreads of their errors.
The lower-variance sensor gets the larger weight. For unbiased sensors, smaller spread means higher precision.

g.q: With inverse-variance weighting, which sensor gets the larger weight?
o: The higher-variance sensor
A larger variance means more spread and gets a smaller reciprocal weight.
The lower-variance sensor
A smaller variance gives a larger reciprocal weight.

p.x: Weighted least squares multiplies each squared mismatch by a weight before summing.
For independent errors with known positive variances, use the reciprocal of each variance. Variance is the square of standard deviation.
If measurement errors are correlated, their mismatches cannot be weighted [[separately]] using only their own variances.
Use the inverse of the error covariance matrix when it is invertible. Covariance measures how errors vary together.
Under the assumed error model, poorly measured directions receive smaller penalties.
A small fitting residual says the predictions match the measured data closely in that metric. It does not establish that the assumed physics is right.

cards: In plain English: SVD reveals how a matrix stretches orthogonal directions.
The singular value decomposition separates a matrix into orthogonal input directions, nonnegative stretches, and orthogonal output directions.
Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of the transpose-times-matrix product. They apply to rectangular matrices too.
Why it happens: that symmetric product measures the squared output norm associated with each input direction.
title: Singular values and principal stretches
plain: SVD reveals how a matrix stretches orthogonal directions.

qs.q: “Those eigenvalues are squared singular values.”
qs.ans: Take their nonnegative square roots.
wrong: Use the eigenvalues unchanged as singular values always.
Keep negative square roots as additional singular values.
Assume singular values exist only for square matrices.
qs.why: The norm relation introduces a square; singular values are nonnegative and support rectangular maps.

qs.q: A dimensionless matrix has eigenvalues 9 and 4 in AᵀA. Find its largest singular value.
qs.why: The singular values are 3 and 2; the largest is 3.

qs.q: If AᵀA has eigenvalue 16, what is the corresponding singular value of A?
qs.why: Singular values are nonnegative square roots. Sixteen omits the root, eight divides by two, and negative four chooses a forbidden negative stretch.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
qs.why: Singular value means nonnegative principal stretch factor. Right singular vector means principal input direction. Left singular vector means corresponding principal output direction.

qs.q: Order an SVD interpretation.
items: Map to the corresponding orthogonal output directions
qs.why: SVD separates direction changes from magnitude changes.

demoNeeded: Map a unit circle to an ellipse, showing singular directions and singular values.

p.x: A matrix can send some input directions to zero. **Singular values** measure the stretch magnitudes of chosen unit input directions.
Singular values are nonnegative. A zero singular value represents a direction that collapses.

g.q: Can a stretch magnitude be negative?
o: No
A stretch magnitude is an output length and may be zero.
Yes
A direction reversal changes orientation, but does not give a negative length.

p.x: **Right singular vectors** are orthonormal input directions. **Left singular vectors** are orthonormal output directions.
The **singular value decomposition**, or **SVD**, pairs each right direction that has positive stretch with a left direction. The image points along that left direction.
For real matrix $A$, $λ$ is an eigenvalue of $A^T A$, where $T$ swaps rows and columns. The associated stretch is $σ$.

p.cap: real matrix and Euclidean length

p.x: The product $A^T A$ is square even when $A$ is rectangular.
Along a unit eigenvector of $A^T A$, the eigenvalue is the [[square]] of the output length.
Taking its nonnegative square root converts squared output length to stretch.

cards: In plain English: A generalized inverse selects a well-defined solution even when ordinary inversion is unavailable.
The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse provides a minimum-norm least-squares solution. It handles rectangular and rank-deficient matrices.
In SVD coordinates, invert nonzero singular values and map zero singular directions to zero. Numerical thresholds must be stated.
Why it happens: null-space components do not improve the residual, so setting them to zero minimizes the solution norm.
title: Pseudoinverse and minimum-norm solutions
plain: A generalized inverse selects a well-defined solution even when ordinary inversion is unavailable.

qs.q: “Choose the least-squares solution with no unnecessary null component.”
qs.ans: Use the minimum-norm pseudoinverse solution.
wrong: Add arbitrary null-space components to reduce the norm always.
Invert zero singular values as ordinary reciprocals.
Assume every least-squares solution is automatically unique.
qs.why: Null additions generally increase minimum norm, zero reciprocals are undefined, and rank deficiency allows multiple fits.

qs.q: Find the minimum-Euclidean-norm dimensionless solution of x1+x2=4. What is x1?
qs.why: Equal components minimize x1²+x2² under the sum constraint, giving (2,2).

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Generalized inverse selecting minimum-norm least squares
Numerical cutoff for treating singular values as zero
qs.why: Pseudoinverse means generalized inverse selecting minimum-norm least squares. Minimum norm means smallest euclidean solution magnitude. Rank threshold means numerical cutoff for treating singular values as zero.

qs.q: Which pseudoinverse implementation is flawed?
lines: Inspect the singular values
State a numerical rank threshold
Invert retained nonzero singular values
Divide by every singular value including exact zeros
qs.why: Zero singular values must not be inverted.
qs.ans: Divide by every singular value including exact zeros
wrong: Inspect the singular values
State a numerical rank threshold
Invert retained nonzero singular values

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for pseudoinverse and minimum-norm solutions, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Multiple inputs can give the same best fit when the map has **null directions**, which have zero output.
Set the null component to zero. The remaining perpendicular components keep the same fit.

g.q: Which change to a null component can reduce the input length while keeping the fit?
o: Make it larger
That increases input length without affecting the output.
Set it to zero
The fit is unchanged, and removing a perpendicular null component reduces the length.

p.x: The **Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse** returns the least-squares solution with smallest Euclidean norm.
It works for rectangular matrices. It also works when the matrix is **rank-deficient**, meaning its rank is smaller than both its row count and its column count.
In singular-vector coordinates, divide by a nonzero singular stretch to undo it. Zero-stretch directions are [[left out]].
A **rank threshold** is the cutoff below which software treats stretches as zero. State it, since it changes which directions are kept.
The **null space** is perpendicular to the input directions with nonzero stretch.
Changing the null part cannot improve the fit. It adds a nonnegative squared length to the solution, so setting it to zero gives the minimum norm.

cards: In plain English: A small number of dominant directions can summarize much of a dataset.
Truncated SVD retains the largest singular values and corresponding directions. It gives best rank-limited approximation in spectral and Frobenius norms.
Principal component analysis of centered data identifies directions of greatest variance. Centering and feature scaling affect interpretation.
Why it happens: orthogonal modal contributions separate squared approximation error, so discarding the smallest stretches loses the least energy.
title: Low-rank approximation and PCA
plain: A small number of dominant directions can summarize much of a dataset.

qs.q: “Center the data before interpreting variance directions.”
qs.ans: Remove the feature means for standard covariance PCA.
wrong: Treat the data mean as irrelevant without centering.
Assume changing feature units never changes principal directions.
Retain the smallest singular values as the dominant variance modes.
qs.why: Means and scaling affect covariance; dominant modes correspond to the largest singular values.

qs.q: A dimensionless matrix has singular values 5,3,1. What is the spectral-norm error of its best rank-two approximation?
qs.why: The spectral error equals the largest discarded singular value, which is 1.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Approximation retaining selected largest singular modes
qs.why: Truncated SVD means approximation retaining selected largest singular modes. Principal component means direction of high centered-data variance. Spectral norm means largest singular value.

qs.q: Order a standard centered-data PCA workflow.
items: Compute principal directions and their explained variance
Retain and validate the desired number of components
qs.why: Centering and scaling define the geometry before decomposition.

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for low-rank approximation and pca, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: A **rank limit** caps the number of independent directions the approximation can keep.
Keep the largest singular values and their paired directions. This is **truncated SVD**.

g.q: Which singular stretches should an optimal truncated SVD keep?
o: The largest
Keeping the largest avoids throwing away the strongest contributions.
The smallest
That leaves the strongest contributions in the error.

p.x: The **spectral norm** measures the largest stretch of a matrix. The spectral error of truncation is the largest discarded stretch, or zero if none are lost.
The **Frobenius norm** is the root of the sum of squared entries. Squared Frobenius truncation error sums the squares of discarded stretches.
In standard covariance **principal component analysis** (PCA), center each feature [[before]] finding variance directions.
Subtract each feature mean. With observations as rows, the centered matrix's right singular vectors give the **principal components**, ordered by decreasing variance.
PCA orders directions by variance. Features such as length and mass can have very different scales.
A change in feature scale can change which PCA directions dominate. Pick scales that make variance meaningful.

g.q: Can changing one feature's scale change which direction PCA ranks first?
o: No
Centering removes offsets but does not undo rescaling.
Yes
Rescaling changes that feature's variance relative to the others.

cards: In plain English: A controlled penalty can stabilize an inverse problem by accepting some bias.
Tikhonov regularization adds a squared solution penalty to squared residual error. Its strength trades data fit against solution magnitude.
Tiny singular values amplify measurement noise during inversion. Regularization reduces that amplification but does not recover information that was never measured.
Why it happens: a penalty discourages extreme coefficients in weakly observed directions, improving stability at the cost of bias.
title: Regularization and ill-posed inverses
plain: A controlled penalty can stabilize an inverse problem by accepting some bias.

qs.q: “The penalty stabilizes the weakly observed directions.”
qs.ans: Expect a bias-versus-noise-amplification tradeoff.
wrong: Assume the penalty creates missing measurement information.
Assume more regularization always improves every prediction.
Require regularization to leave the least-squares solution unchanged.
qs.why: Regularization changes the estimator and trades errors; it neither creates information nor improves every metric monotonically.

qs.q: Minimize dimensionless (2x−4)²+x². What is the regularized minimizer?
qs.why: Differentiating gives 4(2x−4)+2x=10x−16=0, so x=1.6.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Inverse problem lacking robust unique recovery
Systematic estimator shift introduced by assumptions or penalties
qs.why: Regularization means penalty or constraint stabilizing estimation. Ill-posed inverse means inverse problem lacking robust unique recovery. Bias means systematic estimator shift introduced by assumptions or penalties.

qs.q: Which inverse-problem claim is flawed?
lines: Inspect weak singular directions
Select a penalty using justified criteria
Report the fit-stability tradeoff
Claim regularization reconstructs all unmeasured information exactly
qs.why: A penalty adds assumptions, not new measurements.
qs.ans: Claim regularization reconstructs all unmeasured information exactly
wrong: Inspect weak singular directions
Select a penalty using justified criteria
Report the fit-stability tradeoff

demoNeeded: Create an interactive example for regularization and ill-posed inverses, linking adjustable inputs to the lesson’s stated result and highlighting where its assumptions fail.

p.x: Suppose a map barely responds to a direction, but the measurements along its output direction contain noise.
Dividing by a tiny stretch amplifies noise. An inverse can therefore be very sensitive to data errors.

g.q: What does dividing by the tiny singular value do to that noise?
o: Amplifies it
Division by a small positive stretch makes the inferred noise component larger.
Suppresses it
Suppression would require damping the inverse instead of fully dividing by the stretch.

p.x: **Tikhonov regularization** here adds a penalty proportional to squared solution length to the squared residual error.
The **residual** is data minus prediction. Adding a penalty for solution length can favor a smaller solution with a larger residual.
A stronger penalty favors [[smaller]] coefficients in weakly observed directions.
The solution becomes less sensitive to noisy measurements but can be pulled away from the true value even for clean data. That systematic shift is **bias**.
An **ill-posed** inverse may fail to have a unique solution or may change sharply under tiny data changes.
Regularization can stabilize the estimate by favoring some inputs. It cannot restore data about a direction that was never measured.

cards: In plain English: In a requirements document, a few small words decide what is promised, what is hoped for and what is merely allowed.

In requirements writing each verb has one job. “Shall” states a binding requirement that must be verified. “Should” states a goal. “May” grants permission. “Will” states a fact or intent, not a requirement.
Why it matters: only “shall” statements get verified and paid for. A need written as “should” can be skipped without breaking the contract, because nobody promised it.
Some organizations write “must” instead of “shall” for plain language. Either works if the document defines it once and uses it the same way everywhere.
Keep one requirement per sentence. “The pump shall deliver 20 L/min and run quietly” hides two requirements, and the vague one cannot be tested.

How it sounds at work: “Is that a shall or a should?” asks whether something is promised or only hoped for. “That’s a will statement” means the line describes a fact, so nobody has to test it. “Two shalls in one sentence” means split the sentence so each promise can be checked on its own.
title: Shall, will, should, may
plain: In a requirements document, a few small words decide what is promised, what is hoped for and what is merely allowed.
talk: “Is that a shall or a should?”
“That’s a will statement, not a requirement.”
“Split that, it’s two shalls in one sentence.”

qs.q: Match each word to what it means in a requirements document.
qs.why: Shall binds and is verified, should is a goal, may permits and will describes something that is true or planned.

qs.q: “We’d really like it to weigh under 2 kg, but it isn’t a deal-breaker.”
qs.ans: The mass should be less than 2 kg.
wrong: The mass shall be less than 2 kg.
The mass will be less than 2 kg.
The mass may be less than 2 kg.
qs.why: A wish that is not binding is a goal, which takes “should”. “Shall” would make it a pass or fail requirement; “will” claims it as fact; “may” only grants permission.

qs.q: “That’s a will, not a shall. Nobody has to verify it.”
qs.ans: The sentence describes intent, so no test is owed for it.
wrong: The sentence is binding, so it needs a test plan.
The sentence is a goal, so it is tested only if time allows.
The sentence grants permission, so the supplier decides.
