qs.why: “Will” states a fact or intent. Only “shall” statements carry verification; goals take “should” and permission takes “may”.

qs.q: A spec extract. Which line is written so it cannot be verified as a single requirement?
lines: The enclosure shall be rated IP65.
The fan shall move at least 40 m³/h at 12 V.
The display shall be readable and should look modern.
The supplier may use either M4 or M5 fasteners.
qs.why: It packs a requirement and a goal into one sentence, and both are vague. Split it and give “readable” a measurable condition, such as a viewing distance and lighting level.
qs.ans: The display shall be readable and should look modern.
wrong: The enclosure shall be rated IP65.
The fan shall move at least 40 m³/h at 12 V.
The supplier may use either M4 or M5 fasteners.

qs.q: A document writes “must” for every requirement and never uses “shall”. What is the best reading?
qs.ans: Fine, if “must” is defined once and used consistently
wrong: Invalid, because only “shall” creates a requirement
Unclear, because “must” always means a goal
Risky, because “must” means the buyer pays extra
qs.why: Plain-language style guides favor “must”. What matters is a single defined meaning applied the same way throughout the document.

qs.q: Order these words from the strongest commitment to the weakest.
qs.why: “Shall” is a promise that gets verified. “Should” is a goal the team aims for but can miss without breaking the contract. “May” only gives permission and commits nobody to anything.

cards: In plain English: A good requirement says exactly what “done” looks like, so two people would agree whether the product passes.
A testable requirement names the subject, a measurable quantity, a value with units and a tolerance, and the conditions. “The motor shall reach 3000 ± 50 rpm within 2 s at 24 V, 25 °C.”
Why vague words fail: “adequate”, “fast”, “user-friendly”, “minimize” and “as required” have no pass line. Two honest engineers can test the same part and disagree.
Each requirement gets a verification method: inspection (look or measure), analysis (calculation or model), demonstration (operate it, no instruments) or test (operate it and record measured data).
Add a rationale: one line saying why the number exists. When someone asks to relax it later, the rationale tells you what breaks.
How it sounds at work: “What’s the pass line on ‘lightweight’?” “Verification method: test, not analysis.” “Put the rationale in, or this number gets negotiated away.”
title: Write a testable requirement
plain: A good requirement says exactly what “done” looks like, so two people would agree whether the product passes.
talk: “What’s the pass line on ‘lightweight’?”
“Verification method: test, not analysis.”
“Put the rationale in, or this number gets negotiated away.”

qs.q: Which requirement can be verified as written?
lines: The latch shall be easy to open.
The latch shall open with no more than 20 N at the handle.
The latch shall open as quickly as possible.
The latch shall have adequate strength.
qs.ans: The latch shall open with no more than 20 N at the handle.
qs.why: Only the 20 N line gives a quantity, a value and a limit someone can measure. The others use “easy”, “as quickly as possible” and “adequate”, which have no pass line.
wrong: The latch shall be easy to open.
The latch shall open as quickly as possible.
The latch shall have adequate strength.

qs.q: Match each verification method to an example.
pairs: Measure the bore with a gauge
Log temperature during a 2 h run
qs.why: Inspection checks by looking or measuring, analysis by calculation, demonstration by operating without recorded data and test by operating with measured, recorded data.

qs.q: “Verification is by analysis, but I want a test at the end.”
qs.ans: A calculation proves it now, and a measured run must confirm it later.
wrong: A visual check proves it now, and a calculation confirms it later.
A measured run proves it now, and a design review confirms it later.
A demonstration proves it now, and an audit confirms it later.
qs.why: Analysis means calculation or modeling. A test means operating the item and recording measured data, so the customer wants measured confirmation on top of the calculation.

qs.q: “It needs to be pretty fast at warming up.”
qs.ans: The heater shall reach 60 °C within 90 s from 20 °C.
wrong: The heater shall warm up quickly from 20 °C.
The heater shall reach 60 °C as fast as practical.
The heater shall reach operating temperature without delay.
qs.why: Only the first gives start and end values with a time limit. “Quickly”, “as fast as practical” and “without delay” cannot be measured against a pass line.

qs.q: A requirement reads “speed shall be 3000 ± 50 rpm”. What is the highest acceptable speed, in rpm?
qs.why: 3000 + 50 = 3050 rpm. The tolerance applies both ways, so the band is 2950 to 3050 rpm.

qs.q: Order the steps for turning a vague need into a requirement.
items: Name what the need is about
Pick the quantity that shows it
Set a value, units and tolerance
qs.why: Subject first, then the measurable quantity, the number, the conditions it holds under and finally how it will be checked.

cards: In plain English: Big goals get broken into smaller promises for each part, and every small promise should point back to the goal it serves.
Flow-down splits a system requirement into subsystem requirements. A 5 kg drone mass limit becomes budgets for frame, battery, motors and payload, with a margin held back.
A derived requirement comes from a design choice, not the customer. Picking a 6S battery creates a requirement that the motor controller accepts 25.2 V.
Traceability links every child requirement to its parent. Why: when a parent changes, you can find every child it affects; a child with no parent is either missing a link or gold plating.
TBD (to be determined) means no value yet. TBR (to be resolved) means a value exists but is not confirmed. Each should carry an owner and a closure date.
How it sounds at work: “Who owns that TBD and when does it close?” “That’s a derived requirement off the battery choice.” “This one has no parent. Is it gold plating?”
title: Flow-down, TBD and traceability
plain: Big goals get broken into smaller promises for each part, and every small promise should point back to the goal it serves.
talk: “Who owns that TBD and when does it close?”
“That’s a derived requirement off the battery choice.”
“This one has no parent. Is it gold plating?”

qs.q: A drone has a 5.0 kg mass limit and the team holds 10% of it as margin. The frame is 1.2 kg, battery 1.6 kg and motors 0.8 kg. How much mass, in kg, is left for the payload?
qs.why: Allocatable mass is 5.0 × 0.9 = 4.5 kg. 4.5 − 1.2 − 1.6 − 0.8 = 0.9 kg. Forgetting the margin gives 1.4 kg.

qs.q: “That requirement’s an orphan.”
qs.ans: It has no link to any parent requirement.
wrong: It has no verification method assigned yet.
It has no value assigned and is still open.
It has no supplier assigned to deliver it.
qs.why: An orphan is a requirement that traces to no parent. It may be a missing link, or work nobody asked for.

qs.q: The spec says “max current 2.0 A (TBR)”. What does TBR tell you?
qs.ans: A value exists but still needs confirmation
wrong: No value has been chosen yet
The value is final and approved
The value applies only during test
qs.why: TBR means to be resolved: a working number is in place. TBD would mean no number yet.

qs.q: “We picked a 6S battery, so now the controller has to handle 25.2 volts.”
qs.ans: The battery choice created a derived requirement.
wrong: The battery choice created a customer requirement.
The battery choice created a waived requirement.
The battery choice created an orphan requirement.
qs.why: A requirement that follows from a design decision, not from the customer, is derived. It should still trace to the parent it supports.

qs.q: Review this mass flow-down. Which line is the problem?
lines: System mass shall not exceed 5.0 kg.
Frame mass shall not exceed 1.2 kg.
Battery mass shall not exceed 1.6 kg.
Payload mass shall not exceed 2.4 kg.
qs.why: 1.2 + 1.6 + 2.4 = 5.2 kg already passes the 5.0 kg limit before motors or margin. The children cannot all be met while meeting the parent.
qs.ans: Payload mass shall not exceed 2.4 kg.
wrong: System mass shall not exceed 5.0 kg.
Frame mass shall not exceed 1.2 kg.
Battery mass shall not exceed 1.6 kg.

qs.q: A parent requirement changes. Order the response.
items: Find every child that traces to it
Check each child against the new value
Update or retire the affected children
Re-run verification for the changed ones
qs.why: Traceability exists for this: trace down, assess, change, then re-verify what changed.

cards: In plain English: Engineering contracts use a handful of phrases that decide who does what and which document wins when two disagree.
A statement of work (SOW) says what work the supplier does. A specification says what the product must be. Mixing them buries requirements where nobody verifies them.
An order-of-precedence clause ranks the documents. Why it exists: drawings, specs and the contract will eventually disagree, and the clause settles which one governs.
“Furnish” means supply. “Install” means put in place. “Furnish and install” means both. A missing word decides who buys or who fits the part.
“Including but not limited to” marks a list as examples, not a complete list. “And/or” is ambiguous; good practice writes “A, B or both”.
How it sounds at work: “Check the order of precedence before you argue the drawing.” “Is that furnish only, or furnish and install?” “That’s SOW language, it belongs in the spec.”
title: Contract wording engineers meet
plain: Engineering contracts use a handful of phrases that decide who does what and which document wins when two disagree.
talk: “Check the order of precedence before you argue the drawing.”
“Is that furnish only, or furnish and install?”
“That’s SOW language, it belongs in the spec.”

qs.q: “Per the order of precedence, the spec governs over the drawing.”
qs.ans: Where they conflict, follow the specification.
wrong: Where they conflict, follow the newer document.
Where they conflict, ask the supplier which to follow.
Where they conflict, follow the drawing’s notes.
qs.why: An order-of-precedence clause ranks the documents ahead of time, so a conflict is settled by the ranking, not by dates or by asking.

qs.q: Match each phrase to its meaning.
qs.why: Furnish supplies, install fits, “including but not limited to” makes a list non-exhaustive and order of precedence ranks documents.

qs.q: “You buy the valves, we’ll mount them.”
qs.ans: The supplier shall furnish the valves; installation is by the buyer.
wrong: The supplier shall furnish and install the valves.
The supplier shall install the valves furnished by others.
The supplier may furnish the valves at the buyer’s option.
qs.why: The supplier supplies (furnishes) and the buyer installs. “Furnish and install” gives both to the supplier, and “may” makes supply optional.

qs.q: Contract extract. Which line will cause an argument later?
lines: The supplier shall deliver drawings in PDF and STEP.
Acceptance tests shall follow procedure ATP-102 rev C.
The supplier shall provide calibration and/or training.
Payment is due 30 days after acceptance.
qs.why: “And/or” leaves open whether one or both are owed. Write “calibration, training or both, at the buyer’s choice”, or name exactly what is required.
qs.ans: The supplier shall provide calibration and/or training.
wrong: The supplier shall deliver drawings in PDF and STEP.
Acceptance tests shall follow procedure ATP-102 rev C.
Payment is due 30 days after acceptance.

qs.q: A temperature limit appears only in the statement of work, not in the product specification. What is the main risk?
qs.ans: It may never be verified, because tests follow the specification
wrong: It becomes unenforceable, because only drawings are binding
It doubles in strictness, because both documents apply
It transfers to the buyer, because the SOW is the buyer’s
qs.why: Test procedures are written from the specification. A product requirement hidden in the SOW is easy to miss when verification is planned.

qs.q: A drawing and the specification disagree on a surface finish. Order the response.
items: Follow the document it ranks higher
Raise the conflict formally with the other party
qs.why: The clause tells you which governs today; a formal query and correction stop the same conflict recurring.

cards: In plain English: When a part will not, or did not, match its drawing, there are formal ways to decide whether it can still be used.
A deviation is permission, granted before building, to depart from a requirement for a set number of units or a set time. A waiver accepts items already built that do not conform.
Some programs fold both into one term, a variance. Either way, the requirement itself does not change; that takes an engineering change.
A material review board (MRB) decides what to do with nonconforming parts: use as is, rework, repair, scrap or return to the supplier.
Why rework and repair differ: rework brings the part fully back to the drawing. Repair makes it usable but still nonconforming, so it usually needs customer approval.
How it sounds at work: “We’ll need a deviation for the next fifty housings.” “MRB dispositioned it repair, not rework.” “Don’t waive it every lot. Change the drawing.”
title: Deviations, waivers and MRB
plain: When a part will not, or did not, match its drawing, there are formal ways to decide whether it can still be used.
talk: “We’ll need a deviation for the next fifty housings.”
“MRB dispositioned it repair, not rework.”
“Don’t waive it every lot. Change the drawing.”

qs.q: Match each MRB disposition to what happens to the part.
pairs: Brought back fully to the drawing
qs.why: Use as is accepts it, rework restores full conformance, repair makes it usable while still nonconforming and scrap removes it.

qs.q: Before production starts, a supplier knows 40 castings will miss a wall-thickness callout. What should they request?
qs.ans: A deviation for those 40 units
wrong: A waiver for those 40 units
A drawing change for all future units
An MRB disposition after inspection
qs.why: A deviation is approved before the parts are made, for a set quantity. A waiver covers parts already built; a drawing change alters the requirement permanently.

qs.q: “That’s the fourth waiver on this callout. Fix the drawing.”
qs.ans: The requirement keeps being missed, so change the requirement itself.
wrong: The parts keep failing, so scrap the remaining stock.
The supplier keeps slipping, so find another supplier.
The test keeps failing, so rewrite the test procedure.
qs.why: Repeated waivers on one requirement suggest the requirement is wrong or unachievable. An engineering change fixes the source instead of excusing each lot.

qs.q: “We machined the bore oversize, sleeved it back to nominal, and it still isn’t what the drawing shows.”
qs.ans: The part was repaired, not reworked.
wrong: The part was reworked, not repaired.
The part was deviated, not waived.
The part was scrapped, not repaired.
qs.why: A sleeve makes the part work but it no longer matches the drawing, which is repair. Rework would mean it fully conforms again.

qs.q: Review this nonconformance record. Which line is wrong?
lines: Finding: 3 brackets with hole position out by 0.15 mm
Disposition: rework by re-drilling to the drawing position
Disposition: repair with bushing; customer approval attached
Disposition: use as is; drawing updated by this waiver
qs.ans: Disposition: use as is; drawing updated by this waiver
qs.why: A waiver accepts the parts but does not change the drawing. Changing the requirement needs a separate engineering change.
wrong: Finding: 3 brackets with hole position out by 0.15 mm
Disposition: rework by re-drilling to the drawing position
Disposition: repair with bushing; customer approval attached

qs.q: Order the path of a nonconforming part.
items: The part is tagged and segregated
The review board sets a disposition
The disposition is carried out and recorded
qs.why: Find it, quarantine it so it cannot be used by mistake, decide, then act and document.

cards: In plain English: Small words like “within”, “up to” and “between” can make the same number mean two different things.
“Not to exceed 50 °C” and “≤ 50 °C” match. “Less than 50 °C” excludes 50 itself. When the edge value matters, say whether it is included.
“Within 5%” needs a reference: 5% of the nominal, the reading or full scale? A ±5% of full-scale sensor on a 100 kPa range is ±5 kPa at every reading.
“Shall be capable of” promises ability, not performance. “The pump shall be capable of 20 L/min” passes even if the installed pump never delivers it.
Why passive voice is risky: “The data shall be archived” hides who archives it. Name the actor: “The ground station shall archive the data.”
How it sounds at work: “Five percent of what: reading or full scale?” “Is fifty inclusive?” “Who’s the subject of that shall?”
title: Limits, bounds and ambiguity
plain: Small words like “within”, “up to” and “between” can make the same number mean two different things.
talk: “Five percent of what: reading or full scale?”
“Is fifty inclusive?”
“Who’s the subject of that shall?”

qs.q: A pressure sensor has accuracy ±2% of full scale on a 0–500 kPa range. At a reading of 100 kPa, what is the error band, in ±kPa?
qs.why: 2% of the 500 kPa full scale is ±10 kPa at any reading. Taking 2% of the 100 kPa reading would give ±2 kPa, five times too optimistic.

qs.q: Which wording includes exactly 50 °C as passing?
qs.ans: Shall not exceed 50 °C
wrong: Shall be less than 50 °C
Shall be below 50 °C
Shall stay under 50 °C
qs.why: “Not exceed” means at most 50, so 50 passes. “Less than”, “below” and “under” all exclude the value itself.

qs.q: “That’s a capable-of requirement. It won’t catch an install problem.”
qs.ans: It checks the part can do it, not that it does it in the system.
wrong: It checks the system does it, not that the part can.
It checks the drawing shows it, not that the part has it.
It checks the supplier claims it, not that a test exists.
qs.why: “Capable of” verifies ability, usually on the bench. A plumbing restriction in the installed system could still keep flow below target.

qs.q: “Somebody needs to back up the logs every night.”
qs.ans: The server shall back up the logs every 24 h.
wrong: The logs shall be backed up every 24 h.
Logs should be backed up nightly as needed.
The logs will be backed up every 24 h.
qs.why: Naming the actor makes ownership and verification clear. The passive version hides who does it, “should” makes it a goal and “will” only states intent.

qs.q: Review these limits. Which one is ambiguous as written?
lines: Supply voltage shall be 12.0 ± 0.5 V.
Flow shall be at least 20 L/min at 2 bar.
Housing temperature shall not exceed 60 °C.
Output shall be accurate within 1%.
qs.why: “Within 1%” gives no reference: of reading, of full scale or of nominal? The answer changes the allowed error by a large factor at low readings.
qs.ans: Output shall be accurate within 1%.
wrong: Supply voltage shall be 12.0 ± 0.5 V.
Flow shall be at least 20 L/min at 2 bar.
Housing temperature shall not exceed 60 °C.

qs.q: Rank these sensor specs by allowed error at a 20 kPa reading on a 0–200 kPa sensor, largest first.
qs.why: Errors: 2% of 200 = 4 kPa; 1% of 200 = 2 kPa; 5% of 20 = 1 kPa; 2% of 20 = 0.4 kPa.

cards: In plain English: A pin pulled sideways tends to get sliced. Giving it two places to share the load halves the stress.
Shear stress is a force parallel to a surface divided by that surface’s area: τ = V/A. A pin loaded sideways is sliced, not stretched, so its cross-section A = πd²/4 resists.
Single shear: one plane cuts the pin, as in a lap joint. Double shear: a clevis puts two planes through the pin, each carrying half the load, so τ = F/(2A).
Why it matters: moving from single to double shear halves the stress with the same pin. That is why clevises and yokes are common on heavily loaded pivots.
τ = V/A is an average. The true peak in a round pin is higher, near its center, and the plate holes must also be checked in bearing.
How it sounds at work: “It’s in double shear, so the pin’s fine.” “Check bearing on the clevis holes too.”
title: Pins and bolts in shear
plain: A pin pulled sideways tends to get sliced. Giving it two places to share the load halves the stress.
talk: “It’s in double shear, so the pin’s fine.”
“Check bearing on the clevis holes too.”

qs.q: A 10 mm diameter pin carries 8 kN in single shear. What is the average shear stress, in MPa?
The same 8 kN load goes through the same 10 mm pin, now in double shear. What is the average shear stress, in MPa?
qs.why: Two planes share the load: τ = 8000/(2 × 78.54) = 50.93 MPa, half the single-shear value.

qs.q: Which change halves the shear stress in a pin without changing the load or the pin?
qs.ans: Moving it from single to double shear
wrong: Halving the length of the pin
Doubling the thickness of each plate
Using a pin with twice the yield strength
qs.why: Double shear doubles the area resisting the load. Length and plate thickness don’t change the sheared area, and a stronger material raises capacity, not stress.

qs.q: “The pin gets cut in two places, so each cut only sees half the load.”
qs.ans: The pin is in double shear.
wrong: The pin is in single shear.
The pin is in bearing.
The pin is in tension.
qs.why: Two shear planes is double shear. Bearing is the crushing contact between pin and hole; tension pulls along the pin’s axis.

qs.q: “Pin’s fine in shear; it’s the holes I’m worried about in bearing.”
qs.ans: The plate holes may crush or stretch before the pin shears.
wrong: The pin may bend before the plate holes see any load.
The holes may be drilled too small for the pin to fit.
The pin may stretch along its axis under the load.
qs.why: Bearing stress is the contact pressure between the pin and the hole wall, roughly F/(d × t). Thin plates can fail there first.

qs.q: Each joint carries 10 kN. Rank by average pin shear stress, highest first.
qs.why: τ = F/(n·πd²/4): 199, 99.5, 88.4 and 44.2 MPa. A 50% larger diameter more than doubles the area.

p.x: Pull two joined plates sideways in opposite directions. They push on the pin where they meet.
The pin can fail across that cut. A joint can spread the same force over two cuts through the pin instead of one.
The force creating **shear stress** acts [[parallel]] to the surface it acts on.

p.cap: Average across one shear plane

p.x: If a cut crosses a round pin of diameter $d$, the area is $πd^2/4$.
A **lap joint** overlaps two plates, so the pin takes the total force $F$ across one cut. This is single shear.
A **clevis** is a fork with a plate between its ears. A centered load puts half of $F$ across each cut. This is double shear.

p.cap: Symmetric double shear, with area A per cut

g.q: If both ears of a symmetric clevis share the load evenly, how much force crosses each cut through its pin?
o: Half the total force
The two cuts carry equal shares, which add to the total force.
One third of the total force
There are three plates, but the load crosses two cuts through the pin.
All of the total force
That is the single-shear result. Two equal load paths each carry only half.

p.x: Compare a 10.0 mm pin carrying 8.00 kN in single shear and symmetric double shear.
With the same pin and load, double shear halves the average stress. That's why a forked joint is useful on a heavily loaded pivot.
The stress from $V/A$ is an [[average]] across the cut.
The local stress can be higher. In the ideal round beam model it peaks at mid-depth, away from the outside faces.
Also check **bearing**, the contact pressure on a hole wall. Average bearing stress uses the contact force divided by pin diameter times plate thickness.
“The pin passes the double-shear check. Check bearing on the clevis holes too.”
Both averages fall to a quarter of their original values. The pin area grows with $d^2$ and the projected hole area with diameter times thickness.
Check both failure modes. A pin can pass a shear check while pressure at a hole deforms its plate.

g.q: Double the pin diameter and plate thickness. Keep the force and load split fixed. Which average stress falls by a larger fraction?
o: Hole bearing stress
Bearing area quadruples, but the pin's cross-section quadruples too.
Pin shear stress
The pin's cross-section quadruples. The projected bearing area also quadruples because both dimensions double.
They fall by the same fraction
Both resisting areas quadruple under the same force.

cards: In plain English: Inside a loaded beam, layers try to slide past each other. That sliding stress is strongest at the middle of the beam’s height.
A beam carrying a shear force V has shear stress inside it: τ = VQ/(Ib). Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level checked, I the second moment, b the width there.
Why it peaks in the middle: Q is largest at the neutral axis, where the most area lies beyond the cut, and zero at the top and bottom faces, which are free surfaces.
For a rectangle the profile is a parabola with τmax = 1.5 V/A. For a solid circle τmax = 4V/(3A). The average V/A understates the peak.
In an I-beam the narrow web makes b small, so the web carries most of the shear and τmax ≈ V divided by the web area. The flanges carry the bending.
How it sounds at work: “Shear’s carried by the web.” “Peak shear is at the neutral axis, one and a half times the average.”
title: Transverse shear in beams
plain: Inside a loaded beam, layers try to slide past each other. That sliding stress is strongest at the middle of the beam’s height.
talk: “Shear’s carried by the web.”
“Peak shear is at the neutral axis, one and a half times the average.”

qs.q: A rectangular beam 50 mm wide and 100 mm tall carries a shear force V = 10 kN. What is the maximum transverse shear stress, in MPa?
qs.why: A = 5000 mm², so V/A = 2.0 MPa. For a rectangle τmax = 1.5 V/A = 3.0 MPa, at the neutral axis.

qs.q: Where across the height of a rectangular beam is transverse shear stress largest?
qs.ans: At the neutral axis
wrong: At the top and bottom faces
Halfway between the axis and each face
Equal everywhere across the height
qs.why: Q is largest at the neutral axis and zero at the free top and bottom faces, so the parabola peaks in the middle.

qs.q: A solid round shaft 20 mm in diameter carries a transverse shear force of 6 kN. What is the maximum transverse shear stress, in MPa?
qs.why: A = π × 20²/4 = 314.2 mm², V/A = 19.10 MPa. For a solid circle τmax = 4V/(3A) = 25.46 MPa.

qs.q: “The thin vertical part of the I-beam is doing almost all of the shear work.”
qs.ans: The web carries the shear.
wrong: The flanges carry the shear.
The neutral axis carries the bending.
The fillets carry the torsion.
qs.why: The web is the vertical plate of an I-beam. Its small width b makes τ = VQ/(Ib) large there, so it carries most of V.

qs.q: A shear check on a 50 × 100 mm rectangular beam with V = 10 kN. Which line is wrong?
lines: Average shear: V/A = 10 kN / 5000 mm² = 2.0 MPa
Shear stress is zero at the top and bottom faces
Peak shear sits at the neutral axis
Peak shear equals the average, 2.0 MPa
qs.why: For a rectangle the peak is 1.5 times the average: 3.0 MPa. Using the average understates it by a third.
qs.ans: Peak shear equals the average, 2.0 MPa
wrong: Average shear: V/A = 10 kN / 5000 mm² = 2.0 MPa
Shear stress is zero at the top and bottom faces
Peak shear sits at the neutral axis

qs.q: A thin-walled round tube carries a transverse shear force V. About how large is its peak transverse shear stress?
qs.ans: 2 V/A
wrong: V/A
qs.why: For a thin-walled tube the peak, at the neutral axis, is about twice the average. 1.5 is the rectangle and 4/3 the solid circle.

p.x: Load a beam sideways and imagine it as a stack of thin layers. The load makes the layers try to slide past each other.
That sliding action creates **transverse shear stress**. In a rectangular section it is strongest at mid-depth.

vars: whole section's second area moment about the neutral axis
width where you check the stress

p.x: The **neutral axis** is where bending produces no lengthwise stretch. $Q$ is the area beyond the cut times its center's distance from that axis.
Hold $V$, $Q$ and $I$ fixed. Shear stress then varies [[inversely]] with the width at the cut.

p.cap: Elastic beam theory, away from concentrated loads

p.x: In a rectangular beam the width is constant. To find $Q$ at any height, take the area above that cut and multiply by its center's distance from the neutral axis.
At the top face there is no area above the cut. $Q$ and the shear stress are zero there.
At the bottom, the entire section's area balances about the neutral axis, so $Q$ is zero again. The largest $Q$ is at the neutral axis.

g.q: At the free top face of a rectangular beam, how large is the transverse shear stress?
o: Zero
No area lies above that cut, and a free face has no applied sliding force.
Greater than zero
That assumes some load transfers across the free face. The layers above the cut have vanished.

p.x: With cross-sectional area $A$, the average shear stress is $V/A$. For these solid sections, elastic beam theory gives a larger peak at mid-depth.
A 50.0 mm by 100 mm rectangle has area 5,000 mm². With 10.0 kN of shear force, its average is 2.00 MPa and its peak is 3.00 MPa.
The **web** is the thin upright plate in an I-beam. The **flanges** are its wide top and bottom plates.
The web carries most of the vertical shear. The flanges carry most of the bending through tension and compression.
For a thin web, its small width makes $VQ/(Ib)$ large there. A first estimate of peak shear is $V$ divided by the web area.

g.q: In a typical I-beam, which part carries most of the vertical shear force?
o: The web
Shear stress stays comparatively high along the tall, narrow web.
The flanges
The flanges sit far from the neutral axis, which helps them resist bending. Vertical shear is concentrated in the web.

p.x: “The web carries the shear” identifies the main shear path in an I-beam. The peak stress still depends on the section's shape.
For transverse shear on a thin-walled round tube, the peak is [[greater than]] the average $V/A$.
Use the factor for the shape you're checking. A solid rectangle peaks at $1.50 V/A$.

cards: A point inside a loaded part has normal stresses σx and σy and a shear τxy on a tiny x–y square. Turn that square and the three numbers change, even though the load didn’t.
Mohr’s circle draws every turned square at once. Plot X = (σx, τxy) for the x face and Y = (σy, −τxy) for the y face. The line between them is a diameter.
Center C = (σx + σy)/2, the average normal stress. Radius R = √(((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²).
Where the circle crosses the σ axis the shear is zero. Those are the principal stresses: σ1 = C + R and σ2 = C − R. The top of the circle is the largest in-plane shear, τmax = R.
Turning the part by θ moves you 2θ around the circle. The σ1 direction is θp = ½·atan(2τxy/(σx − σy)) from the x axis.
title: Mohr’s circle

qs.q: σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = 40 MPa. Where is the center of Mohr’s circle, in MPa?
Same element: σx = 80, σy = 20, τxy = 40 MPa. What is the radius of the circle, in MPa?
With C = 50 MPa and R = 50 MPa, what is the largest principal stress σ1, in MPa?
qs.why: σ1 = C + R = 100 MPa, and σ2 = C − R = 0.

qs.q: Where on Mohr’s circle is the largest in-plane shear stress?
qs.ans: At the top and bottom of the circle, where τ = R
wrong: Where the circle crosses the σ axis
At the center of the circle
At point X, the x face
qs.why: Shear is the vertical coordinate, so it peaks at the top and bottom, equal to the radius. The σ-axis crossings have zero shear.

qs.q: You turn the stress element 30° on the drawing. How far around Mohr’s circle do you move?
qs.why: Angles on the circle are double the angles on the part.

qs.q: Pure shear: σx = σy = 0 and τxy = 30 MPa. What is σ1, in MPa?
qs.why: C = 0 and R = 30, so σ1 = +30 MPa and σ2 = −30 MPa: pure shear is equal tension and compression on planes at 45°.

qs.q: Match each part of Mohr’s circle to what it means.
qs.why: Those four facts are enough to read any Mohr’s circle.

p.x: Imagine a tiny square around a point in a loaded part. This **stress element** shows what acts across its faces.
**Normal stress** acts perpendicular to a face. Call it $σ_x$ on the x face and $σ_y$ on the y face.
**Shear stress** acts along the face. Let $τ_{xy}$ be shear in the y direction on the x face.
The stress components [[change with]] the square's orientation. You're looking at the same load on differently angled faces.
**Mohr's circle** collects the normal and shear stress pairs for every orientation in the x–y plane. Normal stress is horizontal and shear is vertical.
Draw the line from $X$ to $Y$. It is a **diameter**, a straight line across the circle through its center.
The center $C$ is the average normal stress. The signed gap $d$ from the center to point $X$ is half the normal-stress difference. Here $τ$ is the x-face shear.

p.cap: Use the same stress units on both axes.

p.x: For a circle with nonzero radius, follow it to the left and right ends, where it meets the horizontal axis.
Shear is zero at both crossings. The normal stresses there are the **principal stresses**, $σ_1$ on the right and $σ_2$ on the left.
The largest in-plane shear magnitude is $R$. The top and bottom have signed shear $+R$ and $−R$.

g.q: What is the shear stress where the circle crosses the horizontal axis?
o: Zero
Shear is the vertical coordinate. The horizontal axis has no vertical offset.
The radius
The radius is the shear magnitude at the top and bottom of the circle.

p.x: Rotate the x face by an angle $θ$. On Mohr's circle the angle swept from $X$ is [[twice]] that angle in magnitude.
The direction $θ_p$ of $σ_1$ is measured from the x axis. With the shear convention on these cards, use **atan2**, the arctangent that uses both signs to pick the direction.

p.cap: d is the signed gap defined earlier. For R = 0, every orientation is principal.

cards: Mach number M = V/a compares flight speed with the local speed of sound. Below about Mach 0.8 the flow stays subsonic everywhere; above Mach 1 the aircraft is supersonic.
The speed of sound depends only on temperature: a = √(γRT). For air γ = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg·K), so a ≈ 340 m/s at 288 K and about 295 m/s at airliner cruise altitude (217 K).
Above Mach 1, pressure waves can’t run ahead of the aircraft. They pile up on a Mach cone with half-angle μ = asin(1/M).
Turning or slowing supersonic flow sharply makes a shock: a sudden jump in pressure, temperature and density, with a loss of total pressure. Behind a normal shock the flow is subsonic.
That loss shows up as wave drag. Thin wings, sharp leading edges and sweep keep shocks weak, which is why supersonic jets look like darts.
title: Supersonic flow and shocks

qs.q: At 217 K the speed of sound is 295 m/s. An airliner cruises at 250 m/s. What is its Mach number?
For air at 288 K, a = √(1.4 × 287 × 288). What is the speed of sound, in m/s?
A jet flies at Mach 2. What is the half-angle of its Mach cone, in degrees?
What happens to the flow just behind a normal shock?
qs.ans: It becomes subsonic, with higher pressure and temperature
wrong: It speeds up to a higher Mach number
Its total pressure goes up
Its temperature drops below the oncoming air
qs.why: A normal shock slows supersonic flow to subsonic and compresses and heats it. Total pressure drops across it; that loss is the cost of the shock.

qs.q: Why do supersonic aircraft use thin, sharp, swept wings?
qs.ans: To keep the shocks weak and cut wave drag
wrong: To raise lift at low speed
To make the Mach cone wider
To lower the speed of sound around the wing
qs.why: Weaker shocks lose less total pressure, so there is less wave drag. Thin sharp wings are worse at low speed, which is the trade-off.

qs.q: Rank these by Mach cone half-angle, widest first.
qs.why: μ = asin(1/M): about 56°, 42°, 30° and 19°. Faster means a narrower cone.

p.x: For a typical wing, below about Mach 0.8 the flow stays subsonic everywhere around the aircraft. Above Mach 1, the aircraft is supersonic.
For an ideal gas, the speed of sound depends only on temperature:
Colder air, slower sound: $a ∝ √{T}$

g.q: Air at cruise altitude is about 217 K. Sound travels there…
o: slower
a grows with √T, and √(217/288) = 0.87, so about 340 × 0.87 ≈ 295 m/s.
faster
Thinner air doesn't speed sound up. For an ideal gas only temperature enters a = √(γRT), and it's colder up there.
at the same speed
Pressure and density drop out of a = √(γRT), but temperature doesn't.

p.x: Above Mach 1, pressure waves can't run ahead of the aircraft. They pile up on a cone trailing behind it.

p.cap: M > 1, weak pressure waves

p.x: Faster flight, narrower cone.

g.q: Speed up to Mach 2. The Mach cone gets…
o: narrower
1/M shrinks, so μ = asin(1/M) drops, from 56° at Mach 1.2 to 30° at Mach 2.
wider
The aircraft outruns its waves by more, so they trail at a sharper angle: μ = asin(1/M) falls.

p.x: Turning or slowing supersonic flow sharply makes a shock: a very thin front where the flow properties jump.
Behind a normal shock the flow is [[subsonic]].
The total-pressure loss across shocks shows up as **wave drag**.
Thin wings, sharp leading edges and sweep keep the shocks [[weak]].
That's why supersonic jets look like darts.

cards: In plain English: Shorten a proposed move until it improves the result enough.
For a smooth dimensionless objective f at fixed point x, the gradient ∇f gives local slopes. The direction p = -∇f descends because ∇fᵀp is negative unless the gradient vanishes.
For fixed x and descent direction p, accept step α when f(x+αp) ≤ f(x)+μ₁α∇fᵀp. Here α is step size and 0<μ₁<1 sets sufficient decrease; all quantities are dimensionless.

Why it happens: a smooth objective initially follows its directional slope. Holding x and p fixed, repeated α ← ρα with contraction factor 0<ρ<1 eventually satisfies Armijo for a genuine descent direction.
With dimensionless f=2x₁²+x₂² fixed, x=(1,2) gives p=(-4,-4). At α=1 and μ₁=0.0001, the trial objective is 22; threshold 5.9968 rejects it.
For that fixed quadratic and start, halve α using ρ=0.5: α=0.5 gives objective 2 and threshold 5.9984, so accept. Backtracking seeks sufficient decrease, not the exact minimum along the direction.
title: Backtracking and Armijo
plain: Shorten a proposed move until it improves the result enough.

qs.q: For dimensionless f(x₁,x₂)=3x₁²+2x₂² at x=(2,-1), form p=-∇f. What is p₁?
qs.why: Differentiate before substituting: ∇f=(6x₁,4x₂)=(12,-4). Negating gives p=(-12,4), so p₁=-12.00. Using -6 drops x₁; using +12 forgets the descent sign.

qs.q: For dimensionless f(x₁,x₂)=3x₁²+2x₂² at x=(2,-1), use p=-∇f, α=0.08 and μ₁=0.02. Calculate the Armijo threshold f(x)+μ₁α∇fᵀp.
qs.why: First f=3(2²)+2(-1)²=14 and ∇f=(12,-4). Then p=(-12,4), so ∇fᵀp=-144-16=-160. Threshold=14+0.02(0.08)(-160)=13.744, or 13.74. The dot product uses both coordinates and is negative.

qs.q: A dimensionless calibration objective is f(q)=4(q-3)². At q=1, hold p=-f′(1) fixed; start α=0.8, use ρ=0.4 and μ₁=0.05. What is the first accepted α?
qs.why: f=16, f′=-16 and p=16, so the threshold is 16-12.8α. At α=0.8, f(13.8)=466.56>5.76; at α=0.32, f(6.12)=38.9376>11.904. At α=0.128, f(3.048)=0.009216≤14.3616. Accept 0.1280; keep the original point and direction fixed during rejection.

qs.q: In MATLAB, `g` and `p` are real column vectors, and `p=-g`. Which expression gives the scalar Armijo directional slope, and why?
qs.ans: `g'*p`: inner product gives the directional slope.
wrong: `g.*p`: coordinate products give the directional slope.
`g*p'`: the outer product gives the directional slope.
`sum(g)*sum(p)`: separate sums give the directional slope.
qs.why: The derivative of f(x+αp) at α=0 is gᵀp, coded `g'*p`. Elementwise-product mistake: `g.*p` is a vector, not its sum. Outer-product mistake: `g*p'` is a matrix. Product-of-sums mistake: `sum(g)*sum(p)` adds cross terms absent from the dot product.

qs.q: Order backtracking for a differentiable objective and a nonzero gradient. Reject trials without moving the base point.
items: Evaluate the base objective and gradient; choose a descent direction.
Set the initial step and form the trial point.
Compare the trial objective with the Armijo threshold.
If rejected, shrink the step and repeat the trial test from the same base.
When accepted, move to the accepted trial point.
qs.why: The base gradient defines the directional derivative used in every rejection test. Trial evaluation precedes comparison; rejection changes the step, not the base point. Acceptance ends the loop. Recomputing the direction after every rejection would be a different procedure.

qs.q: “The objective decreased, but I still rejected the step.” What does the analyst mean?
qs.ans: The reduction failed the Armijo sufficient-decrease test.
wrong: The reduction proved that the direction was not descending.
The reduction passed Armijo but missed the exact line minimum.
The reduction required a new base gradient before comparison.
qs.why: Armijo requires a specified amount of decrease, so a small reduction can still fail. Direction-confusion mistake: a rejected trial does not prove a non-descent direction. Exact-search mistake: Armijo does not require the line minimum. Moving-base mistake: the base gradient stays fixed during backtracking.

p.x: You have a direction to move in and a trial step along it. The trial does not improve the objective enough.
Backtracking shortens the step along the same direction and tries again.
Accept the first trial that improves the objective enough.

g.q: What does backtracking try next?
o: A shorter step
Moving less far can keep the trial in the region where the direction helps.
A longer step
Moving farther can overshoot. Backtracking reduces the step along the chosen direction.

p.x: Along the negative gradient, the directional slope $∇f^T p$ is [[negative]] whenever the gradient is nonzero.

p.cap: Zero only when the gradient vanishes.

p.x: Armijo accepts a step only when the objective drops [[sufficiently]] compared with the drop predicted by the local slope.

vars: fixed base point and descent direction
required fraction of the predicted drop

p.cap: All quantities are dimensionless. 0 < μ₁ < 1.

p.x: Start with a smooth objective and a direction with negative slope. Keep the base point and direction fixed.

p.cap: α is the trial step and 0 < ρ < 1 is a fixed shrink factor.

p.x: A small enough step passes Armijo. Close to the base point, the actual drop approaches the drop predicted by the slope.

g.q: If we keep shrinking the step, will a trial pass?
o: Yes, eventually
Near the base point the drop approaches the linear prediction. Armijo asks for only a fraction of it.
It may never pass
That can happen without a descent direction. A negative slope guarantees sufficient decrease for small positive steps.

p.x: Use $f(x)=2x_1^2+x_2^2$ with coordinates $x_1,x_2$ and start at $(1,2)$. All values are dimensionless.
The starting value is $6$. The negative gradient gives direction $p=(−4,−4)$ and slope $−32$.
Reject step size $1$. The trial exceeds the Armijo bound for decrease fraction $0.0001$.
Keep the same quadratic, base point and direction. The base value stays $6$ and the slope stays $−32$.
Use shrink factor $0.5$ to halve the rejected step size from $1$ to $0.5$.
Accept. The trial is below the bound. Backtracking only needs sufficient decrease.

cards: In plain English: Different optimization methods turn the same local information into different moves.
For dimensionless quadratic f=ax₁²+x₂², fixed a>0 controls curvature. Let g=∇f and H be its Hessian. Gradient descent uses x_new=x-αg, with dimensionless step α.

For this fixed positive-definite quadratic, full-step Newton solves Hp=-g for step p, then moves x_new=x+p. Why it happens: its quadratic approximation is exact, so one step reaches the unique minimum.
At fixed a=2 and x=(1,2), gradient descent with α=0.1 reaches (0.6,1.6); full-step Newton reaches (0,0). This exact Newton result depends on the quadratic model and nonsingular Hessian.

Adam uses x_new=x-α_Av̂/(√ŝ+ε) coordinatewise, with bias-corrected mean v̂ and mean-square ŝ. Starting with zero moments, neglect stabilizer ε: step α_A=0.3 from the fixed demo point reaches (0.7,1.7); all quantities are dimensionless.

With fixed a≥1, gradient descent converges from every start only for 0<α<1/a. Adam normalizes coordinates separately, so its first direction matches gradient descent only for special gradient components.
title: Gradient descent, Newton and Adam
plain: Different optimization methods turn the same local information into different moves.

qs.q: For dimensionless f=4x₁²+3x₂² at x=(1.5,-2), take one gradient-descent step with α=0.06. Derive the x₁ shrink factor, then report the new x₁.
qs.why: ∇f=(8x₁,6x₂)=(12,-12). Thus x_new=(1.5,-2)-0.06(12,-12)=(0.78,-1.28), so x₁,new=0.7800. The x₁ factor is 1-8(0.06)=0.52, so 0.52×1.5=0.78. The factor 2 in differentiating each squared term is essential.

qs.q: For dimensionless f=5(x₁-2)²+2(x₂+3)², start at x=(-1,1). Solve Hp=-∇f for a full Newton step. What is p₂?
qs.why: ∇f=(10(x₁-2),4(x₂+3))=(-30,16), and H=diag(10,4). Hence p=-H⁻¹∇f=(3,-4), so p₂=-4.000. This is the displacement; the updated second coordinate is -3, not -4.

qs.q: For a dimensionless calibration problem, Adam starts with zero moments at x=(2.5,-1.5), and its first gradient is g=(6,-9). With bias correction, α_A=0.2 and ε neglected, what is the new x₂?
qs.why: At the first iteration, v̂=g and ŝ=g²=(36,81), regardless of admissible moment decay factors. The second-coordinate step is -0.2(-9)/√81=+0.2; x₂,new=-1.5+0.2=-1.300. Using -α_Ag₂ without normalization would instead take an erroneous +1.8 step.

qs.q: For a dimensionless strictly convex quadratic with unequal positive curvatures, which method reaches its minimum in one full step from every starting point, and why?
qs.ans: Newton, because its local quadratic model is exact.
wrong: Gradient descent, because every negative gradient points directly to the minimum.
Adam, because bias correction replaces its normalization with the inverse Hessian.
All three, because positive curvature makes every full step optimal.
qs.why: Newton solves Hp=-g, exactly cancelling the quadratic gradient at the new point. Gradient-direction mistake: unequal curvature generally prevents the negative gradient from aiming at the minimizer. Moment/Hessian mistake: bias correction is not an inverse Hessian. Convexity/step-size mistake: convexity does not make arbitrary full steps optimal.

qs.q: Order one fixed-step gradient-descent stability audit for f=ax₁²+x₂² with dimensionless a≥1 and positive α.
items: Substitute into the update to obtain factors 1-2aα and 1-2α.
Require both factor magnitudes to be strictly below one.
Check the chosen step, including equality boundaries.
qs.why: Each coordinate repeats multiplication by its factor. For positive a and α, |1-2aα|<1 gives α<1/a and |1-2α|<1 gives α<1; a≥1 makes the first bound decisive. Equality can leave a nondecaying alternating component. Positive definiteness alone does not guarantee fixed-step convergence.

qs.q: MATLAB: `x`, `g`, `vhat`, and `shat` are equal-length real column vectors with at least two entries. `alpha` and positive `epsilon` are scalars. Which line breaks coordinatewise Adam?
lines: `g = grad_f(x);`
`v = beta_v*v + (1-beta_v)*g;`
`shat = (beta_s*s + (1-beta_s)*(g.^2))/(1-beta_s^(iter+1));`
`vhat = v/(1-beta_v^(iter+1));`
`x = x - alpha*(vhat / (epsilon + sqrt(shat)));`
qs.why: Line 5 uses matrix right-division between column vectors, producing a matrix rather than coordinatewise scaling. Replace it with `x = x - alpha*(vhat ./ (epsilon + sqrt(shat)));`. The gradient squares correctly use `.^2`; divisions by scalar bias-correction denominators in the other lines are valid. Assume old `s` is supplied and iteration counting starts at zero.

p.x: The gradient tells you how the objective changes near your current point.
Gradient descent scales the negative gradient as a whole. Newton uses curvature to choose its step.
Adam [[rescales]] the move separately in each coordinate.
Adam divides each coordinate's gradient average by a scale built from that coordinate's squared gradients.

p.cap: a > 0 sets curvature along coordinate x₁.

vars: Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives

p.cap: All quantities are dimensionless.

p.x: For this positive-definite quadratic, the local quadratic model is the whole objective.

p.cap: H is the Hessian, g is the gradient and p is the step.

p.x: Add $p$ to the current point. The full Newton step reaches the unique minimum in one move.

g.q: Where does that full step land?
o: At the minimum
The quadratic model is exact, and solving the Newton system minimizes it.
Partway there
A shortened step could stop partway. A full step minimizes the exact quadratic.

p.x: Set $a=2$ in the fixed quadratic and start at $x=(1,2)$. The gradient $g$ is $(4,4)$.
The Hessian is diagonal with entries $4$ and $2$. Divide the negative gradient by those entries to get Newton's step $p=(−1,−2)$.
Newton lands exactly because the model is quadratic and the Hessian is nonsingular.

vars: bias-corrected averages of gradients and squared gradients

p.cap: All quantities are dimensionless.

p.x: Take $a=2$ and start at $(1,2)$, so $g=(4,4)$. With zero initial moments, each first corrected average is $4$ and each squared average is $16$. Use $α_A=0.3$; $ε$ is negligible beside $√{16}$.
For $f(x)=ax_1^2+x_2^2$ with fixed $a ≥ 1$, gradient descent converges from every start within this step-size range.

p.cap: α is the fixed step size. Each coordinate must contract.

p.x: Adam can point in a different direction. With zero initial moments and negligible stabilizer, each nonzero gradient component becomes its sign in the first step.
The directions agree when all nonzero gradient components have the same magnitude.

g.q: Must Adam's first step point along the negative gradient?
o: Yes
A shared scale would preserve direction. Adam divides each coordinate by its own scale.
No
Separate scales can change the ratio between components and turn the direction.

cards: In plain English: A valid constrained optimum must balance improvement against the direction the boundary blocks.
For dimensionless objective f=(x₁+1)²+x₂², fix boundary c and constraint g=x₁-c≤0. A feasible point obeys the bound; an active point touches it, meaning g=0.
For this differentiable problem, multiplier σ is dimensionless. KKT requires stationarity ∇f+σ∇g=0, feasibility g≤0, σ≥0, and complementary slackness σg=0. An inactive constraint forces σ=0.
At fixed c=1, boundary candidate (1,0) needs σ=-4 by stationarity, violating σ≥0. Interior candidate (-1,0) has g=-2 and σ=0, satisfying all four conditions.
Why it happens: a negative multiplier at this upper boundary means moving inward reduces the objective. The boundary cannot be optimal when feasible descent remains.
For this convex quadratic with affine constraint, KKT is sufficient. Holding c fixed, x₁*=min(c,-1) and x₂*=0. At c=-1, the constraint is active even though its multiplier is zero.
title: KKT conditions
plain: A valid constrained optimum must balance improvement against the direction the boundary blocks.

qs.q: Minimize dimensionless f=(x₁+2)²+3x₂² with g=x₁+4≤0. At candidate (-4,0), calculate σ from stationarity ∇f+σ∇g=0.
qs.why: ∇f=(2(x₁+2),6x₂)=(-4,0), and ∇g=(1,0). Stationarity gives -4+σ=0, so σ=4.000. Feasibility holds with g=0; σ≥0 and complementary slackness σg=0 also hold. Convexity makes this a constrained minimum.

qs.q: For dimensionless f=(x₁-3)²+2x₂² subject to g=x₁-4≤0, find the constrained optimum first. What is g there?
qs.why: The unconstrained minimum solves ∇f=0, giving (3,0), which is feasible. At that point g=3-4=-1.000. Stationarity holds with σ=0; feasibility, σ≥0 and complementary slackness all hold. Forcing x₁=4 would mistake a feasible bound for a required equality.

qs.q: Minimize dimensionless f=2(x₁-1)²+x₂² with g=x₁+2≤0. Use stationarity, feasibility, σ≥0 and complementary slackness to identify the optimum. What is f*?
qs.why: The unconstrained x₁=1 violates x₁≤-2. The optimum is (-2,0): ∇f=(-12,0), so stationarity requires σ=12≥0; g=0 gives feasibility and complementary slackness. Therefore f*=2(-2-1)²=18.00. Evaluating at the infeasible unconstrained minimum would incorrectly give zero.

qs.q: MATLAB: all quantities are dimensionless real columns. At a candidate for one inequality, `gf=[-6;0]`, `gg=[2;0]`, and `gval=0`. Which stationarity calculation and KKT conclusion are correct?
qs.ans: `sigma=-(gg'*gf)/(gg'*gg);` gives 3; all KKT conditions hold.
wrong: `sigma=(gg'*gf)/(gg'*gg);` gives -3; stationarity alone certifies the minimum.
`sigma=-(gg.*gf)./(gg.*gg);` gives component ratios; each is a valid multiplier.
`sigma=-(gg'*gf);` gives 12; an active constraint removes the stationarity check.
qs.why: The scalar calculation gives -(-12)/4=3 and the full residual gf+3gg=(0,0). Stationarity, feasibility gval=0, σ≥0 and complementary slackness all hold. Missing-minus mistake: the first alternative gives the wrong multiplier. Elementwise-division mistake: the second makes 0/0 in one coordinate and cannot produce one scalar σ. Missing-normalization mistake: the third omits ggᵀgg and leaves a nonzero stationarity residual; activity does not waive stationarity.

qs.q: For a differentiable convex objective and affine inequality g≤0, order this candidate-check workflow.
items: Evaluate the objective gradient, constraint gradient and constraint value at the candidate.
Use stationarity to solve for the candidate multiplier.
Check feasibility g≤0, the sign condition σ≥0 and complementary slackness σg=0.
Accept the KKT certificate only if every condition holds.
qs.why: Stationarity ∇f+σ∇g=0 gives σ, so it comes before the tests that use σ: feasibility g≤0, dual feasibility σ≥0 and complementary slackness σg=0. Accepting comes last because it needs every test. Convexity and an affine constraint make the conditions sufficient.

qs.q: “The bound is active, but its multiplier is zero.” Which interpretation is justified?
qs.ans: The point touches the bound; zero multiplier is allowed.
wrong: The point lies strictly inside; zero multiplier proves inactivity.
The point violates stationarity; every active multiplier must be positive.
The point violates feasibility; a boundary value must be negative.
qs.why: Active means g=0, whereas σ≥0 permits σ=0. Zero-multiplier mistake: complementary slackness does not make the converse inference from σ=0 to g<0. Strict-positivity mistake: active constraints need not have σ>0. Strict-feasibility mistake: g≤0 includes equality. Stationarity must still be checked separately.

p.x: A constrained optimum has to be feasible. Your best move in the unconstrained problem might point outside the allowed region.
At a boundary optimum, there is no feasible direction that improves the objective to first order.
Minimize $f=(x_1+1)^2+x_2^2$ for coordinates $x_1,x_2$. A fixed upper bound $c$ limits $x_1$.
The constraint is [[active]] where the point touches that bound.

p.cap: g measures the signed offset from the boundary. All quantities are dimensionless.

p.x: Inside the feasible region, $g<0$. On the boundary, $g=0$.
An inactive constraint has $g<0$, so its multiplier must be zero.

g.q: Interior point. What must the multiplier be at a KKT point?
o: Zero
The constraint has slack, so only a zero multiplier makes the product zero.
Positive
A positive multiplier can occur at an active constraint. In the interior it would make the product nonzero.

p.x: Fix the upper bound at $c=1$. Compare the boundary point $(1,0)$ with the unconstrained minimum $(−1,0)$.
The boundary point fails the multiplier sign test. The interior point satisfies all four conditions.
A candidate lies on the upper bound for $x_1$. The stationary multiplier comes out negative.
Move inward by lowering $x_1$. The objective falls locally, so the boundary point cannot be optimal.
The multiplier's sign tells you whether the boundary blocks improvement or leaves a feasible way to improve.

g.q: What happens to the objective if you move a little inward?
o: It falls
The slope in the outward direction is positive, so reversing direction gives descent.
It rises
That would require a negative outward slope and a positive multiplier. Here the sign is the other way around.

p.x: The objective is convex and the constraint is affine, so a point satisfying KKT is optimal.
At $c=−1$ the bound just touches the unconstrained minimum. The constraint is active with a [[zero]] multiplier.

p.cap: The starred coordinates give the constrained minimum.

p.x: At the touching point the objective gradient vanishes, so stationarity needs no boundary correction.

cards: In plain English: A penalty discourages constraint violations; a multiplier learns the correction needed at the boundary.
For dimensionless f=(x+1)² and g=x+2≤0, fix positive penalty μ. Exterior penalty minimizes f̂=f+(μ/2)max(0,g)². Violations cost extra; feasible points receive no penalty.
With this fixed quadratic, μ=1 gives minimizer x=-1.333 and g=0.6667. Why it happens: a finite quadratic penalty trades objective improvement against some remaining constraint violation.
For the same inequality, fix dimensionless multiplier estimate λ̄≥0 and μ>0. Define clipped constraint ḡ=max(g,-λ̄/μ). Augmented objective f̂=f+λ̄ḡ+(μ/2)ḡ² adds a linear correction.
With μ=1 and initial λ̄=0, the augmented model matches the penalty: distance to true optimum x*=-2 is 0.6667. Updating λ̄_new=max(0,λ̄+μg) gives 0.6667.

For this convex model and fixed μ>0, λ̄=2 places the augmented minimum exactly at x=-2. Each outer iteration minimizes at fixed estimates, updates the projected multiplier, then checks constraint and stationarity residuals.
title: Penalty and augmented Lagrangian
plain: A penalty discourages constraint violations; a multiplier learns the correction needed at the boundary.

qs.q: For dimensionless f=(x-1)², g=x+3≤0 and μ=6, minimize f̂=f+(μ/2)max(0,g)². What is the minimizer x?
qs.why: In the violating branch, f̂′=2(x-1)+6(x+3)=8x+16, so x=-2.000. Its g=1>0 confirms that branch. The convex objective has this unique minimum; the finite penalty leaves violation instead of forcing the true constrained optimum x=-3.

qs.q: For dimensionless f=(x-1)² and g=x+3≤0, minimize the clipped augmented objective with μ=4 and λ̄=6, then calculate λ̄_new=max(0,λ̄+μg).
qs.why: In the active clipped branch, stationarity is 2(x-1)+6+4(x+3)=6x+16=0, so x=-8/3 and g=1/3. This satisfies g≥-λ̄/μ=-1.5. Thus λ̄_new=6+4/3=22/3=7.333. Updating before minimizing would use the wrong constraint residual.

qs.q: A dimensionless constrained calibration has f=3(x-2)² and g=x+1≤0. What multiplier estimate λ̄ makes the exact constrained optimum stationary for the augmented model for any μ>0?
qs.why: The constrained optimum is x*=-1. There g=0 and f′=6(x-2)=-18. Augmented stationarity at the active boundary requires -18+λ̄=0, giving λ̄=18.00. The μg term vanishes at the boundary, so this result is independent of positive μ; convexity makes stationarity sufficient.

qs.q: With exact inner solves for a smooth convex problem whose inequality optimum has positive multiplier, why can an augmented Lagrangian enforce the active bound at finite μ?
qs.ans: The correct multiplier supplies the missing boundary gradient.
wrong: The squared penalty alone supplies a nonzero gradient at zero violation.
The multiplier update removes the objective gradient from every inner solve.
Any positive multiplier makes the inner objective ignore constraint violations.
qs.why: At an active optimum, ∇f+λ̄∇g=0 can hold at finite μ when λ̄ matches the KKT multiplier. Penalty-gradient mistake: a squared violation has zero gradient at zero violation and cannot balance a nonzero objective gradient there. Dropped-objective mistake: the inner solve still includes ∇f. Arbitrary-multiplier mistake: the estimate must converge to the appropriate value, not merely be positive.

qs.q: Order an inequality augmented-Lagrangian outer iteration with positive penalty and nonnegative multiplier estimate.
items: Freeze the current penalty and multiplier estimate for the inner solve.
Minimize the clipped augmented objective to the chosen inner tolerance.
Evaluate the original constraint at the returned point.
Update the multiplier with max(0, current multiplier + penalty × constraint).
Check KKT residuals; if needed, adjust the penalty and repeat.
qs.why: For g≤0, ḡ=max(g,-λ̄/μ) implies λ̄+μḡ=max(0,λ̄+μg). Projection preserves nonnegative multipliers. Inner minimization must use fixed current estimates; the returned point supplies the update residual. Feasibility alone is not convergence: stationarity and complementary slackness also matter. Increasing μ is a policy choice, not a substitute for the multiplier update.

qs.q: MATLAB extension to two inequalities: `g(x)` and fixed `lambda` are real 2-by-1 columns, `lambda>=0`, and `mu>0` is scalar. The augmented objective must be scalar, using the sum of squared clipped constraints. Which line is wrong?
lines: `gbar = @(x) max(g(x), -lambda/mu);`
`fhat = @(x) f(x) + lambda' * gbar(x) + (mu/2)*sum(gbar(x)^2);`
`xstar = inner_minimize(fhat);`
`lambda_new = max(0, lambda + mu*g(xstar));`
qs.why: Line 2 needs `sum(gbar(x).^2)`. Matrix-power mistake: a 2-by-1 column cannot be squared with `^2`; `.^2` squares each clipped constraint before summing. The transpose product supplies a scalar multiplier term, componentwise max gives the specified clipping, and the last line projects each updated multiplier to remain nonnegative.

p.x: A penalty adds a cost when a trial point breaks a constraint. The optimizer minimizes the objective plus that cost.
Some violation can remain if it saves more in the original objective than it costs in penalty.
A multiplier estimate adds a correction that can balance the objective's slope at the boundary.

g.q: Can the minimum of the penalized objective still violate the constraint?
o: Yes
A small violation can cost less than the objective improvement it buys.
No
That would require enforcing a hard bound. A finite quadratic penalty charges for crossing it.

p.x: Minimize $f=(x+1)^2$ over scalar $x$ subject to $g=x+2≤0$. All values are dimensionless.
The exterior penalty charges [[extra]] for infeasible points and leaves feasible points at their original cost.

p.cap: Hold the positive penalty weight μ fixed.

p.x: Set penalty weight $μ=1$ for the fixed quadratic. On the violating side, $x>−2$, both the objective and penalty contribute to the slope.
The finite penalty leaves a violation. The objective improves enough to pay for it.
The augmented objective adds a term that varies [[linearly]] with the clipped constraint, alongside the quadratic penalty.
With weight $μ=1$ and multiplier estimate $λ̄=0$, the augmented objective reduces to the exterior penalty.
Its minimizer violates the bound by about $0.6667$. That is also its distance from the true optimum $x^{*}=−2$.

p.cap: Use the constraint value g at the current minimizer.

p.x: At the true optimum $x=−2$, the objective slope is $−2$. A multiplier estimate $λ̄=2$ supplies the opposite slope.
For this convex model, that puts the augmented minimum exactly at the bound for any fixed penalty weight $μ>0$.
Minimize with estimates fixed, project the updated multiplier onto nonnegative values, then check feasibility and stationarity.

cards: In plain English: Fit the observations, then check whether the model explains variation and predicts new data.
For eight fixed dimensionless observations, ordinary least squares minimizes Sᵣ, summed squared residuals. The demo gives intercept a₀=0.5064 and slope a₁=0.5986 in prediction ŷ=a₀+a₁x, with input x.
For that fixed dataset, Sₜ is summed squared deviation from the observed mean. With Sₜ>0, r²=1-Sᵣ/Sₜ. Demo values Sᵣ=0.4571 and Sₜ=15.51 give r²=0.9705 using unrounded sums.
For dimensionless polynomial inputs xᵢ and fixed degree m, design-matrix row i is [1,xᵢ,…,xᵢᵐ]. With full column rank, solve ZᵀZ a=Zᵀy for coefficient vector a and observation vector y.

For fixed predictions and n observations, RMSE=√(Sᵣ/n), the root-mean-square error. Training RMSE measures fitted-data error; test RMSE uses held-out observations. With dimensionless observations, RMSE is dimensionless too.

Why it happens: added polynomial terms can fit noise as well as signal. On fixed data, nested unregularized exact fits cannot increase training error; test error can rise. Prefer held-out evidence over training improvement.
title: Linear fits and r²
plain: Fit the observations, then check whether the model explains variation and predicts new data.

qs.q: Fit the dimensionless model ŷ=a₀+a₁x by ordinary least squares with an intercept. For n=5, Σx=15, Σx²=55, Σy=27 and Σxy=91, calculate a₁.
qs.why: The normal equations give a₁=[nΣxy-(Σx)(Σy)]/[nΣx²-(Σx)²]=(5×91-15×27)/(5×55-15²)=50/50=1.000. Then a₀=(27-1×15)/5=2.4. Omitting the mean-correction terms would force the wrong through-origin model.

qs.q: For an intercept-containing least-squares fit of dimensionless observations, residual sum Sᵣ=3.6 and total sum about the observed mean Sₜ=24. Calculate r².
qs.why: r²=(Sₜ-Sᵣ)/Sₜ=(24-3.6)/24=20.4/24=0.8500. Dividing Sᵣ by Sₜ gives the unexplained fraction 0.15; taking its square root confuses r² with a correlation magnitude. Positive Sₜ makes this ratio defined.

qs.q: A fixed dimensionless polynomial has coefficient vector a=[1;2;0.5]. On held-out inputs x=[0;2], use rows [1,x,x²]; observations are y=[2;6]. Compute test RMSE.
qs.why: Construct Z_test=[[1,0,0],[1,2,4]]. Predictions Z_test a=[1;7]; residuals prediction minus observation are [-1;1]. Test Sᵣ=1+1=2 and n=2, so RMSE=√(2/2)=1.000. This uses the fixed training coefficients, not a refit to test observations; dividing by n-3 would confuse RMSE with a degrees-of-freedom estimate.

qs.q: For exact unregularized nested polynomial fits on the same dimensionless training data, a cubic has higher training r² and lower training RMSE but higher held-out RMSE than a line. Which conclusion and reason are supported?
qs.ans: The cubic may overfit because its added terms capture training noise.
wrong: The cubic generalizes better because lower training RMSE guarantees lower population error.
The line is invalid because polynomial models must improve both reported errors.
The cubic is underfit because higher held-out RMSE proves insufficient polynomial degree.
qs.why: With fixed nonzero Sₜ, a lower Sᵣ raises r²=1-Sᵣ/Sₜ and lowers training RMSE. The held-out increase nevertheless suggests possible overfitting. Training/test-confusion mistake: training improvement does not guarantee generalization. Nested-model mistake: only the exact unregularized training optimum is guaranteed not to worsen. Bias/variance mistake: higher test error alone does not prove too little capacity; here increasing capacity worsened it.

qs.q: Order polynomial least squares followed by an honest test-set evaluation. Keep the test observations out of the fitting solve.
items: Choose the degree and construct training rows [1,x,…,x^m].
Check full column rank and form the training normal equations.
Solve for the training coefficient vector.
Construct held-out rows using the same powers and predict without refitting.
Compute held-out residuals, square and average them, then take the square root.
qs.why: The intercept column is the zeroth power. For full rank, ZᵀZ a=Zᵀy defines the least-squares coefficients; MATLAB can use `(Z' * Z) \ (Z' * y)`, though QR-based `Z\y` is generally preferable numerically. Test RMSE uses fixed fitted coefficients. Refitting on held-out data causes leakage and no longer measures unseen-data prediction.

qs.q: MATLAB polynomial design matrix: `x` and `y` are real n-by-1 columns with n>1; degree m≥1. Which line prevents correct construction?
lines: `Z = zeros(n,m+1);`
`for j = 0:m`
`end`
qs.why: Line 3 needs `x.^j`, not `x^j`: each sample is raised to the power separately, while matrix powers require a square matrix. MATLAB column j+1 correctly accommodates power j=0 as the all-ones intercept column. Starting columns at zero would instead violate MATLAB indexing; omitting j=0 would drop the intercept.

p.x: A fitted line summarizes how the observed response varies with the input.
To assess prediction, test it on observations that were held out of the fit.
The training fit tells you how much variation the line explains in the observations it already saw.

g.q: Which data better test how the fitted line predicts new observations?
o: Held-out data
These observations had no influence on the fitted coefficients, so they test prediction.
Fitting data
The coefficients were chosen to fit those data. Their error can understate new prediction error.

p.x: For eight fixed, dimensionless observations, ordinary least squares minimizes $S_r$, the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted responses.

vars: sum of squared residuals from the fit
sum of squared deviations from the observed mean
fraction of observed variation explained by the fitted line

p.cap: For this fixed dataset and a fit with an intercept. Requires Sₜ > 0.

p.x: The demo gives $S_r≈0.4571$ and $S_t≈15.51$.
Use the unrounded sums to compute the ratio.
In a polynomial fit, each observed input $x_i$ gives one row of design matrix $Z$. For fixed degree $m$, its powers appear in [[increasing]] order.

p.cap: For dimensionless inputs.
a holds the coefficients. y holds the observed responses.

p.x: If the columns of $Z$ are linearly independent, the least-squares coefficients are unique.
Training RMSE uses the observations used for fitting. Test RMSE uses observations [[held out]] from fitting.

vars: sum of squared residuals on the set being scored
number of observations in that set

p.cap: Use fixed predictions and a nonempty set.

p.x: RMSE has the same units as the response. Here it is dimensionless.
Fit nested polynomial models by exact, unregularized least squares on the same training data. The larger model can reproduce the smaller fit, so training error cannot rise.
Held-out error can rise. The extra terms may follow noise that will not repeat in new observations.
Compare models on held-out data when prediction matters.

g.q: Can test error rise as you add polynomial terms?
o: Yes
The extra terms can fit training noise and give worse predictions on unseen observations.
No
The smaller fit is available to the larger model, but the fit minimizes training error. Test error has no such guarantee.

cards: In plain English: A small table shows when increasing feedback gain makes oscillations grow.

The setup: a controller with gain K drives the plant (the thing being controlled, like a motor), here G(s) = K/[s(s+1)(s+5)]. The output is measured and subtracted from the command: that’s unity negative feedback. s is the Laplace variable; 1 and 5 s⁻¹ are the plant’s rates.

Closing the loop gives s³ + 6s² + 5s + K = 0; its roots decide whether the response dies out. The Routh table: row s³: 1, 5. Row s²: 6, K. Row s¹: (6 × 5 − K)/6. Row s⁰: K. Read down the first column: 1, 6, (30 − K)/6, K. If every entry is positive, the loop is stable, so 0 < K < 30.

How to read it: go down the first column and count sign changes. Each change from + to − or − to + is one pole in the right half-plane, an unstable mode that grows. No changes (all positive) means stable. A zero in the column needs a special step, so don’t call that stable.
At fixed K=10 s⁻³, the s¹ entry is 3.333 s⁻², and every first-column entry is positive. With zero initial state and a unit-step command, the output settles to one.
At K=30 s⁻³ for this plant, the polynomial factors as (s+6)(s²+5). Oscillation frequency is √5=2.236 rad/s; imaginary-axis poles prevent settling. Asymptotic stability requires 0<K<30 s⁻³.
title: Routh and gain limits
plain: A small table shows when increasing feedback gain makes oscillations grow.

qs.q: With time in seconds, a closed-loop characteristic polynomial is s³+7s²+10s+28; coefficients carry their corresponding SI units. Calculate its Routh s¹ first-column entry.
qs.why: For a cubic s³+as²+bs+c, the s¹ entry is (ab-c)/a. With a=7 s⁻¹, b=10 s⁻² and c=28 s⁻³, it is (70-28)/7=6.000 s⁻². Simply copying b=10 omits the coupling to the constant term. First-column entries 1,7,6,28 are positive.

qs.q: A unity-negative-feedback plant is G(s)=K/[s(s+2)(s+6)], with rates 2 and 6 s⁻¹ and positive K in s⁻³. Find the upper gain boundary for asymptotic stability; equality is excluded.
qs.why: Expand the denominator: s(s+2)(s+6)=s³+8s²+12s. Feedback adds K, so the Routh entry is (8×12-K)/8. Requiring it positive gives K<96 s⁻³, together with K>0. The requested upper boundary is 96.00 s⁻³, not an included stable gain.
qs.hint: Expand s(s+2)(s+6) into s³ + as² + bs. The loop is stable while K < a·b.

qs.q: For unity feedback around K/[s(s+3)(s+7)] with rates 3 and 7 s⁻¹, at what frequency does the loop oscillate at its marginal gain, in rad/s?
qs.why: The characteristic polynomial is s³+10s²+21s+K. Routh gives K_crit=10×21=210 s⁻³. At that gain it factors as (s+10)(s²+21), so the imaginary poles are ±j√21 and ω=4.583 rad/s. The frequency is not the real pole magnitude 10 or the gain 210.

qs.q: A loop’s characteristic polynomial is s³ + 8s² + 12s + 120. Its Routh first column is 1, 8, −3, 120. Which verdict is correct?
qs.ans: Unstable: the signs change twice, so two poles are unstable
wrong: Stable: every polynomial coefficient is positive
Stable: only one entry is negative
Marginal: a negative entry means the loop sits on the edge
qs.why: Signs +, +, −, + change twice (8 to −3, then −3 to 120): two right-half-plane poles. Positive coefficients are necessary but not enough. One negative entry still causes two sign changes. Marginal stability shows up as a zero row, not a negative entry.

qs.q: Order the steps of a Routh check for s³ + as² + bs + c.
items: Write the rows [1, b] and [a, c]
Read down the first column: 1, a, (ab − c)/a, c
Call it stable only if every entry is positive
qs.why: The two coefficient rows come first, because the s¹ entry is built from them. Then read the whole column, and only then judge: all positive means stable.

qs.q: “At the gain limit I get (s+8)(s²+12), so the step never settles.” What does the reviewer mean?
qs.ans: At that gain the output oscillates forever instead of settling
wrong: The output grows without bound in one direction
The output settles with no overshoot
The steady-state error is zero, so it’s fine
qs.why: s² + 12 = 0 gives s = ±j3.46: a pure oscillation at 3.46 rad/s that never dies out (the −8 root does die out). Growth in one direction needs a positive real root; settling needs every root in the left half-plane; a zero error can’t help if the output never settles.

p.x: The **Routh table** is a small table that shows, without solving for the roots, when raising the feedback gain makes oscillations grow.
The question here: how high can the gain $K$ go before the loop goes unstable?
A controller with gain $K$ drives the **plant**: the thing being controlled, like a motor.
The output is measured and subtracted from the command: **unity negative feedback**.

p.cap: from 1 + G(s) = 0; its roots decide if the response dies out

p.x: First column all positive needs $K > 0$ and $30 − K > 0$: stable for $0 < K < 30$.

g.q: Stable means every first-column entry is positive. So K must be…
o: K > 0 from the s⁰ row, and (30 − K)/6 > 0 from the s¹ row.
Above 30 the s¹ entry goes negative: two sign changes, two unstable poles.
5 is a coefficient in the table, not the limit. The s¹ entry stays positive up to K = 30.

p.x: Read down the first column and count the sign changes.
Each change, + to − or − to +, is one [[unstable]] pole: a root in the right half-plane, a mode that grows.
No changes, all positive: stable. A zero in the column needs a special step, so don't call that stable.
First column: 1, 6, 3.333, 10. All positive, so the loop is stable.
Starting at rest with a unit-step command, the output settles to exactly 1: the closed-loop gain at $s = 0$ is $K/K = 1$.
At $K = 30$, the $s^1$ entry is zero: the edge.
Poles on the imaginary axis: an oscillation at √5 = 2.236 rad/s that never dies out. Settling needs $0 < K < 30$.

g.q: Poles at −6 and ±j2.236. The step response…
o: oscillates forever
Imaginary-axis poles have zero decay rate: the oscillation neither grows nor dies.
settles slowly
Settling needs every pole in the left half-plane. These two have zero real part.
grows without bound
That needs a right-half-plane pole. At exactly K = 30 they sit on the axis.

cards: In plain English: Position feedback turns the spacecraft toward its target, and rate feedback stops it from swinging past.
For an ideal rigid axis, fix inertia J=10 kg·m². Angle θ is radians; actuator torque u is N·m. With no natural damping or disturbances, Jθ̈=u, starting from rest.
For fixed J and command θ_ref, PD uses u=Kp(θ_ref-θ)-Kdθ̇. Kp (N·m/rad) supplies restoring torque; Kd (N·m·s/rad) supplies damping. Why it happens: rate feedback opposes angular motion.
For this linear unsaturated model, natural frequency ωₙ=√(Kp/J) in rad/s and dimensionless damping ratio ζ=Kd/(2√(KpJ)). Fixed Kp=10, Kd=14 and J=10 give ωₙ=1.000 and ζ=0.700.
For its zero-initial-state unit step and 0<ζ<1, percent overshoot is 100exp(-ζπ/√(1-ζ²)). With fixed demo gains, it is 4.60%. With Kd=0, undamped oscillations persist.
For this underdamped second-order model, 2% settling time tₛ≈4/(ζωₙ), in seconds. Fixed demo gains give 5.71 s. This estimate does not certify overdamped settling; inspect the slow pole instead.
title: Spacecraft attitude with PD
plain: Position feedback turns the spacecraft toward its target, and rate feedback stops it from swinging past.

qs.q: An ideal undamped spacecraft axis has J=8 kg·m², Kp=32 N·m/rad and rate gain Kd=16 N·m·s/rad. Derive its PD characteristic polynomial, then calculate ζ.
qs.why: The closed-loop equation is 8θ̈+16θ̇+32θ=32θ_ref. Dividing by 8 gives s²+2s+4, so ωₙ=√4=2 rad/s and 2ζωₙ=2. Thus ζ=2/(2×2)=0.5000. Omitting normalization by inertia gives incorrect coefficient matching.

qs.q: For a rigid axis with J=6 kg·m², Kp=24 N·m/rad and Kd=12 N·m·s/rad, starting at rest, calculate percent overshoot to a constant angle step. Assume ideal linear PD and no extra poles.
qs.why: First ωₙ=√(24/6)=2 rad/s and ζ=12/(2√(24×6))=0.5. Then percent overshoot=100exp[-0.5π/√(1-0.5²)]=16.30335%, rounded to 16.30%. Reporting 0.1630 would confuse overshoot fraction with percent.

qs.q: A rigid-axis PD model has J=7.5 kg·m², Kp=30 N·m/rad and Kd=12 N·m·s/rad. Check that it is underdamped, then estimate its 2% settling time.
qs.why: ωₙ=√(30/7.5)=2 rad/s and ζ=12/(2√225)=0.4, which lies between zero and one. Hence tₛ≈4/(0.4×2)=5.000 s. Using 4/ωₙ ignores damping; this is an approximate 2% criterion, not an exact settling time.

qs.q: For a rigid axis with fixed J=7 kg·m² and Kp=28 N·m/rad, which change removes undamped oscillation, and why? Assume ideal rate feedback.
qs.ans: Raise Kd from zero to 18 N·m·s/rad; rate feedback adds damping.
wrong: Raise Kp while keeping Kd zero; restoring torque alone supplies dissipative damping.
Lower J while keeping Kd zero; faster motion makes the undamped system dissipate energy.
Raise the fixed command while keeping Kd zero; a larger target increases the damping ratio.
qs.why: Positive Kd introduces a θ̇ term: with Kd=18, ζ=18/(2√(28×7))=18/28=0.6429 and the poles have negative real parts. Stiffness/damping mistake: Kp changes restoring stiffness, not dissipation.
