Inertia/damping mistake: changing J alone leaves ζ=0. Command/dynamics mistake: changing a constant reference does not change the linear characteristic polynomial.

qs.q: Order the underdamped settling-time calculation for an ideal rigid axis with positive inertia and PD gains.
items: Write the characteristic polynomial Js²+Kd s+Kp.
Divide through by J and match s²+2ζωₙs+ωₙ².
Calculate ωₙ and ζ from the matched coefficients.
Check that 0<ζ<1 before using the underdamped estimate.
qs.why: Normalizing first preserves the correct units: ωₙ²=Kp/J and 2ζωₙ=Kd/J. Their product gives ζωₙ=Kd/(2J), so the estimate is also 8J/Kd when its underdamped assumptions hold. At zero damping the response does not settle; for overdamping the slow real pole requires separate attention.

qs.q: “My rigid-axis gains give poles -0.5 and -4.5 s⁻¹, so I should not trust the underdamped settling formula.” What is the reviewer flagging?
qs.ans: The slow real pole controls an overdamped settling tail.
wrong: The faster real pole alone controls the final settling tail.
The negative poles imply instability because no oscillation frequency is present.
The underdamped estimate becomes exact whenever both poles are real.
qs.why: For example, J=4 kg·m², Kp=9 N·m/rad and Kd=20 N·m·s/rad give 4s²+20s+9=4(s+0.5)(s+4.5). Here ωₙ=1.5 rad/s and ζ=5/3>1; the slow -0.5 pole governs late decay. Fast-pole mistake: the -4.5 mode vanishes sooner. Stability-sign mistake: both negative real poles are stable. Formula-range mistake: 4/(ζωₙ)=1.6 s is not a reliable overdamped settling estimate.

p.x: Angle feedback turns the spacecraft toward its target.
Rate feedback stops it from [[swinging past]].

p.cap: no natural damping or disturbance torques, starts at rest

p.x: With no damping of its own, any torque keeps the spacecraft turning until another torque stops it.
The $K_p$ term acts like a [[spring]] pulling toward the target.
The $K_d$ term acts like a damper: it opposes the rotation rate.

p.cap: linear, unsaturated model
unit step from rest, 0 < ζ < 1

p.x: With $K_d$ = 0, ζ = 0: no damping at all, so it swings back and forth forever.

g.q: Now set K_d = 0. The response…
o: oscillates forever
ζ = K_d/(2√(K_pJ)) = 0, and the rigid axis has no damping of its own.
settles after a while
Settling needs some damping. With K_d = 0 there is none anywhere in the loop.

p.cap: underdamped second-order model

p.x: This estimate holds for underdamped loops only. For an overdamped one ($ζ > 1$), check the slow pole instead.

cards: In plain English: A hovering vehicle needs thrust even after it stops moving, so feedback must account for its weight.
For ideal vertical motion, fix mass m=1.2 kg and gravity g=9.81 m/s². Altitude z is metres; thrust T is newtons. Without drag or saturation, mz̈=T-mg.
For fixed reference z_ref, define error e=z_ref-z. PD uses T=Kp e-Kdż, with Kp in N/m and Kd in N·s/m. Why it happens: at rest, nonzero error supplies weight-supporting thrust.
With fixed demo Kp=40 N/m, Kd=10 N·s/m and z_ref=1 m, stable PD equilibrium gives e_ss=mg/Kp=0.2943 m and final altitude 0.7057 m.

For this unsaturated model, exact gravity feedforward adds mg; PID instead adds Ki∫e dt, with Ki in N/(m·s). Either removes constant-gravity offset when its closed-loop output is asymptotically stable.
With positive m,Kp,Kd, PID requires Ki>0 and KdKp>mKi for asymptotic stability. Demo Ki=40 gives 400>48, so error tends to zero. At Ki=0, it reduces to PD and retains offset.
title: Gravity and steady-state error
plain: A hovering vehicle needs thrust even after it stops moving, so feedback must account for its weight.

qs.q: An ideal vertical vehicle has mass m=1.8 kg and g=9.81 m/s². Its stable PD thrust is T=Kp(z_ref-z)-Kdż, with Kp=45 N/m, Kd=12 N·s/m and z_ref=1.6 m. Find steady-state error.
qs.why: At equilibrium ż=z̈=0, so T=mg=1.8×9.81=17.658 N. PD then requires Kp e_ss=17.658, giving e_ss=17.658/45=0.3924 m. The corresponding altitude is 1.6-0.3924=1.2076 m. Derivative gain cannot supply static weight support because velocity is zero.

qs.q: A stable PD altitude loop uses Kp=50 N/m and gravity feedforward m_hat g. Actual mass is 2.0 kg, estimated mass m_hat=1.7 kg, and g=9.81 m/s². With no saturation or other disturbances, find steady-state error.
qs.why: At rest, Kp e_ss+m_hat g=mg. The uncancelled force is (2.0-1.7)×9.81=2.943 N, so e_ss=2.943/50=0.05886 m. Using full mg/Kp ignores feedforward; assuming zero error ignores the mass-estimation mismatch.

qs.q: A vertical PID loop has m=1.5 kg, Kp=36 N/m and Kd=7.5 N·s/m. Find the upper Ki boundary for asymptotic stability, in N/(m·s); equality is excluded.
qs.why: The characteristic polynomial is 1.5s³+7.5s²+36s+Ki. With all gains positive, Routh requires 7.5×36>1.5Ki, so Ki<270/1.5=180.0 N/(m·s), and Ki>0. The boundary gives an imaginary pair; it is not an included stable setting.

qs.q: In an ideal unsaturated altitude loop with accurate mass and stable dynamics, which controller removes gravity offset without integrating error, and why?
qs.ans: PD plus gravity feedforward, because added weight thrust cancels the disturbance.
wrong: PD with larger derivative gain, because damping produces constant thrust at rest.
PD with finite larger proportional gain, because any increased stiffness makes static error zero.
PID with zero integral gain, because its stored integral still produces adjustable thrust.
qs.why: Accurate feedforward adds mg, leaving Kp e_ss=0 and hence e_ss=0. Derivative-at-rest mistake: the damping term vanishes at zero velocity. Finite-gain mistake: finite Kp reduces mg/Kp but does not make it zero for nonzero weight. Zero-integral-gain mistake: multiplying the integral by Ki=0 removes its thrust contribution.

qs.q: Order an altitude steady-state error analysis for a constant reference and gravity disturbance.
items: Write the vertical force balance and the actual controller, including feedforward or integral terms.
Derive the closed-loop characteristic polynomial and check output stability.
If the output settles, set vertical velocity and acceleration to zero.
For active stable integral control, also enforce zero error from the integral-state equilibrium.
Solve the remaining force balance for error and final altitude.
qs.why: The force equation is mz̈=T-mg. Stable PD gives Kp e_ss=mg minus feedforward thrust. Stable PID with Ki>0 also needs the integral-state derivative e to vanish, so the integral supplies the remaining weight thrust. An unstable or marginal loop has no general steady-state limit; applying equilibrium algebra alone does not prove that it is reached.

qs.q: “The PID eliminates gravity error on paper, but Routh gives two sign changes.” What should the reviewer conclude?
qs.ans: The unstable response invalidates the claimed steady-state tracking result.
wrong: The integrator guarantees the claimed zero error despite the unstable response.
The constant gravity force changes the Routh sign count after the transient.
The formal zero-error equilibrium makes both unstable modes disappear automatically.
qs.why: Zero steady-state error requires a reached stable equilibrium or valid final-value-theorem conditions. Integrator-guarantee mistake: integral action can destabilize the loop. Disturbance/pole mistake: constant gravity is a forcing term in this ideal linear model, not a change in characteristic coefficients. Equilibrium/stability mistake: an existing equilibrium does not eliminate growing modes.

p.x: A hovering vehicle needs thrust even when it isn't moving, just to hold up its weight.
So the controller must supply that thrust somehow, and how it does decides the steady error.

p.cap: no drag, thrust not saturated

p.x: At rest $ż = 0$, so the thrust is just $K_p e$.
To hold up the weight, $K_p e = mg$: a steady nonzero error remains.

g.q: Hovering at rest under PD, the altitude error is…
o: zero
With e = 0 and ż = 0, PD gives zero thrust, and the vehicle would fall.
a steady offset
Only the K_p e term is left at rest, so e must stay nonzero to make thrust mg.

p.x: At rest, $K_p e = m g$:
It hovers about 29 cm below the target.
Two ways to remove the offset, each adding to the PD thrust $T_{PD}$:

p.cap: K_i in N/(m·s)

p.x: Either removes a constant-gravity offset, if the closed loop is asymptotically stable.
Feedforward works only if $m g$ is known [[exactly]]. The integral finds the needed thrust on its own.

p.eq: K_i > 0  and  K_d K_p > m K_i
p.cap: positive m, K_p, K_d; linear, unsaturated

p.x: 400 > 48, so with $K_i$ = 40 the error tends to zero. At $K_i$ = 0 it is PD again, and the offset returns.

cards: In plain English: Translate response limits into a region where the system’s poles are allowed to sit.
For a standard zero-free second-order system, poles are σ±jωd: σ is decay rate (s⁻¹), ωd is damped frequency (rad/s), and j²=-1. Stable oscillatory poles have σ<0 and ωd>0.
For its zero-initial-state step, let M be allowed overshoot fraction, 0<M<1. Minimum damping ratio ζ_min=-ln(M)/√(π²+ln²(M)) defines a wedge. Fixed demo M=0.10 gives ζ_min=0.5912.
For this underdamped model, the approximate 2% settling time tₛ=4/|σ| seconds. Fixed demo limit tₛ≤2 s requires σ≤-2 s⁻¹, in addition to the overshoot wedge.
At fixed demo poles -3±3j s⁻¹, ζ=|σ|/√(σ²+ωd²)=0.7071. For the standard step model, overshoot is 4.32% and tₛ≈1.333 s, meeting both limits.

Why it happens: farther-left poles make transients decay faster, while larger damping suppresses overshoot. Both tests matter. Zeros or additional slow poles can invalidate predictions from a selected pole pair alone.
title: Specs to pole locations
plain: Translate response limits into a region where the system’s poles are allowed to sit.

qs.q: For a standard zero-free second-order step response, maximum overshoot is 15%. Convert it to fraction M and calculate ζ_min=-ln(M)/√(π²+ln²(M)).
qs.why: Convert 15% to M=0.15. Then -ln(M)=1.897119985 and ζ_min=1.897119985/√(π²+1.897119985²)=0.5169309, rounded to 0.5169. Inserting 15 instead of 0.15 reverses the logarithm sign and cannot represent a positive damping requirement.

qs.q: A standard underdamped second-order design requires approximate 2% settling time no greater than 1.6 s. Using tₛ≈4/|σ|, find the limiting real part σ; more-negative values are allowed.
qs.why: From 4/|σ|≤1.6, obtain |σ|≥2.5 s⁻¹. Stability selects the negative side, so σ≤-2.500 s⁻¹. The requested boundary is -2.500, not +2.500. Reversing the inequality would admit slower poles close to the imaginary axis.

qs.q: For a zero-free standard second-order system with poles -4±2j s⁻¹ and zero initial conditions, calculate the unit-step overshoot percentage. Derive ζ before evaluating the overshoot formula.
qs.why: ωₙ=√(4²+2²)=√20=4.472136 rad/s and ζ=4/√20=0.8944272. Since √(1-ζ²)=2/√20, percent overshoot=100exp[-π(4/2)]=100exp(-2π)=0.1867443%, or 0.1867%. Using ωₙ instead of ωd in the simplified exponent gives the wrong damping dependence.

qs.q: A standard zero-free second-order loop has poles -1.5±1j s⁻¹. Limits are at most 8% overshoot and approximate 2% settling within 2.4 s. Which verdict and reason are correct?
qs.ans: Fails settling only: overshoot passes, but the decay is too slow.
wrong: Passes both: settling uses the full pole magnitude instead of its real part.
Fails overshoot only: settling passes because the damping ratio is high.
Passes both: negative real parts alone guarantee both numerical response limits.
qs.why: Overshoot=100exp[-π(1.5/1)]=0.8983291%, below 8%. Settling tₛ≈4/1.5=2.666667 s exceeds 2.4 s. Pole-magnitude mistake: 4/√(1.5²+1²)=2.2188 s is not the decay-based estimate. Damping/settling mistake: high damping alone does not enforce the time bound. Stability/specification mistake: stability is weaker than meeting both response limits.

qs.q: Order pole-region design for a standard zero-free second-order system with specified maximum overshoot and approximate 2% settling time.
items: Convert the overshoot percentage to a fraction between zero and one.
Calculate the minimum damping ratio and its left-half-plane wedge.
Convert the settling-time limit to a maximum allowed real part.
Intersect the wedge with the region left of the real-part boundary.
Check the candidate pair against both bounds and confirm the second-order model applies.
qs.why: The damping bound comes from ζ_min=-ln(M)/√(π²+ln²(M)). The decay bound is σ≤-4/tₛ,max. Their intersection, not their union, enforces both requirements. Negative real parts alone establish only stability; added zeros or significant extra modes require a fuller response calculation.

qs.q: “The pair -6±8j s⁻¹ meets our 12% and 1.5 s limits, but an uncancelled pole at -0.25 s⁻¹ remains.” What does that warning mean? Assume that slow mode has appreciable output amplitude.
qs.ans: The extra slow mode can dominate settling despite the selected pair.
wrong: The selected pair guarantees settling regardless of other excited system modes.
The extra pole cancels itself because its real part is negative.
The extra stable pole necessarily makes the full system unstable.
qs.why: For the selected pair, ζ=6/10=0.6, overshoot=100exp(-0.75π)=9.478022%, and tₛ≈4/6=0.6666667 s, so the pair passes. But the -0.25 mode decays on a 4 s time scale and may control settling when appreciably excited. Selected-pair mistake: pair predictions are not a full-system certificate. Cancellation mistake: cancellation requires a matching zero, not just a negative pole. Stability/performance mistake: a slow stable pole harms speed without itself causing instability.

p.x: Response limits, such as maximum overshoot and settling time, can be turned into a region of the complex plane.
Put the system's poles inside it and the response meets the limits.
A standard second-order system with no zeros has its poles at $σ ± jω_d$.
Stable poles sit in the [[left half]] of the plane, $σ < 0$. Oscillating ones also have $ω_d > 0$.

widens

The pair's transient is gone by 1.3 s, but the slow pole's mode is still decaying.

cards: In plain English: One number tells you whether a flow slides smoothly or churns.

Reynolds number compares inertia (a fluid’s tendency to keep moving) with viscosity (its internal friction): Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. ρ is density (kg/m³), V mean velocity (m/s), D pipe diameter (m), μ dynamic viscosity (Pa·s) and ν = μ/ρ kinematic viscosity (m²/s). Re has no units.

For a straight, smooth, round pipe away from the entrance: below about 2300 the flow is laminar (smooth layers); above about 4000 it is usually turbulent (chaotic eddies); in between it is transitional. These are typical values: disturbances can trip turbulence earlier, and very quiet flows can stay laminar longer.

Why it matters: laminar pipe friction follows f = 64/Re, while turbulent friction depends on Re and wall roughness and is higher at the same Re. Mixing and heat transfer also jump in turbulent flow. Engineers check Re first to pick the right correlation.
Example: water at 20 °C (ν ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s) at 1 m/s in a 20 mm pipe gives Re = 1 × 0.020 / 1.0×10⁻⁶ = 20,000, which is turbulent. Many everyday water and air flows are turbulent.

Scaling: at a fixed flow rate Q, V = 4Q/(πD²), so Re = 4ρQ/(πμD). The same flow in a bigger pipe has a lower Re. Other shapes use a characteristic length instead of D (plate length, wing chord, hydraulic diameter), with their own thresholds.
title: Reynolds number: laminar or turbulent
plain: One number tells you whether a flow slides smoothly or churns.

demo.title: Reynolds number and flow regime
demo.hint: Re grows with speed and size and falls with viscosity. Air (ν ≈ 15 mm²/s) needs about 15 times the speed of water (ν ≈ 1 mm²/s) for the same Re in the same pipe. Thresholds are for smooth round pipes.

qs.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.0010 Pa·s) flows at 0.50 m/s in a 25 mm pipe. What is the Reynolds number?
qs.hint: Re = ρVD/μ, with D in metres.
qs.why: Re = ρVD/μ = 1000 × 0.50 × 0.025 / 0.0010 = 12,500. Leaving D as 25 instead of 0.025 m gives 12.5 million.

qs.q: A smooth round pipe flow has Re = 12,500. Which regime is it in?
qs.ans: Turbulent: well above about 4000
wrong: Laminar, because 0.5 m/s is a slow flow
Transitional, because it is below 40,000
It can’t be judged without the pipe length
qs.why: Above about 4000 a pipe flow is usually turbulent. Speed alone doesn’t decide it; Re combines speed, size and viscosity. The transitional band is about 2300–4000, not up to 40,000. Pipe length matters for pressure drop, not for Re.

qs.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.0010 Pa·s) flows in a 10 mm tube. Taking Re = 2300 as the laminar limit, what is the highest laminar velocity, in m/s?
Air (ρ = 1.20 kg/m³, μ = 1.80×10⁻⁵ Pa·s) flows at 10.0 m/s along a flat plate 0.200 m long. What is the Reynolds number based on that length?
qs.hint: Same formula, with the plate length as the characteristic length.
qs.why: Re = ρVL/μ = 1.20 × 10.0 × 0.200 / 1.80×10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.33×10⁵. Along a flat plate, transition is usually quoted near 5×10⁵, so the 2300 pipe value doesn’t apply here.

qs.q: The same volume flow rate is sent through a pipe with twice the diameter. What happens to Re?
qs.ans: It halves
wrong: It doubles
It stays the same
It drops to a quarter
qs.why: V = 4Q/(πD²) drops to a quarter while D doubles, so Re ∝ VD halves. “Doubles” forgets that V falls; “a quarter” tracks V but forgets D in Re; “stays the same” treats Re as a fluid property.

qs.q: Rank these flows by Reynolds number, highest first. Water has ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s.
items: Water at 2 m/s in a 50 mm pipe
Air (ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s) at 5 m/s in a 100 mm duct
Water at 0.1 m/s in a 20 mm tube
Oil (ν = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m²/s) at 1 m/s in a 50 mm pipe
qs.why: Re = VD/ν gives 100,000, about 33,300, 2,000 and 500. Air’s ν is 15 times water’s, so it needs more speed or size to match; the oil is laminar.

qs.q: “At that flow the line is running transitional, so don’t trust the friction factor to better than a factor of two.”
qs.ans: Re is between about 2300 and 4000, where the flow switches between laminar and turbulent and friction is uncertain
wrong: The flow is speeding up as it moves along the pipe
The liquid is starting to boil into gas
The pipe is changing diameter partway along
qs.why: Transitional means the Re band between laminar and turbulent, where the flow flips unpredictably and neither friction correlation fits well. Speeding up, boiling and a diameter change are different effects.

p.x: Watch a dye streak in flowing water. It may stretch into a smooth thread or break up into swirling patches.
The Reynolds number helps predict which kind of motion to expect.
**Inertia** is a fluid's tendency to keep moving. **Viscosity** measures how strongly neighboring layers resist sliding past each other.

p.cap: round pipe; inertia relative to viscosity; no units

p.x: In a straight, smooth, round pipe away from the entrance, the transitional band lies [[between]] the smooth and turbulent regimes.
Transitional flow can switch between the two. Disturbances can trigger turbulence sooner, and quiet flows can remain laminar longer.
Imagine injecting a narrow streak of dye into a pipe. In both regimes, moving fluid carries it downstream.
Turbulent eddies carry dye across the flow faster. They also mix heat across the pipe faster.
The Darcy friction factor $f$ describes resistance to pipe flow. In fully developed laminar flow in a round pipe, $f = 64/Re$.
Turbulent friction depends on $Re$ and wall roughness, and is higher at the same $Re$ where the regimes overlap. In transition, friction is hard to predict.

g.q: Which regime typically spreads the dye sideways faster?
o: Laminar
Smooth layers leave molecular diffusion to do most of the sideways mixing.
Turbulent
Swirling eddies carry dye across the pipe as well as down it.

g.q: If the inner diameter doubles at the same flow rate, how does Reynolds number change?
o: It doubles
That tracks the change in diameter but assumes the mean speed stays fixed.
It halves
Speed falls to one quarter in the larger area. Diameter doubles, so their product halves.
It drops to one quarter
That tracks speed alone. The doubled diameter also multiplies Reynolds number.

cards: In plain English: Bring a moon too close to its planet and the planet’s tides pull it apart.

The planet pulls harder on a moon’s near side than on its far side. That difference, the tidal force, tries to stretch the moon. A moon held together only by its own gravity has a distance inside which the stretching wins: the Roche limit.

For a fluid-like moon, d ≈ 2.44·R·(ρp/ρm)^(1/3), with R the planet’s radius and ρp, ρm the planet’s and moon’s densities. A rigid moon holds on closer, about 1.26·R·(ρp/ρm)^(1/3); real moons fall between. Assumes a circular orbit and a moon held together by gravity alone.
The moon’s size cancels out: only the density ratio matters, and only as a cube root. A denser moon can orbit closer; a fluffy, icy one breaks up farther out.

Example: Earth (R = 6371 km, ρ = 5514 kg/m³) and the Moon (ρ = 3344 kg/m³) give a fluid limit of about 18 400 km. The Moon orbits at 384 400 km, about 21 times farther out. Saturn’s bright rings sit close to or inside its Roche limit, where loose ice can’t gather into a moon.

Why spacecraft don’t care: the ISS orbits about 400 km up, deep inside Earth’s Roche limit, but bolts and metal hold it together, not its own gravity. The tidal stretch on it is tiny compared with its strength.
How it sounds at work: “It’s inside the Roche limit, so it’ll never clump into a moon.” “The comet got torn apart on its close pass.”
title: The Roche limit
plain: Bring a moon too close to its planet and the planet’s tides pull it apart.
talk: “It’s inside the Roche limit, so it’ll never clump into a moon.”
“The comet got torn apart on its close pass.”

qs.q: Earth has R = 6371 km and density 5514 kg/m³; the Moon’s density is 3344 kg/m³. Using d = 2.44·R·(ρp/ρm)^(1/3), what is the fluid Roche limit, in km?
qs.why: 5514/3344 = 1.649, cube root 1.181, so d = 2.44 × 6371 × 1.181 ≈ 18 360 km. Forgetting the cube root gives about 25 600 km; using 1.26 instead of 2.44 gives the rigid limit, about 9 480 km.

qs.q: A small moon held together only by its own gravity drifts inside its planet’s Roche limit. What happens?
qs.ans: Tides pull it apart into a ring of debris
wrong: It falls straight into the planet
It speeds up and escapes its orbit
Nothing: its own gravity holds it together
qs.why: Inside the limit the planet’s pull on the near side exceeds the far side by more than the moon’s gravity can resist, so it breaks up and spreads along its orbit. Breaking up doesn’t change the orbit itself, so it neither falls in nor escapes; self-gravity is exactly what loses.

qs.q: Two moons orbit the same planet. One is twice as dense as the other. Whose Roche limit is closer to the planet?
qs.ans: The denser moon’s
wrong: The less dense moon’s
They are the same, since the planet is the same
The larger moon’s, whatever its density
qs.why: d ∝ (ρp/ρm)^(1/3): a denser moon lowers the ratio, so it can orbit closer before breaking up. The planet being the same doesn’t make the limits equal, and the moon’s size cancels out of the formula.

qs.q: A moon’s density is 8 times lower than another’s, around the same planet. By what factor is its Roche limit farther out?
qs.why: d ∝ (ρp/ρm)^(1/3), so the factor is 8^(1/3) = 2. Answering 8 forgets the cube root.

qs.q: Why can the ISS orbit far inside Earth’s Roche limit without breaking apart?
qs.ans: Its structure, not its own gravity, holds it together
wrong: It orbits too fast for tides to act
The Roche limit applies only to the Moon
It is denser than Earth
qs.why: The Roche limit is for bodies held together by self-gravity. The ISS is held by bolts and metal, which are far stronger than the tiny tidal stretch. Speed doesn’t switch tides off, the limit applies to any self-gravitating body, and the ISS is much less dense than Earth.

False
